paragraphs.text:
ALL THE EXTANT WORKS OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS JOHN CHRYSOSTOM. A DISCOURSE OF EXHORTATION AT THE BEGINNING OF HOLY LENT.

1. I rejoice and am glad to see the Church of God adorned today with the multitude of her own children, and all of you gathered here with great delight. When I look at your bright faces, I take them as the strongest proof of the pleasure in your souls. As a certain wise man said, "When the heart is glad, the face flourishes." That is why I have risen to speak today with greater eagerness. I want to share this spiritual gladness with you, and I also want to announce to you the arrival of holy Lent, which I call the medicine of our souls. The common Master of us all is like an affectionate father. He wishes to wash away the sins we have committed throughout the year, and so he has devised a cure for us through the holy fast as well. So let no one be downcast, and let no one look gloomy. Rather, let everyone leap and rejoice and glorify the guardian of our souls, who has cut this excellent road for us, and let everyone welcome the fast's arrival with great delight.

Let the Greeks be ashamed and the Jews hide their faces when they see with what cheerful eagerness we welcome its arrival. Let them learn by experience how great the difference is between us and them. Let them call drunkenness, every other kind of licentiousness and the indecencies these probably bring upon them "festivals" and "celebrations." But the Church of God, in contrast to them, calls fasting a festival: contempt for the belly, and all the virtue that follows from it. For this is a true festival, where there is salvation of souls, where there is peace and concord, and where all worldly display has been driven out. Here shouting and uproar, cooks running to and fro and the slaughter of animals are put out of the way. In their place, complete quiet and calm hold sway, with love, joy, peace, gentleness and countless other good things. Come then, I beg you, let us speak a little about the fast with you, my beloved. But first I urge you to receive our words in deep quiet, so that you may gain something noble here and take it home with you. We do not gather here idly or at random, so that one person speaks, the others merely applaud what is said, and then we leave. We gather so that we too may gain something useful, something of what pertains to salvation [?]

[?] be slaves without thought, but manage our affairs with reason. Will we gain anything from today's gluttony and heavy drinking? Why do I even speak of gain? There is great loss instead, and unbearable harm. When reason is drowned in a flood of wine, it shuts out the benefit of the fast from the very start. Tell me, what is more disgusting and more shameful than people who drain unmixed wine until midnight and then, at dawn, as the sun's first rays rise, reek as though they had just gorged themselves on wine? They disgust everyone they meet. Their servants despise them, and everyone with any sense of what is proper laughs at them. Above all, through this great self-indulgence and this untimely, useless excess they bring God's indignation upon themselves. "For drunkards," it says, "will not inherit the kingdom of God." What could be more wretched than people who are thrown out from the very doorway of the kingdom for the sake of a brief and harmful pleasure? May none of those gathered here be caught by this passion! Instead, may you feast today too with all self-discipline and moderation, free from the storm and surge that drunkenness naturally produces, and so reach the harbor of our souls, by which I mean the fast. Then we will be able to reap its good things in abundance.

Gluttony has become the cause and the source of countless evils for the human race. In the same way, fasting and contempt for the belly have always been the cause of unspeakable blessings for us. When God formed man in the beginning, he knew that man needed this medicine most of all for the salvation of his soul. So at once, at the very outset, he gave the first-formed man this commandment: "From every tree in paradise you shall eat for food; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat." To say "Eat this, but do not eat that" was a figure of fasting. Adam ought to have kept the commandment, but he did not. Overcome by the craving of his belly, he disobeyed and was condemned to death. That wicked demon, the enemy of our nature, saw how the first-formed man lived in paradise: that life free of toil, and how he lived on earth like an angel, even though he was bound up in a body. The demon wanted to trip him up and throw him down, and by holding out the hope of greater promises he cast him out even from what he already had in hand. That is what comes of not staying within one's own bounds and craving greater things. A certain wise man made this very point when he said, "Through the envy of the devil death entered the world." Do you see, beloved, how death made its entry through gluttony right from the beginning? Look again at how divine Scripture, after this, continually condemns luxury. At one point it says, "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." At another it says, "He ate and drank and grew fat and thick, and the beloved kicked." And the inhabitants of Sodom, along with their other evils, brought upon themselves from this the inexorable wrath [?]

[?] gain, and not to push away its benefit out of laziness, nor be annoyed at its coming, but to rejoice and exult, as blessed Paul says: "For as much as our outer self is wasting away, so much is the inner self being renewed." Fasting is food for the soul. Just as bodily food fattens the body, fasting makes the soul more vigorous. It makes the soul's wing light and lifts it on high. It enables the soul to contemplate the things above, and it raises the soul above the pleasures and delights of the present life. Light ships cross the seas more swiftly, while ships weighed down with a heavy cargo sink. In the same way, fasting makes the mind lighter and prepares it to cross the sea of the present life with ease. It makes the mind long for heaven and the things in heaven, count present things as nothing, and pass them by as more worthless than shadows and dreams. Drunkenness and gluttony, on the other hand, weigh down the mind and fatten the flesh, and so they take the soul captive. They besiege it on every side and do not let reason's judgment stay strong. They drive the soul over precipices and make it do everything against its own salvation. So let us not manage our salvation carelessly, beloved. We know how many evils are born of this, so let us flee the harm it brings.

Luxury is forbidden not only in the New Testament, where the discipline of the philosophic life is more demanding, the contests greater, the sweat heavy, the prizes many and the crowns beyond words. It was forbidden in the Old Testament as well. At that time people still sat beside the shadow and were fixed on the lamp, and they were being led forward little by little, like infants fed on milk. Even then they were not permitted to live in luxury. In case you think we say this merely because we like to condemn luxury, listen to the prophet: "Woe to those who are coming to an evil day, who sleep on beds of ivory and live wantonly on their couches, who eat kids from the flocks and suckling calves from the midst of the herds, who drink strained wine and anoint themselves with the finest ointments, as though they reckoned these things lasting and not fleeting." Do you see how strong an indictment of luxury the prophet made? And he made it while speaking to Jews: insensible, ungrateful people who gorged themselves every day. Notice how precise his words are. First he denounced their gluttony and their heavy drunkenness. Then he added, "as though they reckoned these things lasting and not fleeting." In this way he all but shows that enjoyment reaches only as far as the throat and the lips, and no further [?]

[?] the pleasure is brief and passing, but the pain is lasting and has no end. "Though they learned this by experience," he says, "they reckoned all these things lasting" and permanent, "and not fleeting." That is, they did not see them as things that fly away and do not stay even for a moment. All human and fleshly things are like this: they have scarcely arrived before they have flown away. Luxury is like this, and so are human glory and power, wealth, and all the prosperity of the present life. None of it has anything secure, stable or fixed. It runs past faster than the streams of rivers, and [leaves people] desolate and naked [?]

[?] let us discuss some things with you, my beloved, and today let us venture on subtler thoughts, setting before you teachings from the divine Scriptures. If we do not do this now, when there is fasting and contempt for the belly, and our reasoning enjoys such calm, when will we be able to set these things before you? When there is luxury and gluttony and much [?]? At such a time we would not do it properly. Nor would you be able to receive anything that is said, since the storm of your thoughts would drown you as if in a fog. But now, if ever, is the time for such teachings. For the servant no longer rebels against her mistress. She has become docile and shows great compliance and obedience. She has calmed the leaping of the flesh and stays within her own bounds. Fasting is the calm of our souls. It is the adornment of the old, the tutor of the young and the teacher of the self-controlled. It adorns every age and every nature as if with a diadem. Today there is no uproar anywhere, no shouting, no chopping of meat, no cooks running to and fro. All these have been driven out, and our city now resembles a decorous, modest and sober free woman.

When I consider the sudden change that has come about today, and think of yesterday's disorder, I marvel and am astonished at the power of fasting. It has entered each person's conscience, reshaped the mind and cleansed the understanding. It has done this not only for rulers but also for private citizens, not only for the free but also for slaves, not only for men but also for women, not only for the rich but also for the poor, and not only for those educated in the Greek language but also for barbarians. But why do I speak of rulers and private citizens? Fasting has brought even the conscience of the man who wears the diadem to obey it, just like everyone else. Today you can see no difference between the rich man's table and the poor man's. Everywhere the fare is simple, free of pomp and display. And today people come to their plain tables with greater pleasure than when many rich dishes and much unmixed wine were set before them.

2. Do you see, beloved, the power of fasting from its very beginning? For this reason I take up my discourse to you today with greater eagerness than before. I know that I am sowing seed in rich, deep soil, which can quickly return us a harvest many times greater than what was sown. So, if you please, let us study the meaning of the words of blessed Moses that were read to us today. But I beg you, pay close attention to what we say. We do not speak our own words, but whatever the grace of God supplies for your benefit. What are these words? "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." Here it is worth asking why this blessed prophet, who lived many generations later, sets these things out for us. He does not do it idly or at random. When God formed man in the beginning, he himself spoke with men in a way that men could hear. This is how he came to Adam, and this is how he came to Cain [?]

[?] the great extent of his condescension. He says nothing about the invisible powers. He does not say, "In the beginning God made the angels" or "the archangels." It was not out of incompleteness or at random that he cut this path of teaching for us. He was speaking to Jews, who were enthralled with present things and could not conceive of anything that can only be grasped by the mind. So for the time being he leads them from the things the senses perceive to the Creator of all things. In this way, learning about the Craftsman of the universe from his works, they would worship the Maker and not stop short at the creatures. Even with this teaching they did not stop making gods of created things and showing reverence to the most contemptible of animals. Had he not used such condescension, into what madness would they not have run aground?

Do not be surprised, beloved, that Moses takes this path, since he was speaking at the very beginning to the cruder Jews. Even Paul did the same in the age of grace, when the preaching of the gospel had made such progress. When he was about to address the people of Athens, he based his teaching on visible things, saying, "The God who made the world and everything in it, he who is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands, nor is he served by human hands." He knew this teaching suited them, so he took this path. Led by the Spirit, he shaped his teaching to fit those who were receiving his instruction. You can see that the difference between audiences, and the dullness of the hearers, is the reason for this. Listen to him when he wrote to the Colossians. There he no longer takes this path but speaks to them differently, saying, "For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and for him." And John, the son of thunder, cried out, "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." Moses did not speak this way, and with good reason. It was not fitting to give solid food to those who still needed to be fed on milk. Teachers who receive children from their parents hand on the first elements to them, while those who take the children over from these teachers instill the more advanced lessons. Blessed Moses, the teacher of the Gentiles and the son of thunder did the same. Moses took human nature in hand at the beginning and trained his hearers in the first elements. Paul and John took over from Moses and went on to hand down the more perfect teachings.

So far, then, we have learned the reason for the condescension. We have also learned that Moses, speaking by the Spirit, set out everything in a way that suited his hearers. By saying "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth," he pulled up by the roots all at once every heresy that springs up in the Church like tares. Suppose a Manichee comes to you saying that matter existed beforehand, or Marcion, or Valentinus, or the children of the Greeks. Say to them [?]

[?] "But the earth," he says, "was invisible and unformed." Tell me, why did he bring forth the heaven bright and complete, but show the earth shapeless? He did not do this idly either. He did it so that, once you had learned of his workmanship in the better part of creation, you would no longer doubt at all, nor think that the earth's shapelessness came from any weakness in his power. He also brought the earth forth shapeless for another reason. The earth is our nurse and our mother. From it we came into being and from it we are fed. It is our homeland and our common tomb, and to it we return again. Through it we enjoy countless good things. Because people need it so much, the human race might honor it beyond its worth. To prevent this, he shows it to you first shapeless and unformed. Then you will not credit its benefits to the nature of the earth, but to him who brought it from nonbeing into being. That is why he says, "But the earth was invisible and unformed."

Perhaps we have strained your minds with subtler thoughts right at the start, so it is fitting to end the discourse here. I urge you, my beloved, to remember what has been said and always to keep it ringing in your ears. When you leave here, set the spiritual table alongside the bodily one. Let the husband repeat some of what was said here, and let the wife listen. Let the children learn, and let the servants be taught. Let the house become a church. Then the devil will be put to flight, and that wicked demon, the enemy of our salvation, will run away. The grace of the Holy Spirit will rest there, and all peace and concord will surround those who live there. If you remember what has already been said, you will receive more eagerly what is sown afterwards. We, for our part, will speak with greater eagerness and abundance what God's grace supplies, once we see the earlier seed sprouting. When a farmer sees his seeds growing, he surveys his fields with great eagerness and readily hurries to sow more.

5. So, to make us more eager, show that you are keeping what has been said safely. Along with right doctrine, take great care over the way you live. "Let your light shine," it says, "before others, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." In this way your life will agree with your doctrine, and your doctrine will proclaim your life. For faith without works is dead, and works without faith are dead. If we hold sound doctrine but neglect our way of life, the doctrine will do us no good. Again, if we take care of our life but limp in doctrine, we will gain nothing that way either. So this spiritual building must be bound together on both sides. "For everyone," he says, "who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man." See how he wants us not only to hear but also to do, and to show our obedience through our works. He called this person wise, the one who [?]

…the grace of the Spirit gives its grace in abundance to fervent desire and an alert mind. So let us withdraw from all the affairs of this life, cut away the cares that can choke our thinking like thorns, and turn our whole mind to the desire for spiritual things. Then we may receive much benefit here and go away having gained something great and noble. But to make the discussion clearer to you, let us remind your love briefly of what was said yesterday, so that we may join today's words to yesterday's as one body. Yesterday, as you remember, we showed how blessed Moses, telling us of the creation of these visible elements, said: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed." We taught you the reason why he brought the earth forth shapeless and without form, and I think you all hold it precisely in mind. Today, then, we must go on to what follows. Having said, "But the earth was invisible and unformed," he teaches us exactly why it was invisible and unformed, saying: "And darkness was upon the abyss, and the Spirit of God was moving over the water." Notice here, I beg you, the blessed prophet's economy of words. He does not recount in detail everything that was created. Having taught us the elements that hold everything together, and having mentioned heaven and earth, he leaves out the rest. Nowhere does he speak of the creation of the waters, yet he says: "And darkness was upon the abyss, and the Spirit of God was moving over the water." For this is what covered the face of the earth: the darkness, I mean, and the abyss of waters. From this we have learned that everything visible was an abyss of waters covered with darkness, and it needed the wise Creator to take away all this shapelessness and bring everything into good order. "And darkness," he says, "was upon the abyss, and the Spirit of God was moving over the water." What does this saying mean? "The Spirit of God," he says, "was moving over the water." To me it seems to signify that a certain life-giving energy was present in the waters. It was not simply water standing still and motionless, but moving and possessing a certain vital power. For what is motionless is wholly useless, but what moves is fit for many purposes. 2. So, to teach us that this water, vast and immeasurable, had a certain vital power, he says: "And the Spirit of God was moving over the water." Divine Scripture does not say this in advance without reason. As it goes on it will tell us that living creatures too were brought forth from these waters at the command of the Creator of all. That is why it already teaches the hearer here that this was not simply water standing still, but moving, running about, and flooding everything. Since, then, great shapelessness had been poured over everything visible, God the supreme craftsman gave his command, the shapelessness was scattered, and this immeasurable beauty of visible light was brought forth, and the darkness [?]… [Textual notes, partly illegible: [?] Savile in the margin: "removing" [?]. Below, Coislin: "the benefit and salvation" [?]. "And we taught you" [?] "us". Coislin: "and I was teaching the cause." [?] "to resist" (Latin: resistere).]

…[belo]ved, how great the condescension of the words is here. What then? Did he not know before it came to be that it was good, so that only after it was brought forth did the sight show the Creator the beauty of what he had made? What person of sense would say that? If a man working at some craft sees the purpose his work will serve before he builds it and before he shapes it, then much more did the Creator of all, who by a word brought everything from non-being into being, know that light was good even before it was created. Why, then, did he use this expression? The blessed prophet speaks this way to come down to human custom. When people have worked at something with great care and brought their labours to an end, they then praise what they have made after testing it. In the same way divine Scripture, coming down here to the weakness of our hearing, says: "And God saw the light, that it was good." And then it adds: "And God separated between the light and between the darkness; and God called the light day, and the darkness he called night." He assigned each its own place and fixed certain boundaries for each from the very beginning, so as to keep them unhindered forever. Anyone with good sense can see how from then until now neither has the light overstepped its own bounds nor has the darkness passed beyond its own order and caused confusion and disorder. This alone is enough to bring those who choose to be unreasonable to trust and obey what divine Scripture says, so that they may at least imitate the order of the elements, which keep their course unhindered, and not overstep their own measures but recognize their own nature. Then, having given each its name, he brings both together and says: "And there was evening, and there was morning, one day." He named the end of the day and the end of the night as one, to establish order and sequence in what was done, so that there should be no confusion. Taught by the Holy Spirit through the tongue of this blessed prophet, we are able to know what was created on the first day and what on the others. This too comes from the condescension of God, who loves humankind. His all-powerful hand and his infinite wisdom were not at a loss to bring everything forth in a single day. Why do I say in a single day? Even in a split second. But he did not bring any created thing into being because he needed it, for he needs nothing and lacks nothing. He made everything out of love for humankind and goodness. That is why he creates step by step and, through the tongue of the blessed prophet, gives us clear teaching about what came to be: so that, having learned it precisely, we may not stumble along with those who are driven by human reasonings. For even though these things came to be in this way, there are some who say that everything that exists came about by itself. If he had not used such… [Textual notes, partly illegible: Savile: "builds" (subjunctive). One Regius manuscript and Coislin: "when … something." [?] "to those who do not wish to be unreasonable." [?] Coislin: "of the elements that keep their course unhindered." Then one Regius: "its own nature." Coislin: "condescension; for it was enough." [?] Coislin: "if he brought forth the things that exist." Colbert: "brought forth all things."]

…he says, "whoever leads his neighbour by the hand, or guides him from vice to virtue, imitates me as far as human power allows." For he too, being God, took on our flesh for no other reason, and became man for the salvation of the human race. And why do I say that he took on our flesh and endured everything else that is human, when he even accepted the cross to free us from the curse, we who had been handed over to it by our sins? Paul proclaims this when he says: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us." If, then, he who is God and possesses that ineffable essence accepted all these things for us and for our salvation, out of love for humankind beyond words, what ought we not to show toward our own kin and our own members? We ought to snatch them even from the devil's throat and lead them by the hand onto the road of virtue. As much as the soul is better than the body, so much greater are the rewards granted to those who, by exhortation and constant teaching, bring the careless and the fallen back to the straight road, showing them the ugliness of vice and the great beauty of godly virtue, than to those who help the needy with money. 5. Knowing all this, then, let us talk with our neighbours about the salvation of the soul before every other worldly matter, and draw them into this concern. It is a thing to be prized, truly prized, if the soul, with these things constantly ringing in its ears, can rise up out of the abyss of evils that whirl about in our midst and overcome the uprising of the passions, which besiege our soul without ceasing. That is why we need great watchfulness: our war is unceasing and never has a truce. So Paul said, writing to the Ephesians: "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." Do not think, he says, that the contest set before us is an ordinary one. Our struggle is not against our own kind, and the battle is not on equal terms. Bound up in a body, we have been ordered to wrestle with bodiless powers. But do not be afraid: even if the fight is unequal, the power of our weapons is great. He went on, as if to say: now that you know the nature of your enemies, do not lose heart or grow numb before the struggle, but "Therefore take up the whole armour of God, so that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil." His schemes are many, that is, the ways by which he tries to trip up the more careless. We must know them precisely, so as to escape his grip and give him no way in. We must show care over the tongue, guard over the eyes, purity of mind, and be always on the alert, as though some wild beast were coming at us and trying to do us harm. For this reason that soul as high as heaven, the teacher of the Gentiles, the tongue of the world, who for the sake of his disciples [?]… [?] [Textual note: Coislin: "For how many."]

[?] Homily [?]. …where there is often much ingratitude and much excess among the grasping. For many even of very honest people have not repaid the lenders even the sum borrowed, either through ingratitude or, often, because poverty prevented them. With the Lord of all, nothing of the kind can be imagined. The loan remains intact; he promises to give back a hundredfold for what is deposited, and on top of that he stores up for us the life to come. What excuse, then, is left for us if we do not hurry and press on to receive a hundredfold in place of a little, things to come in place of things present, eternal things in place of passing ones, but gladly lock our money behind doors and bolts, and refuse to give to the needy now what lies there idle and to no purpose, so that in the age to come we might enjoy their protection? "Make friends for yourselves by means of the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail they may receive you into their eternal dwellings." I know that many not only fail to accept what we say, but pay no attention to our words, hearing them as a kind of nonsense and fable. This is exactly why I am stung and pained: neither the experience of events, nor God's great promise, nor fear of what is to come, nor our daily exhortations have been able to reach such people. Yet even so I will not stop giving this advice until, by sheer persistence, I am able to prevail, bring them to sobriety, and raise them up from the stupor and drunkenness that the desire for money has brought on them by darkening their reason. For I know, I know, that after God's grace, the persistence of our words and the diligence that comes from fasting will be able, even if late, to free them from this grievous disease and bring them back to full health. Then they too will be freed from the punishment hanging over such people, and we will be rid of our sorrow, and for all things we will send up glory to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

"And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water. And it was so."

1. Seeing, beloved, how eagerly you gather here every day, I take great pleasure in it, and I do not cease glorifying God, who loves humankind, for your progress. Just as hunger is a sign of bodily health, so eagerness to hear the divine words can be taken as the greatest proof of the soul's health. That is why our Lord Jesus Christ said in those beatitudes spoken on the mountain: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." Who, then, could praise you as you deserve, you who have once received the beatitude from the Lord of all and look for countless good things from him? For such is our Lord: when he sees a soul approaching spiritual things with great desire and intense eagerness, he lavishes his grace on it and bestows rich gifts of his own. So I expect that for your benefit a fuller word of teaching will be given to us too, for the building up of the… [Textual notes, partly illegible: So Savile; [?] manuscripts. Morel: "with the … and … stores up" [?]. One Regius: "does not …" [?]. The other manuscripts: "was able" (singular). Morel: "were able" (plural). And so [?]. Coislin: "richly bestows his own gifts; whence let us expect for us too through our…"]

…from the radiance sent out from there. Let us always fortify ourselves with these weapons, I beg you, and go out so armed into the marketplace, meet our friends, and handle our affairs. And why do I say into the marketplace? When we come to church too, let us have them on, and when we go home, and when we sleep and when we rise, and let us never take them off our whole life long. They go with us when we depart, and they become our greatest ground for confidence there. They do not weigh the body down as visible weapons do. Instead they lighten it, lift it up, and increase its strength, so long as we polish them every day, so that they shine and with their own flash blind the eyes of the evil demon, who devises every scheme against our salvation. Come, then, now that we have armed you well enough, let us set before you the usual table and put before your love what follows from what we said yesterday, again taking as our host that wonderful man, blessed Moses, the great prophet, as leader of this fine teaching. Let us see what he wants to teach us today too, and pay careful attention to what he says. For he does not speak by his own power. Whatever the grace of the Spirit sounds within him, that he utters with his own tongue, teaching human nature. Having completed his account of the first day, and having said after the creation of light, "There was evening, and there was morning, one day," he goes on: "And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water." Notice here, beloved, the order of the teaching. He told us earlier, after the creation of heaven and earth, that "the earth was invisible and unformed," and added the reason: it was invisible because it was covered by the darkness and the waters, for everything was water and darkness and nothing else. Then, at the Lord's command, light was brought forth, light and darkness were separated, and the one received the name of day while the other took the name of night. Now he wants to teach us again that, just as he divided the darkness by bringing forth light and gave each its fitting name, so too the mass of waters by command…

[?] …see a power beyond words, surpassing all human reasoning. He only commands, and one of the elements is brought forth while the other gives way. "And God said," it says, "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water." What does "Let there be a firmament" mean? To put it in human language, a kind of wall and partition dividing between them and making a separation. And so that you may learn the great obedience of the elements and the surpassing power of the Creator, it says: "And it was so." He only spoke, and the deed followed. "And God made," it says, "the firmament, and God divided between the water that was under the firmament and between the water above the firmament." Once the firmament had come to be, it says, he commanded some of the waters to be under… [Textual notes, partly illegible: Coislin: "let us handle affairs" [?]; [?] "let us manage." [?] "came to be" (aorist). Eight manuscripts: "came to be" (perfect). Morel. One: "comes about."]

…not only those trained in the Hebrew language, but all who live throughout the world might reap the benefit of them. And what is wonderful and unexpected is that it was not one of those who held to the Jewish religion who took this trouble, but a man devoted to idols and opposed to true worship. Such is everything our Lord arranges: he always makes the commands of truth grow by means of their opposites. I have not told your love these things without purpose, but so that you may know that they were not composed in this language, our own I mean, but in Hebrew. Now those who are precisely trained in that language say that among the Hebrews the name of heaven is used in the plural, and those who know the Syrian language agree. In their language, they say, one would not say "the heaven" but "the heavens." That is why blessed David's words are put this way, "the heavens of the heavens": not because there are many heavens, for blessed Moses did not teach us that, but because it is customary in the Hebrew language to name a single thing in the plural. If there had been many, the Holy Spirit would not have failed to teach us the creation of the others too, through the tongue of this blessed prophet. Hold these things firmly, I beg you, so that you can silence those who want to bring in doctrines contrary to the Church, and so that you may know with certainty the meaning of what is written in the divine Scriptures. That is why you come here so constantly and why we teach you so often: so that you may be ready to give an account to everyone who asks you. But let us return to the sequence, if you agree. "And God called the firmament heaven," it says. "And God saw that it was good." Consider how great the condescension of the words is, for the sake of human weakness. Just as he said of the light, "He saw that it was good," so now of the heaven, or firmament: "And God saw," it says, "that it was good," teaching us by this its immeasurable beauty. Who would not be amazed and astonished that over so long a time it has kept its beauty in full bloom, and that the further time advances, the more its beauty increases? What could be lovelier than what has received the Creator's praise? If, when we see a finished work of human hands, we admire its shape, its position, its beauty, its proportion, its harmony, and all the rest, how could anyone praise as it deserves what God has created, especially when it has received praise from the Lord himself? This was said in condescension to us. You will see him say it of each thing that comes to be, cutting off in advance the boldness of those who would later sharpen their tongues against God's creation and say, "Why was this or that made?" To check in advance those who attempt to say such things, he says: "And God saw that it was good." When you hear that God saw and praised, understand it in a way fitting for God… [Textual notes, partly illegible: [?] and Savile [?] "having acquired." A in the margin: "the Syrian language." All manuscripts: "bring in" (epeispherein). Savile: epipherein. Morel: eispherein. Savile: "to give you an account"; in Morel "to give" is missing. Three manuscripts and Coislin: "checking in advance those who now attempt to say these things … when therefore you hear." Patrologia Graeca 53.]

…they would not have turned to such folly. But even so we will not stop sounding in their ears what comes from the divine Scripture, while walling off our own hearing from their ruinous teachings.

6. But somehow, carried away again by the momentum of the discourse into these matters, we have lost our thread; so we must bring the discourse back to what came before. "And God called the firmament heaven," it says, "and God saw that it was good. And there was evening, and there was morning, a second day." Having given the firmament its name and praised what had been made, he brought the second day to its close, and says: "And there was evening, and there was morning, a second day." Do you see how precisely it teaches us? It calls the end of the light evening and the end of the night morning, and names the whole a day, so that we may not go astray or suppose that evening is the end of the day, but may know clearly that the length of both together makes up one day. Evening may rightly be called the end of the light, and dawn, that is, the end of the night, the completion of the day. This is what the divine Scripture wants to show when it says, "And there was evening, and there was morning, a second day."

Perhaps we have stretched the discourse to great length, not willingly, but swept along, as one might say, by the very sequence of the words, as by a most violent torrent. And you are responsible for this too, you who listen with pleasure to what we say. For nothing can so rouse a speaker and lead him to a greater wealth of ideas as the eagerness of his hearers. Just as listless and lazy hearers make even a capable speaker more sluggish, so you, by the grace of God, even if we were more voiceless than the very stones, are able to rouse our sluggishness, shake off our sleep, and compel us to say something useful to you and conducive to your edification. Since, then, you are such people, taught by God and able, as blessed Paul says, to admonish others as well, come, let us urge you, now if ever, in this season of the fast, to take great care for virtue as God wills. And do not let the discourse become tiresome to you if we speak to you every day about the same things; for to say the same things is not irksome to me, as blessed Paul says, and for you it is safe. For our soul, being lazy, needs constant reminding. And just as this body needs bodily food every day so as not to fall into great weakness and lie inert, so too the soul needs spiritual food and the best way of life, so that, growing accustomed to what is good, it may thereafter stand unconquerable by the plots of the evil one.

7. Every day, then, let us carefully examine its strength, and never stop searching ourselves. Let us keep an account of ourselves, of what is brought in and what is sent out: what we have said usefully and what idle word we have let slip; and again, what profitable things we have brought into the soul through hearing, and what things capable of harm we have let into it. And let us set certain rules and limits for the tongue, so that we first chew over… [text breaks off]

[Notes: Five manuscripts read "swept along very violently by some [torrent]". Almost all [?] read "of the matter"; others, "of the command".]

…[if a ruler on] earth had laid down a law that one must serve one's enemies, or else the penalty would be death, would not everyone, for fear of this bodily death, have rushed to fulfil the law? How deserving of condemnation would it be, then, to consent to do anything for fear of bodily death, which the debt of nature will certainly bring upon us in any case, and yet, when it comes to the death in which no consolation can be found, to care less for the law laid down by the Master of all?

8. But I did not notice that I was saying these things to people who do not even show equal love to those who love them. Who, then, will rescue us from that punishment, when we are not only far removed from that commandment, but do not even do as much as the tax collectors? "For if you love those who love you," it says, "what great thing are you doing? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?" When not even this is done by us, what hope of salvation have we? Therefore I beg you, let us not be heartless, but let us tame our thoughts. First, let us train them to outdo our neighbour in love, and, as blessed Paul says, to "outdo one another in showing honour", counting others better than ourselves; not to put up with being outdone, but to win; not to be surpassed, but to show an even greater and warmer disposition toward those who love us. For this is what above all holds our life together and binds it fast, and by this we differ from irrational creatures and wild beasts: that we are able, if we wish, to keep the rank proper to us and to show great concord with our neighbours. Then let us rein in our thoughts and tear to pieces this untamed beast—anger, I mean—and set before it the ordeal of the fearful judgment seat, and teach it that if it undertakes to make peace with its enemies it will obtain great blessings, but if it goes on quarrelling it will suffer heavy punishment.

For we ought not to spend our time idly and at random, but every day and every hour keep the Lord's judgment seat before our eyes, and consider what can win us great confidence and what increases our punishment. And so, turning these things over in our minds, let us master the passions, check the wild leapings of the flesh, and put to death, as blessed Paul says, "what is earthly in us: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire, anger, greed, vainglory, envy." If we make ourselves dead to these passions, so that they cannot work in us, we will be able to receive the fruit of the Spirit, which is "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control." Let this be the difference between the Christian and the unbeliever; let these be our distinguishing marks. Let us not pride ourselves on the name alone, nor think highly of our outward appearance; or rather, not even if we acquire these things… [?] …let us not become careless about keeping [them] [?]…

[Notes, largely illegible [?]: "nevertheless, but"; Morel: "let us not become heartless, but"; … [?] in the margin.]

[?] St John Chrysostom

…[those who] expect an attack by enemies, how much forethought they show in guarding [their possessions]? Some shut them away behind doors and bars and take every precaution; others even bury them in the ground itself, so that they may escape everyone's notice. In the same way we too, once we have gathered the wealth of virtue, ought to guard it with great care, and not display it before everyone's eyes, but hide it in the safest storeroom of the mind and wall off every approach from the one who is eager to steal it, so that, having kept it safe from capture, we may have provisions for the journey hence when we depart this life. For just as those living in a foreign land, when they are about to return to their own homeland, hurry little by little long beforehand and press on to gather as many provisions as will suffice for the length of the journey, so that they do not unawares give themselves over to hunger, in the same way we too, being here as in a foreign land (for we are all strangers and sojourners), should already take thought here and lay up for ourselves in advance the provisions that come through spiritual virtue; so that when the Master commands us to return to our own homeland we may be ready, and may take some with us and have sent the rest on ahead. For such is the nature of these provisions: whatever we choose to lay up beforehand for ourselves by performing these good works arrives there before us, opens for us the doors of confidence before the Master, and prepares our entrance in advance, so that we may go in with complete freedom and find great goodwill with the judge.

2. And so that you may learn, beloved, that this is so, consider that the one who gives alms generously both lives here nourished by a good conscience and, when he departs from here, finds great kindness with the judge, and will hear with the rest those blessed words: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me food." One would find the same happening with the other virtues as well; so it will be with the confession of sins and with prayers offered earnestly. For when in the present life we are able to wash away our offences through confession and to find forgiveness from the Master, we go there clean of sins, and shall find great confidence granted to us. For it is no longer possible for anyone who has not washed away his sins in the present life to find any consolation there. "For in Hades," it says, "who will confess to you?" And rightly so: for this is the time of the arena, of contests and wrestling bouts; that is the time of crowns, rewards and prizes. Let us therefore contend while we are still in the stadium, so that when the time comes to receive the crown and the rewards for our labours, we may not be among those put to shame, but among those who receive the crown on their heads with confidence.

We do not offer these opening remarks to your charity idly or in vain, but because we wish every day to remind you of good works, so that you may be perfect and complete…

[Notes: Others read "of the virtues". "From here already." One Royal manuscript reads "to bind on the crown".]

…he commanded [some] to occupy [the place above], and the rest to be beneath the firmament. So now too he commands these very waters, those beneath the firmament, to run together into one gathering, so that the dry land may appear; and then he gives it too its proper name, as he did with light and darkness. "For the waters were gathered," it says, "into their gatherings, and the dry land appeared, and God called the dry land earth." Do you see, beloved, how, though it was invisible and unformed, covered by the waters as by curtains, he unveiled it, so to speak, and now at last shows us its face, giving it its proper name? "And the gatherings of the waters," it says, "he called seas." See, the waters too received their proper name. For just as a first-rate craftsman, when he is about to fashion some vessel by his skill, does not give it its proper name until he has put the finishing touch [?] on the thing he is making, so too the loving Master does not give names to the elements until he has set them in their proper place by his command. When, then, the earth had received its own name and had returned to its proper [?], the waters too, once gathered together, were in turn granted their own name. "For he called the gatherings of the waters seas," it says, and again it added, "And God saw that it was good." For since human nature, being weak, was not equal to praising God's works as they deserve, the divine Scripture forestalls us and teaches us the praise given by the Creator himself.

4. When, then, you learn that the things that were made appeared good even to the one who brought them into being, you will marvel the more, but you will be able to add nothing further by way of praise and encomium. For such is the Master you have, who does such works that they cannot even receive praise from us. For how could human nature ever praise or hymn the works of God as they deserve?

And observe here, I pray, from what follows, the ineffable wisdom of our resourceful God. Since he had shown us the face of the earth plainly, he now by his command bestows on it a fitting beauty, adorning its face with a variety of seeds. "And God said," it says, "Let the earth bring forth green plants, yielding seed according to their kind and according to their likeness, and fruit trees bearing fruit, whose seed is in them according to their likeness, according to their kind, upon the earth. And it was so." What does "And it was so" mean? The Master commanded, it says, and at once the earth, rousing its own birth pangs, made itself ready for the sprouting of seeds. "And the earth brought forth," it says, "green plants, yielding seed according to their kind and according to their likeness, and fruit trees bearing fruit, whose seed is in them according to their kind, upon the earth." Consider here, beloved, how by the word of the Master everything came about for the earth. For there was no man working it, no plough, no help from oxen, no other care given to it; it only heard the command, and at once displayed what it had to give. From this we learn that even now it is not the care of farmers, nor the toil and all the other hardship that farming involves, that grants us the yield of crops, but, before all these, the word of God that was spoken to the earth at the beginning. And besides, the divine Scripture, correcting the ingratitude that men would later show, recounts everything to us precisely in the order in which it happened, in order to silence the drivel, born of their own reasonings, of those who babble idly, of those who undertake to say… [text breaks off]

[Notes: [?] had "the name of beauty" [?]; in the margin, "maimed". Savile in the text and Morel: "maimed".]

But let them await the wages of their own folly. As for us, who have been counted worthy to receive the radiance of the sun of righteousness, let us obey the teaching of the divine Scripture, and, following its rule, store sound doctrines in the storerooms of our mind; and while guarding them, let us take great care for our own salvation and flee the things that corrupt the health of our soul, abstaining from all such things as from deadly poisons. For this harm is much greater—as much greater as the soul is better than the body. Those poisons bring on this bodily death, but the things that corrupt the health of the soul procure eternal death for us.

And what are the things that corrupt us? They are many and various, but above all being infatuated with human glory and not knowing how to despise it. For this becomes the cause of many evils for us; if we have any spiritual wealth, it empties it out and leaves us bereft of the benefit we would have had from it. What could be more ruinous than this corruption, when it makes even what we seem to possess fly away from us? This is how that Pharisee became inferior to the tax collector: he could not control his own tongue, but through it, as through a window, he poured out all his wealth. So great an evil is vainglory.

6. For tell me, why and for what reason are you infatuated with the praise of men? Do you not know that, like a shadow, or anything even flimsier than that, the praise they give is scattered into the air and vanishes? Besides, human nature is easily swayed and changeable, and the same people now praise and now blame the same person; but with God's verdict this could never happen. Let us not, then, be foolish, nor deceive ourselves idly and in vain. For even if we do something good, unless we pursue it for this reason alone, to fulfil our Master's commandment and to be known to him alone, we endure the toil in vain and deprive ourselves of its fruit. For whoever does a good deed in order to hunt for glory from men—whether he manages to enjoy it or not (for often, though he does everything for its sake, he will not even be able to obtain it)—whether, then, he obtains it or fails, has received his reward here in full, and will receive no recompense for it there. Why? Because he has already deprived himself of the judge's munificence, preferring the present to the future, and the glory that comes from men to the verdict of the just judge. On the other hand, if we perform any spiritual work for this alone, to please only that sleepless eye before which all things are naked and laid bare, then our treasure remains beyond the reach of thieves, our reward stays intact, and our good hope already gives us great consolation here; and besides that reward being kept for us in an inviolable treasury, the glory that comes from men would follow as well. For we enjoy it all the more abundantly when we despise it, when we do not seek it, when we do not chase after it. And why are you surprised if, in the case of those [who pursue] spiritual philosophy… [text breaks off]

[Notes: Almost all manuscripts and Savile read "the health" (dative); Morel "the health" (accusative), and below he has "you", here "corrupting us". So Savile and the manuscripts; Morel reads "the present [praise] of these". [?] "the repayment". Shortly after, Morel reads "from the judge".]

…and the great ease of virtue, if we are willing to stay sober. Or do you not know that the divine Scripture compares to dogs those who are so careless of their own salvation that they sometimes come here and at other times hand themselves over to the devil's nets? "For a man," it says, "who turns away from his sin and goes back to it again is like a dog returning to its own vomit." Do you see what those who ran off to that lawless spectacle resemble? Have you not heard Christ saying, "Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand; and the rivers came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was its fall"? But those who ran off to the horse races have become even worse than this. For that man's house at least collapsed only after the assault (he spoke of rivers and winds not to hint to us at a mass of water and the violence of winds, but at the violent onset of temptations; and of the collapse of the house, not so that we should think of a physical house, for the word concerns the soul that collapses under the assault of troubles and cannot hold out). But in your case no wind stirred, no rivers beat against you; just a little devilish breeze blew, and it blew you all away. What could be worse than this folly? What use is the fast, tell me? What is the gain of gathering here?

Who would not groan for you, and call us wretched? Groan for you, because you have poured out in one moment [?] all that you had gathered, and flung open the doors of your mind to the evil demon, so that he could come in and with great ease carry off all your spiritual wealth; and he would rightly call us wretched, because we are sounding into ears so dead and suffering such loss every day, sowing but able to reap nothing. For surely we are not eager to speak merely to delight your ears, or because we crave your praise? If you are not going to gain anything from what we say, it is better for us to be silent from now on. For I do not wish to bring greater condemnation upon you.

For just as a merchant who has gathered a large cargo and has his ship full of great wealth, when a sudden squall strikes, the force of the winds overpowers it, and it sinks, crew and all, becomes a pitiful sight to everyone, suddenly seen stripped bare and reduced from great and untold wealth to utter poverty, in the same way the devil has now treated you. Finding your spiritual ship full of great wealth, and seeing the untold treasure you had been able to gather both from the fast and from the constant teaching, he let loose, like a squall, that profitless and harmful racing of horses, and through it left you destitute and stripped of all your riches.

2. I know that I have rebuked you sharply, but forgive me, I beg you; for such is a soul in pain. I do not say these things out of hostility, but out of concern and a loving heart. Therefore, relaxing my sharpness a little, since the spreading of the sore itself… [text breaks off]

[Notes: [?] and Coislin read "having run together". Coislin reads "hint to us at a mass" [?]. In Coislin: "and those who are idle" [?].]

[...] and that, after so much exhortation from us, you not run off again to those satanic gatherings: this I must solemnly charge you. For it is not always good to apply gentle remedies. When the wound is stubborn, one must also apply astringent and stinging ones, so that the healing may come quickly. 3. Let all who are guilty of these charges learn, then, that if they persist in the same negligence even after this exhortation of ours, we will not tolerate it. Using the laws of the Church, we will teach them with great severity not to commit such offenses, and not to listen to the divine oracles with such contempt. I do not say this about everyone gathered here, but about those who are guilty of what has been said. For the word speaks to everyone, but let each hearer take the remedy that suits him. The one guilty of the sin should take it so as to halt his negligence here and go no further, and recover himself by his zeal from now on and correct his lapses. The one who is not guilty should become more secure, so that he is never caught and never becomes guilty. But we want to persuade your love by the facts themselves that we were led to say these things out of affection and great concern, stung in soul and very much afraid for your salvation. So come, let us nourish ourselves again with good hopes and set before you our customary teaching, and so show you the fatherly goodwill we have toward you. But [?] pay close attention to what is said, so that you may [?] gain something more, and so return home. Now I must speak to your love about the passages that were read. "And God said," it says, "Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth, to divide between the day and the night. And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years. And let them be for light in the firmament of heaven, so as to shine upon the earth. And it was so." Yesterday blessed Moses taught us how the Creator of all adorned the formless earth with plants, with the variety of flowers, and with the sprouting of seeds; so today he has turned his discourse to the adornment of heaven. Just as the earth is adorned by what springs up from it, so he made this visible heaven brighter and more splendid, studding it with the variety of the stars and with the creation of the two great lights, I mean the sun and the moon. "And God made," it says, "the two great lights: the great light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars." Do you see the wisdom of the Creator? He only spoke, and this element was brought forth, this marvelous thing, I mean the sun. For this is what he calls the great light, and he says it was made to rule the day. It makes the day brighter, sending out its rays like flashes of light, displaying its own beauty in full bloom every day, appearing at dawn and rousing all humankind to pursue their work. The blessed prophet shows its beauty when he says: "And he, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, will rejoice like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit to the end of heaven." Do you see how he has shown us both its beauty and the speed of its work? For in saying, "His going forth is from the end of heaven," [?] ... to make the light of the day brighter [?]

[?] [...] we might say the same of the lesser light too, I mean the moon, for there had been three nights before it was created. Yet once it was brought forth, it too contributes its own service. It dispels the darkness of the night and, one might almost say, does the same as the sun in every other respect. For the one was assigned "to rule the day," and the other "to rule the night." What do "to rule the day" and "to rule the night" mean? The one, he says, received authority over the day and the other over the night. The one was to make the day brighter with its rays; the other was to dispel the darkness and, by its light, enable human beings to pursue their occupations with ease. For then the traveler confidently sets out on his journey, the sailor launches his ship and crosses the seas, and each person who follows a trade practises his skill with great freedom. Then, having taught us the use of these lights, he says: "And the stars. And God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth, and to rule over the day and the night, and to divide between the light and the darkness." 5. Consider how great a use he has shown us that these have too. "He set them," it says, "in the firmament of heaven." What does "he set" mean? Does it mean, as one might say, "he fixed" them? Not at all! For we often see them cross a great distance in a single moment. They never stand in one place, but complete the course that the Master appointed them to run. What then does "he set" mean? It means that he commanded them to be in heaven. As Scripture goes on, one can see it saying elsewhere too that "He set Adam in paradise." This is not because he fixed him in paradise, but because he commanded him to be in paradise. In the same way, then, we might say of the stars that he commanded them to be in the firmament of heaven and send out their light upon the earth. For consider with me, beloved: what meadows and gardens are as delightful to see as the sky studded with stars in the middle of the night, adorned with the variety of the stars as if with flowers, as they send abundant light down to the earth? This is the purpose for which they were appointed: "to shine upon the earth, and to rule over the day and the night." This is said generally of the great lights as well. For having taught us about the creation of the two lights and of the stars, he speaks of them all together and says: "And to rule over the day and the night, and to divide between the light and the darkness." By day one cannot see the stars moving across the sky, for the sun's light hides their service by its great brilliance. In the same way the sun would never appear at night, since the moon's light is enough to brighten the gloom of the night. Each of the elements stays within its own bounds and never oversteps its proper measure, but keeps the Master's ordinance and fulfills its own function. Who could tell all the other things that the service of these lights and stars does for human life? "Let them be," it says, "for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years." What does "for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years" mean? Divine Scripture wants to teach us that their course gives us knowledge of the seasons and of the changes of the solstices, the number of the days, and the course of the year, and from these we are able to discern [...] [Notes: Morel.: "Each element ... oversteps," wrongly. Below [?]. Savil.: "What could one say of the other things."]

[...] to sit by [?], and not lift the eye of the mind to the one who brought them forth, and to obey blessed Paul, who says: "For since the creation of the world his invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made." What do you say, O man? When you see the heaven, do you marvel at its beauty, the variety of the stars, its surpassing brightness? Do not stop there, but stretch your mind out to their Creator. Again, the sun's light amazes you. You see how useful it is and are roused to wonder, and when you see its rays lighting up your eyes, you marvel at the beauty of the element. But do not stop there either. Consider this: if the thing created is so marvelous and extraordinary, surpassing all human understanding, what must he be like who brought it forth by word and command alone? Think the same about the earth. When you see it adorned with flowers, with the growth of plants spread over it on every side like an embroidered garment, do not credit what is born from it to the power of the earth, or to the help of the sun and moon. Consider gratefully that to create these too he only said, "Let the earth bring forth the herb of grass," and at once the whole face of the earth grew bright. If we turn these things over in our thoughts every day, we will be grateful ourselves, and we will offer the Master fitting praise, or rather, praise as far as we are able. And we will glorify him not by this alone but [?] by the best way of life: if we do not fall into the same faults again, but bid a firm farewell to the devil's deceits and draw down goodwill from above by our attentiveness from now on, by great zeal, and by earnest confession. For in his great love for mankind it is enough for him that we simply turn away from wickedness. If we choose this, we will readily press on to doing good works as well. So from now on, I beg you, let no one appear at the horse races, or waste the hours of the day in idle gatherings. Let no one give himself over to dice, and the shouting they give rise to, and the rest of the corruption. For tell me, what is the profit of fasting, when you go all day without food but give yourself over to dice and useless chatter, and often spend the whole day in false oaths and blasphemies? Let us not, I beg you, be so careless about our own salvation. Rather, let our conversation always be about spiritual things. Let each person take a divine book in his hands, call his neighbors together, and water both his own mind and the minds of his companions with the divine words. In this way we may be able to escape the devices of the evil one, reap great goods from the fast, and enjoy the loving-kindness of God, by the grace and compassion of his only-begotten Son, with whom be glory, power, and honor to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

"And God said: Let the waters bring forth creeping things that have life, and birds flying over the earth along the firmament of heaven. And it was so. And God made the great sea creatures, and every living creature that creeps, which the waters brought forth according to their kinds." 1. Yesterday we rebuked well enough those who deserted to the horse races. We showed them how great a harm they had suffered, since they had poured out all at once the spiritual wealth they had gathered from the fast, and [...] [Notes: Morel.: "before the creation of this." Morel.: "readily to the practice of works." [?]: "eagerness."]

[...] and they dare to blaspheme the common Master, and think that the negligence of others gives them a cover for their own error. 2. That this brings the greatest danger on those who give them occasion for blasphemy, let us hear from the prophet, who cries out in the person of God: "Woe to you, because through you my name is blasphemed among the Gentiles." A fearful word, full of dread! For this "woe" is, as it were, the voice of one lamenting those who are about to fall under that inescapable punishment. Just as so great a penalty awaits those who give others cause for blasphemy through their own negligence, so for those who care for virtue the same thing becomes the occasion of countless crowns. Christ taught this very thing when he said: "Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." Some people are scandalized by the negligence of others and sharpen their tongues against our Master. In the same way, he says, when you pursue virtue, people who see you do not stop at praising you. When they see your works shining and lighting up their eyes, they are moved to glorify your Father in heaven. And when they do this, our reward is multiplied again, and in return for their praise the Master grants us countless goods: "For those who glorify me," he says, "I will glorify." So let us do everything, beloved, so that our Master is glorified, and let us give no one cause to stumble. This is what blessed Paul, the teacher of the world, continually teaches us. At one point he says: "If food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat"; and elsewhere he says: "When you sin in this way against the brethren and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ." A severe threat, carrying a great condemnation! For do not think, he says, that the harm will fall on that man alone; it passes on to Christ himself, who was crucified for him. If your Master did not refuse to be crucified for him, will you not bring yourself to do everything you can to give him no occasion to stumble? You will find Paul giving this counsel to his disciples everywhere, for this is what holds our life together. That is why, writing elsewhere, he said: "Let each of you look not to his own interests, but each also to those of others"; and elsewhere again: "All things are lawful for me, but not all things build up." Do you see the apostle's understanding? Even if it is lawful for me to do something, he says, and it does me no harm, I would not bring myself to do it if it did not build up my neighbor. Do you see his loving soul, how he never looks to his own interest, but shows in everything that the greatest virtue is to take great care for building up one's neighbors? Since we know all this, I beg you, let us be on our guard. Let us keep away from whatever can ruin the wealth of our virtue, and never do anything that does our neighbor any harm. For this both makes the sin worse and brings a heavier punishment on us. And let us not despise even an ordinary person, or say those cold words: "What do I care if so-and-so is scandalized?" What are you saying? Tell [me] [...] [Note: Morel.: "the good works." Others have "good" [?].]

[...] to teach humankind through the tongue of the prophet, so that we might know both the order of the things created and the power of the Creator: how his word became deed, and his utterance gave them their existence and their passage into being? 4. But there are some ungrateful people who, even after so much teaching, try to disbelieve and will not allow that the visible world has a Creator. Some declare that things exist of themselves; others, that they came from some underlying matter. See how great the devil's deceit is, how he has exploited the easy credulity of those enslaved to error. That is why blessed [Moses] [?], inspired by the divine Spirit, teaches us so precisely: so that we may not suffer the same fate as these people, but may know clearly both the sequence of the things created and how each was created [?]. For if God had not guided the prophet's tongue in this way out of care for our salvation, it would have been enough to say that God made the heaven and the earth and the sea and the animals, without setting out the order of what came first and what came later. But so that those who choose to be ungrateful are left no pretext for an excuse, he clearly sets out both the order of what came into being and the number of the days. He teaches us everything with great condescension, so that once we have learned the whole truth, we may no longer heed the error of those who say everything out of their own reasonings, but may know the ineffable power of our Creator. "And it was so," it says. He said, "Let the waters bring forth creeping things that have life, and birds flying over the earth along the firmament of heaven," and the element obeyed and fulfilled the command. "And it was so," it says, as the Master ordered. "And God made the great sea creatures, and every living creature that creeps, which the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that they were good. And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth." Here again, I ask you, see how great the wisdom of the Spirit is. Having said, "It was so," blessed Moses teaches us in detail, adding: "And God made the great sea creatures, and every living creature that creeps, which the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that they were good." Here again he cuts down the audacity of those who say everything without thinking. Someone might say, "Why were the sea creatures made? What use are they to us? What benefit is there in their creation?" To prevent this, after saying, "God made the great sea creatures, and every living creature that creeps, and the birds," he at once added, "And God saw that they were good." Do not, he says, try to find fault with the creatures just because you do not know the reason they were made. You have heard the Master giving his verdict and saying that they are good. How then are you so mad as to dare to say, "Why were they made?" and to disparage their creation as superfluous? If you are grateful, you will be able to learn even from their creation both the power of your Master and his ineffable loving-kindness. You will learn his power, in that by word and command he caused such creatures to be brought forth from the waters; and his loving-kindness, in that, having brought them forth, he also gave them a place of their own, and the immense part of the [...] [Notes: [?] "I said earlier," placed here. Coislin.: "into the honor that is to come."]

"And God made," it says, "the wild beasts of the earth according to their kind, and the cattle according to their kind, and all the reptiles of the earth according to their kind. And God saw that they were good." Where now are those who dare to ask, "Why wild beasts? Why reptiles?" Let them listen to divine Scripture when it says, "And God saw that they were good." Tell me: the Maker himself praises what has been made, and you dare to find fault? What madness could be greater than this? Among the seeds and plants, too, the earth brought forth not only fruit-bearing trees but also fruitless ones, and it produces not only useless herbs but also ones unknown to us, often even harmful ones. Yet no one will dare on that account to find fault with what has been made, for nothing has come into being in vain or without purpose. It would not have received the Master's praise had it not been made for some beneficial use. Among the trees, then, not all bear fruit; many are fruitless, and these too give us a wonderful use no less than the fruit-bearing ones, contributing to our comfort. From them we build houses and make many other things that serve our comfort. In short, there is nothing that was not made for some reason, even if human nature cannot know the reason for everything with precision. So, as with the trees, so with the animals: some are suited to be our food, others to serve us. The various kinds of wild beasts and reptiles also give us no small benefit. If anyone is willing to learn with a fair mind, he will find even now, when we have lost our dominion over them through the disobedience of the first-formed man, that we gain much benefit from them. For the sons of physicians take many things from them too and make preparations that can contribute to the [55] health of our bodies. Besides, what harm came from the creation of the wild beasts, when they, like the tame ones, were to be under the authority of the one who was soon to be created? I say this for the moment. 6. Now, so that you may learn the surpassing love for humanity that the Master of all shows toward our race: he stretched out the heaven, spread out the earth, and made the firmament to divide the waters like a wall set in the middle. Then he commanded the waters to be gathered together, and named them seas, and the dry land earth, and then he adorned the earth with sprouting seeds and the other plants. Next he went on to make the two great lights and the variety of the stars, and through them he adorned the beauty of the heaven. Then he brought forth the living creatures from the waters, and the birds that fly over the earth across the firmament of heaven. When he had completed the count of five days, and the creatures of the earth also had to be made, he commanded them too to be brought forth: those fit for food, those useful for service, and the wild beasts and the reptiles. Then at last, once he had adorned everything and given the visible world its proper order and arrangement, and had prepared a costly table filled with varied foods of every kind, rich in abundance and wealth, and had made the palace, so to speak, splendid on every side, the things above, the things [?] Coislin: "fruitful" (εὔκαρπα). [?] Some mss.: "he showed the excess of his love for humanity..., for since" [?]

and that all are liable for the same things. Consider, then, how much punishment such people deserve, when they not only heap up the unquenchable fire upon themselves, but also cause others to stay fixed in error and to stop their ears against the teaching of virtue. Besides this, they give occasion for slander against those who practice virtue, and, worst of all, through them the Master is blasphemed. Do you see how great the ruin caused by wickedness is? Do you see that those who practice wickedness make themselves liable to no ordinary punishment, but to a very heavy one, since they will have to give account for all of it: not only for their own destruction, but also for the stumbling of those led astray, for the accusations against those who practice virtue, and for the blasphemy against God? Bearing all this in mind, let us not neglect our own salvation, but let us take great care for a godly way of life, knowing that it is chiefly on this account that we are either condemned or counted worthy of his love for humanity. Let us, then, do everything in such a way that we ourselves live with a good conscience, that we lead by the hand to the truth those still in error through our godly conduct, that through us all others ranked with us enjoy a good reputation, and, above all, that our Master is glorified and shows still greater care for us. For when people look at us and profit, and give praise to God, we too shall enjoy greater help from him. What could be more blessed than a person who lives in such a way that those who see him are amazed and say, "Glory to you, O God! What sort of people are the Christians? What wisdom they show! How they look down on present things! How they regard everything as a shadow and a dream, cling to nothing that is seen, and do everything as though living in a foreign land, hastening every day toward their departure from here!" How great a reward from God do you think these words already bring, here and now, to those who live this way? And what is wonderful and surprising is that the very people who pass such judgments on us will soon turn away from error and return to the truth. Everyone can see how much confidence before God this wins for such people there. Knowing, then, that we are answerable for both the benefit and the harm of our neighbors, let us so order our lives that we do not merely suffice for ourselves but become a source of teaching for others.
