So may we draw much help from God here, and in the age to come abundantly enjoy God's love for humanity, by the grace and compassion of his only-begotten Son, with whom to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, be glory, might, and honor, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

"And God said, 'Let us make man in our image and after our likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of heaven, and the cattle, and the wild beasts, and all the earth, and all the reptiles that creep upon the earth.'" 1. Come now, since yesterday you listened with great eagerness to what we said, today too let us set before your [?] the passages just read

our image and likeness." For the other day we heard him say, after the making of heaven and earth, "Let there be light," and "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water," and again, "Let the water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear," and "Let there be lights," and "Let the waters bring forth reptiles with living souls." Did you see the whole creation made in the five days by word and command alone? Consider today how great the difference in the words is. He no longer says, "Let man come into being," but what? "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness." What is new here? What is strange? Who is this being that is made, that the Maker needed so much deliberation and consideration to form him? Do not be surprised, beloved. Man is more honored than all the visible creatures, and it was for his sake that all these were brought forth: heaven, earth, sea, sun, moon, stars, reptiles, cattle, all the irrational animals. "Then why," someone says, "if he is more honored than all of these, was he brought forth last?" With good reason. When a king is about to enter a city, his bodyguards and all the rest must go ahead of him, so that the king may arrive at a palace made ready. In the same way here, since God was about to set man as a kind of king and ruler over everything on earth, he first built all this ordered world, and only then brought forth the one who was to be set over it, showing us by the very facts how greatly this creature is honored. But let us ask the Jew and see what he says: to whom was it said, "Let us make man in our image"? These are the writings of Moses, whom they say they believe but do not believe, as Christ also says: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me." The letters are with them, but the meaning is with us. To whom, then, was it said, "Let us make man," and with whom does the Master share this deliberation? Not because he needs deliberation and consideration—God forbid!—but by the form of the words he wishes to show us the surpassing honor he bestows on the man being made. What, then, do these people say, who still have the veil lying over their hearts and refuse to understand anything that is written? "He says this to an angel," they say, "or to an archangel." What madness! What great shamelessness! How could it make sense, O man, for an angel to share in the Master's counsel, or for creatures to share the Creator's? It belongs to angels not to share in counsel but to stand by and fulfill their service. To learn this, listen to Isaiah, most loud-voiced of prophets, speaking about the powers above the angels: "I saw the cherubim standing at the right hand of God, and the seraphim, and they covered their faces with their wings, and their feet"—clearly because they could not bear the brightness flashing from there, but stood with great fear and trembling. For it is proper to creatures to stand before the Master. 3. But these people, understanding nothing of what is written, simply say whatever comes to mind. Therefore it is fitting [to refute] their nonsense [?] Two mss.: "the reptiles, the swimming creatures, all." Coislin: "the reptiles, the moving creatures, the swimming creatures, all." Savile: "O the folly! O the great..." Coislin: "O the folly! O [?]..." One Regius ms. and Coislin: "with their wings."

[if they say that] "image" was said [of form], we will reply to them: then clearly not only the man but the woman too [is the image], for both have the same form. But this would make no sense. Listen to Paul saying, "A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man." For he rules, and she is subject, as God also said to her from the beginning: "Your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you." Since man received the image with respect to rule and not with respect to form, and man rules over all while the woman is subject, Paul therefore says of the man that he is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man. If he had been speaking of form, he would not have made the distinction, for man and woman have the same shape. Do you see the abundance of the truth, how it leaves no pretext for defense to those who wish to be shameless? Yet even so, let us not stop showing great patience toward them, in case God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to knowledge of the truth. Let us not grow weary, then, but show great gentleness, to see if we can snatch them from the devil's deceit. And, if you like, let us again set before them blessed Paul, who says to the inhabitants of Athens: "We ought not to think that the Deity is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man." Do you see the wise teacher, how precisely he cut away all their deceit? For he said not only that the Deity is free from bodily shape, but also that human imagination cannot even form any such thing. Keep speaking with them about these things constantly, and do not stop contributing your own part, in case they may give way, in case they may be willing to look up toward the truth. Do not stop speaking with them with great gentleness and care; but as for you yourselves, [62] I urge you, hold fast to the doctrines of the Church with precision, without confusing the sequence of what has been said. When speaking with Jews, speak in a fitting way, and show that these words were not said to any of the ministering powers, but to the only-begotten Son of God himself. Against those who hold the views of Arius, show from this same passage the Son's equality of honor with the Father. And against those who imagine that the Deity has human form, bring forward what blessed Paul said. So overthrow the deadly diseases that spring up like tares among the doctrines of the Church, and be eager to strengthen the godly teachings in yourselves. For I wish and pray that all of you may hold the rank of teachers, and not only be hearers of what we say, but also carry it across to others and draw into the net those still astray, toward the way of truth. As Paul also says, "Build one another up," and, "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." In this way our Church will grow in number, and you will enjoy greater help from above, taking great care of your fellow members. 5. For God does not want the Christian to suffice only for himself, but to build up others as well, not only by teaching but also by his life and conduct. Nothing leads people to the way of truth so much as a strict way of life. For neither to the things [said] by us [?] Two mss.: "Let us not then be content" [?]. Morel: "if perhaps they give way" is missing in two mss. All have "be eager" (σπουδάζετε) except [?], which has σπουδάσατε. Savile and some mss.: περιωρίσθω; Morel: περιορίζεσθαι.

to make petitions to God, and, as far as one can, to provide oneself with the help that comes through almsgiving. For this commandment, this above all, can blot out all our sins and snatch us from the fire of Gehenna, provided only that we practice it generously and do not do it for show before people. And why do I say, not for show? If we were right-minded, we ought to practice it for the sake of the good alone and out of compassion for our fellow human beings, not for the rewards promised by the Master. But since we cannot imagine anything lofty, let us at least practice it for that reason, and never hunt for glory from people, so that we do not bear the expense and also lose the reward. Let us take care of this not only in almsgiving but in every spiritual good deed, and do nothing with an eye to people's praise. Otherwise there will be no benefit for us, whether we fast, or pray, or give alms, or do anything else, unless it is done for him alone, who knows even what is hidden [64] and what lies stored in the depths of our minds. For if you expect your reward from him, O man, why do you want to be praised by your fellow man? And why do I say praised? Often he does not praise but envies. There are many so wickedly disposed that they twist even our good deeds into the opposite. Tell me, then, why do you set such store by their corrupt judgment? Nothing we do escapes that sleepless eye, and bearing this in mind we must order our lives with such care, as people who will soon give account of our words, our deeds, and even our thoughts. Let us not, then, despise our own salvation. Nothing is equal to virtue, beloved. For in the age to come it will snatch us from Gehenna and grant us the enjoyment of the kingdom of heaven, and in the present life it sets us above all who try vainly and to no purpose to plot against us. It makes us stronger not only than men but also than the demons themselves, and than the enemy of our salvation—I mean the devil. What then could equal it, when it makes those who pursue it superior not only to the people who plot against them but even to the demons? Virtue is to look down on all human things, to picture the things to come at every hour, to be excited by nothing in the present, but to know that all human things are a shadow and a dream, and whatever is more worthless still. Virtue is to be disposed toward the affairs of this life as if dead: toward whatever harms the salvation of the soul, to be inactive as a dead man is, and to live and be active only toward spiritual things, as Paul also said: "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." Let us too, then, beloved, having put on Christ, do everything accordingly, and not [grieve?] the Holy Spirit. So when we are troubled by passion, or by improper desire, or anger, or rage, or envy, let us remember the one who dwells in us and drive every such thought far away. Let us revere [?] the grace given to us by God [?] Some mss.: "to be praised and admired." [?]: "all such desire and thought."

those who receive it. Such is our Master: when he sees a wakeful soul and a burning longing, he supplies his own wealth abundantly, exceeding what is asked out of his own generosity. 2. Knowing this, then, beloved, cleanse your minds of worldly affairs, widen the breadth of your understanding, and receive with great eagerness what the Spirit supplies, so that, like rich and fertile soil, you may multiply what is sown and bear fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. In the past days you heard of the unspeakable wisdom of the one who fashioned all visible things, and how he brought everything forth by word and will alone. For he said, "Let it be," and it was, and at once all the elements were brought forth. The word was enough to establish what was made, not because it was merely a word, but because it was the word of God. You remember the arguments we raised then against those who say that existing things came from pre-existing matter, and who bring their own nonsense into the doctrines of the Church. You learned why he brought forth heaven complete, but the earth formless and unshaped. We gave two reasons then. One was so that, having learned the Master's power from the better element, we would no longer doubt it, thinking this happened through weakness of power. The other was that the earth has become both mother and nurse to us: from it we are fed and enjoy all other things, and to it we return again, for it is both our homeland and our tomb. So, lest the necessity of our need lead us to imagine something great about it, he shows it formless at the beginning, so that we may be taught by the facts themselves no longer to credit all the things mentioned above to the nature of the earth, but to the power of the one who brought it forth. You learned again how he divided the waters, commanding this visible firmament to be brought forth. You saw living creatures brought forth from the waters and from the earth. It is not idly or in vain that I feel bound to go over these things again and repeat them to you, my beloved, but so that for those who heard them it may serve as a reminder and they may store them more securely in their minds, and for those who were not present then the teaching may be sufficient, and they may suffer no loss from having been absent. A loving father, too, keeps the leftovers of the table for children who were away, so that when they come they may find in what was kept a consolation for their absence. For this reason we too, caring for all who gather here as our own members, and counting your progress as our own good name, desire [67] that all may be shown perfect and complete, to the glory of God, to the good name of the Church, and to our own boast. And if I do not seem to be troubling you, come, let us briefly remind you, my beloved, of what we said yesterday too. You saw the difference between the making of the creatures and the forming of man. You heard what honor he granted the founder of our race, and how in the very forming, through the words themselves and the weight of the expressions, he revealed the honor shown to the one about to be made, saying, "Let us make man in our image" Coislin: "we enjoy all good things." One ms.: "from the presence."

[?] shows that God's promise was false. In the beginning things were not like this. The wild beasts feared and trembled, and bowed down before their master. But when he lost his freedom of speech with God through his disobedience, his authority was cut short as well. To see that everything was once subject to man, listen to the Scripture saying: "He brought the wild beasts and all the irrational creatures to Adam, to see what he would call them." And seeing the beasts come close to him, he did not leap away. Instead, just as a master gives names to the servants under him, so he gave names to them all. "And whatever Adam called it," it says, "that was its name." This too is a sign of lordship. That is why God, wishing to teach him the dignity of his authority by this as well, entrusted to him the giving of names. This is enough to show that at the beginning the wild beasts were not fearsome to man. But there is another proof, no weaker than this and in fact much clearer. What is it? The serpent's conversation with the woman. If the wild beasts had been fearsome to man, the woman would not have stayed when she saw the serpent. She would not have accepted its advice or talked with it so fearlessly. She would have been terrified at the sight of it at once, and leapt away. But in fact she converses with it and is not afraid, for this fear did not yet exist. But once sin entered, the honor and the authority were taken away. Among household slaves, those who are in good standing are feared even by their fellow servants, while those who have given offense are afraid even of their fellow servants. So it happened with man. As long as he had freedom of speech with God, he was fearsome even to the wild beasts; but when he gave offense, he came to fear even the lowest of his fellow servants. If you will not accept what we say, show me that the wild beasts were fearsome to man before the sin. You cannot. And if the fear came in afterward, this too is the greatest proof of God's love for mankind. For if, after man had broken the commandment, the honor given to him had remained untouched, he would not easily have risen from his fall. When people enjoy the same honor whether they disobey or not, they are trained all the more in wickedness and are slow to turn away from evil. If even now, with fears and punishments and penalties hanging over them, they will not bring themselves to be self-controlled, what would they be like if they suffered nothing terrible for their offenses? So it was out of care and concern for us that he cast us out of that authority. But come with me, beloved, and consider from this too God's unspeakable love for mankind. Adam overturned the whole commandment and transgressed the entire law. Yet God, being loving toward mankind and overcoming our offenses with his goodness, did not dissolve the whole of his honor or cast him out of all his lordship. He let only those animals fall outside his authority which did not contribute much to the needs of his life. The necessary and useful ones, which render great service to our life, he allowed to remain in subjection and servitude. So he left us herds of oxen, so that we might draw the plow, cut open the earth, and sow the seed. He left us the kinds of beasts of burden, so that they might share our labors in carrying loads. He left us the flocks of sheep [...]

[Notes:] [?] read "fellow servants" (syndoulous), and below "of the fellow servants" (ton syndoulon), where our manuscripts and two others have homodoulous and homodoulon. Morel reads "the offenses" (ta plemmelemata); others read ta peplemmelemena.

St. John Chrysostom

[...] that the Master is pleased with such souls, listen to him saying: "On whom will I look, if not on the one who is gentle and quiet and trembles at my words?" That is why Christ also said when he taught: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." The one who truly humbles himself could never be carried away into rage or grow angry with his neighbor, because his soul is calm and attends to its own affairs. And what could be more blessed than a soul in that condition? Such a person sits always in harbor, free of every storm, delighting in the calm of his thoughts. That is why Christ said: "And you will find rest for your souls." Just as the one who has lulled these passions to sleep enjoys great rest, so the careless and slack person, who cannot properly rein in the passions that arise within him, lives in constant turmoil. He has war at home; he is troubled when no one is even there; he endures a great storm. So he is tossed on the crests of the waves, and when the gale of the evil spirits comes upon him, he is often swamped, his ship sunk through the helmsman's inexperience. That is why we must be sober and watchful, and keep a constant and unceasing concern for the salvation of our souls. The Christian must always stand in battle array against the passions of the flesh. He must keep fresh in his ears the laws given us by the common Master of all, wall himself in with them, and make proper use of God's great patience toward us. He must not wait to learn by experience and only then restrain himself, so that it may not be said of us too: "When he slew them, then they sought him." So then, beloved, since we have the presence of the fast as our ally, let us all hasten to confess our offenses, abstain from all evil, and pursue every virtue. This is what the blessed prophet David teaches when he says: "Turn away from evil and do good." If we order our lives in this way, and along with abstaining from food we also show abstinence from evil, we too will be able to enjoy greater freedom of speech with God, and to be counted worthy of more abundant love from him, both in this present life and on that fearful day to come, through the prayers and intercessions of those who have pleased him, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, might and honor to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

An exhortation to those who were ashamed, after the bodily meal, to come to the evening assembly; and on the words that follow "Let us make man in our image and likeness," as far as "And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them."

1. Our gathering is smaller today, and the audience of those who have come together is small. For what reason, and why? Perhaps some were ashamed to come to this spiritual banquet after the material table, and this became the cause of their absence. But let them listen to a wise man saying: "There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace." It is no cause for shame to have partaken of a table [?], since when [?]

[...] not to deprive themselves, but rather to show all the more zeal for this. 2. For there are, there truly are, ways much greater than abstaining from food, which can open to us the doors of freedom of speech before God. So let the one who takes food and cannot fast show more generous almsgiving. Let him have fervent prayers, and an eager zeal for hearing the divine oracles; here bodily weakness is no hindrance to us. Let him be reconciled with his enemies, and drive every grudge out of his soul. If he is willing to accomplish these things, he has shown the true fast, the one the Master requires of us above all. Indeed, the reason he commands this abstinence from food is that, by bridling the leaps of the flesh, we may make it obedient to the rein for fulfilling the commandments. But if, because of bodily weakness, we are not going to bring ourselves even the help of fasting, and then show still greater carelessness, we are unwittingly doing ourselves the greatest harm. For if, even with fasting, the lack of the good works I mentioned does us no good, how much more if we cannot even use the medicine of fasting and then show greater carelessness! Now that you have learned this from us, I urge those of you who can fast to increase, as far as you are able, this good and praiseworthy zeal. "For as far as our outer man is wasting away, so far the inner man is being renewed." Fasting subdues the body and bridles its unruly leaps, but it makes the soul brighter, gives it wings, and makes it lofty and light. And as for your brothers who cannot fast because of bodily weakness, urge them not to stay away from this spiritual food. Teach them, pass on to them what you hear from us, and show them that the one who has eaten and drunk in moderation is not unworthy of this hearing, but only the one who is careless and dissipated. And tell them also the apostolic saying: "The one who eats, eats to the Lord, and the one who does not eat, abstains to the Lord, and gives thanks to God." So the one who fasts gives thanks to God because he has had strength able to hold out against the labor of fasting; and the one who eats in turn gives thanks to God because this cannot harm him at all in the salvation of his soul, if he is willing. For God, who loves mankind, has cut for us so many roads, more than can be told, by which we can, if we wish, share in the highest freedom of speech. We have said enough about this for the sake of those who stayed away, removing their excuse of shame and showing that they should not be ashamed of this. It is not eating that brings us shame, but doing something evil. Sin is a great shame. If we commit it, we ought not only to be ashamed but also to hide our faces, and to bewail ourselves like those who have given offense. Or rather, not even then should we despair of ourselves, but we should hasten to confession and to a right disposition. For we have such a Master, who asks nothing else of us [?]

[...] in these brief words. For this blessed prophet, speaking by the Spirit, wants to teach us now some hidden truths. He said, "Let us make man," and the Creator of all added, so to speak, deliberation and consideration. By this form of speech he showed the honor belonging to the one who was about to be formed, and even before the forming he taught us the greatness of the authority he was about to entrust to the one about to be created. So having said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," he went on: "And let them rule over the fish of the sea." See how from the very opening he points out to us the hidden treasure. For the prophet, speaking by the divine Spirit, sees even things that do not yet exist as already existing and done. Tell me, then: why, having said, "Let us make man," does he now say, "And let them rule"? From this he already hints at a mystery hidden from us. Who are "they" who are to rule? Clearly he said this as a hint at the forming of the woman. You see how nothing in the divine Scripture is set down idly or at random, but even an ordinary-seeming word holds a great treasure stored up within it. 4. And do not be surprised, beloved, at what I have said. It is the custom of all the prophets to speak of things that have not yet happened as though they had happened. Since with spiritual eyes they saw what would happen after a great number of years, they spoke of everything as though they were looking at events already lying before their eyes. To learn this clearly, listen to the blessed David, prophesying so many generations beforehand the events of Christ's cross, and crying out: "They pierced my hands and my feet"; and again, "They divided my garments among themselves." You see how he proclaimed in advance things that would happen long afterward as though they had already happened? In the same way this blessed prophet, already hinting to us at the forming of the woman, says in a veiled way, "And let them rule over the fish of the sea." Then, going further, he says more clearly: "And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them." See how much precision he uses, saying the same thing once and a second time, so that his words may be stored up in the minds of his hearers. If this had not been his concern, it would have been enough to say, "And God made man." But he adds again, "In the image of God he made him." Since he had taught us in what went before in what sense "in the image" is said, here he takes up the same word again and says, "In the image of God he made him." And so as not to leave even a shameless excuse to those who want to fight against the doctrines of the Church, a little further on he teaches the same thing again: that it was in respect of ruling and having all created things subject to him that he used the word "image." Meanwhile, let us see what he says: "And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he made them." What he hinted at above when he said, "And let them rule," he has said here more clearly. Yet even this he taught us in a hidden way, for before teaching us about the forming, or saying where the woman came from, he says: "Male and female he made them."

[Note:] Coislin and another manuscript read "the present things."

[...] every green plant for food. And it was so." Everything the Creator commanded, it says, was carried out, and everything was set in its proper order. That is why it immediately added: "And God saw all the things he had made, and behold, they were very good." 6. Who could worthily praise the precision of the divine Scripture? Look: here too, by saying in a single phrase, "And God saw all the things he had made," it has stopped the mouths of all who would later try to contradict it. "And God saw all the things he had made," it says, "and behold, they were very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day." For with each of the things created it had said, "And God saw that it was good." Now, when everything was finished, and the works of the sixth day had reached their end, and the one who was to enjoy all the things created had been brought into the midst, it says: "And God saw all the things he had made, and behold, they were very good." See how, gathering together all created things by this word "all," it has assigned praise to everything created. It was not content to say "all," but added "that he had made." Nor did it stop there, but said, "and behold, they were good," and "very good," that is, exceedingly good. When the Master, who brought them from nothing into being, calls his creatures good and exceedingly good, who would dare, even if filled with utter madness, to open his mouth and speak against what God has said? Among visible things, not only was light created, but also darkness, opposed to light; not only day, but also night, opposed to day. Among the plants springing from the earth there were not only useful herbs but also deadly ones, and not only fruitful trees but also barren ones. There were animals not only tame but also wild and untamable. Among the creatures brought forth from the waters there were not only fish but also sea monsters and other beasts of the sea. There was land not only inhabited but also uninhabitable, and not only level plains but also mountains and glens. Among the birds there were not only tame ones fit for our food, but also wild and unclean creatures, kites and vultures and many others like them. Among the creatures brought forth from the earth there were not only tame animals, but also snakes, vipers, serpents, lions and leopards. And in the air, again, there were not only seasonable rains and winds, but also hail and snow. Anyone who wanted to go through them one by one would find many things in each part of creation that are thought not merely useful to us but harmful. So that none of those who later looked at creation might be able to find fault with what was made, and say, "Why this? What is this for?" and, "This was made well, but that was not," the holy Scripture, stopping the mouths, so to speak, of all who would try to be ungrateful, says on the sixth day, after the creation of everything: "And God saw all the things he had made, and behold, they were very good." What could equal this for trustworthiness, when the Creator of all himself gives his verdict and says that all things made are good, and very good? So when you see someone, out of his own reasonings, [...]

[...] because nothing was created on it, he counts it worthy of blessing. "And God blessed the seventh day," it says, "and sanctified it." What then? Were the other days not blessed? Yes, it says, but for them, instead of any blessing, it was enough that created things were brought forth on each of them. That is why for those days it did not say "he blessed," but only for the seventh, and having said this it added, "and he sanctified it." What does "and he sanctified it" mean? He set it apart. Then the divine Scripture, teaching us also the reason why it said "and he sanctified it," added: "Because on it he rested from all his works which God had begun to make." Already here, from the very beginning, God gives us a teaching in a veiled way, training us to dedicate the whole of one day in the cycle of the week and set it apart for spiritual work. This is why the Master, having completed all of creation in six days, counted the seventh worthy of blessing and sanctified it, because on it he rested from his works which he had begun to make. But here again I see a vast sea of thoughts opening up before us, and I do not want to pass it by lightly, but to take you too as partners in this spiritual trade. What, then, is the question that arises for us here? Here the divine Scripture says that God rested from his works, yet in the Gospels Christ says: "My Father is working until now, and I am working." Does there not seem, from the wording, to be a contradiction between these statements? Far from it! Nothing in the divine Scripture contradicts anything else. When the Scripture says here that God rested from his works, it teaches us that on the seventh day he ceased from creating and from bringing things out of nothing into being. But when Christ says, "My Father is working until now, and I am working," he is pointing to God's constant providence. He calls it work to hold together the things that have been made, to grant them their continued existence, and to guide them through all time. If this were not so, how could this universe hold together, if the hand from above were not steering and governing all visible things and the human race? And if anyone, with great gratitude, wishes to look closely at each of the things the Creator of all accomplishes every day for our benefit, he will find an abyss of love for mankind. What reasoning, what mind will be able to reach the unspeakable goodness he shows to the human race, making the sun rise on the evil and the good, sending rain on the righteous and the unrighteous, and supplying every other abundance? Perhaps we have stretched our discourse further than we should. But we did not do this idly or at random. We did it so that those who stayed away might learn through you how much they have lost by depriving themselves of spiritual teaching for the sake of bodily food. But so that their discouragement may not grow, show them your brotherly goodwill by passing on to them what we have said, for this is the proof of genuine love. For if, in the case of material foods, those who do this, and the [...]

[Notes:] Four manuscripts read "here." Shortly after, Coislin reads "opening up to us." Coislin reads "from all the works." [?] One Regius manuscript reads "his continued existence"; Coislin and another read "continued existence to it." One Regius manuscript reads "of the dishonor."

[?] This is why today I want to set a simpler teaching before you. When the body has been dried out by fasting, it needs a little relief, so that it can strip again for the contests of the fast with its eagerness at full strength. In the same way the soul needs rest and relief. We should not always be straining, nor always relaxing; we should do now the one and now the other, and so keep the reins on both the condition of the soul and the restless leaps of the flesh. Constant straining at our labours wears us out and makes us collapse, and constant relaxing leads to laziness. Anyone can see that this happens with the soul as well as with the body. That is why balance is good in everything. The God of all teaches us this very thing through the works he created and brought forth to sustain us. So that you may understand, let us test the point on day and night, that is, on light and darkness. He set the day apart for human beings to work, and the darkness of night for rest and a break from their labours, and he fixed measures and limits for each, so that all of us might enjoy the benefit that comes from them. That the light is the time for the day's work, hear David saying: "Man shall go out to his work, and to his labour until evening." He was right to say "until evening." When evening comes the light withdraws, and the darkness that follows puts human nature to sleep. It rests the weary body and relaxes all the senses. Like an excellent nurse, it relieves all the organs of sense from their toils [85] and fatigues by its own care. Then, when the measure of the night is filled, the light arrives and wakes them, and it makes the senses ready, at full strength, to meet the rays of the sun and to take up their usual work with fresh and fervent eagerness. You can see the same thing happening in the turning of the seasons of the year. Spring follows winter, and when summer has come autumn takes its place. In this way the changing temperature of the air gives our bodies rest. They are not destroyed by long freezing in the cold, nor broken down by long heating in the fierce summer. That is why he has us train for winter beforehand in autumn, and for summer in spring. If anyone is willing to look at everything fairly, he will find a certain order and reason in all created things, and nothing made at random or without purpose. One can observe this also in the seeds that spring up from the earth. The earth does not yield everything at the same time, nor is the same time suited to the care of everything that grows from it. The farmer knows the right time, having learned it from the wisdom God gave. He knows when to sow the seed, and when to entrust the young trees and the vine to the bosom of the earth. He knows when to sharpen the sickle for the harvest, when to gather the fruit of the vine and cut the clusters, and at what season to pick the fruit of the olive. And you will find, if you wish [?]

[?] to the gain of our salvation. [?] so that the one who is mad for money may give up his passion and prepare himself for almsgiving and [?] of the poor. People who pursue the affairs of this life would never agree to take up any business without first carefully examining the profit it will bring. It is much more right for us to do the same. We should not simply run through the weeks of the fast, but search our conscience, put our thoughts to the test, and consider what we achieved in this week and what in the other, what progress we have made toward the coming one, and which of our passions we have corrected. If we are not going to manage ourselves in this way and take this much care of our own souls, we will get no benefit from the fast or from the going without food that we endure. That is especially so if we turn out to be worse than those who put so much effort into amassing money. You will find that each of them shows complete vigilance, so as to add something each day to what he had before. He is never satisfied: the more his wealth grows, the more his desire and his effort stretch out. Where the effort is useless, and the wealth often does great damage to the salvation of the soul, they show this much vigilance. How much more must we do the same where the effort brings great benefit, the reward is beyond words, and the gain has no limit? In their case there is great uncertainty on top of all this, because the possession of money is insecure. When death comes, the money stays here and is of no use to the one who gathered it. Worse, while the money stays here, he is compelled to give an account for it, and with great severity. Often, even before death, after much toil and sweat and hardship, a reversal of fortune strikes like a sudden storm, and the man who owned great wealth is all at once poorer than the very poor. You can see this happening every day. In spiritual trade, however, there is never anything of this kind to fear. It stays secure and unshaken, and just where we need it most, it gives us great comfort. 3. So, while we have time, I urge you: let us at least bring the same effort as they do to this spiritual trade. Let us never stop asking ourselves whether we have achieved anything, and whether through great vigilance we have put to flight any of the passions that trouble us. Then, with the assurance that comes from our conscience, we may reap great joy. What is required is not only that we come here every day, hear the same things over and over, and fast through the whole of Lent. Suppose we gain nothing from coming here constantly and hearing these exhortations, and bring nothing useful for our souls out of the season of the fast. Then these things will not only do us no good; they will become grounds for greater condemnation. For after enjoying so much care, we stay the same: the irritable man does not become gentle, the hot-tempered man does not change to mildness, and the [?] … [?] any spiritual work? For if Paul, so great and so eminent, who heard those unspeakable words that no one has known to this day, cried out, saying [?]

[?] that death came to him every day. What nature did not allow, since we are all subject to only one death, the ardour of his will achieved. [?] since he shared the same nature with us, was subject to the same passions, and lived in such difficult times [?], even though the God who loves mankind kept him alive longer for the salvation of others. He was adorned with so many achievements and seemed like an angel on earth. Yet every day he strove to gain more, to stand in battle against the dangers faced for the sake of the truth, to gather spiritual merchandise for himself, and never to stand still. What defence, then, could we have? Not only are we empty of all achievements, we are subject to so many failings, any one of which is enough to drag us down into the very pit of destruction, and we make no effort even to correct them. Often the same person is found with not just one failing but several: he is irritable, self-indulgent, greedy, envious and hot-tempered, and he neither wants to correct these faults nor to take up the works of virtue. What hope of salvation can there be for him? I say these things, and I will not stop saying them, so that each of my hearers may take from what I say the remedy that suits him, and hurry to be rid of the passions that trouble him, recover his health, and make himself fit for the work of virtue. Think of the sick. A doctor may apply his remedies ten thousand times, but the patient may not bear to persist with the treatment. He may often grow impatient after the doctor applies it, throw it off because he cannot bear the pain, and refuse the benefit it brings. No one with any sense would blame the doctor, who has done everything he could. In the same way, here too we prepare the remedy of spiritual teaching and apply it. It is then up to you to bear the pain, to profit from the treatment, and to be rid of the disease and return to true health. In this way you will clearly feel the benefit, and we will have no small comfort when we see those who were sick before return to health so quickly. So I urge each of you: even if you did not do so before, at least from now on make an effort to cut out of your soul the failing you know troubles you more than your other passions. Use devout reasoning like a spiritual knife, and in this way free yourself from the passion. God has given us reasoning that is sufficient, and able, if only we are willing to look a little more closely, to overcome each of the passions that arise in us. [88] That is why the grace of the Spirit has left us the lives and conduct of all the saints written down in the divine Scriptures. We learn that they shared the same nature as us and achieved every kind of virtue, so that we may not grow lazy in practising it. 5. Did the blessed Paul not have the same nature as we do? I burn with love for the man, and that is why I never stop turning back to him. I gaze into his soul as into an original image, and I am amazed at his disdain for the passions, his surpassing courage and the burning fire of his love for God. And I reflect that one man, by choosing to, achieved the whole gathering of the virtues, while each of us is unwilling to achieve even a little. Who [?]

[?] doing everything under the cloak of piety and unsettling the minds of the simpler people. So after saying, "I am more," he goes on to list the achievements of his courage. He says: "in labours far more, in beatings beyond measure, in deaths often." What are you saying? What you say is strange and astonishing. Is it possible to undergo death often? "Yes," he says, "if not in fact, then in intention." He is teaching us that, for the sake of the preaching, he constantly exposed himself to dangers that brought death upon him, but the grace of God kept the athlete safe in the very midst of the dangers, so that his disciples might gain great benefit from him. "In deaths often," he says. "From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I have spent in the deep. On journeys often, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers among false brothers, dangers in cities, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea." Beloved, let us not just skim over these words, for each of them on its own shows us an ocean of trials. He did not simply speak of one journey, but said, "on journeys often." Nor did he speak of one danger from rivers, but of many different dangers, and he endured all of them to an extraordinary degree. [90] And after all this he goes on: "in toil and hardship, in sleepless nights often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness, apart from the other things." 7. See another ocean of trials opening up before us. By saying "apart from the other things," he hinted that what he left out was probably more than what he mentioned. Nor did he stop there. He goes on to tell us of the attacks and the plots he endured: "There is the pressure on me every day, the anxiety for all the churches." This too would be an achievement enough on its own to raise him to the very summit of virtue. "The anxiety," he says, "for all the churches": not for one or two or three, but for all the churches throughout the world. As much of the earth as the sun travels over when it sends out its rays, that much did this blessed man hold in his anxious care. Do you see the breadth of his soul? Do you see the greatness of his mind? And what he adds next overshadows, so to speak, everything he has said: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" Ah, how great was this man's tender love! How great his vigilance, how great his care! What mother is so torn in her heart when her child lies feverish in bed, as this blessed man was weaker than those who were weak in every place, and burned for those who were made to stumble? Notice the force of the expression. He did not say, "Who is made to stumble, and I am not grieved?" He said, "I burn." In this way he shows us how intense his pain was, and all but shows himself on fire and burning within for those who suffer stumbling blocks. I know I have stretched my teaching to great length, though I had decided today to keep it short so that you might get a little relief from the toil of the fast. But somehow I fell upon the wealth of this saint's achievements and was carried along as if by a very powerful flood of water, and so [?] … to set out [?] the spiritual [?]. Before attending to our brothers,

if we had abandoned our exhortation to them in order to keep to the order of the readings, and so neglected them in their sickness, someone might rightly have blamed us for letting the proper moment go by. Now, though, nothing within our power has been left undone. We have given the word of teaching, paid out the silver, and entrusted the seeds to this spiritual soil. So it follows that we should once more set before you what was read from the blessed Moses, so that we may reap the gain from it before we go home. Let us hear what it is. "This," it says, "is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when it came to be, on the day God made heaven and earth, and every green thing of the field before it appeared on the earth, and every plant of the field before it sprang up. For God had not sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to work the earth. But a spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth." Notice again the wisdom of this wonderful prophet, or rather the teaching of the Holy Spirit. He has described to us in detail everything about creation, gone through the works of the six days, and told of the creation of man and of the authority given to him over all visible things. Now he sums everything up again and says: "This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when it came to be." Here it is worth asking why he calls it the book of heaven and earth, when the book contains many other things. It teaches us about many other matters too: about the virtue of the righteous, about the love of God for mankind, about the condescension he showed to the first-formed man and to the whole human race, and about many other things it is not the moment to list now. Do not be surprised, beloved. This is the custom of divine Scripture: it does not always tell us everything in detail. It starts from the most essential points and leaves the rest to be worked out by those who receive its words with a fair-minded ear. So that you may learn that this is how things are, I will make it clear to you from the very passage that has just been read. In the earlier passages divine Scripture taught us the creation of all things in detail. Now it does not mention them all, but says: "This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when it came to be, on the day God made heaven and earth," and so on. 2. Do you see how it turns the whole account toward heaven and earth, and leaves us to infer everything else from them? When it says "heaven and earth," it has summed up everything at once, both what is on earth and what is in heaven. In its account of the created things it did not mention them all in order. It recalled the most essential ones and did not go on to describe everything to us one by one. In the same way it has named the whole book "the book of the generation of heaven and earth," even though the book contains many other things. It leaves us to reason, from the mention of these two, that this book must contain all visible things, both those in heaven and those on earth. "On the day," it says, "God made heaven and earth, and every green thing of the field before it appeared on the earth, and every plant of the field before it sprang up. For God had not sent rain upon the earth, [95] and there was no man to work the earth. A spring [?]"

…let us exercise our discourse on the subject before us, and only then move on to another. For this very thing is contrary to the nature of water, to bear so heavy a body; and again it is contrary to the earth's nature to have its seat on such a foundation. And why are you amazed? If you are willing to examine each of the things that have come into being, you will find that the power of their Maker is boundless, and that by his own [?] all visible things [?]. You can see this happening with fire too. Fire has a consuming energy; it overcomes everything and easily devours every material, stones and wood and bodies and iron. Yet when the Creator gave the command, it did not touch tender, perishable bodies, but kept the young men unharmed in the middle of the furnace. And do not be amazed only that it did not touch their bodies; this irrational element showed a discipline so great that it cannot be put into words. It did not even damage their hair. It surrounded them and held them within, but the substance of the fire, as though carrying out an act of obedience and serving its Master's command, kept those wonderful young men whole and unharmed, and they spent their time in the furnace as fearlessly as if they were walking in a meadow or a garden. And so that no one would think that what was seen was not the action of fire, the loving Master did not bind its energy. He let its burning energy remain, but made his own servants superior to the harm that came from it. And so that those who had thrown them in might also learn how great is the power of the God of the universe, the fire showed its own energy on them: the same fire that wrapped the young men round inside burned up and consumed the men standing outside. Do you see how, whenever the Master wishes, he changes each of the elements into the opposite nature? For he is Creator and Master, and he orders all things according to his own will. Would you like to see the same thing happen with water too? Just as here the fire kept away from those who were inside and forgot its own energy, yet did its proper work on those who were outside, so we shall see the waters drowning some and giving way to others, so that they passed through unharmed. Call to mind now Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and the people of the Hebrews: how the Hebrews, at the Master's command, with the great Moses leading them, crossed the Red Sea as if on dry land, while the Egyptians with Pharaoh, wanting to take the same road after them, were swallowed up and drowned. So the elements, too, know how to show reverence to the Master's servants and to hold back their own force. Let us who are hot-tempered, who are prone to anger, who through sloth are caught by our other passions and betray our own salvation, listen, and let us who have been honored with reason imitate the great obedience of these irrational elements. For if fire, so consuming and so fierce, kept away from bodies so perishable and so tender, what pardon will a man receive if, at his Master's command, he will not rein in his own temper and cast out his anger against his neighbor? What is more, fire, whose nature is to burn, did not display its own energy; but man, the gentle creature, the rational, the reasonable, does what is contrary to his own nature, and through sloth [sinks] into the savagery of wild beasts. [?]

…and these things were said in this way with great condescension and because of our weakness. For the very statement, “God formed man, and breathed into him,” is unworthy of God. But for our sake and because of our weakness the divine Scripture tells these things in this way, condescending to us, so that, having been granted this condescension, we may be able to rise up to that height. “And God formed man,” it says, “taking dust from the earth.” For a start, if we are willing to be sober, no small lesson in humility comes to us from this. For when we consider where our nature had the beginning of its make-up, even if we raise our eyebrows ten thousand times, we are checked and humbled; reckoning up our own substance, we are taught to be modest. This is why God, caring for our salvation, guided the prophet's tongue in this way for our instruction. The divine Scripture had already said, “And God made man; in the image of God he made him,” and had handed over to him rule over all visible things. Then, so that man would not, in ignorance of how his own substance was made, imagine great things of himself and overstep his proper limits, Scripture takes the matter up again and teaches the manner of his making, the beginning of his origin, where the first man was brought forth from and how he was brought forth. For consider: even after this teaching, even after learning that he has the beginning of his make-up from the earth, from which come the seeds and the irrational animals (even if his formation and the incorporeal substance of his soul [gave] him precedence [?], granted through God's love for humankind, for through it he received both rationality and rule over all things), even after learning all this, the one formed from the earth imagined, through the serpent's deceit, that he could be equal to God. If this blessed prophet had been content with the first account, and had not taken it up again and taught us everything with precision, what madness would we not have run aground on?

5. So it is of the greatest value for our instruction in the true philosophy to learn where the make-up of our substance came from in the beginning. “And God formed man,” it says, “taking dust from the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life.” Since he was speaking to people who could not hear otherwise than as we were able to hear, he uses such coarse language. He also wanted to teach us that the Master's love for humankind willed that this being formed from the earth should have the substance of a rational soul as well, through which this living creature was shown to be complete and perfect. “And he breathed into his face,” it says, “the breath of life.” That is, the breathing bestowed a life-giving energy on the one formed from the earth, and this became the make-up of the substance of the soul. Then it goes on: “And man became a living soul.” The one who was formed from the dust, having received the breathing-in, the breath of life, “became,” it says, “a living soul.” What does “a living soul” mean? An active soul, which has the members of the body serving its operations and following its will. But I do not know how we have turned this order upside down. The excess of wickedness has become so great that we force the soul to follow the desires of the flesh. [?]

…let us flee wickedness and do everything not to make ourselves unworthy of those ineffable good things. May we all attain them, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, might and honor to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

“And the Lord God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, and placed there the man whom he had formed.”

1. I see your insatiable longing and great desire, your attentive minds, all of you eager and with wings spread for spiritual teaching. So although I am well aware of my own great poverty, I make every effort to set this poor, plain table before you continually, every day. I am confident that, burning with desire as you are, you will receive what is said with eagerness, since one can see the same thing happen with ordinary food. When the guests have a lively appetite, even if the table is poor and the host is a person of humble means, they eat what is set before them with great pleasure. But when those being entertained have lost their appetite, even if the table is lavish and the dishes are varied, it is no use, since there is no one able to enjoy what has been prepared. Here, however, by God's grace your eagerness is lively and the table is spiritual, so we too speak with great longing, knowing that we are setting these divine teachings before sober ears. So too a farmer, when he finds rich, deep soil, does everything he can for it: he cuts the furrows, drags the plow, pulls up the thorns, and sows his seed generously. Already nourished by good hopes, he waits every day for what he has sown to sprout, trusting in the fertility of the soil, and ready to receive a harvest many times greater than the seed. In the same way we too, seeing your eagerness grow each day, your longing at its height and your zeal increasing, have good hopes for you, and we ourselves hasten with greater eagerness and zeal to contribute what lies within our power, for the building up of your love, for the glory of God, and for the boast of God's Church.

Come then, if you agree, let us take up briefly some of what was said the other day, and then go on in order with what has been read today. We must say what our subject was the other day, and how far we had taken our discourse when we ended the teaching. “And God formed man,” it says, “taking dust from the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” What I said then I will say now, and I will never stop saying it: great and inexpressible is the love of the common Master of all for our race. For he used great condescension for our salvation, and he counted this living creature, man I mean, worthy of great honor, showing by words and deeds that he shows him more care than all visible things. [?] And they say that [souls] pass even into the substance of the most dishonorable irrational animals. [?] What could be worse than this folly? For since their reasoning was darkened, and [?]

…they did not know the true meaning of Scripture. As though their mind's eye had been blinded, they rush over the cliffs in opposite directions, some raising it above its worth, others dragging it down below its worth. For if, because Scripture says, “He breathed into his face,” they are going to give God a mouth, they must also attach hands to him, since it said, “He formed man.” But so that we are not forced, by setting their nonsense before you, to say unfitting things ourselves, come, let us turn away from their folly and their great insanity, and follow the purpose of the divine Scripture, which interprets itself. We need only not fix our attention on the coarseness of the words, but bear in mind that the cause of this coarseness of expression is our own weakness. Human hearing could not have received what was said in any other way unless it had enjoyed so great a condescension. So, bearing in mind both our own weakness and the fact that the things said are about God, let us receive what has been said as it is fitting to speak of God. Let us not drag the Godhead down to bodily shape and the composition of members, but understand everything in a way worthy of God. For the Godhead is simple, uncompounded and without shape. If we set out from our own ideas and also attribute a composition of members to God, we shall slip without noticing into the impiety of the pagans. So when you hear Scripture say, “God formed man,” understand it to have the same force as “Let there be.” And again, when you hear that “he breathed into his face the breath of life,” consider this: that it pleased him, just as he brought the incorporeal powers into being, so also to give this body made of dust a rational soul able to use the members of the body. For once this body had been fashioned at the Master's command, it lay there like an instrument needing someone to move it, or rather like a lyre needing someone who, by his own skill and wisdom, could use the members within it, as if they were strings, to offer up a fitting melody to the Master. “He breathed,” it says, “into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” What does “He breathed the breath of life” mean? It means that he willed and commanded that this body which had been fashioned should have a life-giving power, which became in the creature a living soul, that is, an active one, able to display its own skill through the movement of the members.

3. Notice in this very point the difference between this wonderful rational creature and the creation of the irrational animals. For of them he says, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls,” and at once living, ensouled creatures rose up from the waters; and likewise again on land: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” But with man it was not so. First the body is fashioned from the dust, and after that the life-giving power is given to it, which is the substance of the soul. That is why Moses said of the irrational animals, “Its blood is its soul.” But in the case of man, the soul is an incorporeal and immortal substance, far superior to the body, as superior as the incorporeal must be to the corporeal. But perhaps someone will say: if the soul is more precious than the body, why is the lesser thing fashioned first, and only then the greater and superior one? Do you not see, beloved, that the same thing happened in creation as well? [?]

…[not to keep to what is] set down in Scripture, but to bring in other things from one's own mind, I think brings great danger to those who dare to do it. “And he placed there,” it says, “the man whom…”

4. See at once how much honor he shows him. Having fashioned him outside paradise, he immediately brought him in. He led him into paradise so as to give him, through the facts themselves, a sense of the kindness done to him, and so that he might recognize from what was done the honor being shown to him: “And he placed there the man whom he had formed.” Let us again understand “placed” to mean “commanded him to live there,” so that both the sight of it and his life there might give him great pleasure and stir him to grateful thanksgiving, as he considered how much kindness he had received before he had yet done anything. So do not be put off by the word “placed.” It is always Scripture's custom, for our sake and for our benefit, to use human words. And to learn this, see how earlier, in describing the creation of the stars, it used the same word, saying, “And he placed them in the firmament of heaven.” This was not so that we would think they are fixed into the heaven (for each of them runs its own course, moving from place to place), but to teach that he commanded them to be in the heaven, just as he commanded man to live in paradise.

“And God,” it says, “also made to spring up out of the earth every tree that is beautiful to look at and good for food, and the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of knowing what is known of good and evil.” See here another kind of kindness again, because of the honor shown to the one he had made. Since he wished him to live in paradise, he commanded various trees to spring up from the earth, both able to delight him by the sight of them and suitable for food. “Every tree,” it says, “beautiful to look at,” that is, to behold, “and good for food”: that is, able to gladden him by their appearance and give him great pleasure in eating, and by their number and abundance to bring great joy to the one who was going to enjoy them. For he caused “every tree,” it says, every one you could name, to spring up. Do you see a life free of hardship? Do you see a wonderful life? Man spent his time on earth like an angel. He was clothed in a body, yet he was free of bodily necessities. Like a king adorned with purple robe and diadem and dressed in purple, he luxuriated in his life in paradise, fearlessly enjoying great abundance. “And the tree of life,” it says, “in the middle of paradise, and the tree of knowing what is known of good and evil.” After teaching us that the earth brought forth every tree at the Master's command, beautiful to look at and good for food, it then says, “And the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of knowing what is known of good and evil.” For the loving Master, as Creator, foresaw the harm that would arise from too much freedom as time went on. So he made the tree of life spring up in the middle of paradise, and the tree of knowing what is known of good and evil, since a little later he was going to command him to abstain from it. He did this so that man might know that he enjoyed these things by grace and love for humankind, and that there is a Master and [Creator]. [Notes: Savile and Coislin read “to thanksgiving and gratitude”; Morel [?]. Ibid., Morel: “how he had received kindness.” [?] “in the middle of paradise,” and so three times below; one manuscript [?] “purple” [?]; others “by grace and generosity”; Morel “by grace and love for humankind.” Ibid., Savile: “and that there is a Master and Creator”; one royal manuscript: “and that he is Master and Creator”; Morel: “and he is Master and Creator.”]

“And the Lord God took the man whom he had formed and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and keep it.”

1. Again today, if you wish, we will take up the thread of what was said yesterday and try to weave our spiritual teaching for you from there. For great is the power hidden even in the passage just read, and we ought to go down into its depths and, after examining everything carefully, reap its fruit. For if those who want to find stones in the sea endure so much toil and hardship, giving themselves over to the force of the waters so as to obtain what they seek, much more should we fix our minds intently and, after searching out the depths of what has been said, lay hold of these precious stones. But do not be afraid, beloved, when you hear of depth. For here there is no disorderly rush of waters, but the grace of the Spirit, which lights up our mind, makes it easy for us to find what we seek, and lightens every toil. The finding of those stones has not greatly benefited the one who found them; often it has even harmed him and become the occasion of countless shipwrecks for him. He has not reaped as much joy from the finding as the unpleasantness he has suffered after it, having roused the eyes of the envious against himself and stirred up the greedy to make war on him. So the finding of those stones not only brings no benefit into our life, but even becomes the occasion of many wars. For they are fuel for greed, and kindling a furnace of avarice, they besiege the souls of those they have captured. But with these spiritual and precious stones there is nothing of this kind to fear. The wealth gathered from them is beyond words, and the pleasure is unfading, far surpassing all the joy that comes to people from those other stones. Listen to David saying this: “Your words are more desirable than gold and much precious stone.” Do you see how he brought forward the materials thought most precious, and was not content with this comparison alone, but added “much,” and only then showed us the superiority of the divine words? “More than gold,” it says, “and much precious stone.” Not that the divine words are only that much more desirable; but since he saw that among people these materials alone held the very highest rank, he brought them forward and so showed the superiority, and that the desire for the words of the Spirit is more intense. And so that you may learn that it is always the custom of divine Scripture to compare the benefit of the divine words with things perceived by the senses, and in this way to show their superiority, listen also to what follows. For he went on: “And sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” Here too, it is not that they are only that much sweeter, nor that they can give only that much pleasure; but since he had nothing else among things of the senses to compare with the pleasure of the divine words, he mentioned these and so again gave them the superiority, saying that the pleasure of spiritual teachings is greater. You will find Christ using the same rule in the Gospels. For when he was talking with the disciples, and they wanted to learn the interpretation of the parable of the… [Notes: “We will try”: so some manuscripts and Savile; Morel [?]. [?] who has “the materials.” Savile and six manuscripts: “to compare with the pleasure of the divine words.”]

[?] …: "One God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." Do you see how he gave the name "Lord" to the Son? So what would they say? That the title "Lord" is greater than "God"? See how absurd this is, and how far the blasphemy goes. When someone will not be content to follow the rule of divine Scripture, and wants to give room to his own reasonings instead, he throws his mind into confusion. He brings disputes about words and endless questionings to bear on the sound correctness of doctrine. "And the Lord God took the man whom he had formed," it says, "and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and to guard it." See how much forethought he shows for the man he created. Yesterday blessed Moses taught us that God planted the paradise and placed the man there, which means that God wanted man to make his home there and live in the enjoyment of paradise. Today he shows us once more the unspeakable love God displays toward man, and taking up the account again he says: "And the Lord God took the man whom he had formed, and placed him in the paradise of delight." He did not simply say "in the paradise" but added "of delight," to show us how surpassing was the pleasure man enjoyed from living there. And having said "he placed him in the paradise of delight," he goes on, "to work it and to guard it." This too shows great care. Life there was full of every delight, holding both the pleasure of the sight and the gladness of the enjoyment. So that man might not grow unruly from too much ease (for "idleness has taught every evil," as it says), he commanded him to work it and guard it. "What then?" someone says. "Did paradise need his care?" That is not what I am saying. God wanted him, for the time being, to have some small and moderate concern for guarding and working it. Had he been freed from all labour, he would at once have slipped into sloth, enjoying great ease. As it was, doing a kind of work that was painless and free of hardship, he would be more soberly disposed. Nor were the words "to guard it" added idly. They are a condescension in the wording, so that he might know fully, it says, that he was subject to a Master. That Master had granted him such enjoyment, and along with the enjoyment had entrusted him with guarding it. For God does and arranges everything for our benefit, and along with this he bestows both enjoyment and ease. Out of his surpassing love for us he prepared those ineffable goods for us even before he brought us into being, as he himself says: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." If so, how much more will he provide everything here in abundance! 3. He had conferred so many benefits on the creature he made. First he brought him from nonbeing into being and deigned to form a body from the dust. After that he granted the more important thing, the incorporeal soul, through the inbreathing. Then he commanded paradise to come into being and bade him dwell there. After this, once again, like a father [?] … [?] more]. "which he enjoyed"; b Savile and [?]: [?] "the work; for the work was still free of all toil, and it gave him" (Reg. "and it gave him") "some painless occupation, free of hardship." Reg. [?] "without hardship, and [?]" [?] Clu[?]. d Coislin [?].

[?] … "not only do I command you not to touch it, but I also set a great penalty, so that, kept in check at least by fear, you may keep the commandment I have given you." He acts as a generous master might if he entrusted a great house to someone and, so that his own ownership might remain intact, stipulated that the man pay him some small sum of money. In the same way our loving Master granted him the enjoyment of everything in paradise and ordered him to keep away from one tree alone. He did this so that man might know that he is under a Master, and that it is fitting for him to obey and [?] what that Master commands …

4. Who could admire as it deserves the generosity of the common Master of all? Man had as yet shown nothing, and yet see how great a kindness God thought him worthy of! He did not give him only half of the enjoyment. Nor did he order him to keep away from most things and enjoy the rest. He wanted him to share in everything in paradise, and commanded him to keep away from one tree only. By this act he showed that he did it for no other reason than that man might know who was the author of such great benefits. Along with everything else, consider God's goodness here too: how much honour he shows even to the woman who was about to be formed from the man. She had not yet been brought forth, yet he gives the command as though to both, saying: "You shall not eat of it; and on the day you eat of it, you shall surely die." Thereby he shows from the very beginning that man and woman are one, as Paul also says: "The head of the woman is the man." That is why he speaks as though to both: so that afterwards, when he had formed the woman from him, he might give the man occasion to make known to her what he had been commanded. I know, of course, that this question about the tree is much discussed. Many who speak carelessly try to shift the blame from man to God, and dare to say: "Why did he give him the commandment, knowing that he would transgress it?" and again, "Why did he order the tree to be in paradise?" and much else besides. But we must not seem to leap ahead now and explain these things before we reach the moment of the transgression. We too must wait for blessed Moses' narrative. Then, when we arrive at that place at the proper time, we shall raise this question, if God's grace allows it, and teach your love the true sense of Scripture. In this way you will know the truth of what is written and offer the fitting glory to the Master. You will not pass over the one who sinned and shift the blame onto God, who is blameless. For the present, if you agree, let us go through what comes next in the reading. "And the Lord God said," it says, "It is not good for the man to be alone." See, once again it says "the Lord God," just as before, so that we may fix what is said in our minds and not think human reasonings more authoritative than divine Scripture. "And the Lord God said," it says, "It is not good for the man to be alone." See how the good God does not stop, but adds benefits to benefits. Rich in goodness, he wishes to surround this rational creature with every honour, and along with the honour to grant him an easy life. "For the Lord God said," it says, "It is not good for the [man] …" [?] the enjoyment [?]. [?] and [?] this. [?] after the same words, "of what is written." Morel.

… all the creatures fiercer than these came to him as to a master, in complete submission, and received their names, and Adam feared none of these wild beasts. So let no one find fault with what the Master has made, or sharpen his tongue against the Creator (or rather, against his own head), or speak those useless words: "Why were the wild beasts brought into being?" The giving of the names shows us precisely that all of them, just like the tame animals, acknowledged their servitude and his lordship. The names he gave them remain to this day. God ratified them so that we might have a perpetual reminder of two things. One is the honour man received from the Master of all at the beginning, when these creatures were made subject to him. The other is that we should lay the blame for losing that honour on man himself, who maimed his own authority through sin. "And Adam gave names," it says, "to all the cattle, and to all the birds of the sky, and to all the beasts of the earth." From this, beloved, consider the freedom of his will and the surpassing greatness of his understanding. Do not say that he did not know what was good and what was evil. He was able to give fitting names to the cattle, the birds and the wild beasts without confusing their order. He did not give wild animals the names suited to tame ones, nor assign to tame animals the names that belonged to wild ones, but gave each its fitting name. How then was he not filled with all wisdom and understanding? Reckon from this how great was the power of that inbreathing, and how great the wisdom of the incorporeal soul that the Master granted. He composed this wondrous, rational creature from two substances and joined the incorporeal substance of the soul to the body, like a most excellent craftsman to his instrument. So when you consider the great wisdom of this creature, be amazed at the power of its Creator. When a grateful observer sees the beauty of heaven, it leads him to glorify its Creator. Much more, then, will this rational creature, man, be able to praise without ceasing the one who brought him into being, and offer the Master glory as far as he can, when he reflects on his own formation, on the surpassing honour granted him, on the greatness of the gifts and on the unspeakable benefits. I wanted to go on to what follows as well. But we must stop our teaching here, so that we do not bury the memory of what has already been said under a mass of words. Our aim is not simply to say a great deal. We speak so that you may keep these things fixed in your minds at all times. Then you will not only know for yourselves what the divine Scriptures contain, but will also become teachers to others, able to admonish them as well. So I urge each of you, as you leave here, to go over the memory of what has been said with your neighbour. Let each contribute what he remembers and receive what the other has recalled. [114] Gather everything together in this way, keep the memory of it ringing in your ears, and go home. There, by yourselves, ruminate on these divine teachings. Then, with all your care given to them and your minds occupied with them, you may with ease [?] … [?] and so reads the Latin translator. e Coislin: "neighbour, but let him take [?], [?] to me who sow [?]"; and so also one Colbert manuscript.

… let us set before your love. Just now you heard divine Scripture say: "But for Adam there was not found a helper like him." What does this short phrase mean, "But for Adam"? Why did it add the conjunction? Would it not have been enough to say "for Adam"? We do not search into these things idly, out of needless ambition.
