We interpret everything precisely to train you not to pass over even a short phrase or a single syllable of what is in the divine Scriptures. These are not mere words; they are words of the Holy Spirit, and that is why one can find a great treasure even in a single syllable. So pay careful attention, I beg you. Let no one be sluggish, no one drowsy; all of you, give me alert minds. Let no one's thoughts wander outside, and let no one stand here dragging worldly cares along with him. Let each consider the dignity of this spiritual assembly, and that we are hearing God speak to us through the tongue of the prophets. Let him lend his ear accordingly and keep his mind attentive. Then none of the seeds we sow will fall on rock, or by the road, or among thorns. The whole seed will fall on the good ground (I mean the breadth of your minds), so that it can bear you abundant fruit and multiply what we sow. But now let us see what this joining by the conjunction means for us. "But for Adam," it says, "there was not found a helper like him." Observe the precision of divine Scripture. Having said, "But for Adam there was not found a helper," it did not stop there, but added "like him." By this addition it hints to us why it used the conjunction. I expect that those who can grasp things more sharply already foresee what we are about to say. But since we are teaching everyone in common, we must make what we say clear to all. So come, let us teach you why it spoke as it did. [11?] Bear with me a little. In what was said the other day, as you remember, divine Scripture said, "Let us make him a helper like him," and immediately taught us about the creation of the wild beasts, the reptiles and all the irrational creatures. For it says: "And God formed further out of the earth all the wild beasts and the birds of the sky, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them." And like a master he gave names to them all. According to the wisdom granted him, he assigned its proper name to each kind of beast, bird and irrational creature. This was so that we might know that all those creatures are nevertheless irrational and fall far short of man, even if they perform some service and share in his labours. It was also so that we might not think it was of them that he said, "Let us make him a helper." For even if they help, and have become useful to man in many ways, they are nevertheless irrational. That they help, experience itself shows. Some are suited to carrying our loads, others to working the land. The ox draws the plough, cuts furrows, and serves us in much else for farming. The [donkey?], in turn, is of great service in carrying loads, and many other irrational creatures … [?] Coislin: "let him lend his mind, to keep it attentive." d Savile and Coislin: "a helper like him." ° Coislin: "[?] be hostile to the creature being formed."

… [?] he was unaware of it at the moment of removal, but he was going to recognize afterwards what had happened. God did not want the removal to cause him pain, nor the loss to make him dejected afterwards. So he arranged both matters: he removed the rib painlessly, filled up what was lacking, and did not allow Adam to perceive anything of what happened. "So taking this rib," it says, "the Lord God built it into a woman." The statement is astonishing and far surpasses our reasoning. Indeed, all the works of the Master are of this kind; this is no less a wonder than man's being formed from the dust. And see the condescension of divine Scripture, how many words it uses because of our weakness. "And he took," it says, "one of his ribs." Do not understand what is said in a human way. Put down the coarseness of the expressions to human weakness. For had it not [118] used these words, how could we have learned these ineffable mysteries? So let us not stop at the words alone, but understand everything in a way that befits God, since it concerns God. Expressions like "he took" are used because of our weakness. Notice how here again it follows the same custom as in the case of Adam. There it said once, twice and many times: "And the Lord God took the man whom he had formed," and again, "And the Lord God commanded Adam," and again, "And the Lord God said, Let us make him a helper like him." So now too it says, "And the Lord God built the rib which he took from Adam into a woman," and above, "And the Lord God cast a trance upon Adam." This is so that you may learn that the expressions make no difference between Father and Son. Because the two are of one substance, Scripture uses the names interchangeably. See, then, how in the formation of the woman too it followed the same custom, saying, "And the Lord God built the rib which he took from Adam into a woman." What would the heretics say here? They want to pry into everything, and think they have comprehended the generation of the Creator of all. What word can explain this? What mind can comprehend it? "He took one rib," it says. How did he form the whole creature from this one rib? But why do I ask how he formed the creature from this one rib? Tell me, how did the removal take place? How did Adam not perceive it? You will not be able to answer any of these questions; only he who performed the creation knows. We do not comprehend even these things that lie close at hand, the details of how a creature of our own kind was formed. How great a madness and folly would it be, then, to pry into what concerns the Creator, and to claim to have comprehended things of which not even the incorporeal and divine powers have exact knowledge? They only go on glorifying him unceasingly with fear and trembling. 3. "And the Lord God built," it says, "the rib which he took from Adam into a woman." See the precision of Scripture. It no longer said "formed" but "built," since he took the part from what had already been formed and, as one might say, supplied what was lacking. That is why it says "and he built": he did not make another formation [?] … [?] one [?]; so some manuscripts. b [?] "formed." [?] one "was taking the part." … but woman from man; and man was not created for the sake of the

woman, but woman for the sake of the man." "Yes," someone says, "but these words show that the woman came from the man." Wait, and you will see the exact teaching [120] in what follows. For he says: "Nevertheless, neither is man without woman, nor woman without man." He is teaching us that from then on both man and woman would come into existence through the union of the two. That is why Adam too said: "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." 4. Next, so that you may learn how precise his prophecy was, and how what he said shines forth until now and will until the end of the world, hear also what follows: "She shall be called woman," it says, "because she was taken from her man. For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." Do you see how he opened everything up to us, making each thing clear precisely by his own prophecy? "She shall be called woman," it says, "because she was taken from her man." Again it hints to us at the removal of the rib. Then, showing what was going to happen, it says: "For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh." Tell me, where did it come to him to utter these things? How did he know the future, and that the human race would grow into a multitude? How did he know that there would be a union of man and woman? For intercourse came after the transgression. Until then they lived in paradise like angels. They were not inflamed by desire, not besieged by other passions, not subject to the necessities of nature. They had been created wholly incorruptible and immortal, so that they did not even need clothes to cover them. "For the two were naked," it says, "and were not ashamed." Since sin and disobedience had not yet crept in, they were clothed in glory from above, and that is why they were not ashamed. But after the commandment was transgressed, shame entered, and with it the knowledge of nakedness. So tell me, where did it come to him to utter these things? Is it not clear that he shared in the prophetic gift before the disobedience, and saw all these things with spiritual eyes? I point this out not idly but for two reasons. First, so that you may learn the surpassing love that God showed toward man. From the beginning he granted him an angelic life and conferred countless benefits on him, and along with all the rest thought him worthy of the prophetic gift. Second, so that when you see man's negligence after such great benefits, you may no longer shift the blame to God but lay all of it on man. For he himself became the cause of all his evils, as you will learn later: both of his fall from such great goods and of the condemnation he suffered for his disobedience. For when I consider the condition of life the Master granted him, showing him such abundant benefits, I think first that even before forming him he brought this whole created world into being for his sake, [121] and only then created him, so that once made he might enjoy [?] … Savile and some manuscripts: "having crept in" [ἐπεισελθούσης]; Morel, like others, "having crept in" [ὑπεισελθούσης]. [?] "to utter" [present]; others "to utter" [aorist]. So Savile and many. Others [?] "and having done countless benefits to him." One: "and countless [?] to him [?]" [?] "having entrusted." Boisius: "having laid down." d Coislin: "his creation, this." PATROL. GR. LIII.

Let anyone who is rash with his tongue, and simply blurts out whatever comes into his head, again imitate the blessed prophet and say, "Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door to fence in my lips." And let him never utter words carelessly and at random, but listen to Paul, who says, "Let all clamor and anger and slander and filthy talk and coarse joking be put away from you, along with all malice"; and again, "But only such speech as is good for building up, as the need requires, so that it may give grace to those who hear." And let him shun oaths altogether, heeding the ruling of Christ, which says, "It was said to those of old, You shall not swear falsely; but I say to you, Do not swear at all." So do not tell me, "I swear in a just cause"; for it is not permitted to swear in a just cause or in an unjust one. Let us then keep our mouth pure of oaths, and with all these things let us wall in our tongue, our lips and our mind, so that none of the evil thoughts is either conceived within or brought out through the tongue. Let us also stop up our ears securely, so as not to receive an idle report, as the blessed Moses commanded when he said, "You shall not receive an idle report"; and again the blessed David said, "Whoever slandered his neighbor in secret, him I drove away." Do you see, beloved, how much vigilance we need, how much toil for the sake of virtue? How even one small part, if neglected, brings total danger upon us? That is why in another place too the blessed David cried out, rebuking the one who does this: "You sat and spoke against your brother, and against your mother's son you laid a stumbling block." If we wall in all our members in this way, we shall be able to rouse ourselves to the works of virtue as well: to occupy the tongue with praise and hymns to the God of all; the hearing with listening to and learning the divine oracles; the mind with understanding the spiritual teachings; the hands not with robbery and greed, but with almsgiving and the doing of good deeds; and the feet not with theaters and horse races and harmful spectacles, but with the church and houses of prayer and the tombs of the holy martyrs, so that, reaping the blessing that comes from them, we may make ourselves unconquerable by the snares of the devil. If we are careful in this way and concerned for our own salvation, we shall be able to reap the gain of the fast, escape the devices of the Evil One, and draw down abundant help from above. May we all enjoy it by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, might and honor to the Father together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

On the transgression of the first-formed. "And they were both naked [?], Adam and his wife, and were not ashamed."

1. I wish today, beloved, to open up for you a spiritual treasure, which is shared out and never spent [?]...

Notes: One Regius manuscript reads "let him banish altogether." [?] "let us then keep [our mouth pure] of oaths" [?]... "Homily 16 [?], on the [?] of the statues [?]. "You heard yesterday how" [?]... [?] "on the transgression of the first-formed" are missing in [?], but are found in others. Two read "I wish today too."

...which the Lord God had made. Using this creature as a kind of instrument, through it he lures the guileless and weaker vessel, the woman I mean, into his deceit by means of conversation. "And the serpent," it says, "said to the woman." Consider from this, beloved, how at the beginning none of the wild beasts that had been made was fearsome either to the man or to the woman. They recognized their subjection and man's mastery, and just as the tame animals are now, so then even the wild and untamed ones were docile.

2. But perhaps someone may be puzzled here and want to learn whether the beast also had a share in reason. Not so, God forbid! Rather, always following Scripture, we must reckon that the words were the devil's, who was roused to this deceit by his own envy, and that he used this beast as a suitable instrument, so that by casting in the bait of his deceit he might trip up first the woman, as one always more easily deceived, and then through her the first-formed man as well. So, using this irrational creature to construct his plot, he speaks to the woman through it and says, "Why is it that God said, You shall not eat of every tree of paradise?" Notice here the extreme subtlety of his malice. He brings in what God had not said, in the form of advice and a question, as if he were showing concern for them; for this is what he means to show by saying, "Why is it that God said, You shall not eat of every tree of paradise?" This evil demon is all but saying: Why has he deprived you of so great an enjoyment? Why does he not allow you to share in the good things in paradise, but has granted you the enjoyment of looking at them, yet does not let you partake of them and reap a greater pleasure? "Why is it that God said?" Why, he means, is this so? What is the use of living in paradise when you may not enjoy what is in it, but suffer all the more pain precisely because the sight is there, but the enjoyment that comes from partaking is not? Do you see how he injects his venom through his words, like bait? The woman ought to have perceived, from the very attempt, the extremity of his madness, and that he was deliberately saying what was not so, and supposedly out of concern, in order to find out what God had commanded them and so draw them into transgression. She could have seen through his deceit at once and turned away from any further conversation with him, since he was talking nonsense, and not have brought herself down to such a low level; but she was unwilling. For she ought not to have tolerated conversation with him from the start, but to have talked only with the one for whose sake she had been brought into being, who had become her partner in dignity, and for whose help she had been created. But since, swept away somehow, I know not how, she tolerated the conversation with the serpent and received the deadly words of the devil through it as through an instrument, the right thing would have been for her, learning at once from what he said how contrary his words were, and that the Creator had commanded one thing while this creature was saying another, directly opposed to the Creator, to turn away and flee from any further conversation with him, and to loathe the one who had dared to whet his tongue against the command given to them. But through her great heedlessness she not only did not turn away, but even reveals the whole command to him, sets the pearls before the swine, and...

Notes: Others read "having used." [?] "and following." [?] "of that in paradise." Some manuscripts read "that from the sight." Colbertinus reads "but he another."

...[the enemy of our] salvation introduces counsel contrary to the Master. For when the loving God, out of his great care, had forbidden them to partake, so that they would not become mortal through disobedience, this creature says to the woman, "You will not surely die." What pardon could anyone think the woman deserves for even consenting at all to lend her ears to one who uttered such audacious things? For when God said, "You shall not die" [?]...

Then, not content with contradicting what had been said by [God], he also slanders the Creator as envious, so that in this way he might bring in his deceit and, having tripped up the woman, accomplish his own aim. "You will not surely die," he says. "For God knew that on the day you eat of it [?], your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." See, there is the bait [?]. Having filled the cup with deadly poison, he handed it to the woman; and she, not [?] to see what was worthy [?] (for she could have recognized this from the start, had she wished), but hearing from him that "God forbade you to partake for this reason, because he knew that your eyes would be opened, and you would be like gods, knowing good and evil," was puffed up by the hope of equality with God [?]... when he raises someone to a great height through deception, then [he casts him down] into the deep pit [?]. For having [hoped for] equality with God, she hastened to partake, and from then on she bent her reasoning and her mind in that direction and looked to nothing else but how to drain the cup mixed by the evil demon. For after she had received that deadly poison through the serpent's counsel, so that you may learn that she was eager about these things [?]... "saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasing to the eyes to see, and beautiful to contemplate; and she took of its fruit and ate." Truly, bad company corrupts good morals [?]! For why did she experience nothing of the kind before the counsel of that evil demon? Why did she not consider the tree or see its beauty? Because she feared God's command and the penalty that would follow from partaking. But now, since she had been deceived by this wicked beast into believing that not only would they not suffer this, but would even be equal to God, the hope held out by the promise drove her to partake. And not enduring to remain within her own limits, but thinking the enemy and foe of our salvation more trustworthy than the words of God, she learned by experience itself, not long afterward, how deadly the counsel was, and what calamity would overtake them from partaking. For "seeing," it says, "that the tree was good for food, and pleasing to the eyes to see, and beautiful to contemplate," she reasoned with herself, perhaps as a result of the deceit the devil had brought to her through the serpent: "If the tree is good for food, and can delight [?] the eyes, and there is an indescribable beauty in it, and partaking of it also gives us the highest honor, so that we shall have the same dignity as the Creator, why should we not partake of it?"

4. Do you see how the devil led her away captive, drew her reasoning astray, and induced her to aspire to things above her own dignity, so that, [puffed up] by empty hopes...

Notes: Others read "one who uttered." Others read "might be able." One Regius, Savile and Coislin read "the deliberation." [?] one Colbertinus "of the demon" [?]. Savile and manuscripts read "O woman, why [did you accept] the deadly counsel [?]." [?] "partner in authority." [?] and manuscripts read "such great generosity."

...and who granted [you] a life free of all toil. For were you not allowed to enjoy all the other things in paradise in abundance? Why did you too refuse to keep a command so easy to keep? But when you heard from the woman the promise held out by that deadly counsel, you too were puffed up by the hope and readily shared the food. That is why the penalty falls on both of them, and the outcome of events will teach you not to consider the counsel of the evil demon more trustworthy than God. "And she gave also to her husband, and they ate, and the eyes of the two were opened, and they knew that they were naked."

5. A very great question arises for us here, one which I promised your love [the other day?]. For one might rightly ask what power that tree had, that eating from it opened their eyes, and why it is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And if you wish, bear with me; for I want to speak to you a little about this too, and to teach your love that, if we are willing to receive with good sense what is said in the divine Scripture, nothing of what is said will seem difficult to us. For it was not the eating of the tree that opened their eyes, since they could see even before they ate. But eating from it was the occasion of disobedience and of the transgression of the command God had given, and for this reason they were also stripped of the glory that clothed them, having made themselves unworthy of so great an honor. That is why Scripture, following its own custom, says, "They ate, and their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked." Stripped of the help from above because they transgressed the command, they also become aware of their bodily nakedness, so that through the shame that overtook them they might know exactly into what a fall transgressing the Master's command had brought them. For those who before this had enjoyed such freedom of speech with God, and did not even know that they were naked (indeed they were not naked, for the glory from above covered them better than any garment), after the eating, that is, after transgressing what had been commanded, were brought down to such lowliness as to look for a covering, because they could not bear the shame. For when the transgression of the command came in, it stripped off that new and wondrous garment, the garment of glory, I mean, and of favor from above, with which they had been clothed, and it both made them aware of their nakedness and wrapped them in unspeakable [?] shame. "And they sewed fig leaves," it says, "and made themselves aprons." Consider with me, beloved, from what a height the devil's counsel brought them down into a deep pit. Those who had been clothed in such glory now sew fig leaves and make themselves aprons. This is the profit of the devil's deceit; this is the trick of his counsel: not only does it fail to procure the greater things, it leaves one naked and bereft even of what one has. Since, then, the pretext of eating brought about the disobedience, Scripture therefore says, "And they ate, and their eyes were opened," speaking not of the bodily eyes but of the perception of the mind. For since they transgressed...

Notes: Savile and most read "here." [?] "to stir up." [?] "the transgressing" ... "was caught by the counsel" [?]. [?] one Colbertinus [?] "and ... declare [?]." Coislin reads "they ate and were filled, and were opened."

...the transgression of the command took place at it, and from then on the knowledge of sin came in, and shame; that is why it was so called. For divine Scripture has the custom of naming places after the events that happen in them. That, then, is why divine Scripture named the tree too "of the knowledge of good and evil": because it was over it that the command was either transgressed or kept. For the loving Master, instructing man from the very beginning and from the outset, and wishing to teach him that he has a creator and maker who brought all visible things into being and fashioned him too, wished to show his own lordship over him by this small command. A generous master who has given someone a large and wonderful house to enjoy wants to receive from him not its proper value but some small portion, so that his own ownership may be preserved, and the other may know well that he is not the owner of the property but enjoys its use by favor and generosity. In the same way our Master, having entrusted all visible things to man, and having granted him life in paradise and the enjoyment of everything in it, commands him to abstain from one tree, setting a severe penalty if he should transgress. He does this lest, little by little, man's mind should be drawn astray, so that he thought visible things had come about of themselves and imagined himself something greater than his own dignity; rather, he was to know that he was under a master, and that he shared in the rest because of the master's generosity. But since, being very heedless, he fell along with the woman into this slip by transgressing the command he had been given and tasting the tree, for this reason he named it the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Not because before this he was ignorant of good and evil (he was so far from ignorant that the woman, speaking with the serpent, said, "God said, You shall not eat of it, lest you die"; so she knew that death was the punishment if they transgressed the command), but because after eating it they were both stripped of the glory from above and experienced bodily nakedness. That is why he named it "of the knowledge of good and evil": because it was over it, so to speak, that obedience and disobedience were put to the test. Have you learned why it said, "Their eyes were opened, and they knew that they were naked"? Have you understood why the tree is called "of the knowledge of good and evil"? Consider how full of shame they became afterward, when they had eaten it and transgressed the Master's command: "For they sewed fig leaves and made themselves aprons." See from what glory to what poverty they were brought down! Those who before this lived like angels on earth now devise for themselves a covering of leaves. So great an evil is sin. For it not only separates us from the favor from above, but also brings us down into great shame and lowliness, and, having robbed us of the good things we already possessed, takes away all our freedom of speech. But so as not to make our whole discourse gloomy by dwelling on sin, the sin that overtook man from eating the tree and from disobedience, come, if you please, from the tree...

Notes: Eight manuscripts read "it was so called." Below, one Regius reads "to the [things] of." Almost all read "not [owner] of the creation"; Morel reads "not of the property." "Having granted" before "the enjoyment" was missing in Morel, but [?] ... "they were stripped of grace and glory, and experienced bodily knowledge."

...[that] you may learn the ineffable condescension of God, it is necessary to listen to what has been read. "And they heard," it says, "the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the evening, and Adam and his wife hid from the presence of the Lord in the midst of the trees of paradise." Let us not pass over lightly, beloved, what the divine Scripture says, nor stop short at the words. Let us bear in mind that the words are lowly because of our weakness, and that everything is done in a manner befitting God for the sake of our salvation. For tell me, if we chose to follow the bare sound of the words, and not take what is said in a way befitting God, would not many absurdities follow? Look, let us examine it from the very beginning of the reading: "And they heard," it says, "the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the evening, and they hid." What are you saying? God walks? Shall we fasten feet on him? And shall we conceive nothing lofty from this? God does not walk; God forbid! How could he, who is present everywhere and fills all things? He whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, is he contained in paradise? What person of sense would say this? What, then, does "They heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the evening" mean? He wished to give them such an awareness as would throw them into anguish, and this is indeed what happened. For their awareness was such that when God came near they tried to hide. Sin and transgression had come in, and shame was poured over them. For the incorruptible judge, conscience I mean, rose up against them and cried out with a clear voice, accusing, pointing out, and as it were painting before their eyes the magnitude of their sins. For this is why the loving Master, when he fashioned man from the very beginning and from the outset, placed conscience within him as an unceasing accuser, one that cannot be misled or ever be deceived. Even if someone who has sinned and done some wicked deed could escape the notice of all men, he cannot escape that accuser. He goes about continually with it inside him, troubling, lacerating and scourging him, never resting, but assailing him in the marketplace, in gatherings, at table, as he sleeps and as he rises, demanding a penalty for his offenses, and setting before his eyes the wickedness of his sins and the punishment that follows them. Like an excellent physician, it never stops applying its remedies; even if it sees the patient resisting, it does not withdraw even then, but keeps up its care without ceasing.

2. For this is its work: to keep up a constant reminder, never to let a person forget what he has done, but to set it before his eyes, so that at least in this way it may make us slower to fall into the same sins. For if even with this support, the help that comes from conscience, with this vehement accuser pressing upon us, scourging our conscience, lacerating our heart, and bearing down on us more heavily than any executioner, most of us still do not overcome our sloth, where would we not quickly have run aground if we did not have this help? That is why also [?]...

Notes: [?] "which indeed happened; for they had such [an awareness]." Shortly after, [?] "when [God] came near, they try to hide; for there came in." Shortly after, one Regius reads "was poured upon." Below, others read "cried aloud," and shortly after "of the sins committed." Savile [?] "its work, the unceasing [thing], a reminder." In Morel "the" is missing. Four manuscripts and Savile read "trampling more heavily."

3. Let us hear, then, if you will, what the judge asks, what the condemned answer, what punishments they receive, and what sentence falls on the one who devised so great a plot against them. But I beg you, give me your full attention, and listen to what is said with great fear. When we see an earthly judge sitting on a high tribunal, bringing the condemned into the midst, tearing at them and punishing them, we stand by in great dread, eager to hear what the judge says and what the accused answers. How much more right is it for us to do so now, when we see the Creator of nature exacting justice from those he created! And if you pay close attention, you will see how great a gulf there is between God's love for humankind and the harshness of human beings toward their own kind. "And the Lord God called Adam and said to him, Adam, where are you?" From this very question we should be astonished at God's surpassing love for humankind. Not only did he call, he called in person, something human beings would never consent to do with their own kind, who share the same nature with them. For you know that when they sit on a high tribunal and exact justice from evildoers, they do not deign to reply to them in person, and in this way they show them how much dishonor they have brought on themselves by their wicked deeds. The judge gives his answer, but someone else standing by conveys it from the judge to the accused, and then carries the accused's words back to the judge. This is the custom you will find among judges everywhere. But God does not act so. What does he do? He calls in person: "And the Lord God called Adam," it says, "and said to him, Adam, where are you?" See how much power is stored up in this brief word. The very act of calling shows great and unspeakable love for humankind; and to give an opening, by means of the question, to one who was put to shame and did not dare to open his mouth or loosen his tongue shows great goodness. And saying "Where are you?" carries great force as well as love. For by it he all but hints to him, as if to say: What has happened? I left you in one place, and now I find you in another. I left you clothed in a different glory, and now I have found you naked. Where are you? How did this happen to you? Who brought about such a change in you? What robber and housebreaker has taken all the abundance of your wealth at one stroke and left you in such poverty? Where did your awareness of nakedness come from? Who is to blame for the stripping of that marvelous garment you used to wear? What is this sudden change? What storm so violent has so quickly sunk your whole cargo? What has happened, that you try to hide from the one who showed you so many kindnesses and raised you to such honor? Whom do you fear now, that you are so eager to escape notice? Has an accuser appeared? Have witnesses come forward? Where did such cowardice and fear come from, poured out over you? "I heard your voice," it says, "as you walked in the garden, and I was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid." Where did your knowledge of nakedness come from? Tell me: what is this new and strange thing? Who could ever have an[nounced] [?] this— Morel.: "which any human being… would endure… them." Reg. and others [?]: "nor to part [the mouth]." Savil.: "to move the tongue." [?] Savil. [?]: "to part"; [?] Savil.: "to move the tongue." [?]: "was improvised."

[?] …to display his own love for humankind? Let us hear, then, what the condemned man answers to this. "And Adam said," it says, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me from the tree, and I ate." Pitiable words, full of great lament, and enough to draw the Master to compassion, he who is so gentle and overcomes our offenses with his goodness. For by his great forbearance he had shaken Adam's mind and shown him how great his sin was, and so Adam, all but composing a defense, says to him: "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me from the tree, and I ate." I know, he says, that I have sinned; but the woman whom you gave to be with me, of whom you yourself said, "Let us make for him a helper like him," she has been the cause of my fall. "The woman whom you gave to be with me." When did I ever expect that she would cover me with this shame, she who was created to bring me her comfort? You gave her to me; you brought her to me. And she, moved by I know not what, gave me from the tree, and I ate. These words seem to offer some defense, but they are devoid of any claim to pardon. For what pardon could you deserve, he says, when you forgot my commandments and valued the woman's gift above what I had said? Even if the woman gave it, my commandment and the fear of the penalty were enough to make you shun the eating. Did you not know? Were you unaware? I spoke in advance precisely because I cared for you, so that you would not fall into this. So even if the woman abetted you in transgressing the commandment, you will still not be free of guilt. You should have regarded my commandment as more trustworthy, and not only refused the food yourself but also shown the woman how great the sin was. For you are the head of the woman, and she was brought into being for your sake. But you turned the order upside down: not only did you fail to correct her, you were dragged down along with her. The rest of the body ought to follow the head, but the opposite has happened: the head has followed the rest of the body, and everything has been turned upside down. Therefore, since you have overturned the whole order, here you are now in this condition, you who were before clothed in such glory. Who could lament as it deserves your loss of such great blessings? Yet even though all this has befallen you, ascribe the blame to no one else but yourself and your own negligence; for unless you had been willing, the woman could not have led you into this fall. Did she force you? Did she argue with you? Did she deceive you? She merely gave it, and at once, with such readiness, you were led to eat, without any thought of my commandment. Instead, you supposed that I had deceived you, and that I had not allowed you this food so that you would not attain greater things. Yet how could it be reasonable that you were deceived by me, who had bestowed so many kindnesses on you? And how great a kindness was this very thing, that I warned you beforehand and ordered you to abstain, so that you would not fall into what you have now brought on yourself? But you counted all this as nothing, and see, you have learned by experience how great your sin is. From now on, then, do not ascribe the blame to the woman alone, but also to the negligence
of your own. 4. Since, then, he had spoken sufficiently with Adam, and Adam had confessed his sins, though he thought he was shifting the blame onto the woman, see [?] … Gen. [?]

[?] …does he grant him, nor does he question him as he did the man and the woman. Having received their defenses, he moves against this creature as the one responsible for all the evils. As God, who knows even what is hidden, he knew that this creature had served the devil's plot and the envy the devil showed toward humankind. And so that you may learn his goodness, see how, in their case, although he knew, he said to the one, "Where are you? Who told you that you are naked?" and to the other, "What is this you have done?" But with this wicked beast he does nothing of the kind. What does he do? "And the Lord God said to the serpent, Because you have done this." Do you see the difference? To the woman he said, "What is this you have done?" but to the serpent, "Because you have done this." Because you have worked this evil, he says, because you introduced this ruinous counsel, because you served such envy, because you sharpened such jealousy against the one I created, "Cursed are you above all the cattle and above all the wild beasts of the earth. On your breast and belly you shall go, and earth you shall eat all the days of your life. And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. He shall watch for your head, and you shall watch for his heel." 6. Consider here, I pray you, an order and sequence full of love for humankind. In his questioning he began with the man, then moved on to the woman. And when she named the one who had been the cause of her fall, he came to the serpent, and without deigning to let it answer, he imposes the punishment, and such a punishment that it extends through all time, and by its very appearance serves as a perpetual teacher to all who come after, so that they will no longer accept that ruinous counsel or be deceived by the devil's schemes. But perhaps someone might say: If it was the devil who introduced the counsel, working through the serpent, why did the animal suffer such punishment? This too was the work of God's unspeakable love for humankind. A loving father, when punishing the man who killed his son, breaks the knife or sword with which the murder was committed and cuts it into many pieces. In the same way the good God, since this beast served the devil's villainy like a knife, imposes on it a perpetual punishment, so that from this visible, perceptible creature we may reckon how great a dishonor awaits the devil too. For if this creature, which served merely as an instrument, experienced such wrath, what punishment is he likely to receive? Or rather, Christ has already taught us this in the divine Gospels, saying to those standing on his left, "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." That fire was prepared for him long ago, and that unquenchable fire awaits him. What, then, could be more wretched than those who, by neglecting their own salvation, make themselves liable to the punishment prepared for him? And that the kingdom has been prepared for us, if we choose to display virtue and follow the laws laid down by Christ, hear him say again: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." Do you see? For him the unquenchable fire has been prepared, but for us, if we are not negligent, the kingdom. Bearing this in mind, then, let us take care of our lives, and vice— One Reg. ms.: "counsel." [?]

[?] …in the same way I command you, too, to take on another shape of body, to crawl on the ground, and to have earth as your food, so that you may no longer lift your head upward, but remain in this condition forever, and, unlike all the other beasts, feed on earth. And not only this, but "I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed." Nor will I be content with making you crawl on the ground; I will also make the woman your implacable enemy. And not her alone: I will also make her seed a perpetual foe to your seed. "He shall watch for your head, and you shall watch for his heel." For I will give him such strength that he will forever press on your head, while you lie beneath his feet. See, beloved, through the punishment of this beast, how great a care he shows us that he has for human nature. So much for the visible serpent. But anyone who wishes may afterward follow the sequence of what is written and recognize that if these things were said of the visible serpent, all the more should they be understood of the spiritual serpent. For him, too, God has humbled and brought down beneath our feet, and he has made us press on his head. Or is this not what he means when he says, "Tread upon serpents and scorpions"? Then, so that we would not think this was said of visible beasts, he added, "and upon all the power of the Enemy." Have you seen, from the punishment imposed even on the devil's instrument, God's surpassing love for humankind? Let us come back now, if you will, to the woman. Since the serpent introduced the deception, it was the first to receive punishment; and since it deceived the woman first, and she then dragged the man down with her, he punishes her first, with a punishment that carries a great deal of admonition. "And to the woman he said, I will greatly multiply your pains and your groaning; in pains you shall bear children; and your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you." See the Master's goodness, how much gentleness he shows after so great a transgression. "I will greatly multiply your pains and your groaning." I wanted you, he says, to have a life free of pain and toil, released from all grief and despondency, full of every delight, and, though clothed in a body, to feel none of the body's ills. But since you did not use such ease as you should, and the abundance of good things led you into such ingratitude, I am putting a bridle on you, so that you will not leap out of bounds any further, and I condemn you to pains and groaning. "I will greatly multiply your pains and your groaning; in pains you shall bear children." I will see to it, he says, that the occasion of great joy, the succession of children, begins for you with pain, so that you too may have a perpetual reminder, through your labor pains each time and through the griefs that come with each birth, of how great this sin and disobedience was, and so that as time goes on you will not forget what happened, but will know that the deception was the cause of these things for you. Therefore "I will greatly multiply your pains and your groaning; in pains you shall bear children." Here he alludes to the pangs of childbirth and that great travail which must be endured— [?] some mss. [?]. Many mss.: "I condemn"; Morel.: "I will condemn."

[?] …sharing [?], and for whose sake you were created, you chose to enter into conversation with that wicked beast, the serpent, and to accept its counsel. Therefore from now on I subject you to him and declare him your lord, so that you acknowledge his authority; and since you did not know how to rule, learn to be ruled well. "Your turning shall be to your husband, and he shall rule over you." It is better for you to be under him and live under his authority than to enjoy license and power and be carried over cliffs. For a horse, too, it is more profitable to wear a bridle and walk in good order than to be carried over cliffs without one. Looking to your advantage [?], then, I want your turning to be toward him, and you to follow him as the body follows the head, and to acknowledge his authority gladly. I know you are worn out by the length of what has been said. But rouse yourselves a little, I beg you: let us not leave the trial unfinished, nor go away while the judge is still sitting, for we have now reached the very end. 9. Let us see, then, what he says to the man after the woman, and what punishment he imposes on him too. "And to Adam he said, Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, from that alone, and you ate of it, cursed is the ground in your labors. In pains you shall eat of it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the grass of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the ground from which you were taken; for earth you are, and to earth you shall go." Here too the Master's great and unspeakable care for humanity is shown. But let us listen closely to each of the words. "And to Adam he said, Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, from that alone, and you ate of it." Since you listened to your wife, he says, and ate from the tree, and valued her counsel above my commandment, and would not abstain from this one tree alone, of which I commanded you not to eat (did I order you to abstain from many? Only one, and you would not bear even that, but forgot my commandments and obeyed your wife), therefore you will learn from the facts themselves how great an evil you have done. Let men hear; let women hear: the men, so that they do not put up with women who give wicked counsel; the women, so that they do not give such counsel. For if Adam, who shifted the blame onto his wife, was granted no pardon, what defense could anyone have who says, "Because of my wife I committed this or that sin, I did this or that"? This is why she was placed under your authority and you were declared her lord: so that she would follow you, and the head would not follow the feet. Yet we often see the opposite happen: the man who ought to hold the place of the head does not even hold the place of the feet, while the woman who stands in the place of the feet is set in the place of the head. That is why blessed Paul, the teacher of the world, foreseeing all this, cried out, "For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" But let the husband, too, show great vigilance in shaking off a wife who gives ruinous counsel, and let the woman [keep] ringing in her ears [?]— Some mss.: "your lord."

You will endure these things until the end of your life comes upon you and you are dissolved into that from which you were formed. For even though in my love for humankind I granted you the nature of a body, that body, being from the earth, will be earth again. "For earth you are, and to earth you shall go." It was so that these things would not happen that I said, "Do not touch the tree," and added, "On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die." For I did not want this. But since everything on my part had been done, and you brought these things on yourself, lay the blame on no one else, but ascribe it all to your own negligence. But here another question arises for us, which, if you wish, we will briefly resolve and then bring our sermon to an end. God said, it says, "On the day you eat of it, you shall surely die"; yet they are shown to have lived for many years after the disobedience and the eating. To those who read the text superficially this seems to pose a problem; but if one listens with good sense, what is said is clear and raises no problem for the attentive reader. For even though they lived for many years, nevertheless from the moment they heard "Earth you are, and to earth you shall go," they received the sentence of death and became mortal, and from then on one could say they were dead. Scripture hints at this when it says, "On the day you eat, you shall surely die," meaning: you will receive the sentence that from now on you are mortal. It is just as in human law courts: when someone has been sentenced to be beheaded without fail and is then thrown into prison, even if he remains there a long time, he lives no better than the dead and departed, being dead by the sentence. In the same way these two, from the day they received the sentence of mortality, even though they lived on for a long time, were dead by the sentence. I know that much has been said and that our teaching has run on to great length. So since, by God's grace, we have set everything before you as best we could and brought the reading to its end, let us draw the sermon to a close here. 10. We could have added more and shown that even this punishment that was imposed, becoming mortal, holds a great abyss of love for humankind. But so as not to bury your minds under a great mass of words, come, let us urge you, when you leave here, not to give yourselves up to profitless gatherings or untimely chatter. Instead, reflect by yourselves and with one another, gather up what has been said, and remind yourselves of what the judge answered and what defense the accused made: how the man shifted the blame onto the woman, and she onto the serpent; how he punished the serpent too, imposing on it a perpetual punishment that extends through all the ages, and showing fierce wrath against it, thereby displaying his care for those who had been deceived. For by avenging himself so on the deceiver, he made it clear that the deceit had been practiced on those very dear to him. Then go on to remember the woman's penalty and the punishment imposed on her, or rather the admonition; and so, remembering what was said to Adam, and the— Savil. omits "of your life" [?]. Below, two mss.: "becomes earth again." [?]: "lay"; Morel.: "laid" [?]. Another: "transfer." Below, some mss.: "here…" Morel.: "senseless." Savil.: "Eve, which means life." [?] missing in Morel.

…of blessed Paul, I mean, who says: "For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law." What he means is this: those who lived before the law and those who lived after it will not pay the same penalty. Those who sin after the law has been given will suffer heavier punishment. "All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law": that is, not having the teaching and help of the law makes their punishment milder. "And all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law." These, he says, had the law as their teacher, and even so were not brought to their senses but committed the same sins as the others, so they will also pay a greater penalty. But let us also hear what was read today. "And Adam called the name of his wife Eve," it says, "which means life, because she is the mother of all the living." See how precise the divine Scripture is. It did not pass over even this, but taught us that Adam also gave the woman her name. "For he called the name of his wife Eve," it says, "which means life, because she is the mother of all the living": that is, she is the beginning of all who will come from her, the root and foundation of the generations to follow. Then, after teaching us the name given to the woman, it shows us again the goodness of God, how he does not abandon the creatures he made in such shame and nakedness. "And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife garments of skin," it says, "and clothed them." Think of a tender-hearted father with a noble-born son. The son has been brought up with every care, enjoys every luxury, lives in a splendid home, is dressed in silk, and freely uses his father's property and wealth. Then the father sees him run aground, through all this ease, on the cliff of wickedness. So he strips him of all these things, puts him under his own authority, takes away his fine clothing, and often dresses him in a cheap, servile garment, so that he will not be completely naked and disgraced. In the same way God, who loves humankind, acted toward Adam and Eve. They had made themselves unworthy of that bright and radiant garment which covered them and set them above the needs of the body. So he stripped them of all that glory and of the enjoyment they had shared before they fell this grievous fall. Yet he showed them great compassion. He pitied them for their fall, and saw them covered in great shame and not knowing what to do to keep from being naked and disgraced, and so he made garments of skin for them and clothed them. For such are the devil's schemes: when he finds people who listen to him, he trips them up with a brief pleasure, drags them down into the very depths of wickedness, fills them with every shame and dishonor, and leaves them lying below, a pitiful sight to all who see them. But the guardian of our souls, seeing them in great helplessness, cannot bear to overlook them even so. He devises a covering for them, and by the cheapness of the garment shows them what kind of clothing they had made themselves worthy of.

…as gods, and in the hope of becoming equal to God they dared to eat. This is why God, wishing in turn to shame them, to bring them to a sense of their faults, and to show the magnitude of their disobedience and how utterly they had been deceived, says: "Behold, Adam has become like one of us." This saying carries a great rebuke, able to reach the heart of the transgressor. Was it for this, he says, that you despised my commandment, imagining you would be equal to God? Behold, you have become what you expected! Or rather, not what you expected, but what you deserved to become. "Behold," he says, "Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil." For this is what the deceiver, the devil, told them through the serpent: "Your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." "And now, lest he stretch out his hand and touch the tree of life and eat, and live forever." Notice here, I beg you, the Master's love for humankind. We must examine what is said with great care, so that nothing hidden in these depths escapes us. When God gave Adam the commandment, he ordered him to keep away from nothing but that one tree. Adam dared to eat from it and received the penalty of death, which God had laid down when he gave the commandment, in case he transgressed. But God made no stipulation about the tree of life. For, as I think and as one can see, since God had created him immortal, Adam was free, if he wished, to partake of that tree along with the others, since it could secure him unending life. That is why he receives no commandment about it. 3. If anyone, out of curiosity, wants to ask why it was called the tree of life, let him learn that a human being cannot always follow his own reasoning and scrutinize the works of God with precision. It seemed good to the Master that the human being he had made, while living in paradise, should have a training ground for obedience and disobedience, and so he set up these two trees there: one of life, and the other, so to speak, of death. For eating from it, and transgressing the commandment, brought death upon him. So once he had partaken of it and become mortal, and was from then on subject to the needs of the body, and sin had made its entry, and because of this death had been arranged by the Master for his benefit, God no longer lets Adam stay in paradise but orders him to leave it. He shows that he does this for no other reason than his love for him. To understand this precisely, we must read the very words of the divine Scripture again. "And now," it says, "lest he stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life and eat, and live forever." Since he has already given proof of great lack of self-control in the matter of the commandment already given, and has become mortal, God is saying, it is better that he be thrown out of here, so that he will not dare to touch this tree too, the one that gives unending life, and go on sinning without end. So the expulsion from paradise came from care rather than anger. Such is our Master: when he punishes he shows his care for us no less than when he does us good, and he brings punishment on us to correct us. If he knew that we would not grow worse by sinning unpunished, he would not punish at all. But to check our progress toward worse and to cut off wickedness before it advances, he punishes, true to his own love for humankind.

…as that sword, by turning, blocked every road leading there and could give him constant fear and a constant reminder. 4. "Now Adam knew Eve his wife." Consider when this happened. After the disobedience, after the expulsion from paradise: that is when sexual union begins. Before the disobedience they lived like the angels, and there was no mention anywhere of intercourse. How could there be, when they were not even subject to the needs of the body? So from the beginning, from the very start, virginity held the first place. But when disobedience crept in through carelessness and sin gained entry, virginity flew away, since they had become unworthy of so great a good, and from then on the law of intercourse came in. Consider then, beloved, how great the dignity of virginity is: how lofty and great a thing it is, how it rises above human nature and needs help from above. For those who eagerly choose virginity display, while in the body, the life of the bodiless powers. Listen to Christ speaking to the Sadducees. They raised the question of the resurrection and wanted to find out by asking: "Teacher, there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died without children, and left his wife to his brother. The second also died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother; and likewise the third, and the fourth, and the fifth, and the sixth, and the seventh. In the resurrection, then, whose wife of the seven will she be? For they all had her." What did Christ say to them? "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels." Do you see how those who have taken up the lot of virginity for love of Christ imitate the life of the angels while they walk on earth and are bound up with a body? For the greater and loftier the thing is, the greater, indeed far greater, are the crowns, the rewards, and the promised blessings for those who, together with virginity, also show the practice of good works. "Now Adam," it says, "knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain." Since sin had come in through the disobedience, and the sentence had made them mortal, God, so rich in resources, in his wisdom arranged for the continuance of the human race and allowed the race to grow through intercourse. "And she said, 'I have acquired a man through God.'" See how the penalty she received made the woman more sensible. She credits the child she bore not to nature but to God, and so shows her gratitude. Do you see how the punishment became an occasion of correction for them? "For I have acquired a man," she says, "through God." It was not nature, she says, that [gave] me the child [?]

…from his own occupation, and he offered the sacrifice from his flock. "For he too brought," it says, "some of the firstborn of his sheep and of their fat portions." Consider how it hints to us at the devotion of his heart toward God. He did not simply offer from his sheep, but "from the firstborn", that is, from the valuable, choice ones. Then, from these very firstborn, again the more valuable: "and from their fat portions," it says, the richest and most valuable. In Cain's case Scripture mentions nothing of the kind, only that he offered "a sacrifice from the fruits of the earth": whatever came to hand, as one might say, showing no zeal or care. I say it again, and I will not stop saying it: God accepts what we bring not because he needs anything from us, but because he wants our gratitude to be shown through these things too. Someone who brings an offering to God, and brings it from his own goods, ought to consider the gulf between the two natures, and that a human being is counted worthy of such honor. He ought therefore to show what he can on his own part and offer the more valuable things. But notice, I beg you, beloved: Cain had from this the means to perceive what was needed, and so he is rightly called to account for betraying his own salvation through carelessness. For neither did Abel have anyone to teach him, nor did Cain have anyone to advise and counsel him. Each was moved by the teaching of conscience and by the wisdom granted from above to the human race, and set out to make this kind of offering. But the difference in disposition, and the carelessness of the one's choice, made the offering of the one acceptable and that of the other rejected. "And God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts." See how what is said in the Gospel is fulfilled here: "The first will be last, and the last first." For look: Cain had the advantage of being the firstborn and was apparently the first to offer, yet because he did not offer as he should, he was judged inferior to his brother. Both of them offered, the divine Scripture says, "and God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts." What does "looked upon" mean? It means he accepted, he approved the disposition, he crowned the choice, he was pleased, as one might say, with what was done. For even when we speak about God and dare to open our mouths about that pure nature, being human we could not understand these things in any other way than through our human language. But consider the remarkable thing. "God looked," it says, "upon Abel and upon his gifts." It called the offering of the sheep "gifts" because of the value, the choiceness, the spotlessness of what was offered. So he looked upon Abel, because he made his offering with a sound disposition, and upon the gifts that were offered, not only because they were without blemish but because they appeared valuable in every respect: from the disposition of the one who offered them, from their being firstborn, and the choicest of these, and from their fat portions, and the best of those. "And God looked," it says, "upon Abel and upon his gifts; but upon Cain and his sacrifices he did not look." Since Abel offered with an upright disposition and a sincere mind, "God looked," it says, that is, he accepted, he was pleased, he approved. And it called what was offered "gifts", by this too honoring the disposition of the one who offered them. "But upon Cain and his sacrifices he did not look." Consider Scripture's [?]

…why did you not see for yourself what was required? Were you making an offering to a human being, who could be deceived? Did you not know that I had no need of the things offered, but of the sound disposition of those who offer them? "Why have you become very sad, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?" Coming up with the thought of making an offering was praiseworthy, but failing to divide rightly is what caused the offering to be rejected. Someone making an offering to God ought to have shown great care in the dividing, and to have made as great a distinction in the dividing as the gulf between the one who receives and the one who offers. But you thought of none of this and simply brought whatever came to hand. That is why it could not be accepted. Your disposition when you made the offering took no account of the gulf, and so caused the sacrifice you offered to be rejected; in the same way your brother's disposition, being upright and showing great care in the dividing, made his gifts acceptable. Even so I do not exact punishment for the fault. I only point out the sin and give you advice; if you are willing to accept it, you will correct the sin and will not throw yourself into worse evils. What then? You have sinned, and sinned greatly, but I do not punish you for the sin. For I love humankind, and "I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he turn and live." Since you have sinned, then, "be still": bring calm to your thoughts and free yourself from the violent waves that besiege your mind. Calm the turmoil. Do not add another, worse sin to the one before, and do not plot anything beyond remedy. Do not hand yourself over as a captive to the evil demon. "You have sinned; be still." God knew from the start the attack that was going to be made on the brother, and with these words he tries to forestall it. Being God, he knows even the secret places of the mind, and he knew the stirrings of Cain's heart. So by his long exhortation and the condescension of his words he applies a remedy suited to him, doing everything on his own part, even though Cain pushed the medicine away and hurled himself into the pit of fratricide. "You have sinned; be still." Do not think, he says, that because I turned away from your sacrifice on account of your crooked disposition, and accepted your brother's gift on account of his sound choice, I am depriving you of your precedence and casting you out of the rank of the firstborn. Be still. For even if he has been counted worthy of honor from me and his gifts have become acceptable, "his recourse is to you, and you will rule over him." So even after this sin I allow you to keep the privileges of the firstborn, and I command that he be under your authority and under your rule. See the Master's love for humankind, how by these words he wants to calm Cain's anger and frenzy and cut off his impulse. Seeing the stirrings of his mind and knowing the savagery of his murderous disposition, he wants already to soften his thinking beforehand and bring calm to his mind by subjecting his brother to him and not curtailing his authority. But even after such great care and so many remedies, the…

…knowing what stirs in the depths of the mind, he exhorts, he counsels, he tries to hold him back beforehand from the evil attempt. Yet he does not impose compulsion. Having applied the appropriate remedies, he leaves everything to rest on the will of the sick man. This, then, is what happened now with Cain. See into what frenzy he ran aground after such great care. When he recognized his sin, he ought from then on to have busied himself with correcting it. But like a drunken man he added another sore to his earlier passion and wound, and did not accept the cure brought to him with such great care. Instead, eager to carry out the murder he had in mind, he begins with deceit and cunning and tricks his brother with misleading words. So beastly does a human being become when he turns aside to wickedness. For great and precious as this rational creature is, especially when he sets out to practice virtue, when he turns to wickedness he imitates the cruelty of savage beasts. Indeed, once this gentle and rational creature has fallen into their wildness, he far surpasses their ferocity. Let us see, then, what happens here. "And Cain said to Abel his brother," it says, "'Let us go out into the field.'" The words are a brother's, but the intent is murderous. What are you doing, Cain? Do you not know whom you are talking to? Do you not realize that you are speaking with your brother? Do you not reckon that he was born of the same birth pangs as you? Do you not take to heart how abominable this attempt is? Do you not fear the Judge who cannot be deceived? Do you not shudder at the thought of this outrage? Why are you dragging your brother into the field and taking him out of his father's arms? Why are you leaving him without his father's [protection]? What is this strange thing, that now you drag your brother into the field and attempt what you never did before, putting forward brotherly goodwill under the pretense of kindness while you plan to treat him as an enemy? What madness is this? What frenzy? Granted, your reason is blinded and you take no account of brotherly affection, and you do not even recognize nature itself. But why have you become so hostile toward someone who has done you no wrong? What charge do you have against your parents, that you plan to plunge them into such grief, to become the author of this dreadful drama, and to be the first to show them this violent death? Is this how you repay them for raising you? What scheme of the devil spurred you on to this deed? Can you say that the goodwill of the common Master of all toward him made him exalt himself over you? Did not God, anticipating this murderous disposition of yours, subject him to you, put him under your authority, and say, "His recourse is to you, and you will rule over him"? For we must take this as referring to the brother's subjection. There are some who say that God was speaking to him about the sacrifice he had offered, something like this: "Its recourse is to you" (that is, the gift's), "and you will rule over it," meaning, you will enjoy it yourself. So I have stated both views and leave them to your understanding, so that you may accept whichever seems to you more consistent. For my part, I think this was said about the brother. "And it came to pass,

…to be led to confess his offense, and perhaps be able to obtain some pardon and loving-kindness: "Where is Abel your brother?" What then does this ungrateful, unfeeling man do, this reckless and shameless man? He ought to have realized that God was not asking out of ignorance. He was asking for Cain's own confession, and teaching us never to condemn our brothers before there is proof. Cain ought to have recognized the Master's counsel: God had tried to check this attempt of his, and because He knew the movement of his mind even before the deed, He had used preventive remedies. Having considered all this, Cain ought to have stopped his madness there, told what had happened, shown the physician the wound, and accepted the remedies He offered. Instead he makes the wound worse and the spreading of the sores more severe. "And he said," it says, "I do not know." See how shameless the answer is! Are you talking to a man, tell me [?], that you could deceive Him? Do you not know, wretched and miserable man, who it is that is speaking with you? Do you not realize that He asks out of His great goodness? He wants to find some occasion to show His own loving-kindness. And once He has done everything on His side, you will have no defense left, since you will have made yourself liable to punishment. "And he said, I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" Consider here how the conscience accuses him. Driven, so to speak, by his conscience, he did not stop at saying "I do not know" but added "Am I my brother's keeper?", all but convicting himself. And yet if you had done everything properly, according to the law of nature, you ought to have been the keeper of your brother's safety. Nature enjoined this: those who were born of the same womb ought to be each other's keepers. But if you did not want this, and had no wish to be your brother's keeper, why did you also become his slayer? Why did you murder one who had done you no wrong, and imagine you had no one to convict you? Wait, and you will see the very man you killed become your accuser. Lying dead, he will accuse you, the one who lives and walks about, with a loud voice. "And God said, What have you done?" This phrase too carries great force. Why, He says, have you committed this? Why did you do this unholy outrage, this foul attempt, this unpardonable act, this unbearable madness? Why this new and strange murder, the first ever brought into human life, and by your right hand? Why have you done this great and fearful thing, a sin that could not be exceeded? "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth." Am I a man, He says, who hears only the voice the tongue utters? I am God, able to hear even blood crying out as it lies somewhere down on the ground. See how far the voice of this blood flies. It rises from earth to heaven, passes beyond the heaven of heaven and the higher powers, stands beside the royal throne itself, laments your bloodshed, and accuses your unholy deed. "The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth." Was it against a stranger and an alien, He says, that you committed this crime? No [?], it was against your own brother, who had done you no wrong. But perhaps My goodwill toward him gave birth to this murder, and since you could not fight against Me, you poured out your uncontrollable rage on him. For this reason I will bring on you a punishment such that neither your daring deed nor the punishment it brought on you will ever be forgotten. What happens to you will be a lesson in sobriety for everyone who comes after. [Notes: a. One manuscript [?] reads "demanding a defense." b. Five manuscripts read "murderer." Shortly after, one reads "to have the proof." c. Savile and three manuscripts read "crying out against." d. [?] One reads "the good condition of the limbs."]

[?]… For such, he says, is the sin I have committed that it cannot receive pardon. See, it says, he confessed, and confessed very precisely. But it gains him nothing, beloved, because the confession comes too late. He should have done this at the proper time, when he could still have obtained the judge's loving-kindness. Remember now what I said a little while ago. On that fearful day, before that incorruptible tribunal, each of us will repent of our sins as we see those fearful punishments and inexorable reckonings before our eyes. But it will be of no benefit, because the time will have betrayed us. Repentance has its season, and ineffable power, before the punishment is inflicted. So I urge you: while this marvelous remedy can still work, let us reap its benefit. While we are still in the present life, let us apply the healing of repentance to ourselves. Let us learn well that it will do us no good to repent then, after the theater has been emptied and the time for the contests has been taken away.

4. But let us return to our subject. When the Master asked him, "Where is Abel your brother?", that was when he should have confessed his offense, fallen down, pleaded, and asked for pardon. At that time he rejected the healing. Now, after the sentence, after everything has come to an end, after the blood of the one lying dead has accused him with a loud voice, he confesses, and gains nothing by it. That is why the prophet said, "The righteous man is his own accuser in his opening speech." So this man too, if he had confessed before the Master reproved him, might perhaps have been granted some loving-kindness, because the Master's goodness is boundless. No sin, however great, overcomes His loving-kindness, if we show repentance at the proper time and ask for pardon. "And Cain said, My guilt is too great for me to be forgiven." The confession is full enough, but it comes too late. "And he said, If you cast me out today from the face of the earth, I shall be hidden [?] from your face, and I shall be groaning and trembling on the earth; and it will be that everyone who finds me will kill me." See how pitiable the words are. Yet because they come too late, and the time has betrayed them, they have no power. "And he said, If you cast me out today from the face of the earth, I shall be hidden [?] from your face, and I shall be groaning and trembling on the earth; and it will be that everyone who finds me will kill me." If you have made me accursed on the earth, he says, and you yourself have turned away from me and handed me over to such punishment that I groan and tremble, then nothing prevents anyone at all from killing a man in this state, stripped of your support. I will be easy prey, he says, for anyone who wants to kill me. I have no strength to resist, since I carry about limbs that are unstrung and shaken on every side. And because everyone knows I have been stripped of your support, anyone who wants to kill me will be emboldened to rush at me. What then does the loving and good Master do? "And the Lord God said to him, Not so." Do not think, He says, that things will happen this way. No one who wants to kill you is permitted to do it. Instead, by prolonging your life I will make your pain greater, and I will leave you behind as a lesson for the generations to come, so that the sight of you…

…which he committed. Fifth, he murdered his brother, who was born of the same womb as he. Sixth, he was the first to introduce murder into the world. Seventh, when God questioned him, he dared to lie. So whoever tries to kill you, He says, will make himself liable to seven punishments. Do not fear this, then. See, I am setting a sign on you, so that no one who finds you will fail to recognize you. The prolonging [?] of your whole life will benefit the generations that follow. What you did alone, with no one present, everyone will learn when they see you groaning and trembling. Your bodily trembling all but cries out, speaking to everyone and saying: Let no one else dare such things as I did, so that he may not receive such a punishment.

6. Now that we have heard these things, beloved, let us not just pass over what has been said. Let us not consider only whether we enjoy a spiritual table when we gather here each day, for merely hearing does no good without obedience shown in deeds. Let us reflect on how Cain drove himself into this grievous and unpardonable sin. He envied one who had never once tried to wrong him, and out of that envy he dared to take such revenge, or rather to commit such a murder, against his own brother. So let us flee not from suffering harm, but rather from doing harm to others. The one who wants to harm his neighbor is the one who truly suffers harm. To learn that this is true, look here: who suffered harm, the killer or the one killed? Clearly the killer. Why? Because the one killed is praised on everyone's lips to this day. He is proclaimed and crowned as the first martyr of the truth, as the blessed Paul also says: "Though he died, Abel still speaks." The killer, though, lived a more pitiable life at the time than anyone else, and since then he has been assailed by everyone's accusations. Divine Scripture holds him up as an example of one abominable to God and accursed. That is what happens in the present life, which passes away along with us. But in the age to come each of them must meet his lot and receive from the just Judge what fits his own deeds. What words could describe that, whether the good or the opposite? There are none, neither for the good things nor for the painful ones. The one will be welcomed by the kingdom of heaven, the eternal dwellings, the choirs of patriarchs, prophets and apostles, and the company of all the saints, to reign for endless ages with Christ Jesus the King, the only-begotten Son of God and God.
