The other will be taken over by the fire of Gehenna and all the other undying torments, punished for unending ages together with all who have done things like him. This holds especially for those who came after him and were caught by the most shameful passions, since the common Master pronounces a greater punishment on them. Listen to the blessed Paul saying: "All who sinned without the law will also perish without the law"; that is, they will undergo a lighter… [Notes: a. [?] reads "which he committed, and the madness against his own brother." The same [?] reads "that he was the first to introduce murder and violent death, seventh." b. Seven manuscripts read "speaking and saying." c. The Colbert manuscript [?] reads: "so that he may not receive such a punishment. Let us therefore also give thanks to our good and loving God, to whom belong glory, might, honor and worship, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen." [?] are lacking. d. [?] One reads "[?] of the saints."]

…oblivion, but also to teach all who come after to flee completely from this daring deed? Come then, let us take up what follows, and see what this blessed prophet tells us today as well, as the working of the Spirit resounds in him. When Cain had received his sentence, "He went out," it says, "from the presence of God." What does "He went out from the presence of God" mean? It means he was stripped of God's protection because of that abominable deed. "And he dwelt in the land of Nod, opposite Eden." Scripture also tells us the place where he then made his home. It teaches that he too lived not far from paradise, so that, living opposite it, he would always be reminded of what had befallen his father because of the transgression. He would also be reminded of how great his own daring deed was, and of the heavy punishment he received because not even his father's punishment had brought him to his senses. The very place where he lived was an unceasing reminder of tossing and trembling, not only to him but also to the generations after him. For the name Nod is a Hebrew word that means "tossing." So God settled him there, so that even the place would accuse him continually, as though the accusation were written on a bronze pillar. Then it says: "And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch." Now that they had become mortal, they naturally devoted all their efforts to continuing their line through children. But perhaps someone might say: How did Cain get a wife, when Scripture nowhere mentions another woman? Do not be surprised at this, beloved. Up to this point divine Scripture nowhere gives an exact list of the women. It avoids what is superfluous and mentions only some of the men, and not even all of them. It tells the story more briefly, saying, "So-and-so begot sons and daughters, and died." So it is likely that after Cain and Abel, Eve also bore a daughter, whom Cain took as his wife. Since it was the beginning and the human race had to increase, they were permitted to unite even with their sisters. That is why Scripture leaves us to work out the consequence for ourselves and tells only this: "And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and he was building a city, named after his son Enoch." See how little by little they begin to contrive things. Because they had become mortal, they wanted their memory to be preserved forever, both through their offspring and through naming places after their children. One could rightly say that all these things are reminders of their sins and of their fall from that glory. While Adam and Eve were in that glory they needed none of these things, but stood above them all. "And to Enoch was born Irad," it says, "and Irad begot Mehujael, and Mehujael begot Methushael, and Methushael begot Lamech." You see how this blessed man ran through the genealogies. He mentions only the men and nowhere recalls the women. Just as with Cain he said "He knew his wife" without explaining or telling us where he got the wife, so here again he says: "And Lamech took for himself two… [Notes: Some manuscripts read "what he had dared, and that because of the magnitude of what he had dared he received such a punishment." Savile conjectures that it should read "what he had dared, and of the [?] punishment which he received." [?] One reads "they made."]

…and he came to realize that denial had brought Cain a harsher punishment. So he called his wives and, with no one compelling or convicting him, confessed his sins with his own tongue. He compared what he had done with what Cain had committed and fixed his own punishment. Have you seen the Master's care? Even His punishments become occasions for loving-kindness. His loving-kindness does not stop at the one who receives the punishment. He makes the remedy useful to everyone else as well, if they are willing to reap its benefit. Tell me, what else could have moved Lamech to such a confession, unless the memory of what had befallen Cain was constantly shaking his mind? "He said," it says, "Hear my voice, and give ear to my words." See how he sets up a tribunal against himself and makes his appeal to them, so that they will not take what he says lightly. Saying "Hear my voice, and give ear to my words" means this: Focus your minds, he says, and pay careful attention to what I am about to say. I am not going to talk to you about ordinary matters. I will declare to you hidden things, which no one else knows except me and that sleepless Eye. Because I fear that Eye, I hasten and press to make plain to you what I have done, and to how many punishments my unholy deeds have made me liable. "For I have killed a man to my wounding, and a young man to my bruising. For vengeance is taken sevenfold for Cain, but for Lamech seventy times seven." This is a great saying, a very great one, and it shows the man's great candor. He does not only confess what happened and bring into the open the murders he committed. By comparing what Cain did with what he himself did, he also imposes the penalty on himself. What pardon would a man deserve, he says, who was not brought to his senses even by another's punishment? The memory still rang in his ears, and on top of it all he committed a double murder. "For I have killed a man," he says, "to my wounding, and a young man to my bruising." I have not wronged those I killed so much, he says, as myself. I have thrown myself into inescapable punishment by committing sins beyond pardon. If Cain became liable to seven punishments for one murder, I would justly undergo seventy times seven punishments. Why, and for what reason? Cain did commit murder, and the murder of a brother. Yet he had never before seen anyone do such a thing, nor had he watched another man punished for the deed and suffer such great wrath. But both these things increase my punishments [?]. I had before my eyes what Cain dared to do, and I saw how incurable the punishment was, and even so I did not come to my senses. Therefore, even if I undergo his punishments seventy times seven times over, I still will not pay the penalty I deserve.

3. You see, beloved, how God created our will free? Just as we are tripped up when we grow careless, so when we choose to be sober we see what is needed. Tell me, who urged this man to such a confession? No one else but conscience [?]… [?] compunction, confession of the fault, intense perseverance;

and He not only grants healing of the wounds [?: "the mother, by the name she gave, says: 'raised up'"] but also shows them clean of their sins [?: "for God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom (Cain) killed"], and He makes righteous the one who was weighed down before by countless burdens of sins. O the greatness of His loving-kindness! O His surpassing goodness! When sinners confess their sins, ask for pardon, and give assurance for the future, He at once declares them righteous. To learn this clearly, listen to the prophet saying: "Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified." He did not simply say "Tell your iniquities"; he added "first." That is: do not wait for the one who will convict you, do not wait for the accuser. Get ahead of him yourself and seize the opening speech, so that you may silence the accuser's tongue.

4. Have you seen the judge's loving-kindness? In human courts, when someone agrees to do this and confesses what he has done before the proofs are brought, he may perhaps escape the tortures and the punishments heaped one on another, and even that only if he happens to find a mild judge. Even so, he certainly receives the sentence that leads to death. But with our loving God, the physician of our souls, the goodness is ineffable and the generosity surpasses all words. Our adversary, I mean the devil, will stand facing us on that day. Suppose we get ahead of him. Suppose that already in the present life, before we enter the court, we confess what we have done, seize the opening speech, and become our own accusers. Then we will call forth such loving-kindness from the Master that He not only grants us freedom from our sins but also counts us among the righteous. This Lamech had no law given that could teach him, and he heard neither prophets nor any other exhortation. Yet through the tribunal implanted in nature he became aware of what he had dared, brought what he had done into the open, and condemned himself. If he did that, how can we obtain any defense if we do not eagerly show our wounds to the Master and receive healing for them from Him? If we do not do this now, in the season of fasting, when our thoughts are so calm and all luxury is out of the way, when will we ever come to recognize what we have done? So I urge you to be sober and watchful at all times, and to spend the whole of the present life on this, so that by our perseverance we may escape that unbearable punishment and stay clear of the fire of Gehenna. We must do this with greater zeal especially now, when the season of fasting lets you enjoy fuller and more continuous teaching. "And Adam knew Eve his wife," it says, "and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth, saying: For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed." Divine Scripture brought the genealogy down to Lamech and stopped there. Then it returned to Adam and his wife and says: "And Adam knew his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth, saying: For God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed." She bore a son, it says, and called his name Seth; and not content… [Notes: a. One [manuscript] and the Colbert [?] in [?] read "to give assurance for the future." b. Others read "leading to death." Patrologia Graeca 53.]

6. But now that we have begun the story, let us not stretch the teaching out to great length. Like this blessed prophet, let us too bring our discourse to a close here, and keep the interpretation of what follows for next time, if God permits. For the present, though, I want to urge your love to gain something more from what we say. Examine yourselves every day: what did you gain from this teaching, and what from that one? Do not take in what we say only as far as your ears, but store it up in your minds, and make the memory of it firm by constant meditation. For I want you not only to be sufficient for yourselves but also to become teachers of others, so that you can admonish others too. And do this not by words alone; train your neighbours by your deeds as well, toward the achievement of virtue. Just consider: if you were willing to come here every day, reap some small portion, and correct the passions that trouble you, how you would arrive little by little at the very summit of virtue! For we never stop discoursing each day and sounding in your ears the best way of life, so that you may cut out these deadly passions, I mean anger, malice and envy. Once these are removed, the mania for money will be corrected more easily. And once the mania for money has ceased, wicked thoughts and shameful imaginings will be checked with greater freedom. For the love of money is the root of all evils. So if we cut out the root and pull it up from its very depths, we shall get the better of the branches more easily. The citadel of evils, the crown of sins, so to speak, is the madness for money. If we chose to overcome it, nothing would prevent us from escaping this mania too, and with it pulling up and cutting out all the deadly passions. And do not think it something great and burdensome to despise money. I think of how many people, out of empty and useless ambition, have poured out many talents of gold to no purpose except to win the acclaim of market loafers and often worthless people. That acclaim ends before evening. Often it does not even last until evening, but before the day is out it surrounds them with countless evils. [Others, in the grip of the Greek error, are dazzled by human glory and set great store by it. They throw away everything they have, leave themselves only a single cloak and a staff, and spend their whole life that way, choosing to endure all that toil and hardship for the sake of human acclaim.] When I reckon all this up, I do not know what defence or pardon we shall have. We will not bring ourselves to give up even a small fraction of what they give up, though it is for the commandment God has given and for that glory which is immortal and has no end. We become worse even than they are, and do not even consider how great the difference is: that they give up so much for the useless acclaim of their fellow human beings … [?]

Homily 21. "This is the book of the generation of human beings. On the day God made Adam, he made him in the image of God. Male and female he made them, and he named them Adam, on the day he made them." 1. Great and inexpressible, beloved, is the treasure in what has just been read. I know that many look at the list of names, attend only superficially to what was read, and think the passage contains nothing more than mere names. But I urge all of you not to run carelessly past what lies in the divine Scriptures. Nothing written there lacks a great wealth of meaning. The blessed prophets set these things down under the prompting of the divine Spirit, and so these writings, written by the Spirit, hold a great hidden treasure. Do not be surprised that I now promise to show you a great hidden wealth of meaning in a list of names. There is not a syllable, not a single stroke in Scripture, in whose depths a great treasure is not stored up. That is why we must approach the divine oracles guided by grace from above, having received illumination from the Holy Spirit. To understand what is written, divine Scripture needs not human wisdom but the revelation of the Spirit, so that we may learn the true sense of what it contains and draw much benefit from it. In the affairs of this life, documents drawn up by people have often been worn away by time, yet they have still kept great force from the date set at the head of the document, even from a single syllable. How much more can this be found in the divine Scriptures, composed by the Holy Spirit! Only let us be sober and not run carelessly past. Let us strain our minds and examine everything with precision, and not be worse than those who show so much zeal over the things of sense. Those who dig earth that holds metal do not stop at the surface. They go down to a great depth, and when they manage to find the flakes of gold, they separate them from the earth with much toil and vigour. After all that toil they find only slight recompense for their labours. They know that the benefit they reap is less than their labour, and often, after many sleepless nights and much weariness, they have failed of their hope altogether. Even so they do not give up; nourished by hope, they do not feel their labours. If they show such zeal over perishable and fleeting things, where there is great uncertainty as well, how much more ought we to show equal and greater zeal! Here the wealth cannot be taken away, the treasure is inexhaustible, and failure is impossible. So let us strive, that we may attain what we seek, reap the benefit from it, and learn God's inexpressible love for humankind. Then we may become grateful toward our Master, draw his goodwill upon us, and stand proof against the snares of the devil. Come then, let us set before us what was just read and examine each part with precision, so that you may enjoy your usual teaching before you go home. "This is the book," it says, "of the generation of human beings. On the day God made Adam, in the image of God …"

… before your love. But so that we may not for now fall away from the sequence before us, come, let us take up again what was said. "This is the book," it says, "of the generation of human beings. On the day God made Adam, he made him in the image of God. Male and female he made them, and he named them Adam, on the day he made them." See how divine Scripture starts the account again from the beginning and reminds us how great an honour the human being was granted at his creation. "On the day," it says, "he made Adam, he made him in the image of God." That is, he appointed him ruler of all visible things. For this is what "in the image" means: in respect of rule and of lordship. The God of all holds rule over all things, visible and invisible, since he is the creator of all. In the same way, when he created this rational living being, he willed it to have rule over all visible things. That is why he also granted it the substance of a soul, wishing it to be immortal forever. But when through carelessness it slipped and transgressed the commandment given to it, not even then did he turn away from it completely. Imitating his own love for humankind, he deprived it of immortality and condemned it to death, but he left it almost in the same rule. Then the one born from Adam ran aground in such madness. He was the first to introduce murder and to bring that violent death into the world, and he showed great ingratitude by adding a lie to his murder. God chose to correct him with lasting punishment, so that he would not only gain something himself from what had happened to him but would also teach those after him how great his daring had been and how extreme his outrage. But through great carelessness those born from him also wrapped themselves little by little in worse evils. Adam was in deep dejection, not only because of his own transgression but also because of Cain's crime and the unbearable grief he had seen with his own eyes. They did not yet know what death looked like, even though they had received the sentence. His grief was double and triple: they saw death brought into life for the first time, and a violent death at that, dared by his own son against a brother of the same mother and the same father who had done no wrong. So the loving God, wishing to console Adam, so to speak, and to bring him comfort to counterbalance his griefs, gives him another son, Seth. He makes this a sufficient comfort for him, and from him he then establishes the beginning of the generations. That is why the blessed prophet began this way: "This is the book of the generation of human beings." Having promised to recount the generation of human beings, see what sequence he follows: "Adam lived," it says, "two hundred and thirty years, and he begot according to his form and according to his image, and named him Seth. And his days were seven hundred years, and he begot sons and daughters. And all the days of Adam were nine hundred and thirty years, and …"
3. Was I not right in saying at the beginning that nothing is to be found written carelessly and at random in divine Scripture? See now too with what precision the blessed [?]

… of the name of the one born to him, showing his God-loving disposition. "And to Seth," it says, "a son was born, and he named him Enosh. He hoped to call on the name of the Lord God." Do you see a name more splendid than a diadem, brighter than purple? What could be more blessed than such a man, adorned with calling on God and bearing this in place of a name? Do you see how, as I said at the beginning, a great wealth of meaning is stored up even in bare names? This shows not only the parents' love of God but also the great care they took of their children. From the very beginning they trained the children born to them to hold fast to virtue through the names they gave them. They did not name them casually and at random, as people do now. Now people say, "Let the child be called after his grandfather and great-grandfather." The ancients did not do this. They made every effort to give their children names that would lead to virtue not only those who received them, but would also become a lesson in all true wisdom for everyone else and for later generations. We shall see this as the discourse goes on. So let us not give our children just any names either, nor grant them the names of grandfathers, great-grandfathers and distinguished relatives. Let us give them the names of holy men who shone with virtue and had great confidence before God. Or rather, let neither parents nor the children who receive the names simply rely on those names. A name without virtue is no use at all. We must place our hope of salvation in the achievement of virtue. We should not pride ourselves on a name, or on kinship with holy men, or on anything else, except the confidence that comes from our own works. Or rather, we should not pride ourselves even on that. We should be humbler and more modest precisely when we have managed to gather great wealth of virtue. That way we shall keep the wealth we have gathered in safety and draw God's goodwill upon us. This is why Christ said to his disciples, "When you have done everything, say, We are unprofitable servants." Everywhere he humbles their thoughts, persuading them to be modest and not to be puffed up by their achievements, but to know that the greatest virtue of all is for someone to stay modest amid his achievements. 4. But let us return to the sequence of the discourse and look at those born next. As we go on little by little, we are likely to find a greater treasure and a great and inexpressible wealth. "And Enosh," it says (this is Seth's son), "lived one hundred and ninety years and begot Kenan. And Kenan begot Mahalalel, and Mahalalel begot Jared, and Jared begot Enoch. And Enoch lived one hundred and sixty-five years and begot Methuselah. And Enoch," it says, "was well-pleasing to God. Enoch lived two hundred years after he begot Methuselah, and he begot sons and daughters. And the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. And Enoch was well-pleasing to God, and he was not found, because God had translated him." Was I not right in saying that …

… the sentence he had pronounced against Adam. But he does not make it plain, so that fear might serve as a means of correction. That is why he translated Enoch, who had pleased him. Someone may want to pry and ask, "Where did he translate him? And has he survived until now?" Let such a person learn not to follow human reasoning or to meddle in the things of God, but to believe what is said. When God declares something, we must not oppose what he has said. We must hold the words of God more trustworthy than anything else, even if they do not appear to agree with what lies before our eyes. Divine Scripture has said that he translated him. It has said that he translated him alive, without his tasting death, and that by pleasing God he rose above the sentence pronounced against the human race. But where he translated him, and how he lives now, it has not added. 5. Do you see the Master's goodness? He found a man who had achieved virtue and did not deprive him of the dignity he had granted the first-formed man before he transgressed the commandment. This teaches us that Adam too, if he had not preferred the deception to the commandment given him, would have been granted the same things and greater. "And Methuselah lived," it says, "one hundred and eighty-seven years and begot Lamech. And Lamech lived one hundred and eighty years and begot a son, and he named him Noah, saying: This one will give us rest from our works, from the toils of our hands, and from the earth which the Lord God has cursed." See again, in the name of the child now born to Lamech, the greatness of the mysteries, the surpassing nature of the prophecy, and the inexpressible love of our good God for humankind. In his foreknowledge he saw what was to come. He saw human wickedness growing, and through the child's name he foretells the evils that are going to overtake the whole human race, so that, corrected by fear at least, people might keep away from wickedness and choose virtue. And see the Master's long-suffering, how long beforehand he has the prediction made, so as both to show his love for humankind and to deprive of every excuse those who were going to [suffer] the punishment …

But perhaps someone might say: "Where did Lamech get so great a prophecy? Does Scripture mention that he was virtuous and admirable?" Do not be surprised, beloved. The Master is wise and resourceful, and he often allows wonderful and great things to be foretold even through unworthy people. This happens not only in the Old Testament but also in the New. Listen to the evangelist speaking of Caiaphas, the high priest of the Jews: "He did not say this of himself, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus was going to die, not for the people only, but also to gather into one the nations that were scattered." You will find something similar happening with Balaam. He was summoned to curse the people, yet not only did he not curse them, he even prophesied great and wonderful things, not only about the people but also about the Saviour's coming. So do not be surprised that Lamech now gives his child such a name. Attribute it all to God, who by his resourceful wisdom arranges all things …

… [?] care, nor put forward anything else and think it a sufficient defence for living carelessly and negligently. Let us not bring out those feeble and useless words and say: "I am a man of the world, I have a wife, I have to look after my children." Most people usually say this when we urge them to the labours of virtue, or to give great attention to reading the Scriptures. "That is not my business," one says. "Have I renounced the world? Am I a monk?" What are you saying, man? Is pleasing God allotted to them alone? He wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and he wishes no one to neglect virtue. Listen to him saying through the prophet: "I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live." Tell me, was living with a wife or caring for children any hindrance to this righteous man? So I urge you, let us not deceive ourselves. The more we are caught up in these cares, the more we should take the medicines that come from reading the divine Scriptures. Were these men not of the same nature as we are? And did they not have far fewer means to lead them to the practice of virtue? What pardon, then, would we deserve if we do not reach the measure of virtue of the men of old? We enjoy so much teaching, we have been granted so much grace, we enjoy help from above, and we have received the promise of those ineffable good things. If we are willing to be sober, what has been set before us today is enough to rouse us to a longing for virtue, and to keep us from ever thinking that anything stands in our way on its road. If those who lived before the Law reached such virtue from the teaching implanted in nature, what can we say for ourselves? After so much help, after the coming of Christ and countless miracles, we are still far from virtue. So I urge you, let us not skim over what lies in the divine Scriptures, but read their contents attentively. Then, reaping the benefit from them, we may at last, late as it is, take hold of virtue as God wills. If we are going to sound this spiritual teaching in your ears every day while you remain in the same carelessness, what benefit will you get from constant teaching? And what comfort will there be for us, when we see our great labour come to nothing and no progress result from our efforts? Tell me, are we not made up of two substances, I mean soul and body? Why, then, do we not give equal care to both? We are eager to look after the body in every way. We pay money to doctors and take great care of it ourselves. We clothe it in expensive garments, give it more food than it needs, and want it to live in constant comfort, untroubled by any illness at all. If anything at all troubles it, we try every means to correct what is causing it pain. And this we do for the body, which I call the lesser in substance. For tell me, how can soul and body be equal? If you want to see the difference, consider how the body is found to be worth nothing once the soul has departed. So you who take such care of the body, why …

…let them rather transfer the ornament, and adorn the soul with it. For just as these things, when placed on the body, make it uglier even if it is beautiful, so when they are put on the soul, they change it to the height of beauty even if it is ugly. “And how,” someone says, “is it possible to put gold ornaments on the soul?” Again, through the hand of the poor. For when they receive them, they fashion its beauty. Put the gold into their hands and distribute it into their stomachs, and they will give you such beauty of soul that by its loveliness you will draw the true Bridegroom himself, and through this win countless good things for yourself. For when you draw the Master by your beauty, you have the supply of all good things, and you have gained unspeakable wealth. If, then, we wish to become lovely in the Master’s eyes, let us stop being infatuated with adorning the body, and let us attend every day to the beauty of the soul, so that we may draw the goodwill of the God who loves mankind, and attain the ineffable good things, by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, might and honor to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY 22

“And Noah was five hundred years old, and Noah fathered three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. And it came to pass, when men began to be many on the earth, and daughters were born…”

1. I want to set before you today the leftovers of yesterday’s table. But do not be put off, beloved, when you hear “leftovers.” With food for the body, dishes often go stale after a day or two, become useless and unfit to eat. With the spiritual table there is nothing of that sort to fear: the more time passes, the more charm it shows, and it is found fresher and more vigorous. Come, then, let us put into effect the promise we made yesterday, pay off the debt of our teaching, and show our good faith. For this payment is not profitable only to those who receive it, as with ordinary debts, but also to me who pay it. And why do I say “to me who pay it”? Such is the nature of this spiritual debt that the more it is paid off, the more it grows, and it produces greater abundance and unspeakable wealth both for the one who pays and for those who receive. Do you see the new nature of this debt, and the strange kind of repayment? Such are spiritual things: they grow by being distributed, and the more people share in them, the greater the abundance becomes; the one who pays feels no loss from the payment, but his wealth even grows, and those who receive are set in greater abundance. Since, then, such is the nature of these spiritual things, let us hasten with all eagerness to the repayment, and you prepare your ears to receive it, so that each of you may take what we say into the open lap of your mind, and so go home. For I want once more to bring before you the story of righteous Noah, so that you may learn the great virtue of the righteous man, the unspeakable lovingkindness of God, and his long-suffering that surpasses all words. You learned yesterday how, from the very beginning of his birth…

[Notes:] a. Savile: περιτιθέμενα. Other manuscripts: περιτιθέντα; [?] περιτεθέντα. b. Savile and some others [?]: “the gold, distributing it into their…”

…to obtain some [?]. That is why the righteous man, like a spark in the middle of the sea, not only was not extinguished but sent out a brighter light every day, becoming a teacher to all through his own [?]

Do you see how the Master created our nature with free will? Tell me, how was it that they were rushing into wickedness and making themselves liable to punishment, while this man chose virtue, fled from their company, and did not experience the punishment? Is it not obvious that it is because each person chooses virtue by his own free choice? If that were not so, and the power to choose did not lie in our nature, those people ought not to have been punished, nor these to receive rewards for virtue. But since, after the grace from above, he has left everything to our free choice, punishments are laid up for those who sin, and recompense and rewards for those who do right. “And Noah was five hundred years old,” it says, “and fathered three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth.” Notice the precision of divine Scripture. Having told us the number of the righteous man’s years, to show the surpassing long-suffering of the Master, it wants again to make plain to us how great the Master’s forbearance was, and how violent the rush of human wickedness.

2. But let us hear the very words spoken by Moses, for speaking by the Spirit he wants to teach us everything precisely. “And it came to pass,” he says, “when men began to be many on the earth, and daughters were born to them.” He did not add “and daughters were born to them” idly, but to show us the great multitude. For where there is so great a number of roots, many branches must be born. “And when the sons of God saw,” it says, “the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” Let us examine each word of what has been said carefully, so that nothing hidden in the depths may escape us. For it is necessary to make a thorough investigation of this passage and to overturn the fables of those who say everything without thinking: first to state what they dare to say, and, having shown the absurdity of their claims, then to teach your love the true meaning of Scripture, so that you may not simply lend your ears to those who utter those blasphemies and dare to speak them to their own ruin. For they say that this was said not about men but about angels, since it called these “sons of God.” First let them show where angels were called sons of God; but they could not show it anywhere. Men were called sons of God, but angels never. About angels it says, “He who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire”; but about men, “I said, You are gods…”

[Notes:] Others read “of their fall.” Savile adds “from what has been said.”

“…daughters were born to them. And when the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” We have already taught you that it is Scripture’s custom to call men too sons of God. Since, then, these people traced their descent from Seth, and from the one born to him and named Enosh (for he, it says, “hoped to call on the name of the Lord God”), from then on those born after him were called sons of God by divine Scripture, because up to that point they imitated the virtue of their ancestors; while it called “sons of men” those who existed before Seth, those from Cain and those who traced their descent from him. “For it came to pass,” it says, “when men began to be many on the earth, and daughters were born to them, that the sons of God” (those from Seth and Enosh) “saw the daughters of men” (those born to the others, about whom it said, “and daughters were born to them”) “that they were beautiful.” See how by this phrase he has displayed to us all their licentiousness. For they did not rush into this act out of a desire for children, but out of an uncontrolled craving for pleasure: “For when they saw,” it says, “the daughters of men, that they were beautiful.” Desire for good looks brought them to this ruin, and beauty of face became for them the cause of fornication and licentiousness. And he was not content with this, but added, “They took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” This again shows their great licentiousness: they were overcome by beauty and were unwilling to put a bridle on their disorderly desire; overpowered by what they saw, they went under, and by this lawless act deprived themselves of providence from above. And so that we may learn that they did this neither by the law of marriage nor for the sake of children, he says, “Seeing that they were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” What then? Should one blame the eyes for seeing? Not at all. The eye was not the cause of the fall, but the slackness of free choice and the unbridled state of desire. For the eye was created so that, beholding God’s works through it, we might glorify their Maker. Seeing, then, is the eye’s work; but seeing wrongly comes from the reasoning that drives it from within. For the Master created our limbs to be useful for doing good, and allowed them to be driven by the incorporeal substance, I mean the soul. So whenever the soul sinks into slackness and loosens the reins, it is like a charioteer who does not know how to check the unruly leaping of his horses: he gives up the reins and hurls over a cliff both the horses drawing the chariot and himself. In just the same way our free choice, when it does not know how to use the limbs as it should, gives in to disorderly desires and makes itself go under. That is why our Master Christ, knowing how easily our nature is assailed and how slack our free choice is, laid down a law that walls off and forbids idle gazing, so that from a great distance he might put out the fire that is kindled in us, and [?] I give, so that, if you wish, you may wash

[Note:] Six manuscripts read “a woman.”

away your sins by changing for the better, and, choosing virtue, escape the experience of punishment. “For their days,” it says, “shall be a hundred and twenty years. And the giants,” it says, “were on the earth in those days. And after that, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and they bore children for themselves, those were the giants of old, the men of renown.” By “giants” here I think divine Scripture means those strong in body. “From them,” it says, “their generation increased.” For one can see this said elsewhere too: “Giants,” it says, “are coming to put an end to my anger.” Some think this number of a hundred and twenty years is the limit of life; but that is not what it means. Rather, for the time being it wants to show the long-suffering he displays toward them even after so many sins. So, that we may learn that even after his indignation, and his threat, and so long a period of patience, which he gave them for repentance, they not only gained nothing but persisted in the same ways, it says, “When the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and they bore children for themselves, those were the giants of old, the men of renown.” Do you see the height of ingratitude? Do you see a soul past feeling? Neither the fear of punishment nor the time of patience turned them from their wicked deeds; but once they had been carried over the cliff, and had the eye of their mind blinded, they were no longer willing to come back up, plunged as though in drunkenness in their wicked desire, just as a wise man says, “When the ungodly man falls into the depth of evils, he despises.” For it is a terrible thing, beloved, terrible, to be caught in the devil’s snares. For the soul is then caught as in nets, and just as a pig delights in wallowing in mud, so the soul, buried under evil habit, does not even perceive the stench of its sins. Therefore we must be sober and watchful, so as to give the evil demon no entrance at the start, lest he darken our reasoning and blind the mind’s power of sight, and so bring it about that, like people deprived of the light of this sun and unable to look at the rays of the Sun of righteousness, we are carried over the cliff, which is what these people suffered then. For hear again the forbearance of God’s goodness: “And when the Lord God saw,” it says, “that the wickednesses of men were multiplied on the earth.” What is meant by the words “when he saw”? Not that the Master was ignorant—perish the thought! But divine Scripture tells everything with our weakness in mind, to teach us that even after such long-suffering on his part they persisted in the same things, or even wrapped themselves in worse evils. It says: “When he saw that the wickednesses of men were multiplied on the earth.” For from this wicked act, as from a spring, many other sins were also born to them; that is why it says “the wickednesses of men.” For where there is fornication, licentiousness and such great debauchery, it is to be expected that drunkenness, drunken violence, much injustice, greed and countless evils are also born. “And when the Lord God saw,” it says, “that the wickednesses of men were multiplied on the earth, and that everyone was carefully intent in his heart on evil things all his days…”

…that they would come to an awareness of their own failings and so call back my indignation. But since even so they gained nothing more, I must carry out my threat and bring about their complete blotting out, and do away with their race like some evil leaven, so that they may not become teachers of wickedness to the generations that follow as well. “And the Lord God said, I will blot out man, whom I have made, from the face of the earth, from man to beast.” But perhaps someone might say, “Why, when man turned to wickedness, do the irrational animals also suffer the same punishment with him?” Rightly so. For were the irrational animals made for their own needs? They were brought into being for man’s sake. So when he is being taken away, what need would there be for them? That is why they too share in the punishment, so that you may learn how extreme the indignation was. And just as in the beginning, when the first-formed man sinned, the earth received the curse, so now too, when man is about to be done away with, the irrational animals share in the punishment. And just as, when man prospers, creation shares in his good fortune (as Paul too says, “that creation itself also will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God”), so now too, when man is about to be punished for the multitude of his sins and handed over to utter destruction, the cattle, the reptiles and the birds also have their share in the flood that is about to overtake the whole world. And just as in a house, when the steward has fallen under his master’s indignation, it is natural that all his fellow servants share in the gloom, in the same way here too, as in a house where the people are being destroyed, everything in the house and everything under man’s dominion must fall under the same punishment. “And I have considered,” it says, “that I made them.” How full of condescension is this saying! “Did I want,” he says, “to wrap them in such punishment? But by the excess of their lawlessness they provoked so great an indignation.” Then, so that we should not think the human race was being wiped out completely, or that our nature was being destroyed root and branch, but should learn how great an evil sin is and how great a good virtue is, and that one person who does the Lord’s will is better than ten thousand lawless people, it says, “But Noah found favor before the Lord God.” “Even if the whole multitude,” it means, “ran aground on such great wickedness, this righteous man kept the spark of virtue alive, all the while talking to all these people throughout the whole time and urging them to be rid of their wickedness, and keeping himself free from their corruption.” And just as they by their wicked deeds provoked the God who loves mankind to indignation, so this man, choosing virtue, “found favor before the Lord God.” For God shows no partiality; even if he finds only one person in so great a multitude doing what pleases him, he does not overlook him, but counts him worthy of his own providence, and shows him care all the greater because, when so many were dragging him toward wickedness, he chose the road of virtue for himself.

[Note:] Savile and Morel [?] read ἁμαρτόντος; six manuscripts ἁμαρτῶντος.

…or because of some other turn of circumstances, or even fettered by bodily illness, he wants to have memorials of his greed everywhere and, so to speak, in every city, and to keep undying monuments of his wickedness before everyone. The sins from which all this was gathered he heaps on his own head, and he does not feel that he is carrying a heavy load, hard to bear; but the enjoyment of these things he yields to others, not only after his departure from life, but even before his exit from here. For even if he is not stripped of them against his will, all these things are pulled apart and torn to pieces, so to speak, by his own household, and he does not get to enjoy even the smallest part of them. But why do I speak of enjoyment? Even if he wanted to, how could he, having only one stomach, be equal to so great a mass of money?

7. But the cause of all these evils is vainglory, and the wish to have one’s name put on fields, baths and houses. What good is it to you, man, when shortly a fever seizes you, and your soul suddenly flies away and leaves you deserted and naked—or rather, stripped of virtue but clothed in your injustices, robberies and acts of greed, the groans, the lamentation, the tears of orphans, the plots and the deceits? How will you be able, with these great loads of sin lying on you, to pass through that narrow gate, which cannot admit a bulk of such size? You must then stay outside, weighed down by these loads, and repent to no purpose, already seeing before your eyes the punishments made ready, that fearful fire that is never quenched, and the worm that never dies. But if we have any concern for our salvation, while we still have time, let us turn away from wickedness, pursue virtue, and disregard vainglory. For that is why it is called “vain”: because it is empty and has nothing secure or lasting, but is only a deception of the eyes, flying away before it has even appeared. Do we not see the man who today is escorted [?] and surrounded by bodyguards often living in prison tomorrow and moving among criminals? What is more deceptive than this strange and vain glory? And even if no reversal awaits him in the present, death certainly comes and cuts short his prosperity; and the man who swaggered in the marketplace, who threw people into prison, who sat on the throne, puffed up with pride and looking on all men as shadows, the next day suddenly lies a breathless corpse, full of stench, pelted with countless accusations by those he wronged, and by those he did not wrong, who grieve with the wronged. What could be more pitiable than such a man? Everything he gathered, his enemies and foes have often divided among themselves; but he goes away taking with him the sins heaped up on him from it, to be called to account for them with great strictness. Therefore, I urge you, let us flee this vain glory and long for the true glory that lasts for ever; and let neither love of money trip us up, nor desire [?]

[Notes:] Others read ἐκσωρευθέντα [?]. Shortly after, many manuscripts read “for these transgressions” [?].

…sitting in harbour, steering the rudder of virtue in this way, he placed himself beyond the storm that was about to overtake everyone throughout the world. Such a thing is virtue: deathless and unconquerable. It does not give way to the ups and downs of this present life. It flies high above the nets of wickedness and looks down on all human affairs as if from some lofty watchtower, and it feels nothing of what seems painful to others. Someone standing on a high rock laughs at the waves when he sees them dash against the rock and at once dissolve into foam. In just the same way, the one who pursues virtue stands in a safe place and suffers nothing unpleasant from the turmoil of events. He sits in quiet, delighting in the calm of his own thoughts, and reflecting that the affairs of this present life are no different from the currents of rivers, rushing past with such ease and force. We can see the waves of the sea now rising to an indescribable height and then suddenly sinking low again. In the same way we see those who neglect virtue [206] and pursue wickedness: now they are proud, raising their eyebrows and excited about the affairs of this present life, and then they are suddenly brought low and driven into the deepest poverty. The blessed prophet David hinted at such people when he said, “Do not be afraid when a man grows rich, or when the glory of his house increases; for when he dies he will take nothing with him.” He was right to say, “Do not be afraid.” Do not let abundant wealth and splendid glory unsettle you, he means. For before long you will see that man lying on the ground, inert, dead, cast aside, food for worms, stripped of all these things. He was not able to take anything at all away with him, but left it all behind here. So do not be anxious when you see present things, and do not call that man blessed who in a short while will be bereft of them. Such is present prosperity, and such is the nature of wealth: it does not travel with those who depart from here. They leave it all behind here and go away naked and alone, clothed only in their wickedness and in the burdens of sins they have gathered from it. With virtue it is not like this at all. Even here it raises people above those who plot against them and makes them impregnable. It grants them unbroken joy and does not let them feel the ups and downs of events. And when they depart from here it goes with them, above all at the time when we need its alliance. On that fearful day it gives us great help, making the judge’s eye gentle toward us. Just as here, when terrible things are present, it lifts us above them, so in the age to come it snatches those who carry it with them out of those punishments. And not only that: it also secures for us the enjoyment of ineffable good things. To show you that this is so, and that we are not using these words simply and idly to entertain you, I will try to demonstrate it to your love from the passage now before us. See how this wonderful man, Noah I mean, at a time when the whole human race had provoked the loving Master to indignation against them, was able by his own virtue both to escape the experience of that indignation and to draw great goodwill from him. And if you like, for the moment [?] concerning those in the [?] who laughed and wanted to mock; but [208]

this righteous man was not like that. He disregarded not only ten or twenty or a hundred people, but the whole of human nature, so many tens of thousands. It is likely that they all laughed at him, mocked him, jeered at him, and showed him a great deal of drunken insolence. Perhaps they would even have liked to tear him apart, if they could. For wickedness always shows great fury against virtue. Yet not only does it do virtue no harm, but its very warring makes virtue stronger. Such is the strength of virtue that in suffering it overcomes those who inflict the suffering, and in being attacked it stands above its attackers. This can be seen from many examples. But to give you a starting point (“Give a wise man an opportunity,” it says, “and he will become wiser”), I must bring you examples from both the Old and the New Testament. Think of Abel, then. Was he not killed by Cain? Was he not thrown down on the ground? But do not look at the fact that Cain prevailed and won, and killed the one he envied, who had done him no wrong [?]. Consider instead what came afterward. The one who was killed has been proclaimed and crowned from that day to this, and so long a time has not withered his memory. But the one who killed him and prevailed endured, even at that time, a life heavier than death, and from then until now he has been publicly branded and accused by everyone, while Abel is sung every day on the lips of all. That is what happens in this present life. As for the age to come, what word, what mind could describe it? I know that, being intelligent, you will find many other examples of this kind in the Scriptures. They were written for our benefit for this very reason: so that by learning them we may flee wickedness and prefer virtue. Would you like to see the same thing in the New Testament too? Listen to blessed Luke telling the same thing about the apostles: that after being flogged they left the council rejoicing, because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Christ. Yet floggings were no occasion for joy, but for grief and dejection. But floggings for God’s sake, and the cause for which they were flogged, gave birth to joy in them. Meanwhile those who flogged them were left in great perplexity and helplessness, not knowing what to do. Listen to them, still at a loss after the flogging and saying, “What shall we do with these men?” What are you saying? You flogged them, you did them countless harms, and you are still at a loss? So strong and unconquerable a thing is virtue, overcoming those who make it suffer in the very act of suffering. 3. But so as not to make our discourse long, we must come back to this righteous man and marvel at the surpassing greatness of his virtue: how, while so great a multitude laughed at him, trampled on him, jeered and mocked him (I say the same things again, and I will not stop saying them), he was able to disregard them and rise above them. How? I will tell you. Because he looked continually toward the sleepless eye, he kept the eye [209] of his mind fixed there, and so he regarded all these things as nothing. That is how it is. When someone is wounded by that love and stretches himself out in longing for God, he sees nothing else of what is visible, but continually pictures the one he longs for, by night and by day, lying down and rising up. So do not be surprised if this righteous man, having once directed his [?] there [?]. [Variant: six manuscripts and Morel read “overcomes such things.”]

…divine Scripture says, “These are the generations of Noah.” It sets our ears on wing, as if it were about to recount his genealogy: who his father was, where his family came from, how he was brought into life, and everything else that those who narrate genealogies usually tell. But it leaves all that aside, rises above custom, and says: “Noah was a righteous man, perfect in his generation; Noah pleased God.” Do you see a wonderful genealogy? “Noah,” it says, “a man.” Notice how even the common name of our nature becomes praise for the righteous man. Since those others had lost even the status of being human by slipping into the pleasures of the flesh, this man, it says, preserved the image of a human being among so great a multitude. For this is what a human being is: one who pursues virtue. Having a human shape, with eyes and nose and mouth and cheeks and the other limbs, does not make someone a human being, for these are just members of the body. We would call that person a human being who preserves the image of a human being. And what is the image of a human being? Being rational. “What then?” someone says. “Weren’t those people rational?” Yes, but this is not the whole of it. Being virtuous too, fleeing evil, mastering unnatural passions, following the commandments of the Master: this is what a human being is. 4. To show you that it is Scripture’s custom not even to grant the name “human being” to those who pursue wickedness and neglect virtue, listen to God saying, as we said yesterday: “My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” For I, he means, together with the flesh also bestowed the soul and its authority [?]; but they, as though clothed in flesh alone, neglecting the virtue of the soul, have become wholly flesh. [211] Do you see how he calls them flesh, not human beings, because of their wickedness? And a little further on, as you will soon learn, divine Scripture calls them earth, because they had been consumed by earthly thoughts. For it says, “The earth was corrupted before God,” not speaking of the earth we perceive, but calling its inhabitants earth. Elsewhere it calls them neither flesh nor earth, but does not even consider them to exist in this present life, because they are empty of virtue. Listen to the prophet crying out and saying, in the middle of the capital city of Jerusalem, where there were so many tens of thousands, such boundless crowds: “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one to answer.” This was not because they were absent, but because, though present, they were no better off than those who were not. And again elsewhere: “Run about,” it says, “and see if there is one who does judgment and righteousness, and I will be merciful.” Do you see how holy Scripture knows how to call only the one who pursues virtue a human being, while it does not even consider the rest to exist, but sometimes names them flesh and sometimes earth? That is why here too, when it promises to recount the righteous man’s genealogy, divine Scripture says, “Noah, a man.” For he alone was a human being. The rest were not human beings. They had human form, but by the wickedness of their choice they had betrayed the nobility of their nature, and instead of human beings [had sunk] to the [?] of wild beasts…

5. Do you see whom divine Scripture knows how to call human beings? That is also why, from the beginning, when the Master of all saw the one he had fashioned, he said, “Let us make man [Variant: Savile and six manuscripts read “human beings,” the rational ones [?].]

in our image and likeness.” That is, so that he might be ruler of all visible things and of the passions arising within him; so that he might rule and not be ruled. But if he betrays his rule and is ruled rather than ruling, he loses even his being human and transfers himself to the name of the irrational beasts. This is why here too, wanting to proclaim the virtue of this righteous man, divine Scripture says, “These are the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man.” Here is another very great kind of praise: “righteous.” By this title it shows his virtue as a whole, for we are accustomed to use the name “righteous” of those who pursue every virtue. Then, so that you may learn how he reached the very summit of virtue, as much as was demanded of our nature at that time, it says, “righteous, perfect in his generation.” He fulfilled everything, it means, that a man who had chosen [215] virtue ought to show (this is what “perfect” means), falling short in nothing, limping in nothing. He did not succeed in one thing and fail in another, but was perfect in every virtue, for this is what he ought to have shown. Then, to make the righteous man more conspicuous to us from the time and from the comparison, it says, “perfect in his generation”: at that time, in his perverse generation, which had turned aside to such wickedness and had not wanted to show even a trace of virtue. In that generation, then, in those times, this righteous man not only showed virtue but reached the very peak of the virtues, becoming perfect and complete in everything. As I said before, achieving virtue among those who war against it, and showing the same strictness in the midst of those who hinder it, always shows the greater weight of virtue. That is why this righteous man is counted worthy of more praise. And divine Scripture does not stop there in proclaiming him. It shows us the surpassing greatness of his virtue, and that he received a verdict from above. Having said, “perfect in his generation,” it says, “Noah pleased God.” So great was the abundance of his virtue that it drew praise from God. “Noah pleased God,” it says; that is, he became acceptable to God, he pleased that sleepless eye by what he had achieved, and the conduct of his life drew God’s goodwill. This not only freed him from the indignation that was about to be unleashed on all, but also made him the protector of others. “Noah pleased God,” it says. Who could be more blessed than this man, who was able to show such virtue that he had the Master of all as the one who praised him? Of all that he did, this would be more precious to anyone with sense than all wealth, all glory and power, and every other human prosperity. To one who shows genuine love for God, this would be more desirable than a kingdom. For this is the true kingdom: to be able, by the best way of life, to make the Master kind and merciful toward us. Indeed, we ought not to fear and dread hell because of that unquenchable fire, the fearful penalties and the everlasting punishments, but because of offending so good a Master and placing ourselves outside his goodwill. Just as, then, [?] [Variant: others read “because of not offending”; this is better, but Savile [?]. Others read “of the summit.”]

…[?] Is it not clear that by their own zeal they will be able to accomplish these things, after the grace from above, while we, giving ourselves over to our own sloth, betray our salvation and leave ourselves bereft of the goodwill that comes from there? [Interleaved text from another column: …when so many things have been done beforehand [?] for our salvation, we should prove them all useless through sloth [?], betraying our salvation [?]. I call on you to be sober, and not to follow [?] others, but to examine your own life each day, and to know what sins we have committed and what good we have done. So let us correct our sins, so that we may draw help from above and become pleasing to God, as this righteous man was, and attain the kingdom of heaven, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father together with the Holy [Spirit] [?]…] 6. I urge you to consider these things and keep turning them over in your minds, and never to blame the devil, but our own slothful will. I do not say this because I want to free him from blame. Heaven forbid! For he does come like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. I say it because I want to make us safer too, so that we do not think ourselves free of blame when we desert so easily to wickedness, and so that we do not say those feeble words, “Why did God leave him alone, when he is so wicked, so that he trips people up and throws them down?” Such words would show the greatest ingratitude. Instead, consider this for yourself: he left him for this reason above all, so that, driven by fear and expecting the enemy’s attack, we might show great watchfulness and constant sobriety, cutting short all the toil of virtue by the hope of the rewards and the recompense of those eternal and ineffable good things. And why are you surprised that he left the devil for this reason, out of care for our salvation, to rouse us from our sloth and to prepare for us occasions for crowns? He prepared hell itself for this reason, so that the fear of punishment and the unbearable nature of the penalty might drive us toward the kingdom. Do you see the resourceful loving-kindness of the Master? How he does and arranges everything, not only to save those he created, but also to count them worthy of ineffable good things? For this reason he gave us free will, placed the knowledge of wickedness and virtue in our nature and our conscience, allowed the devil to exist, and threatened hell, so that we might never experience hell and might attain the kingdom. And why are you surprised that he arranged all these things, and countless others, for this purpose? He who dwells in the Father’s bosom consented to take the form of a slave and to endure all the other bodily things: to be born of a woman, to be brought forth from a virgin, to be carried in the womb for nine months, to be wrapped in swaddling clothes, to be thought the son of Joseph, Mary’s betrothed, to grow little by little, to be circumcised, to offer sacrifice, to hunger, to thirst, to grow weary, and finally to endure death. And not just any death, but the one thought shameful: the death of the cross, I mean. All this the Creator of all accepted for us and for our salvation: he who is unchangeable, who brought all things from non-being into being, who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, the lightning of whose glory not even the cherubim, those bodiless powers, are able to look upon. Instead they turn their faces away and show us the wonder by the covering of their wings. He whom angels, archangels and countless myriads hymn continually became a man for our sake and for our salvation. [216] He cut for us the road of the best way of life, and by taking our own nature and coming among us, he laid down sufficient teaching. What defence, then, is left to us? In the same way it is fitting that, like those who hunger and thirst, so [we should approach] the spiritual teaching [?]…

…to approach. People like this are not only worthy to be called blessed; they will also obtain what they strive for. For "They shall be filled," he says, that is, they shall be satisfied: they will fulfil their spiritual desire. Since, then, we have such a Master, so good and so generous, come, let us also take refuge in him and draw down his help, so that he too, true to his own loving-kindness, may enlighten our minds to see into the power of the divine Scriptures. And you, for your part, receive the spiritual teaching with great eagerness, like people who hunger and thirst. For perhaps, perhaps, the good and resourceful Master will give us speech when we open our mouths, for his glory and for your building up. We may be lowly and worthy of no account, but he will do it for your sake and for your benefit. So let us cast everything on the grace from above and call on him who makes the blind wise and makes clear the tongues of stammerers. Then let us take up what was read just now, so that whatever he supplies, true to his own loving-kindness, we may set before your love. But I beg you, keep your minds alert. Attend carefully to what is said, and put away from yourselves every worldly thought, so that we may sow the spiritual seed as into rich, deep-soiled ground cleared of weeds and thorns. "These," it says, "are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, perfect in his generation; Noah pleased God." Yesterday's teaching ended at this point, so we must now set out what remains. "And Noah," it says, "begot three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth." The divine Scripture did not point out to us both the time and the number of the righteous man's children for no reason. Even by this it wished to show us quietly how far his virtue surpassed others. Having said above that Noah was five hundred years old, it then added, "And he begot three sons." By this it teaches us the exceeding greatness of his self-control, and that [?] while all the people of that time indulged such incontinence and displayed great lust, and every age, so to speak, had deserted to wickedness… For you hear the divine Scripture saying, "And the Lord saw that the wickednesses of men were multiplied on the earth, and that everyone was diligently devising evil things in his heart from his youth." It shows us clearly that the young outdid the old, that the old raged no less than the young, and that even the age that has no experience of evil was strongly inclined toward wickedness. 2. It says this so that we may learn how this righteous man alone held out, while all these people showed great frenzy and madness. He won the contest of chastity, together with the rest of virtue, until he reached his five-hundredth year. For after saying, "Noah was five hundred years old," it then says, "And Noah begot three sons." Have you seen, beloved, the surpassing self-control of the righteous man? Let us not run past these things carelessly. Let us think about that time, and about the wickedness that spread over the whole human race through great carelessness, and let us consider how great a virtue and how God-loving a disposition, over so long a span of time [?] … but about people clothed in flesh, who had spent themselves on earthly deeds. For it is the custom of Scripture, as we have often said before

your love, to call those who showed a fleshly mind and imagined nothing lofty by the name of "flesh" [?: from the Master. For even if much virtue … to himself]. As blessed Paul also says, "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God." What then? Was the man who said this not clothed in flesh himself? But he does not mean that those clothed in flesh cannot please God. He means those who take no account of virtue but set their minds on everything fleshly, who are dragged down toward the pleasures of the flesh and take no care of the soul, which is bodiless and rational. Through what has been said, then, the divine Scripture taught us how many the sins were, how great the wickedness and how great God's indignation. It also taught us that because they made a practice of lawless deeds it called them "earth" once, twice and three times, and named them "flesh," stripping them of the name of the nature we all share. Now, through what follows, it shows us God's unspeakable loving-kindness and how far he condescends. For what does it say? "And God said to Noah." 3. See how great his goodness is! As a friend to a friend, he now shares with the righteous man the punishment he is about to bring on the human race, and says: "The time of every man has come before me, for the earth is filled with injustice by them. And behold, I am destroying them and the earth." What does "The time of every man has come before me" mean? I have shown great long-suffering, he says, and great forbearance, because I did not wish to bring the punishment that I am about to bring. But the great excess of their sins has brought them to the appointed time itself. An end must now be put to them, and their wickedness must be cut off so that it goes no further. "For the time," he says, "of every man has come before me." See here too how he speaks: just as he said above, "Everyone devises," so now he says, "of every man." For all of them with one accord deserted to lawlessness, he says, and in so great a multitude one cannot find anyone who takes account of virtue. "For the time," he says, "of every man has come before me." "The time" means that the time has arrived when the incision must be made and the spreading of the ulcer checked. "The time of every man has come before me." They gave themselves up to lawless deeds as though no one were watching or about to demand an account of their offences. They did not consider that it is impossible to escape my notice, I who grant the very substance of life, who gave body and soul, and who supplied so many good things. "The time, then, of every man has come before me." Then, as if justifying himself to the righteous man, and showing that the excess of their sins is what calls him to this indignation, he says, "For the earth is filled with injustice by them." For have they left out anything that leads to wickedness? he says. Their wickedness grew so great that it now overflows, and the whole earth is filled with it. "That is why I am destroying both them and the earth. And behold," he says, "I am destroying them and the earth." Since they first destroyed themselves by their lawless deeds, I am bringing utter ruin on them and wiping out both them and the earth. That way the earth can receive a kind of cleansing and be purified of the filth of so many sins. Consider for me, then, what kind of

[?] …a flood of water to destroy all flesh in which there is the breath of life under heaven. "And the cattle," he says, "and the birds, and the wild beasts, and the four-footed creatures, and all that is under heaven will be destroyed." And so that you may learn that nothing will be left, he says, "And all that is on the earth shall die." For the world now needs a cleansing. But do not let this trouble you or confuse your thoughts. I see that their sore is incurable, and I wish to stop the streams of wickedness so that they do not make themselves liable to greater punishments. So now too, true to his own loving-kindness and tempering indignation with goodness, he says: I am bringing a punishment of such a kind that it will be painless for them and they will not feel it. I am not looking at how great their sins are or at what they deserve. I am looking ahead to what will come after: I wish both to bring the fitting punishment on them and to free those who will come later from the corruption they would spread. So do not be downcast or alarmed when you hear these things. For even if a penalty worthy of their sins overtakes them, still, "I will establish my covenant with you." All who came before made themselves unworthy and were ungrateful toward my commandments, so now I will establish my covenant with you. The first-formed man, after so many benefits, let himself be deceived and broke my commandments. Then the one born of him slid down to the very bottom of wickedness, and so he received a lasting punishment along with the curse. Yet not even his punishments brought those after him to their senses. They went further still, so that they were even struck out of the genealogy. After this I found Enoch preserving the image of virtue, and because he pleased me so greatly I took him away alive. I did it to show those who pursue virtue what rewards they are counted worthy of, and because I wished to make those who came after him his imitators, walking the same road as he did. Now everyone has deserted to wickedness, and in so great a multitude I have found you alone able to make good the transgression of our forefather; so I will establish my covenant with you. For the way you have lived shows that you can be trusted to receive my commandments. Then, so that the righteous man would not still be despondent on hearing this, as if he alone were going to be left, God consoles him, so to speak, and says again: "You shall go into the ark, you and your sons, and your wife, and your sons' wives with you." For even if they fell far short of the righteous man's virtue, they were still free of the others' extreme wickedness. Besides, they enjoy salvation for these two reasons. The first is to honour the righteous man. For it is the custom of the loving God to honour his servants and often to grant them the salvation of others. He did this in the case of blessed Paul too, the teacher of the world, who sent out the rays of his teaching everywhere. When Paul was sailing to Rome, a great storm arose at sea. Everyone on the ship feared for their very lives and had no good hope because of the size of the waves. He called them all together and said: "Take heart, men. For there will be no loss of life among you, only of the ship. For there stood by me this night…" [Notes:] a Savile and others: "will be left remaining." b Morel: "to become his imitators."

…before me. This is true virtue: when someone shows it before God, when that unerring eye casts the verdict. Then the loving God teaches us the measure of virtue that he required from the righteous man at that time. For he does not wish the same measure of virtue to be brought by everyone; he looks for a different virtue as the times differ. He says, "For I have seen you righteous before me in this generation," a generation that has turned aside to so much wickedness, an evil generation that has shown such ingratitude. I saw you righteous; I found you alone grateful; I saw you taking great account of virtue. You alone appeared righteous before me while all these are perishing. I command you to go into the ark with all your household, and I bid you bring in seven of each of the clean cattle. Earlier he had commanded, without making any distinction, that one pair of every kind be brought in. That is why he now says, "Of the clean, seven by seven, and of the unclean, two by two, male and female." Then, teaching the reason, he added, "To keep seed alive over all the earth." Here it is worth investigating how the righteous man knew which animals were clean and which unclean. For this distinction, which Moses later laid down in law for the Jews, had not yet been made. How then did he know? From within himself, moved by the teaching stored up in nature, and reason prompted him as well. For nothing that comes from God is unclean. How could we call any created thing unclean, once the verdict from above has been passed on them and the divine Scripture has said, "God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good"? Rather, nature, moving of its own accord, made this distinction. To see that this is true, consider how even now in some places people abstain from certain things as unclean and not customary, while others eat those very things because custom leads them to. So then too, the knowledge stored up within taught the righteous man which animals were fit for food and which were unclean. They were not unclean in fact, only considered so. Tell me, why do we consider the donkey unclean, though it eats nothing but seeds, while we consider other four-footed animals fit for food, though they eat unclean food? In this way the knowledge that God supplied to nature became the teacher of these things. Alternatively, one can say that God, who gave the command, also made the knowledge of these things clear to him. But we have said enough about the clean and the unclean. 6. Another question now arises for us. Why two of each of the unclean animals, but seven of each of the clean? And again, why not six or eight, but seven? Perhaps our sermon is stretching on to great length. But if you are not tired and you wish it, we will briefly teach your love about these things too, as far as the grace of God allows. For many people tell many fables about these things, and use them as a starting point for displaying their superstitions about numbers. That it is not an observance, but the untimely curiosity of [?]… [Note:] Some read "about them," others "concerning them." [?] …but they also roused themselves at what was said, and such

…a turning from evil they made, and their confession was so thorough that they extended it even to the animals. Not that the animals confessed (how could creatures without reason do so?). They did it so that by this means they might draw the good Master to loving-kindness toward them. For it says that the king and those around him proclaimed a fast and commanded that the cattle, the oxen and all the animals should take neither pasture nor water. All humanity there put on sackcloth, and the king himself, who sat on the throne, joined them, and they made a great and fervent confession. And they did this without knowing that they would escape the punishment, for they said, "Who knows whether God will repent of the evil which he said he would do to us?" 7. Have you seen the good sense of barbarians? Have you seen how not even the shortness of the days made them hesitate or drove them to despair? But look at these people of Noah's time. After so many years they heard that in seven more days the flood would come, and even so they did not turn back, but remained unfeeling.
