So it must be agreed that our own free choice is the cause of all evils. For look: these were human beings, and those were human beings too, of the same nature but not of the same choice. That is why they did not meet the same fate. The Ninevites escaped destruction, because the good God, in his loving-kindness, was content with their repentance. The others were swept under the water and handed over to utter ruin. "For in seven more days," he says, "I will bring rain upon the earth." Then, wishing to increase their fear, he says, "forty days and forty nights." What then? If he had wished, could he not have brought all the rain in a single day? And why do I say a single day? In a single [?]… But he does this deliberately, wishing both to heighten their fear and to give them a chance to escape the punishment even when it stood at the very doors. "And I will blot out," he says, "every living thing that I have made from the face of the earth, from man to beast." See how he foretells it once and twice, and even so it does not reach them. He did all this to teach us that he was just to bring such a punishment on them. It was so that none of the foolish could find fault and say, "If he had been patient, perhaps they would have given up wickedness and returned to virtue." That is why he makes the number of years clear to us and commands the building of the ark. And after all this he also gives warning seven days ahead, to muzzle the shameless tongues of those who like to speak rashly. "And Noah did," it says, "all that the Lord commanded him." [?] See how now too the divine Scripture proclaims the good sense and obedience of the righteous man, teaching [?] that he left out none of the things commanded, fulfilling everything [?] of his own virtue, and through this the [?]…
8. Let us too, then, imitate this righteous man and fulfil the commandments given to us by God [?]… [Notes:] [?] "upon the wickedness." Savile: "eager to hunt."

…the present life [?] those endless ages. I know these words sting your ears, but forgive me. I say them because I long for your salvation. I would rather you were stung a little here and escaped eternal punishment than were entertained for a little while and suffered unending torment. For if you bear with my words and shake off your former despondency, you will be able to wash away your sins and draw great loving-kindness from God. This is especially true now, while this short time of holy Lent still remains to you. For the Master does not need many days or much time. If we are willing, we can correct many of our failings even in these two weeks. He granted the Ninevites such loving-kindness because they showed repentance for three days. Much more, then, will he not overlook us, if only we show true repentance, turn away from wickedness and take the road that leads to virtue. For the divine Scripture bears witness about the Ninevites and says, "God saw that each of them turned from his evil way." If, then, he sees that we too have gone over to virtue, turning away from wickedness and hurrying to do good works, he will accept our return as well. He will free us from the burdens of our sins and grant us his gifts. For we do not desire release from our sins and long for salvation as much as he hurries and presses to give us that release and let us enjoy salvation. So I beg you, let us rouse our minds, and let each one examine himself. Has he achieved anything more in the time that has passed? Has he gained any benefit from this constant teaching? Has he reaped anything toward his neighbour's improvement? Has he corrected any of his own faults? Has he received any encouragement toward the life of wisdom from our daily exhortation? Let him look for ways to add to what he has already achieved, and never stop this good work. But someone may see that he is held fast by his habits and persists in the same faults. Let him do violence to his own mind and make it pay the penalty for such great negligence. Let him not allow himself to go any further. Let him halt the course of his bad habit here, cut off the impulse and rein in his thoughts. Let him bring himself to think of that fearful day. Let him reflect on the enjoyment of this awesome table, the brightness of the fire that leaps out from it and its burning power. Let him consider what kind of mind it requires in the one who approaches: pure of all filth and every stain, and shunning the company of improper thoughts. Then, having prepared ourselves in this way during these intervening days and cleansed ourselves as far as we can, we may be able to share in the enjoyment that comes from it. We may also be counted worthy of those ineffable good things which he has promised to those who love him, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit [?]… [Notes:] Savile conjectures "negligence." The same editor has "push away" in the text and "shake off" in the margin. Savile: "mind, let him exact a penalty for such great negligence, nor let him allow…" Two manuscripts: "mind. Let him not exact a penalty for such great negligence, and let him not allow…"

…because they are flesh. In this way he warned them in advance how great his indignation would be. Then, to give them enough time to change and escape the experience of his indignation, he says: "Yet their days shall be a hundred and twenty years." That is: I will still be patient after the five hundred years. For during those five hundred years this righteous man never stopped reminding them all by his very name, and urging them, if they were willing to pay heed, to turn away from wickedness and go over to virtue. "Nevertheless," he says, "even now I promise to be patient for a further hundred and twenty years, so that, using the time in between as they ought, they may flee wickedness and lay hold of virtue." And he was not content with the promise of the hundred and twenty years. He also commands the righteous man to build an ark, so that the very sight of the ark might again give them a sufficient reminder, and no one might be unaware how great the punishment about to be brought would be. For this alone was enough to throw everyone who had any sense into anguish and fear, and to persuade them to appease so gentle and loving a Master: that this righteous man, who had reached the extreme of old age, was showing such zeal over building the ark. For if those barbarians — the Ninevites, I mean; for it is necessary to bring them forward again, so that in this way the surpassing wickedness of the one group and the great good sense of the other may be shown all the more clearly… For indeed our Master, on that fearful day, the day of judgment I mean, brings servants forward alongside servants and so pronounces condemnation, when it is shown that those who enjoyed the same things and shared in the same things did not pursue the same virtue. And often he even makes comparisons between unequal cases, so as to bring a heavier condemnation on the negligent. That is why he said in the Gospels: "The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and look, something greater than Jonah is here." It is as if he were saying: the barbarians, who enjoyed no care, who heard no prophetic teaching, who saw no signs and beheld no miracles, but heard only the words of one man rescued from a shipwreck — words that could have driven them to utter despair and thrown them into helplessness, so that they might even have disregarded what he said — not only did not despise the prophet's words, but, though confined to the narrow span of three days, showed a repentance so exact and so intense that they caused the Master to revoke his sentence. "These, then," he says, "will condemn this generation, which has enjoyed so much care, which has been nourished on the prophetic books, which sees signs and wonders every day." Then, to show the excess of these people's unbelief and the unspeakable good sense of the others, he added: "Because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and look, something greater than Jonah is here." "Those people," he says, "saw in Jonah a lowly man, and yet they received his preaching and showed a most exact repentance; but these, who [?] much…" [?]

…sins they might make themselves liable to a heavier punishment. So the good and loving Master, seeing their impenitence, cut short the time during which he had promised to be patient. For just as, in the case of those who show good sense, he revokes his sentences because of the goodness that belongs to him, welcomes them when they change, and frees them from the punishment hanging over them, so again, whenever he promises to grant some good things or a period for repentance, but sees that people have become unworthy, then too he revokes his promises. That is why he also said through the prophet: "At one moment I will speak against nations and against kingdoms, to destroy and to tear down; and if they repent, I too will repent of what I said I would do to them." And again: "At one moment I will speak concerning nations and kingdoms, to build up; and if they sin, I too will repent of what I said I would do to them." Do you see how he takes from us the occasions both for the love he shows us and for his indignation? That is why now too, since they did not use the extension of time as they ought, he cuts the time short. That is also why blessed Paul said to those who were callously disposed and would not accept the salvation given us through repentance: "Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is leading you to repentance? By your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God's righteous judgment." Do you see how this wonderful teacher of the world taught us clearly that those who do not use as they ought the patience of God granted us for repentance make themselves liable to a heavier penalty and punishment? That is why now too the loving God, as though making his defense and showing the reason why he brought the flood before the appointed time was completed, notes for us the number of the righteous man's years, and says: "Noah was six hundred years old." For those who would not change in a hundred years, what more would they have gained from the twenty years, except to add still more to their sins? Yet to show the surpassing measure of his unspeakable love and goodness, he did not refuse to announce the coming of the flood to them seven days beforehand, so that, pressed at least by the shortness of the time, they might show some change.

3. And see the Master's love, how in various ways, like an excellent physician, he treated their disease. Since their wounds were incurable, he granted them so long a period of grace, wishing that, coming to their senses at least through the length of time, they might make him revoke the sentence of his indignation. For it is always his custom, since he cares for our salvation, to foretell the punishments he is about to bring, and for this reason alone: so that he may not bring them. If he had wanted to bring them, he would not have spoken of them. But he foretells them on purpose, so that we, learning of them and brought to our senses by fear, may turn aside his indignation and make his sentences void. For nothing delights him so much as our conversion and our return from wickedness to virtue. Consider, then, how he treated their disease too: first by giving them so long a period for repentance, then, since… [Note: Morel reads "to work." Savile and others [?] …]

…of Noah, and the three wives of his sons, and all the wild animals according to their kind, just as the Lord God had commanded Noah. When, it says, the flood began, according to the Master's command, Noah went into the ark with his sons and his wife and his sons' wives, and all the wild animals according to their kind. "And the Lord God," it says, "shut the ark from outside him."

4. Consider here too how the language accommodates itself to us. "God shut the ark from outside him," to teach us that he placed the righteous man in great security. He added "shut" and "from outside" for this reason: so that the righteous man could not see the universal destruction taking place and suffer still greater anguish himself. For even as it was, when he reckoned up that terrible storm in his mind and pictured in his thoughts the destruction of the human race, the common end of all the irrational creatures — the annihilation, so to speak, of humans and beasts and of the earth itself — he was confounded and deeply troubled. For even though those who were perishing were wicked, the souls of the righteous are accustomed to show great sympathy whenever they see people being punished. You will find every one of the righteous and of the prophets making earnest supplication for them, as the patriarch did for Sodom, and as all the prophets constantly did. One of them said: "Alas, Lord, will you wipe out the remnant of Israel?" And another says: "Will you make human beings like the fish of the sea, which have no leader?" Since, then, even without seeing it, this righteous man was troubled in his thoughts and confounded in his mind, God shuts him in the ark as in a prison, so that the sight and spectacle might not throw him into still greater anguish, and so that he would not see with his eyes what was happening and be seized by fear. For it was likely that, seeing the flood of waters, he would be anxious that he too would be submerged. So the loving God, caring for him, does not allow him even to watch the rush of the waters, or to see the destruction taking place and the ruin of the whole world. As for me, when I reckon up how this righteous man lived in the ark, I am astonished and amazed, and again I ascribe everything to God's love. For if it had not been that love which gave strength to his mind and made what was hard easy, how, tell me, could he have endured being shut up there as in some jail and harsh prison? How, tell me, could he hold out against such a roaring of the waves? For if people on a ship, using a sail, and seeing the helmsman seated at the tiller and resisting the force of the winds with his skill, nevertheless die of fear when they see the violence of the waves, and fear, so to speak, for their very lives, what would one say about this righteous man? Being in the ark, as I said before, as in a prison, he was carried this way and that, unable to see the sky or lift his eyes anywhere else, but confined within and having nothing at all to look at that could bring him any comfort. For those who sail the sea, even when the waves rise high, can often look up at the sky, catch sight of a mountain peak, and spy a city far off… [Note: one manuscript reads "of the waters"; another "of the waves."]

…the world, and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith. Do you see how faith in God, like a secure anchor, prepared him both to build the ark and to endure living in it? For this was the ground of his salvation. "Through it," it says, "he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith" — not because he himself passed judgment, but because the Master brings condemnation by comparison. For though they had enjoyed the same things as the righteous man, they did not walk the same road of virtue as he did. So by the faith he displayed he condemned those who displayed great unbelief and did not believe the warning. For my part, together with everyone, I am astonished both at the righteous man's virtue and at the Master's goodness and unspeakable love, when I consider how he was able to live among the wild beasts — lions, I mean, and leopards and bears and the rest of the savage and untamed creatures. Recall for me here, beloved, the dignity that the first-formed man enjoyed before the disobedience, and consider God's goodness. For since Adam's transgression had mutilated the authority given to him, but the good Master found another man able to restore the original image, who preserved the features of virtue and showed great obedience to the commandments, he raises him again to that original honor, as if teaching us by the facts themselves how great was the authority Adam had before the disobedience. So the righteous man's virtue, laying hold of God's love, restored the former rule, and the beasts once again acknowledged their subjection. For wherever wild beasts see a righteous man, they forget their own nature — or rather not their nature, but their ferocity; and while they remain in their nature, he changes their ferocity into gentleness. See this happening in the case of Daniel. Surrounded by lions, as though escorted by sheep, he spent his time there without fear; for the righteous man's boldness bridled the nature of the beasts and did not allow them to behave like beasts. In the same way this wonderful man bore his life among the beasts with ease. Neither the cramped space, nor the length of time, nor being shut in like this without even breathing the open air, made him grow numb; but through his faith in God everything seemed light to him, and he lived in that harsh prison as we do in meadows and wooded places. For the Master's command made the hardships seem easy to him. Such is the way of the righteous: whenever they endure something for his sake, they do not look at the outward appearance of what happens, but, reckoning the cause, they bear everything with ease. Paul too, the teacher of the Gentiles, called the prisons, the arrests, the daily dangers, all those many unbearable afflictions, light — not because they were such by nature, but because the cause of what was happening gave him such a disposition that he did not even turn to look at the terrible things that came upon him. Listen to him saying: "For our momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure." "The expectation," he says, "of the glory that is going to come upon us, and of that unending rest, lightly us [?]…" [Note: Morel reads "was preparing." Others, with the biblical text: "and it covered everything."]

…birds of the sky, and all that lived in the mountains — wild beasts, I mean, and other irrational animals. That is why it says: "And it rose fifteen cubits above the mountains," so that you may learn that the Master's sentence was carried out in fact. For he had said: "Yet seven days, and I will bring a flood upon the earth, and I will wipe out every living thing that I have made from the face of the earth, from human being to beast, and from creeping things to the birds of the sky." So divine Scripture recounts these things not simply to teach us how high the waters rose, but so that along with this we may see that nothing at all was left — no irrational creature, no wild beast, no cattle — but everything was wiped out together with the human race. Since all these had been brought into being for humanity's sake, when humanity was about to be destroyed, they too fittingly shared in its destruction. Then, having taught us to what height the waters rose, and that they topped the mountain peaks by another fifteen cubits, Scripture, true to its own precision, says again: "And all flesh that moved on the earth died, of birds and of wild beasts, and every creeping thing that moves on the earth, and every human being, and everything that has the breath of life — all that was on the dry land died." It was not idly that it added the hint, "all that was on the dry land," but to teach you that all perished, and the righteous man alone was saved, together with all those in the ark. For they had gone ahead, in obedience to God's instruction, left the dry land and taken up their dwelling in the ark. "And he wiped out every living thing that was on the face of all the earth, from human being to beast, and creeping things and birds of the sky; and they were wiped out from the earth." See how once, twice and many times it teaches the universal destruction that took place, and that nothing that existed escaped, but all were drowned by the waters, both the human race and the irrational creatures. "And Noah alone was left," it says, "and those with him in the ark. And the water rose upon the earth for a hundred and fifty days." For that many days, it says, the water remained at its height. Consider here again the righteous man's greatness of soul and his surpassing courage. What must he not have suffered, picturing in his mind and seeing, so to speak, in his thoughts the bodies of human beings and of cattle, clean and unclean, which had suffered a common death and were mingled together with no distinction at all? And again, after this, when he reckoned up his own situation — the solitude, the desolation, that painful existence, with no comfort from anywhere, not from company, not from anything to see, not even knowing exactly how long he would have to endure life in that prison? For as long as the crashing and roaring of the waters went on, it produced in him a fear that grew stronger every day. For what good could he reasonably expect, seeing the waters remain unchanged for a hundred and fifty days, rising higher and not abating in the least? Yet he bore it nobly, knowing the Master's resourcefulness, and that, being the creator of nature, he does all things and transforms them as he wills; and he did not chafe at his life there. For the influence of God… [Note: Savile in the margin: "for so many days, he says." [?] … "against the assault of the enemy." Others read: "against the multitude of the enemy."]

…the daily [?]: "The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed to us." "Even if every day," he says, "we were to give ourselves up to death — which nature does not allow, though the will that conquers nature is crowned through the Master's love — we endure nothing worthy of the good things that will await us, and of the glory that is going to be revealed to us." See how great is the glory enjoyed by those who pursue virtue: it surpasses everything that anyone could ever display. For even if one reaches the very summit, one still falls short. For what could a human being display that would be great enough to contend worthily for the Master's generosity? If Paul, so great and so eminent, said, "The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed to us" — he who said, "I die every day," and again, "I have labored more than all of them" — what shall we say, who are unwilling to undertake even the slightest toil for virtue, but always pursue ease and keep looking for ways to avoid any experience of hardship, and that while knowing that it is impossible to obtain the rest of the world to come in any other way, unless we have first desired here a life of struggle? For these afflictions win for us God's favor, and a little toil here grants us great confidence there, if only we are willing to walk according to the counsel of this teacher of the world. Consider, beloved, that even if what befalls us is painful, it is temporary, while the good things that will receive us there are immortal and eternal. "For the things that are seen," he says, "are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal." Let us, then, bear the temporary things nobly and not grow weary in the labors of virtue, so that we may enjoy the eternal and everlasting good things. May we all attain them, by the grace and love of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, power and honor to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

HOMILY [?]

"And God remembered Noah, and all the wild animals, and all the cattle, and all the birds, and all the creeping things that were with him in the ark. And God brought a wind upon the earth, and the water subsided."

1. Great and unspeakable is the love of God shown in the passage just read, and the surpassing measure of his goodness, which he shows not only toward this rational creature — the human being, I mean — but also toward the nature of the irrational animals. For since he is the creator of all things, he extends his goodness to everything he has created, showing us through all things how much providential care he takes of the human race, and that from above and from the beginning he arranged everything for our salvation. So whether he chastises or punishes, he does both out of the same goodness. For he does not inflict punishments out of passion and anger, but because he wishes to cut wickedness short and keep it from advancing too far. So now too, as you hear, he brought the flood for no other reason than his care for those who had given themselves up to such wickedness. "And what sort of care," someone says, "is it for everyone to be destroyed by the waters?" Do not speak thoughtlessly, [my friend?]…

After these things had happened, the one born of him (Cain, I mean) saw with his own eyes his father's expulsion from paradise, his fall from that indescribable glory, and the weight of that curse which said, "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." Yet even so he was not brought to his senses, but entangled himself in still greater evils. If he had not seen what had befallen his father, to what lengths of madness would he not have gone? And the remarkable thing is that even when God punished this man, who had sinned so gravely and stained his right hand with an accursed murder, he mixed loving-kindness into the punishment.

2. You can learn the greatness of God's goodness from the way he dealt with Cain. When Cain insulted God himself, and showed great contempt in the sacrifice he was about to offer, not dividing it rightly but making his offering carelessly and at random, God said nothing harsh or severe to him. And yet the sin was no ordinary one; it was very great indeed. Among human beings, those who wish to honour their fellows give them the first and choicest things, and are eager to offer whatever seems most valuable of all. Should not a man, then, when he makes an offering to God, have offered the more valuable and choicest things? Yet although he had sinned so badly and shown such contempt, God exacted no penalty and inflicted no punishment for what had been done. Instead he spoke to him as a friend speaks to a friend, with all gentleness, saying: "You have sinned; be still." He only pointed out his sin to him and advised him not to go any further. Do you see the surpassing greatness of his goodness? But Cain not only gained nothing from such great forbearance; he added greater sins to the earlier ones and rushed on to the slaughter of his brother. Even so God showed him great patience, first questioning him and giving him room to defend himself. But when he persisted in his shamelessness, then God brought the punishment upon him to correct him, and even that punishment had much of God's loving-kindness mixed into it. Do you see how, when Cain sinned against God himself, and that with no ordinary sin, God let him go; but when he armed his right hand against his brother, then he received both rebuke and curse? Let us also act this way now and imitate our Master. Let us pass over the sins committed against us and forgive those who wrong us; but when a sin is aimed at God, then let us demand satisfaction. Yet somehow we do everything the opposite way. Sins that reach as far as God we make no effort at all to avenge, but if some trifling wrong is done to us, we become fierce investigators and accusers of it, not knowing that in this way we provoke our loving Master even more against ourselves. For it is God's custom often to let pass the sins committed against himself, but to avenge with great severity the sins committed against our neighbours. To see this, listen to blessed Paul when he says: "If any man has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, let him not divorce her. And if any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, let her not divorce him." Do you see how great the condescension is? Even if he is a pagan, Paul says, even if he is an unbeliever, as long as he accepts the marriage, do not reject him. And again: even if the wife happens to be a gentile, even if she is an unbeliever, as long as she wishes to live with you, do not drive her away. What…

…[?] forty nights, during which the torrent of waters poured down, and seeing the waters stay at the same level for a hundred and fifty days without abating at all. What was harder still, he could not even see with his own eyes what had happened. Shut in as he was, and unable to set before his sight from anywhere the calamities that had overtaken the world, he endured a greater anguish and pictured them each day as worse. For my part, I marvel that he was not swallowed up by despondency itself as he considered the destruction of the human race, his own solitude, and that harsh way of life. But the cause of all his blessings was his faith in God. Through it he held out and bore everything nobly, and nourished by hope he felt none of his hardships. Since, then, he had done his own part, had shown his patience, had brought abundant faith, and displayed great endurance, consider the great loving-kindness of the good God toward him. "And God remembered Noah," it says. Scripture did not say "And he remembered" idly. Earlier the divine Scripture had made known to us the testimony God gave about the righteous man when he said, "Enter the ark, for I have seen that you are righteous in this generation." That is why it now says, "And God remembered Noah": that is, he recalled the testimony he had given about him, and he did not overlook the righteous man for long. He was patient only as long as Noah could hold out, and then he granted him his own favour. For he knows the weakness of our nature, and whenever he allows some trial to come upon us, he lets it go on only as long as he knows we are able to bear it, so that he may grant us a sufficient reward for our endurance and also display his own loving-kindness. As Paul too says: "God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond what you are able, but with the testing he will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to bear it." Since, then, this righteous man had shown endurance and patience, putting up with his life in the ark through his faith in God, [248] "God remembered Noah," it says. Then, so that you may learn the bottomless depth of his loving-kindness, the divine Scripture adds: "and all the wild beasts, and all the cattle, and all the birds, and all the creeping things that were with him in the ark." See how he does everything out of honour for man. When human beings perished in the flood, he destroyed the whole race of irrational animals along with them; so here too, when he is about to show his loving-kindness to the righteous man, he extends his goodness, out of honour for Noah, to the irrational animals as well, to the wild beasts, the birds and the creeping things. "And God remembered Noah," it says, "and all the wild beasts, and all the cattle, and the creeping things, and all that were with him in the ark. And God brought a wind upon the earth, and the water subsided." Having remembered Noah, it means, and those who were with him in the ark, he ordered the torrent of waters to be checked. In this way he would show his loving-kindness little by little, let the righteous man breathe again at last, free him from the turmoil of his thoughts and bring him into calm, granting him the enjoyment of light and the breath of the open air. "And God brought," it says, … [Note: One manuscript reads: consider how great.]

…for it is one of the clean animals. "And he sent out the dove from him," it says, "to see whether the water had subsided from the face of the earth. And the dove, finding no rest for its feet, returned to him into the ark, because there was water over the whole face of the earth." Here it is worth asking how the holy Scripture, having said above that the tops of the mountains appeared, now says that the dove found no rest and returned to him into the ark because the water was over the whole face of the earth. Let us read the passage carefully and we shall see the reason. It did not simply say "finding no rest"; it added "for its feet." It did so to teach us that, although the waters had partly receded and the tops of the mountains had appeared, even the mountaintops were still muddy from the great mass of water, or covered with swampy slime. So the dove could not find anywhere to stand or any suitable food, and it returned, teaching the righteous man by its return that the waters were still running high. "And stretching out his hand," it says, "he took it and brought it in to himself into the ark." Do you see how sensible the bird was? By coming back and being present it taught the righteous man to show [250] a little more patience. And so: "And having waited yet seven more days, he sent out the dove from the ark again. And the dove returned to him toward evening, and it had an olive leaf, a twig, in its mouth." The words "toward evening" are not set down here idly or at random. They are there so that we may learn that the dove had fed throughout the whole day, and having found suitable food, it came back toward evening carrying an olive twig in its mouth. For this is the nature of the creature: it is tame and always seeks out what it is used to. That is why it returned, and with the olive twig it brought the righteous man great comfort. But someone may perhaps ask: where did it find the olive leaf? The whole thing came about by God's providence: that the leaf was found, and that the dove took it in its mouth and came back to the righteous man. Besides, the tree is evergreen, and it is likely that when the waters receded the tree still had its crown of leaves. "And having waited yet another seven days," it says, "he sent out the dove, and it did not return to him again." See how the righteous man received ample comfort at every turn. When the dove came back carrying the olive leaf in its mouth, he had good hopes; so now, when it went out and did not return, this gave him the strongest proof that it had found plenty of relief and that the waters had completely ceased. And to see that this is true, listen to what follows: "And it came to pass in the six hundred and first year of Noah's life, in the first month, that the water failed from the face of the earth. And Noah uncovered the roof of the ark that he had made, and saw that the water had failed from the face of the earth."

5. Here again I find myself marvelling and astonished at both the virtue of the righteous man and the loving-kindness of God. Tell me, how was it that after so long a time, when he came out into the open air and raised his eyes to look at the sky, he was not blinded and his eyesight was not damaged? For you know, you know, that this especially… [Note: ³ Others read "to display." Patrologia Graeca 53.]

…[?] the gratitude of the righteous man. With this we bring our discourse to an end, and we urge you, beloved, to keep turning this blessed man over in your minds continually, to study the beauty of his virtue carefully, and to become his imitators. Consider, I ask you, how great the wealth of his virtue is: we have been recounting his story for so many days now, and even today we have not yet [252] been able to bring our treatment of him to a close. And why do I speak of bringing it to a close? However much we say, we cannot reach the end. Even if we were able to say a great deal, and those after us as well, we still could not arrive at the end; so great a thing is virtue. If we are willing, this man will be able to instruct our whole nature and lead it to zeal for virtue. For when this righteous man, living among so many wicked people and unable to find anyone of like mind, was found to have reached such a measure of virtue, what defence shall we have, who face no such obstacles and yet are lazy about achieving it? Do not tell me only of his life over those five hundred years, how he was continually mocked and ridiculed by those who pursued wickedness; consider also his stay in the ark. That one year seems to me to weigh as much as all the rest of his life. So great was the affliction the righteous man was forced to endure there: he was in such cramped quarters that he could hardly breathe, he put up with living alongside wild beasts and irrational animals, and through it all he showed the firmness of his mind, the steadfastness of his will, and the faith he had in God, through which he bore everything calmly and lightly. That is exactly why, since he had contributed everything on his part, he also enjoyed God's gifts in abundance. For though he endured great hardship while living in the ark, he nevertheless escaped that terrible deluge and that universal destruction. And so, after that hardship and that unbearable prison, he enjoyed security and relief, was counted worthy of God's blessing, and in turn fulfilled his own gratitude through his deeds. Everywhere you will find that the first step came from him. In his early years he pursued virtue throughout and kept himself apart from the wickedness of those people, and so he did not share their punishment; while all the rest were drowned, he alone was saved. So too, since he brought great faith and endured his life in the ark with thanksgiving, God's gifts followed in turn with great generosity. Brought out of the ark and restored to his former way of life, he was at once counted worthy of a blessing; and when he again showed his own gratitude and gave thanks as best he could, he was then counted worthy of still greater gifts from the loving God. For this is God's custom: whenever we offer him something small and paltry, provided only that we do offer it, he bestows great generosity on us in return. And so that you may learn both how utterly paltry human offerings are and how generous your Master is, consider this. Even if we want to offer something, what more can we do than show our thanks in words? But his gifts to us are carried out in deeds. How then could [we] equal… [Note: [?] manuscripts: "thus we shall be able to instruct."]

…[?] wishing. Among human beings, the thanks given to benefactors makes them more illustrious; but with the loving God, when we give thanks, it is ourselves we make more illustrious. For he does not want this to happen because he needs our praise, but so that the profit may come back around to us and we may make ourselves worthy of greater help. It is true that we can never do this as he deserves; how could we, bound as we are to so weak a nature? And why do I speak of human nature? Not even the bodiless and invisible powers, the principalities and the authorities, the cherubim and the seraphim, will be able to offer him the glory he deserves when they give thanks. Still, it is right to offer thanks as best we can, and to glorify our Master continually, both by words of praise and by the best way of life. For praise becomes most splendid when we offer up glory through countless tongues. The virtuous man leads everyone who looks at him to sing hymns to his Master, and the glory they give wins for the one who caused it great and indescribable favour from the Master. What, then, could be more blessed for us than this: not only to glorify the good God with our own tongues, but also to rouse all our fellow human beings to give glory on our account? So great is the power of virtue that it can praise the Creator with countless mouths. Nothing could equal the best way of life, beloved. That is why the Lord said, "Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." Do you see how, just as light drives away the darkness when it appears, so virtue, when it is seen, puts wickedness to flight, drives away the darkness of error, and moves the minds of those who see it to give glory? Let us strive, then, to make our works shine so that our Master may be glorified. Christ did not say this so that we would do anything for show (God forbid!), but so that, living carefully and as he wishes, we may give no occasion for blasphemy, and by doing good works may lead those who see us to glorify the God of all. Then, yes then, we shall draw his favour on us in greater measure, and we shall be able to escape punishment and to obtain the ineffable blessings, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus [255] Christ, with whom to the Father together with the Holy Spirit be glory, power and honour, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

"And Noah built an altar to the Lord, and took of all the clean cattle and of all the clean birds, and offered a whole burnt offering on the altar."

1. Yesterday you saw the goodness of our loving Master: how he brought the righteous man out of the ark, freeing him from his life there and releasing him from that harsh and strange prison, and how he repaid him for his patience by saying, "Increase and multiply." Today let us learn about Noah's gratitude and his thankful soul, through which he once more called forth God's favour toward him in fuller and far greater measure. For that is what God is like: whenever he sees, for the…

…to undergo all that is ours, so that he might raise our nature, which lay somewhere down below under the mass of its sins, from earth to heaven. Astonished at this, the son of thunder, thinking about the surpassing greatness of the love God showed to the human race, cried out and said: "For God so loved the world." See how full of wonder the phrase is. He says "so" because he was weighing the greatness of what he was about to say; that is why he began this way. Tell us, then, blessed John: "so" — how? Tell us the measure, tell us the greatness, teach us how far it surpasses all. "For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." Do you see that this was the reason for the Son's coming: that those who were going to perish might find a way to salvation through faith in him? What could anyone think when he considers that great and wonderful generosity, which surpasses all words, that he bestowed on our nature through the gift of baptism, granting us release from all our offences? But what am I to say? The mind is not equal to it, nor does speech have the strength to count up the rest. However much I say, what remains is so great that it outstrips what has already been said. What, then, could anyone think of the way of repentance which, in his indescribable loving-kindness, he granted our race, and the wonderful commandments given after the gift of baptism, through which, if we wish, we shall be able to draw his favour upon us?

2. [257] Do you see, beloved, the bottomless depth of his benefits? Do you see how many we have counted, and yet we have not been able to tell even the smallest fraction of them? For how will a human tongue be able to recount in words what God has done for us? Yet many and great as these are, far greater and more ineffable still are the benefits he has promised in the age to come, after our departure from here, to those who walk the road of virtue. And to show us their surpassing greatness in a few words, blessed Paul says: "What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him." Do you see how surpassing his gifts are? Do you see that his benefits go beyond all human thought? "It has not entered into the human heart," he says. If, then, we are willing to consider these benefits and to give thanks as best we can, we shall be able to draw his favour on us all the more and to be roused more strongly to virtue. For the memory of his benefits is enough to urge us on to the labours of virtue, to make us disregard all present things, to set us longing for the one who has done us so much good, and to make us show our love for him at its height every day. That is why this righteous man enjoyed so much favour and honour from above: because he showed great gratitude for the benefits he had already received. But to make our discourse clearer, I must set before you, beloved, the very beginning of today's reading. When he had come out of the ark at the Master's command, with his sons, his wife, his sons' wives, and all the wild beasts and the birds, and had received from God … [?] the fragrant aroma.

That is why blessed Paul [?] … cheaper than a cup? Yet the intention [?] the reward for him. [?] calls it a sign, saying: "And he gave the sign of circumcision, a seal." To show that circumcision contributes nothing toward righteousness, look: this righteous man also reached such great virtue before circumcision had been made law. And why do I say this? The patriarch Abraham himself was justified by faith alone before he received circumcision. For before circumcision, it says, "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Why then are you so proud of circumcision, you Jew? Learn that many were righteous before it. Abel made his offering by faith, as Paul also says: "By faith Abel offered God a greater sacrifice than Cain." Enoch was taken up. Because of his great righteousness, Noah escaped that terrible [259] flood. And Abraham was proclaimed righteous for his faith in God before circumcision. So from the very beginning the human race obtained salvation by faith. This is also why the loving Lord allowed sacrifices to be offered to him. Our nature was still rather imperfect, and he wanted it both to be able to show its own gratitude and to escape entirely the ruin of idol worship. For if most people did not escape that fall even after so great a condescension, how could anyone have escaped the harm it brings if this had not been done? "And the Lord God smelled a pleasing odor." But it was not so with the ungrateful Jews. How was it then? Hear the prophet saying, "Incense is an abomination to me." He all but points to the wickedness in the intention of those who offered it. Here the virtue of the righteous man made the smoke and the savor of burning fat a pleasing odor. In the same way, with them the wickedness of those offering it caused the fragrant incense to be smelled as an abomination. So, I beg you, let us strive in every case to show a sound intention, for this is the cause of all good things. The good Lord does not usually pay attention to what we do so much as to the inner thought from which we start when we do it. He looks at that, and so either accepts what we do or turns away from it. So whether we pray, or fast, or give alms (for these are our spiritual sacrifices), or carry out any other spiritual work, let us do it from a sound intention, so that we may also receive a crown worthy of our labors. It would be utterly absurd for us to endure the toil and yet be deprived of the reward because we did not pursue virtue according to the laws he has given. Indeed, it is possible, truly possible, through God's inexpressible love for humankind, to receive the crown from intention alone, even without having done the deed. To learn this, consider almsgiving. Suppose you see someone lying in the marketplace, gripped by extreme poverty. You share his pain, and lifting your mind to heaven you give thanks to the Lord for your own circumstances and for the poor man's endurance. Then even if you cannot help him or relieve his hunger, you have received the full reward for your intention. This is why the Lord said: "Whoever gives just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, truly I tell you, he will not lose his reward." What [is cheaper] than cold [?] … (Other manuscripts read "to appear.")

… to the righteous man, but out of his own goodness also to all of human nature that was yet to come [261] into being. For the words "I will not again strike all living flesh," and "as I have done," and "all the days" show that there will never again be such a flood, and that such total destruction will never again overtake the world. Then comes the permanence of his kindness: "In all the days," he says. That is, I promise for all time never again to show such anger, nor to throw into such confusion the balance of the seasons and the order of the elements. That is why he added: "Seed and harvest, cold and heat, summer and spring, day and night shall not cease." This order, he says, will remain unshaken. The earth will never stop supplying the human race with what it produces, or repaying people for their labor and farming. The turning of the seasons will not be disturbed. Cold and heat, summer and spring will come in every yearly cycle. At the time of the flood this whole order was thrown into a kind of confusion, and this righteous man spent the entire time in the ark as if it were a single night. That is why he says: now neither day nor night will fail to keep its own course, and their service will remain unshaken until the end of the age. Do you see a consolation sufficient and able to lift the righteous man's spirits? Do you see what a reward gratitude receives? Hear his inexpressible generosity once more from what follows. "And God blessed Noah and his sons," it says, "and said to them: Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and rule over it. And the dread and fear of you shall be upon all the wild animals of the earth, and upon all the birds of the sky, and upon all that move on the earth, and upon all the fish of the sea. I have given everything into your hands. And every creeping thing that lives shall be food for you. I have given you everything, as I gave the green plants. Only you shall not eat flesh with the blood of its life." Here it is right to marvel at the surpassing goodness of the Lord. See how this righteous man is again counted worthy of the same blessing as Adam, and recovers the dominion that had been taken away, through his own virtue, or rather through the Lord's inexpressible love for humankind. For just as he said in Adam's case, "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and rule over it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and the creeping things, and the birds of the sky, and the wild animals of the earth," so now he says: "And the dread and fear of you shall be upon all the wild animals of the earth, and upon all the birds. And every creeping thing that lives shall be food for you. I have given you everything, as I gave the green plants. Only you shall not eat flesh with the blood of its life." See how the same rule given to the first-formed man is kept here in another form. There, after entrusting him with dominion over everything and granting him the enjoyment of what was in paradise, God commanded him to keep away from one tree only. In the same way here, after the blessing, after making him fearsome to the [262] wild animals, and after putting all the winged creatures and birds under his hand, he says: "Every living creeping thing shall be food for you. I have given you everything, as I gave the green plants." Here the eating of meat begins, not so that into glutton[y] …

… "and multiply, and fill the earth and rule over it." He did not simply say, "But you." It is almost as if he were saying: you few, you who can easily be counted, fill the whole earth and rule over it. That is, you have the dominion, the authority and the enjoyment. See God's love for humankind. First he bestows great benefits, and only then does he give a law and a commandment. With Adam, he first settled him in paradise and granted him such great enjoyment, and only then commanded him to abstain from the tree. In the same way here, he first did a number of things. He promised never again to bring such total destruction or show such anger, but to let all the elements remain unshaken until the end, each completing its own course and keeping its own order. He counted them worthy of blessing, granted them the ancient authority over all irrational creatures, and gave them permission to eat meat. Only then does he say, "Only you shall not eat flesh with the blood of its life." Do you see how he first does good, displaying his inexpressible generosity, and only then gives commands? This would never happen among human beings. People first want their orders carried out. They want those who receive the orders and fulfill them to show great goodwill, and only then do they reward those who have shown great obedience. With the common Lord of all it is the opposite. First he does good and draws our nature to himself by the abundance of his benefits. Only then does he give light and easy commands, so that, roused both by how easy the commands are and by the benefits we have received, we may hurry to fulfill them. 5. So, beloved, let us not grow careless or more sluggish in obeying what has been commanded. Let us think about the benefits we have received, how easy the commands are, and the greatness of the promises stored up for us once we fulfill them. Let us be sober and eager to carry out the commandments God has given us. Let us not throw away the paths he has granted our nature, which lead to the salvation of our souls. Instead, let us use the time of life that remains to us as we ought, wash away our sins, and lay up for ourselves [264] great confidence before God. Let us do this above all now, while what remains of holy Lent is still before us. 6. For the number of days remaining is not small, if we are willing to come to our senses a little. I have said this not because the correction of our sins needs only so much time. I said it because we have a Lord who loves humankind and is gentle, and who does not need a long time. We need only approach him with great fervor and [?], withdrawing from our whole former way of life and fixing ourselves to the help that comes from above. The Ninevites were weighed down by so many sins, yet because they practiced a great and earnest repentance, they needed no more than three days to call forth God's goodness and make void the sentence pronounced against them. And why do I speak of the Ninevites? The thief on the cross did not need even one day. And why do I say one day? He did not need even a short hour. So great is God's love for us. For when he sees the intensity of our … (Savile conjectures "to settle" him.)

… made to him the same plea that he too had made to the master, saying: "Be patient with me, and I will pay you back everything." "But he," it says, "went and threw him into prison" [?] … from those of our own kind), then we shall also draw down the anger … "until he should pay all that was owed to him." What excessive ingratitude! [?] … of the Lord, and the things whose forgiveness we previously … He still had fresh in his memory the great generosity shown to him, yet even so he could not bring himself to feel any compassion. Instead, first he was choking the man, and now he even threw him into prison. 7. But see what happens next. "When his fellow servants saw it," it says, "they were grieved, and they went and told their lord everything that had happened." It was not the man who had suffered who did this. How could he, shut up in prison? It was the fellow servants, who had not been wronged at all, who were as distressed as if they had been wronged themselves, and who went and reported everything. Now see the master's anger. "Then," it says, "he summoned him and said to him: You wicked servant." Here we can truly see how great a ruin it is to hold a grudge. When the man was scheming to escape his ten thousand talents, the master did not call him wicked. He did so now, when the man had been harsh toward his fellow servant. "You wicked servant," he says, "I forgave you all that debt because you begged me." See how he shows how extreme the man's wickedness was. Did you show me anything more? he says. Did you not use mere words? And did I not accept your plea and forgive that whole great and enormous debt? "Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" What [266] pardon could you deserve? I, your master, forgave so great a mass of debts because of those mere words. Yet you did not have mercy on your fellow servant, who is of your own kind. You were not moved. You did not remember what you had received from me and show him some compassion. You became merciless and cruel, and you refused to have mercy on your fellow servant. Therefore you will now learn by experience how many evils you have brought on yourself. "And his lord was angry and handed him over to the torturers." See him now angry because of the man's inhumanity toward his fellow servant, and handing him over to the torturers. What he did not do earlier, when the man was liable for such great debts, he now orders to be done. "He handed him over to the torturers until he should pay all that was owed." That is, until he pays back the ten thousand talents that he had already been forgiven when he went away. Great and inexpressible is God's love for humankind. When the man was scheming to escape his own debt, the master forgave him because he made his plea. But when he learned that the man had been cruel and inhuman toward his fellow servant, he then took back his own generosity. By the facts themselves he showed him that he had wronged himself more than the other man. Just as that man threw his fellow servant into prison until he should pay what was owed, so the master handed him over to the torturers until he should pay back the whole debt. He did not say these things simply about talents and denarii. The story is about sin and the greatness of our offenses. We are to learn that we owe the Lord the penalty for countless offenses, and yet through his inexpressible love for humankind we receive forgiveness from him. But suppose we become cruel and inhuman toward our fellow servants, those of our own kind who share the same nature with us. Suppose we do not forgive the offenses committed against us, but act wickedly over these trifles (for what are a hundred denarii compared to ten thousand ta[lents]?) [?] … ourselves through laziness of such great gifts and of the prizes

… that surpass all reason. Instead, let us strive in every way to achieve this, and let us force our reasoning and train it to yield to God's command. That is why I too have now given this exhortation and set the parable before you. I have shown how great this achievement is and how much profit comes to us from it, so that, while there is still time, each of us who has anyone hostile toward him may make every effort to win him over by much attentiveness and reconcile him to himself. And let no one say to me, "I pleaded once and twice, and he did not accept." If we do this sincerely, let us not [268] stop until we have overcome him by our persistence, drawn him to us, and turned him from his hostility toward us. Are we doing him a favor? The benefit passes to us. We win God's goodwill. We lay up forgiveness of sins for ourselves in advance. We gain great confidence before the Lord. If we achieve this, we will be able to approach this sacred and awesome table with a clean conscience, and to speak with confidence those words that are joined to the prayer. The initiated know what I mean. So I leave it to each one's conscience to know how, if we have fulfilled the commandment, we can say these words with confidence at that awesome moment. But if we are careless, how great a condemnation would come upon us! We would be acting against the very words while daring to utter the words of the prayer lightly and thoughtlessly. We would be heaping greater fire upon ourselves and calling down anger [?] … listening with pleasure to what is said, and showing by your applause that you are eager to be ready and to put this exhortation of the Lord into practice. This is the hospital of our souls, the medicine for our wounds, the best way of pleasing God. The greatest proof of a God-loving soul is this: to accept everything for the sake of the Lord's law, and not to be dragged down by the weakness of our thoughts, but to rise above the passions, keeping in mind the benefits God gives us each day. However much [zeal] we show, we will not be able to reach even the smallest part of what has already been given to us, what is done for us each day, and the good things stored up for us if we choose to carry out his commands. So let each of you, as you leave here, make this your task. Hurry as if to a very great treasure, and do not put it off even a little. Even if we must toil, or search, or travel a long road, even if there are difficulties, let us remove all these obstacles. Let us be intent on one thing only: how we can carry out the Lord's command and receive the reward of obedience. Do I not know that it seems heavy and burdensome to go to someone who is hostile and like an enemy toward you, and to stand there and talk with him? But if you consider the worth of the promise and the greatness of the reward, and that the benefit comes back not to him but to you, everything will seem light and easy to you. So let us turn these things over in our thoughts and overcome habit, and with pious reasoning [?] let us become people who fulfill the commands of Christ. Then we may be counted worthy of the rewards that come from him, by the grace and love for humankind of his goodness. With him, to the Father together with the Holy Spirit, be glory, power and honor, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen. Patrologia Graeca 53.

… and to entrust him with dominion over all irrational creatures, and to give him authority to eat them as freely as he ate green plants, and to command him not to eat flesh with its blood. Yet he was still caring for the righteous man and for those who would come after, and always lavishing kindness on our nature. So he adds still greater benefits and says: "And God said to Noah and to his sons with him: Behold, I establish my covenant with you and with your offspring after you, and with every living soul that is with you, the birds and the cattle, and all the wild animals of the earth that are with you, all that came out of the ark. And I will establish my covenant with you. All flesh shall never again die by the water of the flood, and there shall never again be a flood of water to destroy all the earth." The righteous man was probably still anxious, his mind still crushed by fear. If even a little rain ever happened to fall, he would be distraught and shrink back, as though such a flood were again overtaking the world. The good Lord knew that even some trifling thing that troubled him could throw him into turmoil, for the experience of what had happened was enough to instill great fear. Since this blessed man was likely to be terrified and afraid even of ordinary rain, the good God wanted him and all who came after him to be able to take courage. So, as if making him confident, freeing him from all fear and settling him in great security and good cheer, God promises him never again to bring such a punishment. 2. He had already promised this even before the blessing, saying, as you heard, "I will not again curse the earth." Even if people increase their wickedness, I will still never again subject the human race to such a penalty. To show his inexpressible love for humankind, he promises this again. He wants the righteous man to be confident, and not to reason within himself and say: "He had already counted our race worthy of a blessing and caused it to grow in number, and yet he brought this total destruction." So he wanted to drive all turmoil out of Noah's thoughts and assure him fully that this will never happen again. "Just as I brought the flood out of love for humankind," he says, "to cut short wickedness and stop them from going [271] further, so now, out of my own love for humankind, I promise never to do this again. Then you may live free of all despondency and so complete the present life." That is why he says, "Behold, I establish my covenant." That is, I make an agreement. In human affairs, when someone promises something, he makes an agreement and gives full assurance. In the same way the good Lord says, "Behold, I establish my covenant." And he said "I establish" well, meaning "Behold, I renew" [?] … the total destruction that came about through their transgressions, and "I establish my covenant with you and with your offspring after you." See the Lord's love for humankind. I do not set up the agreement only as far as you, he says. I declare it firm also for those who will be born after you. Then, to display his generosity, he says: "And with every living soul that is with you, the birds and the cattle, and all the wild animals of the earth that are with you, all that came out of the ark. And I will establish my covenant with you. All flesh shall never again die by the water of the flood, and there shall never again be a fl[ood] …" (Two manuscripts read "about to suffer such a thing." Shortly after, some [read] [?])

[?] the surpassing greatness of his [goodness]? "And there shall no longer be water for a flood, so as to wipe out all flesh": there shall never again be such a rain. Since he knows that human nature is afraid of this, see how he makes the promise again and again, all but saying: Even if you see a heavy downpour of rain, do not suspect anything so dreadful even then. For the water shall not become a flood to wipe out all flesh; there shall never again be such a rain; human nature shall never again experience such wrath. "And my bow," he says, "shall be in the cloud, and I will look upon it to remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living soul in all flesh." Consider how, wishing to bring human nature to confidence and full assurance, he uses such lowly language. "And I will look upon it," he says, "to remember my covenant." Does the sight, then, bring him to remembrance? Not so that we should suspect this (perish the thought!), but so that when we see this sign we may take courage in God's promise, since it is impossible for God's promises to fail. "And God said to Noah," it says, "This is the sign of the covenant which I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth." You have received, he says, the sign which I have given between me and all flesh that is on the earth. No longer be troubled in your mind or disturbed in your thoughts, [275] but look at this and have good hopes yourself. Let all who come after you enjoy the comfort it brings, and let the sight of the sign give them courage that no such deluge will ever again overtake the world. For even if people's sins increase, I will still fulfill what I have promised, and I will never again unleash such wrath against everyone. Do you see the surpassing goodness? Do you see the greatness of his condescension? Do you see the intensity of his care? Do you see the promise of his generosity? For he did not extend his kindness to two or three or ten generations; he promised that it would last as long as the world endures, so that we might be brought to our senses by both: by the punishment those people received for the multitude of their sins, and by the promise we have been granted through his unspeakable love for humankind. For those who have sense are drawn to obey the commandments by kindnesses even more than by punishments. Let us not, then, be ungrateful. For if, before we had shown anything good, or rather when we had done things that deserved punishment, he granted us such great kindness, what generosity will he not grant us in turn if we become grateful, show our thanks for what has gone before, and make a great change for the better? For if he does good to the unworthy and shows love to sinners, what shall we not obtain if we turn away from wickedness and pursue virtue? This is why he takes the initiative in bestowing many kindnesses on us, grants pardon again to those who have sinned, and does not bring punishment on us at once: so that he may draw us to himself by every means, both by his kindnesses and by his patience. And often, by punishing some, he wishes to lead others on, so that, brought to their senses by fear of what happened to those, they may escape experiencing the punishment themselves. Do you see his resourceful love for humankind, how everything he does is for this one purpose alone [?] [Other manuscripts: "the resourceful love of God for humankind."]

[?] neither the magnitude of the calamity made him restrain himself, nor the great confinement in the ark. Though the old man had not yet begotten children even then, this man gave himself over to incontinence. At a time when such wrath and such total destruction had overtaken the world, he was busy with intercourse and did not curb his unbridled desire; his disposition had been wicked from the very beginning and from the outset. Since, [275] then, Canaan his son was shortly to receive the curse because of the insult to his father, divine Scripture noted it in advance. It made known to us the name of the son, and with it the incontinence of the father, so that when you later see him showing great ingratitude toward his father, you may know that he had been like this from the very beginning, since not even the calamity humbled him. For such great dejection is enough to quench every pleasure, and nothing can so subdue this flame and this madness as intense dejection and extreme calamity. So the one who, amid evils so great, showed such frenzy and madness for begetting children, what pardon could he deserve?

But from this another question arises for us in turn, that much-discussed one which is bandied about everywhere: why, when the father sinned, does the son receive the curse? But so as not to make our discourse long now, we shall reserve this for the present, so that when we reach that very passage we may then offer the solution too, whatever God may grant. For, as I said before, nothing set down in divine Scripture can be found written without some reason and cause. For now, then, we have learned this: that it was not idly or by chance that Moses mentioned the son's name when he said, "And Ham was the father of Canaan." "These three," it says, "are the sons of Noah, and from them people were scattered over all the earth." Let us not pass over even what has just been said, beloved, but let us consider from this very statement the greatness of God's power. "These three," it says, "were the sons of Noah, and from them people were scattered over all the earth." How did so great a multitude grow from the three? How were they able to survive? How was the whole world established from these few? How did their bodies endure? There was no physician to give them treatment, nor any other care. For they had not yet even built cities. After such great hardship and their stay in the ark they came out as though pickled and worn out, and finding themselves in such isolation and unspeakable desolation, how were they not destroyed? How did they not perish? For tell me, did fear and anguish not shake their minds and throw their thoughts into turmoil? Do not be surprised, beloved: it was God who was working everything, it was the Creator of nature who removed all these obstacles, and that command of his which says, "Increase and multiply, and fill the earth," also granted them their increase. For the Israelites too, when they were worn down in Egypt by brickmaking and clay, increased all the more into a multitude for it; and neither that merciless and cruel command of Pharaoh ordering the males to be thrown into the river, nor the rest [?] … You, beloved, when you hear these things, do not attribute what happens to them, but to the grace from above which strengthens and anoints [?] [Variant: "had distributed cities."] [Some manuscripts: "it also"; others: "to them also."] Peter, when he set upright the man who had been lame from his mother's womb,

and restored him, while everyone was astonished and marveling at them, showed his own right-mindedness and said: "Men, why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?" Why, he says, were you so astounded, and why are you amazed at what has happened? Surely it is not we who did this, or who by our own power brought him back to health and enabled him to walk? Why do you stare at us? We contributed nothing more than lending our tongue; the one who did it all is the Lord and Creator of nature. He, "the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob," whom you claim as your patriarchs; he "whom you handed over and denied before Pilate, when he had decided to release him"; he it is who did these things: "whom you denied, the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you condemned the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead; of this we are witnesses. And by faith in his name, his name has made strong this man whom you see and know; and the faith that comes through him has given him this perfect health in the presence of you all."

6. Great indeed is this surpassing boldness; great and unspeakable is the power of the grace given them from above; the boldness of this blessed man would be the clearest proof of the resurrection. For what greater sign could anyone ask to receive than this? He who before the cross could not bear the threat of a lowly servant girl now rises up in this way against the Jewish populace. With such boldness, before so great a crowd and all alone, he strips for the contest against men raging so wildly, and utters things that could stir up their madness all the more. Do you see, beloved, how what I said at the outset is shown now as well? When someone is fired with longing for God, he no longer cares to look at the things that fall under these bodily eyes. Having acquired other eyes, I mean the eyes of faith, he always pictures those things and keeps his mind intent on them; and though he walks on earth, he does everything as one whose citizenship is in heaven, hindered by nothing human in the race of virtue. For such a person no longer sees the splendors of life, nor its hardships and adversities, but runs past them all, hastening toward his own homeland. Just as one who runs this bodily race with great intensity sees none [278] of those who meet him, even if he bumps into them countless times, but keeps his mind intent on the race, easily runs past everything and hastens toward the goal set before him, so in the same way the one who is eager to run the race of virtue and longs to ascend from earth to heaven leaves behind everything seen below and is wholly absorbed in the race. He does not stop, nor is he held back by any of the things he sees, until he is able to reach the very summit. For to one so disposed even the things that seem fearful in this present life become contemptible. Such a person fears neither sword, nor precipice, nor the teeth of wild beasts, nor tortures, nor the hands of executioners, nor anything else painful in this life. Even if he sees coals spread beneath him, he leaps upon them as if he were looking at meadows and gardens; and if he sees some other kind of punishment being brought against him, he does not grow numb before [?]

and let him listen to blessed Paul saying and urging, "So let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." Nor let anyone who has gone down to the very depths of wickedness despair of his own salvation; let him consider God's unspeakable love for humankind and hear God saying again through the prophet, "Shall the one who falls not rise again? Or shall the one who turns away not return?" And again: "I do not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live." Do you see, beloved, how each thing written in divine Scripture was handed down to memory for no other reason than for our benefit and the salvation of the human race? Bearing this in mind, let each of us take from it the remedies that suit him and apply them to himself. This is why they are set freely before everyone: anyone who wishes may apply the remedy suited to the passion troubling him and quickly regain health, provided only that he does not shake off the treatment of the healing art but shows his own good sense. For there is no passion besetting human nature, whether of soul or of body, that cannot receive healing from here. What do I mean? Tell me. Someone comes in here weighed down by grief and difficult circumstances, and so is buried in dejection. He comes in and at once hears the prophet saying, "Why are you so sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disquiet me? Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God." He goes away having received ample consolation and having shaken off all that dejection. Another, again, oppressed by extreme poverty, is distressed and frets [280] at seeing others overflowing with wealth, puffed up and surrounded with great pomp. He too hears the same prophet saying, "Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will sustain you"; and again: "Do not fear when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house increases, for when he dies he will take nothing with him." Another, again, enduring plots and slanders, is distressed and thinks life unlivable, since he can find no human help anywhere. He too is taught by this blessed prophet not to take refuge in human alliances in such circumstances, for he hears him saying, "They slandered me, but I prayed." Do you see where he seeks his ally? Others, he says, stitch together deceits and slanders and plots, but I flee to the impregnable wall, to the secure anchor, to the calm harbor, to prayer, through which all difficulties become light and easy for me. Another, again, is despised and neglected by those who once courted him, and abandoned by his friends, and this above all confounds and disturbs his mind. But he too, if he wishes, will come here and hear this blessed man saying, "My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me, and my nearest kin stood far off; and those who sought my life used violence, and those who sought my harm spoke vanities [?], and devised deceits all day long." Do you see them stitching together plots to the very point of death, and waging unceasing war? For "all day long" means throughout one's whole life. What then did he do while they were plotting and contriving these things? "But I," he says, "like a deaf man did not hear, and like [?]" [Some manuscripts: "my harm."] [?] [Some manuscripts: "… to be consumed" [?]]

[?] so that when we leave here we may have provisions for the journey, enough not only for ourselves but also to supply others, and be able to set right our wife, our servants, our neighbors, our friend, and even our enemy. For spiritual teachings are such that they are set before all in common, and there is no distinction among those who receive them, except where someone brings an intent mind and fervent zeal and so outstrips his neighbor. Since, then, the profit from the teachings here is so great, come, let us set before you today what has been read, and when we have reaped its profit, [282] let us then return home. "And Noah," it says, "began to be a man who tilled the soil, and he planted a vineyard, and he drank of the wine and became drunk." Consider how great a benefit the very opening of the reading offers us. For when we hear that the righteous man, the perfect man, the one who received testimony from above, drank and became drunk, how shall we, who are drowned in so many other sins, not strive with all our strength to flee the ruin that drunkenness brings?
