And yet it is not the same thing for this righteous man to be caught by the passion as for us to fall into it. For there are many things that show this righteous man to be deserving of pardon. And I say this not to make a defense of drunkenness, but to show that the righteous man was tripped up not through incontinence but rather through ignorance. That he did not simply take to wine-drinking without reason, hear Scripture itself say so, making his defense in its very words: "And Noah," it says, "began to be a man who tilled the soil, and he planted a vineyard, and he drank of the wine and became drunk." The very word "began" shows that he himself was the first to discover wine-drinking, and that through great ignorance, and through not knowing the right measure in partaking, he slid into drunkenness. And not only this: he was also gripped by great dejection and wanted to find consolation for himself from it, as a certain wise man says, "Give wine to those in grief, and strong drink to those in pain." He shows that nothing can be so effective a remedy for dejection as the use of wine, provided only that excess does not spoil the benefit it brings. And who will deny that this righteous man was in grief and dejection? He saw himself in such desolation, with human bodies flung down before his eyes along with cattle and brute beasts, and a common tomb made for them all. For it is the custom of the prophets and of all the righteous to grieve not only for their own affairs but also for the rest of humankind. If anyone cares to count them up, he will find them all showing this compassion. He will hear Isaiah saying, "Do not labor to comfort me over the ruin of the daughter of my people"; Jeremiah, "Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes?"; Ezekiel, "Alas, O Lord, are you wiping out the remnant of Israel?"; Daniel lamenting and saying, "You have made us fewer than all the nations"; Amos, "Repent, O Lord, of this"; and Habakkuk, "Why have you shown me toils and troubles?" and again, "And you will make men like the fish of the sea." And he will hear this same blessed Moses saying, "If you will forgive them their sin, forgive; but if not, blot me out too"; and again, when God promised

But perhaps someone might say: And why was a plant [284] so full of evils brought into our life? Do not just say whatever comes into your head, man. For the plant is not evil, nor is wine wicked; what is evil is its improper use. Deadly sins are born not from wine but from a corrupt will, and from spoiling by excess the benefit that comes from it. That is why it is only now, after the flood, that he shows you the use of wine: so that you may learn that even before wine was used, human nature had run aground on boundless licentiousness and shown a great escalation of sins, and this when wine was nowhere to be seen. So when you see the use of wine, do not blame everything on the wine, but on the will that has been corrupted and has deserted to wickedness. And besides, consider where wine has proved useful, and shudder, man. For the very means of our salvation and of our blessings is accomplished through it. The initiated know what is meant. "And Noah," it says, "began to be a man who tilled the soil, and he planted a vineyard, and he drank of the wine and became drunk, and was uncovered in his house." For drunkenness is a terrible thing, beloved, terrible indeed, able to maim the senses and drown the reason. It takes the rational human being, who has received dominion over all things, binds him as with unbreakable chains, and makes him lie there like a corpse, inert; or rather worse than a corpse. For a corpse is inert toward both good and evil, but this man is inert toward the good while being all the more active toward evil, and he is set out as a common laughingstock for everyone: for his wife, his children, and even his own servants. His friends count the shame as their own and hide their faces in embarrassment, while his enemies gloat, mock and curse him, all but saying: Should this man breathe the air? The brute, the pig! And they say things worse still. Such men are in a worse state than those returning from war with bloodied hands and carried home on stretchers. For most people perhaps even praise those men for their trophies, their victories, their wounds and the slaughter they have done; but these they pity, call wretched, and call down countless evils upon them. For what could be more wretched than a man nailed to drunkenness, who pours out neat wine every day and destroys the judgment of his reason? That is why a certain wise man gave this advice: "The first need of human life is bread and water and clothing, and a house to cover one's shame." So if someone is caught by drunkenness, he should not be paraded about or made a public spectacle, but should be covered by his own household and not set before everyone as an occasion for laughter and disgrace. "And Noah," it says, "began to be a man who tilled the soil, and he planted a vineyard, and he drank of the wine and became drunk." 4. The word "drunkenness," beloved, is not always used in holy Scripture in this sense; [283] it is also used of being filled. This, then, one might say about this righteous man: that it was not through incontinence that he fell into drunkenness, but that being filled did this to him. For hear David saying, "They shall be drunk with the fatness of your house," meaning "they shall be filled." Besides, those who give themselves over to drunkenness never reach the point of being sated; the more neat wine they pour into themselves, the more they burn with thirst, and drinking always becomes fuel for their thirst. And the [?] of pleasure has made even the hearers more careless, and toward [?]

[?] you smeared on folly; and not only that, but you also caused God to be blasphemed. And no one is unaware how great a punishment this brings on those who give occasion for it. So let us shun Ham's example, I beg you, and imitate the modesty these right-minded sons showed toward their father's nakedness. In the same way let us cover over our brothers' sins. We do this not to train them in laziness, but because this is the best way to give them more occasion to be quickly rid of that defilement and to return to the course of virtue. For when few people witness a person's faults, it is easier for him to come to his senses and return. But when a soul has lost all shame and sees that none of its wicked deeds has escaped notice, it is not willing to give them up easily. It is like someone who has fallen into a thicket and into deep water and is dragged down by countless waves: it will hardly be able to come up again, because it has finally fallen into despair and given up on returning. 5. Therefore, I beg you, let us not parade our neighbors' failings. When we learn of them from others, let us not hurry to see the nakedness. Like these right-minded sons, let us cover them up and conceal them, and let us work by exhortation and counsel to raise up the fallen soul. Let us teach it the greatness of God's love for humankind, the surpassing measure of his goodness and the boundlessness of his compassion. Then we may receive an even greater blessing than they did from the God of all, who wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and who does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he should turn and live. "And they did not see," it says, "their father's nakedness." See how, from the very beginning, they fulfilled ahead of time what the written law would later lay down for the instruction of the human race. They took it from the law that is set in nature. What the law said, "Honor your father and your mother, that it may go well with you," and "Whoever speaks evil of father or mother, let him surely die," was already being fulfilled in their deeds. Do you see how nature came first and held teaching enough? "And Noah awoke from his wine," it says, "and knew what his younger son had done to him." "He awoke," it says. Let those who spend their days at drinking parties hear how great this fall was, and let them flee the ruin that comes from drunkenness. "He awoke," it says. What does "he awoke" mean? When madmen come out of their frenzy, we usually say that so-and-so has come to his senses from the demon and been freed from its tyranny. Scripture says the same thing here. For drunkenness truly is a demon that people choose for themselves. It darkens the reason worse than a demon does, and robs its captive of all good sense. When we see someone possessed by a demon, we often pity him, share his pain and show him great sympathy. With a drunkard we do the opposite: we are indignant and annoyed, and we heap countless curses on him. Why is that? Because the one is driven by the evil demon [? the text breaks off here, followed by a garbled editorial note giving the variant "troubled by a demon"; Patrologia Graeca vol. 53]

[?] than he, but younger in judgment, and his rashness cast him out. Because he would not stay within his own bounds, he lost the honor that nature had given him. He betrayed what he had by nature through his own wicked choice, while Japheth gained through sound judgment what he did not have by nature. 6. Do you see that nothing in divine Scripture is set down idly or at random? "What his younger son had done to him," it says. "And he said: Cursed be Canaan, the boy; he shall be a servant to his brothers." Look, we have come to the question that is raised everywhere. You can hear many people asking: when it was the father who sinned and reported the nakedness, why does the son receive the curse? So I beg you, listen carefully and accept the answer. We will say whatever divine grace grants us for your benefit. "And he said: Cursed be Canaan, the boy; he shall be a servant to his brothers." He did not mention the son idly or at random, but for a hidden reason. He wanted to rebuke Ham for his offense and for the insult he had shown him, and at the same time not to spoil the blessing God had already given. For "God blessed Noah," it says, "and his sons, when he came out of the ark." So that he might not seem to curse someone who had once received God's blessing, he lets the insolent son go for the time being and brings the curse on his son instead. "Yes," someone says, "that shows why he did not curse Ham: Ham had enjoyed God's blessing. But why does this boy pay the penalty when the other one sinned?" This too does not happen without reason. Ham suffered the punishment no less than his son did, and he felt the penalty. You know, you surely know, how often fathers have prayed to bear punishment in place of their children. As a punishment, it is heavier for them to see their children punished than to be held liable themselves. So this happened in order that Ham, through his natural love for his child, might suffer greater pain; that God's blessing might remain intact; and that the son who received the curse might pay the penalty for his own sins. For although he now receives the curse because of his father's sin, it was still fitting that he should pay the penalty for his own offenses. He did not receive the curse only because of his father's sin, except perhaps so that through him his father might pay a heavier penalty. In many places the prophets say that fathers do not pay the penalty for their children, nor children for their fathers, but each answers for his own wrongdoing. For example, they say: "The teeth of the one who eats the sour grape will be set on edge"; and, "The soul that sins, it shall die"; and again, "Fathers shall not die for their children, nor children for their fathers." So I beg you, let none of you who do not know the purpose of divine Scripture dare to find fault with what is written. Receive what is said with a right mind, marvel at the precision of divine Scripture, and consider what a great evil sin is. For see, the brother who shared the same birth pangs, the one from the [?] [Note:] "The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children's teeth were set on edge." In Ezekiel (18:2) the reading is ᾑμωδίασαν instead of ἐγομφίασαν, from αἱμωδιάω.

[?] done. That the boy too was wicked in himself, and that all his descendants turned aside to wickedness and became abominable, you can hear from Scripture, which says by way of a curse: "Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite." And again someone else says, as an insult: "Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah." Now that we have heard the rebuke received by the one who paraded his father's nakedness, it is worth hearing what rewards were given to those who showed their father such modesty and honor. "And he said," it says, "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem, and Canaan shall be his servant." Someone may say that this is not a blessing of Shem. On the contrary, he blessed him greatly. When people give thanks to God and bless him, he usually pours out his own blessing more abundantly on those who are the reason he is blessed. So by blessing God, Noah made God a debtor who owed Shem a greater blessing, and he won Shem a greater reward than if he had blessed him himself, on his own account. For just as God grants us great goodwill when he is blessed because of us, so, when others blaspheme him because of us, a greater condemnation falls on us for giving them the occasion. So I beg you, let us be eager to live in such a way, and to show such intense virtue, that those who look at us offer up hymns of blessing to the Lord God. Because he is good and loves humankind, he wants to be glorified through us. This is not because he gains anything for his own glory, since he needs nothing, but so that we may give him occasion to grant us more of his goodwill. "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem, and Canaan shall be his servant." Do you see how fatherly the punishment is that he imposes, a correction rather than a punishment? He was a father, and a loving father. He did not want to inflict the penalty the boy deserved, but to cut short any further wickedness. "That is why," he says, "I condemn you to slavery, so that you may have a constant and indelible reminder." Then he says: "May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant." This is another very great blessing, and it may hold a hidden treasure. "May God enlarge Japheth," it says. No one would be wrong to call the righteous man's blessings a prophecy. His father did not give him his name idly or at random, but prophesied through the name the storm that was to come. Much more, then, this righteous man would not have pronounced his blessings idly or in vain. Through these blessings of Shem and Japheth I think he is hinting at the calling of the two peoples. Through Shem he means the Jews, since from him came the patriarch Abraham, and the Jewish race grew from him. Through Japheth he means the calling of the Gentiles. See how this blessing, too, foretells this. "May God enlarge Japheth," it says, "and let him dwell in the tents of Shem." We see this fulfilled in fact among the Gentiles. By saying "enlarge" he hinted at all the nations. By saying "let him dwell in the tents of Shem" he meant that the nations came to enjoy what had been prepared and made ready for the Jews. "And let Canaan be his servant." 8. Do you see what rewards these men received for their good sense [?] [Note: a marginal conjecture reads "than if he himself had blessed him by himself."]

[?] they drew down help from above, so that their achievement in repentance is celebrated to this day. Let us imitate them, then. We have learned that our ancestors' wickedness does not harm us if we are willing to stay sober, and that our ancestors' virtue cannot help us at all if we are lazy. So let us take great pains to hold fast to virtue and show a right-minded choice. Then we may enjoy the same blessing as Shem and Japheth, be set free from the curse and the slavery that Canaan received, and not become slaves of sin. Instead, may we gain true freedom and obtain those ineffable good things, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, power and honor to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

"And the whole earth was one lip, and there was one language for all." 1. Look, we have now come to the end of holy Lent. We have completed the voyage of the fast and, by God's grace, have at last reached the harbor. But that is no reason to grow slack. All the more, we should show much greater zeal and watchfulness. Think of helmsmen. They cross countless seas with full sails and with cargo piled high. When they are about to enter the harbor, that is when they struggle hardest and take the most care, so that the ship does not strike a reef or a rock and make all their earlier labor useless. Runners do the same: when they reach the end of the course, they run more vigorously, so as to reach the finish and win the prize. Athletes too, after countless bouts and victories, struggle harder when they wrestle the bout for the crown, so that they may take the crown and leave in triumph. Helmsmen, runners and athletes each step up their effort and watchfulness most when they are near the end. In the same way, now that by God's grace we have reached this Great Week, we above all ought to quicken the course of our fasting and pray more fervently. We ought to make a full and exact confession of our sins and work hard at good deeds: generous almsgiving, kindness, gentleness and every other virtue. Then, when we reach the Lord's day with these achievements, we may enjoy the Master's generosity. We call this week Great not because its hours are longer, since other weeks have much longer hours. Nor is it because it has more days, since it has the same number as all the others. Why, then, do we call it Great? Because the good things that came to us in it are great and ineffable. In it the long war was ended, death was extinguished, the curse [? text missing] all were of one voice and one tongue. And that the words "And the whole earth was one lip" refer to

speech, hear Scripture saying elsewhere: "The venom of asps is under their lips." So Scripture is accustomed to use the word "lip" to mean speech. "And it came to pass, as they moved from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they settled there." 2. See how human nature cannot bear to stay within its own bounds, but always grasps for more and reaches for greater things. This is what does the human race the most harm: it will not recognize the limits of its own nature, but always aims at greater things and imagines things beyond its worth. That is why people who are infatuated with the things of this world, once they have surrounded themselves with great wealth and power, seem to forget their own nature. They want to raise themselves higher and higher until they are brought down to the very bottom. You can see this happening every day. Yet even this does not teach others restraint. They shrink back for a little while, but then suddenly forget everything, walk the same road again and are carried over the same cliff. You can see this happening now with these people as well. "And it came to pass, as they moved from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they settled there." See how Scripture teaches us little by little how unstable their minds were. "When they saw the plain," it says, "they moved away, left their earlier home and settled there." Then it says: "Each one said to his neighbor: Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire. And brick served them as stone, and bitumen was their mortar. And they said: Come, let us build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top will reach to heaven; and let us make a name for ourselves before we are scattered over the whole earth." See how they did not use their common language for a proper purpose, and how vain plans for this life become the source of evils. "Come," it says, "let us make bricks and bake them with fire. And brick served them as stone, and bitumen was their mortar." Consider how solid they want to make their building, not knowing that "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain." "And let us build ourselves a city," it says: not for God, but for themselves. See how far their wickedness went. The memory of that universal destruction was still ringing in their ears, yet they ran aground on such madness. "And let us build ourselves a city," it says, "and a tower whose top will reach to heaven." With the word "heaven" divine Scripture wanted to show us how excessive their daring was. "And let us make a name for ourselves," it says. Do you see the root of the wickedness? "Let us enjoy an everlasting memory," they mean. "Let us be remembered forever. Let our deed and our work be such that it is never handed over to oblivion." "And let us do this before we are scattered over the face of the whole earth." "While we are still together," they mean, "let us carry out what we have decided, so that we leave an unfading memory to the generations that follow." Even now there are many who imitate them and want to be remembered for deeds like these: people who build splendid houses, baths, colonnades and promenades. If you ask any of them why he toils and wears himself out and shows such [?]

[?] and the widows, and he presented her alive. If you want to be remembered, and if you love true glory, imitate her. Build buildings like these. Do not waste yourself on lifeless material; show great generosity to your fellow human beings instead. That kind of memory deserves praise and brings great gain. But let us return to our subject and look at the daring of the men of that time. If we are willing to be sober, their failings will be a lesson to us. "And let us build ourselves a city," it says, "and a tower whose top will reach to heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves before we are scattered over the earth." Do you see how at every point they show how corrupt their minds were? "And let us build ourselves a city," it says, and again, "Let us make a name for ourselves." But see how, even after such universal destruction, they again set their hands to evils no smaller than before. What, then, was to happen? How were they to be held back from their madness? God had promised never again to send a flood, true to his own love for humankind. But these people were neither brought to their senses by punishments nor made better by kindnesses. So listen to what follows, and learn how great God's unspeakable love for humankind is. "And the Lord God came down," it says, "to see the city and the tower which the sons of men were building." See how Scripture speaks in human terms. "And the Lord God came down," it says. This is not so that we should understand it in a human way. It is so that we may learn from it never to condemn our brothers rashly, nor to pass sentence on hearsay, until we have first gained full certainty. Everything God does is done for this reason: he comes down to our level in this way to teach human nature. "And the Lord God came down," it says, "to see the city and the tower." See how he does not check their madness at the outset. He shows great patience and waits for them to carry out all their wickedness in deed, and only then cuts off the undertaking. He did not want anyone to be able to say that they had only made plans and had not carried out what they had decided. So he waits for them to complete what they had planned, and then shows them how senseless their undertaking is. "And the Lord God came down," it says, "to see the city and the tower which the sons of men had built." See how extraordinary his love for humankind is. He let them toil and wear themselves out, so that the experience itself might teach them. When he saw the wickedness at its height and the disease growing worse, he did not leave it to the end. He showed his goodness like an excellent physician who sees the disease growing and the wound becoming incurable and makes a quick incision, so as to remove the cause of the disease completely. "And the Lord God said," it says: "Look, they are all one race and one lip," which means one voice and one language. "And this they have begun to do, and now nothing that they set out to do will fail them." 4. See the Master's love for humankind. Since he is about to cut short their impulse, he first sets out a justification. He all but shows them how great their sin is and how far their ingratitude went, and that they did not use their agreement for a proper purpose. "For look," he says, "they are all one race and one lip. And this they have begun to do, and [?] [Note: four manuscripts read "shows the difference"; [?] πῶς before οὐκ [?] ἀναχαιτισθῶσι. Three manuscripts read ἐπινενομένην [?].]

…just as their one shared language made it possible for them to live together, so the division of their language would bring about their dispersion. For if they did not have the same language and speech, how could they live in the same place? "And the Lord God scattered them from there," it says, "over the face of all the earth, and they stopped building the city and the tower." See the Master's loving-kindness, and into what helplessness he threw them! From then on they were like madmen. One would order one thing, and the other would hand him something else, and their whole enterprise became useless to them. That is why "they stopped building the city and the tower. Therefore its name was called Confusion, because there the Lord God confused the lips of all the earth, and from there the Lord God scattered them over all the earth." Consider how many things are done so that the memory of this might stretch through all time. First there is the division of tongues. Or rather, even before that, there is the giving of a name: the name Peleg, which Eber gave to his son, means "division." Then there is the naming of the place: the place was named Confusion, that is, Babylon. Then Eber himself kept the same speech he had before, so that this too might become a clear sign of the division. Do you see by how many means God wanted the memory to be preserved for ever, so that what happened then would never be forgotten? From that time on a father had to tell his child the cause of the different languages, and a child would seek to learn from his father why the place had its name. For the place was named Babylon, which means confusion, for this reason: because there the Lord God confused the lips of all the earth, and from there he scattered them. The name of the place seems to me to signify both things: that he confused their tongues, and that from there they suffered dispersion.

5. You have heard, beloved, how the occasion of their dispersion and of the division of tongues came about. Let us flee from imitating them, I beg you. Let us use what God has given us for its proper purpose. Let us keep our human nature in mind and make our plans as it befits men to plan who are mortal. Let us reckon how perishable the present life is and how short our lifetime, and let us store up for ourselves beforehand great confidence before God by doing good deeds. During these days let us show not only greater strictness in fasting, but also abundant almsgiving and earnest prayers. For prayer must always be yoked to fasting. To see that this is true, hear Christ saying: "This kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting." And again, of the apostles: "Having prayed," it says, "and fasted, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed." And again the Apostle: "Do not deprive one another," he says, "except for prayer and fasting." Do you see how fasting needs the alliance of prayer? For it is then above all that prayers are made with sobriety, when the mind is lighter, weighed down by nothing and not pressed under the wicked burden of luxury. Prayer is a great weapon, a great safety, a great treasure, a great harbor, a place of refuge, if only we approach it soberly [?] … he prayed to be delivered from these, and not once or twice, but many times. "Three times," he says, "I besought the Lord." "Three times" means that he besought him many times,

and did not get what he asked. Let us see, then, how he took it. Was he vexed? Did he grow more sluggish? Did he lose heart? No. What does he say? "He said, My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Not only did God not free him from the troubles that pressed on him; he even let him remain in them. "Yes, but how is it clear that he was not vexed?" Hear Paul saying, once he had learned what the Master had decided: "Most gladly, then, will I boast in my weaknesses." Not only do I no longer seek to be delivered, he says, but I will even boast in these things with all the more pleasure. Do you see a grateful soul? Do you see longing for God? Hear him saying: "For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought." Being human, he says, we cannot know everything exactly. So we must yield to the Creator of our nature and accept with joy and great pleasure whatever he himself approves. We must not look at how events appear on the surface, but at what the Master has decided. For he knows better than we do what is good for us, and he also knows how to arrange our salvation.

6. Let us have one task, then: to persevere in prayer without ceasing. Let us not fret at the delay, but show great patience. For when he puts off our requests, it is not because he refuses them. He is wisely drawing out our perseverance, and he wants to draw us to himself continually. A loving father, too, often does not grant what his child asks. It is not that he does not want to give, but that he is drawing out the child's perseverance by this means. Knowing this, then, let us never give up, and let us never stop coming to him and making our supplications. For if the woman's perseverance forced that cruel and harsh judge, who did not even fear God, and roused him to help her, how much more shall we rouse our gentle and loving Master to help us as his own, if we are willing to imitate that woman? He is compassionate, and he runs to meet our salvation. Let us train ourselves, then, to be hard to tear away and to stay fastened to prayer without ceasing, by day and by night, and especially by night. Then no one disturbs us. Then our thoughts are very calm, all is quiet, and the room is free of commotion. Then there is no one who can interrupt us and draw us away from our approach to God, and the mind is collected and can lay everything carefully before the physician of souls. Blessed David was king and prophet at once. He was harassed by so many affairs and clothed in purple and a diadem, and yet he said: "At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for your righteous judgments." What would we say, then, who lead a private and untroubled life and do not even do what he did? By day he had many distractions, the press of affairs was great, the turmoil was great, and he could find no suitable time for such an approach to God. Others make the hours of rest a time for sleep, lying on soft bedding and tossing this way and that. But the king, who had taken on so great a care, made them a time for approaching God, conversing with him in private, and with sincer[?]…

Some manuscripts read "Was he then vexed?" Three manuscripts read "reading." Others read "gathered."

[?] the words on prayer yesterday, and that you gather so eagerly to listen. This makes us more eager too, and moves us to set this spiritual feast before you more abundantly. A farmer, too, when he sees his field returning the seed sown in it many times over and the crops flourishing, does not stop doing his part every day and giving it proper care. He keeps watch by night and by day in case anything should ruin his labors. In the same way, when I see this spiritual field of yours flourishing so, and this spiritual seed being stored in the folds of your mind, I rejoice and am glad. But I also have a great struggle on my hands, because I know the wickedness of the enemy who plots against our salvation. Pirates at sea, when they see a ship filled with cargo and carrying untold wealth, then above all lay their plots, so as to sink the whole cargo and leave those on board naked and destitute. So too the devil, when he sees great spiritual wealth gathered, zeal boiling, minds awake, and the wealth increasing every day, is stung and gnashes his teeth. Like a pirate he prowls about, devising countless schemes to find some small way in, to leave us naked and destitute, and to plunder all our spiritual wealth. So let us be sober, I beg you. The more our spiritual wealth increases, the more we must sharpen our watchfulness. Let us wall off his approaches on every side, win God's goodwill by living the best kind of life, and so put ourselves beyond the reach of the devil's darts. For the beast is wicked, and his schemes are intricate. Sometimes he cannot drag us down into wickedness directly and lure us by deceit. He does not use force or compulsion, God forbid; he only deceives, and when he sees us careless, he trips us up. So when he cannot openly harm our salvation by wickedness itself, he often lays his bait in the very works of virtue we pursue, and secretly sinks all our wealth. What do I mean? I must say it more clearly, so that once we have learned his plots we may escape the harm they do. He may see that we do not readily accept wickedness in its naked form, but flee licentiousness and embrace chastity, turn away from greed, hate injustice and laugh at luxury, give ourselves to fasting and prayer and devote ourselves to almsgiving. Then he contrives another scheme, by which he can ruin all our riches and make all our good deeds useless to us. Those who have vigorously got the better of his schemes he prompts to think highly of their own good deeds and to look to human glory, so that they fall from the true glory. For anyone who pursues something spiritual while looking to human glory has already received his reward here, and no longer has God as his debtor. He has enjoyed praise from those by whom he sought to be glorified, and he has robbed himself of what the Master promised, preferring the temporary [?]…

"Ruin the labors": so three manuscripts. Patrologia Graeca 53.

praise, but let us be content with the praise that comes from the Master. "For his praise," it says, "is not from men but from God." And the further we advance in virtue, the more we should make ourselves humble and modest. Even if we reach the very summit of virtue, if we gratefully set against it the Master's benefits to us, we will see clearly that we have not repaid even the smallest part of what God has bestowed on us. Indeed, it was by this that each of the saints won renown. To learn this, hear the teacher of the world, that soul which reached to heaven. After so many achievements, and after such great testimony from above ("For he is a chosen vessel to me," it says), he does not forget his own offenses, but keeps turning them over [?]. He had been fully assured that he had received forgiveness for them through baptism, yet he will not let himself forget even these. He cries out and says: "I am the least of the apostles, and I am not fit to be called an apostle." Then, to teach us how far his humility went, he added: "because I persecuted the Church of God." What are you doing, Paul? The Master in his own generosity forgave you and wiped away all your sins, and you keep turning them over? "Yes," he says, "I know. I am not unaware of my Master's pardon. But when I consider what I have done and see the ocean of God's loving-kindness, then I learn well that I am what I am by his grace and loving-kindness." For having said, "I am not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God," he added, "But by the grace of God I am what I am." I showed such madness, he says, but his ineffable goodness and grace granted me forgiveness. Do you see a contrite soul, which always carries about with it the memory of the sins it committed before baptism? Let us too imitate him. Let us remember every day the sins we have committed after baptism, keep turning them over in our minds, and never let ourselves forget them. This will be bridle enough to keep us humble and modest. And why do I speak of Paul, so great and so eminent as he was? Do you want to see that those in the Old Testament too won renown chiefly in this way, by staying humble after countless achievements and an ineffable confidence before God? Hear the patriarch saying, after he had conversed with God and after the promise made to him: "But I am earth and ashes."

3. But since I have mentioned the patriarch, let us, if you agree, lay before your love the passage read today. By unfolding it we may see how surpassing the righteous man's virtue was. "And Terah took," it says, "Abram and Nahor his sons, and Lot the son of his son, and Sarah his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son, and brought them out of the land of the Chaldeans to go into the land of the Canaanites. And he came as far as Haran and settled there. And all the days of Terah in Haran were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran." Let us pay careful attention to what has been read, I beg you, so that we can grasp the sense of what is written. For right at the outset there seems to be a difficulty in these words. When this blessed prophet (Moses, I mean) said "the father's house," why not also the [?]…

place where you command me to go? Why do you not make it known, so that I can at least know how far it is? For how am I to know that the land I am going to will turn out better and more prosperous than the one I am leaving?" But the righteous man neither said nor thought anything of the kind. He looked to the greatness of the one who gave the command, and he preferred what he could not see to what he held in his hands. And yet if he had not had a lofty mind and a philosophical disposition, and if he had not been trained to obey God in everything, he would have had another serious obstacle as well: his father's death. For you know that many people, for the sake of their relatives' tombs, have often chosen to die in the places where their parents ended their lives.

4. It would have been natural, then, for this righteous man too, had he not loved God exceedingly, to reason like this: "Out of love for me my father left his home and disregarded long-standing ties. He rose above everything and came this far, and you might almost say that he ended his life in a foreign land for my sake. And now, even after his death, shall I not be eager to repay him in kind? Shall I go off and leave my father's tomb behind together with my kindred?" Yet none of these things could blunt his eagerness. His love for God made everything seem easy and simple to him. He might also have thought this, if he had wanted to entrust his affairs to human reasoning: "At my age, already heading toward extreme old age, where am I to go? I am not taking my brother along, nor do I have my kinsmen with me. I am cut off from all my family. How am I, alone and a stranger, to reach a foreign land, when I do not even know where my wandering will end? And if I happen to die halfway along the road, what is the use of all this hardship? Who will lay out my body, an old man, a stranger, with no city and no home? Perhaps my wife will beg the neighbors to show some compassion, and will pay for the funeral rites from a collection and from what they contribute. How much better it would be to sit here for the short time we have left to live and end my life here, than to be dragged here and there in my old age and endure everyone's mockery, as a man who could not live in peace even at such an age, but kept moving from place to place and never settled anywhere!" But this righteous man took none of this into account and hastened to obey the command. Perhaps someone might say that it was spur enough for him to be told: "Come into the land that I will show you, and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you." Yet if he had not loved God, this very thing would have been enough to make him slower to obey. Had he been one of the many, he could have said: "Why are you taking me away to a strange land and ordering me to settle in a foreign country? If you want to make me great, why do you not make me great here? Why do you not grant me your blessing while I live in my father's house? For if I happen to be worn out by the toils of the journey and perish and die before I reach the place you command, what use are the promises to me?" But he would not even entertain any of these thoughts. Like a grateful servant, he simply obeyed the command. He did not pry or meddle; he obeyed, and was fully assured [?]…

Four manuscripts read "that he be made equal to the [?]."

makes it plain. "And Abram went," it says, "as the Lord God had told him, and Lot went with him." It does not simply say "Abram went," but "as the Lord God had told him." He did everything, it means, in keeping with the command. God told him to leave everything, kindred and home, and he left it. God told him to go into a land he did not know, and he agreed. God promised to make him into a great nation and to bless him, and he believed that this too would happen. "And as the Lord God had told him, so he went." That is, he believed what God had said. He did not hesitate or doubt. With his mind and his reasoning firmly fixed, he went. That is why he also enjoyed great favor from the Master. "And Lot went with him," it says. God had said, "Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father's house," so why did Abram take Lot with him? It was not that he disobeyed the Master. Perhaps it was because Lot was young and Abram stood in the place of a father to him. Lot, out of affection and because of his gentle character, could hardly be torn away from the righteous man, and for this reason he could not bear to leave him. Besides, Abram treated him as a son, since at his age he could not have children because of Sarah's barrenness. Moreover, the young man's character was not far short of the righteous man's. There were two brothers before him, and he attached himself to the righteous one. How much understanding this very fact shows, that he could discern and test which of his uncles he should entrust himself to! And his choice to go abroad was itself another sign of his well-ordered character. Even if at the end he seemed to go wrong in some things, when he leapt to take the first choice, he was still eager to walk in the righteous man's footsteps. That is why the righteous man took him as his companion on the journey, and why Lot eagerly preferred a foreign land to staying at home. Then, so that we may learn that the Master gave these commands to the patriarch not when he was a young man but when he was already heading into old age, when most people are less willing to travel abroad, it says: "Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran." Do you see how neither his age nor anything else that might have drawn him to stay at home stood in his way? His longing for God rose above everything. When the soul is awake and sober, it cuts through every obstacle and gives itself wholly to the object of its longing. None of the difficulties that appear along the way can stop it. It passes them all by and does not stop until it reaches what it strives for. That is why this righteous man too, though old age and many other things could have held him back, broke all his bonds. Like a young man in the prime of life whom nothing hinders, he hastened and pressed on to carry out the Master's command. For no one who wants to do something noble and courageous can ever carry it out unless he first sets himself in battle order against everything that is going to stand in the way of his undertaking. This righteous man knew this clearly. So he passed everything by, and gave no thought to custom, kindred, his father's house, the tomb, or even old age itself. He directed his mind to one thing alone: how he could fulfill what the Master had commanded. And one could see a truly wondrous sight: a man in extreme old age with his poor wife [?] … the patriarch and Nahor were brothers.

And yet, although his brother had advanced to such virtue, he was still held captive by error. But this man showed everyone, every day, by his very deeds, how his virtue was growing. "And he came," it says, "into the land of Canaan, and Abram passed through the land along its length, as far as the place of Shechem, to the high oak." Scripture tells us the part of the country in which the righteous man now makes his home. Then, so that we may learn what conditions he still faced there, it says, "And the Canaanites were then living in the land." Again, blessed Moses did not note this idly. He did it so that from this too we might learn the patriarch's philosophic mind. Because the places were still occupied by the Canaanites, he was forced to lodge wherever he happened to be, like a wanderer and a stranger, like one of the lowly and the outcast, perhaps without even an inn. And yet even so he did not grow vexed. He did not say: "What is this? I lived in Haran with such honour and so many servants, and now, like a man without a city, a stranger and a newcomer, I am forced to go about at other people's mercy and look for rest in a poor lodging. And I cannot even get that, but must live in tents and huts and bear every other hardship. Is this all he meant when he said, 'Come, and I will make you into a great nation'? So far the beginnings are fine for me! What good can I expect from here on?" But even so the righteous man could not bring himself to say anything of the kind, or to waver. With his whole mind and perfect faith he trusted in God's promises and kept his thoughts unswerving at all times. That is why he was quickly granted comfort from above.

7. But so that we do not stretch our teaching out too long, let us stop here and bring our discourse to a close, after urging you, beloved, to imitate this righteous man's disposition. For it would be most absurd if things stood like this. This righteous man was called from land to land and showed such obedience. Neither old age, nor the other hindrances we listed, nor the hardship of the times, nor anything else that could have held him back was strong enough to make him slower to obey. Instead he broke through every bond, and the old man ran and hurried like a youth in his prime, with his wife, his nephew and his servants, to carry out what God had commanded. We, on the other hand, are called not from land to land but from earth to heaven, and yet we will not show the same eagerness to obey that the righteous man showed. Often we put forward cold and useless excuses. Neither the greatness of the promises, nor the worthlessness of visible things, which are earthly and passing, nor the dignity of the one who calls us draws us on. Instead we show such sloth that we prefer passing things to those that last forever, earth to heaven, and things that fly away before they even appear to things that can never come to an end. Tell me, how long will we be so mad about piling up money? What frenzy is this, to be besieged every day by this cruel desire and never be satisfied, but to be in a worse state than drunkards? For just as they, the more [?]

Some manuscripts read "we put forward defences." So some manuscripts. [?] For he ought to have said: "and the things that fly away before they appear to those that can never come to an end."

[?] so that in this way we may reap the benefit they offer. For somehow what is found through toil and searching sticks more firmly in our minds, while what comes easily flies more quickly out of our hearts. So let us not be slack, I beg you. Let us rouse our minds and look thoroughly into the very depth of what is written, so that we can go home having gained something more from here. For the church of God is a spiritual festival and a hospital for souls. People who come to a festival should gather a great store of goods there before they go home. In the same way, people who come to a hospital should receive the medicines that suit their ailments before they leave. For we do not meet every day just to see one another and then all go our separate ways. We meet so that each of us may learn something useful and receive treatment for the passion that troubles him, and only then go away. How would it not be most absurd? We send our children to school and demand some addition to their lessons from them every day, and we would never put up with their going there aimlessly unless we saw them gaining something more. Yet we, who have reached full age and come to this spiritual school, do not show the same zeal as they do, and this when the gain reaches as far as the salvation of the soul! So let each of us, I beg you, examine himself every day: what did he gain from today's discourse, and what from the next? Then we too will not seem to come here aimlessly. This frees us from all blame, for we contribute everything on our part and leave nothing undone that is in our power. But for those who are impatient, who do not pay careful attention and do not want to gain anything more, it becomes a cause of greater condemnation. To see this, hear Christ saying to the man who buried his talent: "Wicked servant, you ought to have deposited my money with the bankers, and when I came I would have demanded it back with interest." And of the Jews he says: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse." But for our part we are not now asking whether we are free of the charges. We long for your progress, and even if we ourselves are a thousand times blameless, we count our joy cut short unless you too show a zeal worthy of our labours. For this is the ground of our joy: to see you advance in spiritual things. I know, of course, that by the grace of God you are filled with understanding and will be able to admonish others as well. But, following blessed Paul, I remind you and stir up your zeal and eagerness. I urge these things on you constantly because I want you to become perfect and complete. I take this too as no small proof of your progress toward God: that you come here every day with such eagerness and are never satisfied with spiritual teaching. A good appetite for bodily food is a sign of excellent health, and in the same way a desire for spiritual teaching is the clearest evidence that the soul is healthy. That is why I too, knowing your longing, and knowing that even if I drew out the teaching a thousand times over I still could not fill your [?] so that the patriarch's love of God might be shown most clearly, that even

seeing things turn out, for the time being, contrary to the promises, the blessed man was not disturbed or thrown into confusion. He kept his mind unmoved, convinced that what God had once promised him was sure and firm. But let us examine everything little by little. In this way we will learn the resourceful wisdom of the good God, the care he showed for the righteous man, and the patriarch's love for his Master. "And the Lord God appeared," it says, "to Abram." How did he appear? As God alone knows, and in the way Abram was able to see. I will not stop saying this: I do not know the manner. I only hear Scripture saying, "The Lord God appeared to Abram and said to him, 'To your offspring I will give this land.'" Keep careful note of the promises God makes. Then, when you see the righteous man falling into various trials, you will learn how far his philosophy surpassed others, how firm his courage was, and how steady and unshakable his love for God remained. And what happened to this righteous man will teach you never to think it a sign that God has abandoned someone when you see a virtuous person fall into temptations or other troubles of life. Instead, think of how varied God's dispensations are, and leave everything to his incomprehensible providence. For he allows even this righteous man, who loved God so much and showed such obedience, to be tried by things you will hear about very shortly. He does this not because he overlooks his servant, but because he wants to reveal his virtue to everyone else. (This is his custom with each of the righteous. Those of you who study the divine Scriptures diligently will be able, by learning them from the very beginning, to see him ordering the lives of his servants in this way.) How, then, would it not be the height of ingratitude to think that such permission means abandonment, rather than to count it the greatest sign of his great care and his inexpressible love for humankind? So, in showing his surpassing power, he accomplishes two things by this. He makes the endurance and courage of his servants plain to all. He also shows how resourceful his providence is: in the very midst of dangers, when matters are almost past hope, he turns them to what he wills, and the difficulty that has arisen in the meantime does not hinder him at all. "And the Lord God appeared," it says, "to Abram and said to him, 'To your offspring I will give this land.'" Great is the promise, and the righteous man longed for it above all. You know how people who have reached old age, especially those who have been childless all their lives, long for children. So the Master gave him a reward for his obedience. When Abram heard, "Go out from your land," he did not delay or put it off. He obeyed the command and carried out what he was ordered to do. So God says: "To your offspring I will give the

3. Consider how by this word he lifted up his mind and gave him enough to repay his labours. For this reason the righteous man too shows his own gratitude and turns at once to thanksgiving. "And he built there," it says, "an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him." See the proof of a mind that loves God. He consecrated the very place where he had been granted converse with God,

of the righteous man, that he "encamped." It says this to show how lightly the patriarch travelled. Soldiers easily pitch camp now here, now there. In the same way this righteous man, though he brought his wife, his nephew and such a crowd of servants with him, made his moves with even greater ease. Do you see how unencumbered his life was in old age, even with a wife and so many servants? But what I especially find myself admiring is the woman's courage. When I think about the weakness of the female nature and reckon how readily she made these moves with the righteous man, neither complaining herself nor becoming a hindrance to him, I am astonished. I reckon that she too possessed a spirit as lofty and courageous as the righteous man's. We will see this most clearly as we go through what follows in the reading. Do you see how, after hearing "To your offspring I will give this land," the righteous man did not stay put, but moved from here to there [?], and then from there somewhere else? But see him driven out again, even from the wilderness, not by men but by the pressure of famine. "And there was a famine," it says, "in the land." Let those who speak carelessly and thoughtlessly and read omens listen to this. They say: "So-and-so arrived, and that is why a famine came," and "So-and-so came, and that is why this happened." Look: a famine came even while the righteous man was there, and a severe one. Yet the righteous man was not disturbed or overcome by human weakness, and he did not blame his own presence for the famine. But when he saw that nature was being overcome and the famine was prevailing, "Abram went down," it says, "into Egypt to sojourn there, because the famine prevailed in the land."

4. Consider how the contests grew longer for the righteous man. For the Master arranged that he should become a teacher not only to those living in Palestine but also to those in Egypt, and should make the light of his own virtue plain to all. He was like a lamp hidden away in the land of the Chaldeans, and God raised him up from there to lead by the hand those sitting in the darkness of error onto the way of truth. But perhaps someone will say: "Then why did he not arrange for the people in the land of the Chaldeans to be brought to godliness through him?" It is likely that God provided for their salvation too, through others. Even so, hear Christ saying, "A prophet is not without honour except in his own homeland." God had made a promise, saying, "And I will make your name great." To fulfil it, he allows the famine to happen and, through it, makes Abram come to Egypt, so that the people there too may learn how great the man's virtue is. Like an executioner who has thrown chains around them, the famine roused them from the wilderness and dragged them to Egypt. But now let us see what follows, and how great a trial the righteous man fell into, so that we may learn both his courage and the woman's philosophic mind. When they had gone a long way along the road and were now near Egypt, the righteous man grew anxious. Afraid and trembling, so to speak, for his very life, he speaks to his wife. "For it happened," it says, "when Abram drew near to enter Egypt, that he said to Sarai his wife: 'I know that you are a beautiful woman. So it will be, when they see

Perhaps "thither." "That nature was being overcome": nature overcome [?]. Others read: "then forcibly dragged them to Egypt."

[?]. Such is the madness of this thing, and so uncontrollable is jealousy, that it makes anyone it has once caught disregard even his own safety. From this we can learn the righteous man's courage, and also his great intelligence. In such helplessness, caught as if in a net, he was able to find a way to lessen the evil. If he had said she was his wife, and had not played his part and used the name of sister, she would have been taken from the righteous man anyway, since her beauty would have drawn the Egyptians' lustful attention. And the righteous man would have been murdered, so that no one would be left to accuse them of their crime. These two evils were sure to happen because of the men's lust and the king's tyranny. So that they might find some small comfort in their great perplexity, he says: "Say, 'I am his sister.' This may perhaps free me from the dangers. As for you, whether you call yourself sister or wife, no one will deny that it will certainly happen: because of your bodily beauty they will rush to carry you off. But I may well escape their plot if you use the name of sister." Do you see the righteous man's intelligence? Trapped as he was, he was able to find a way and plan how he might get the better of the Egyptians' plot. Here too, please consider both the righteous man's endurance and the woman's goodness. The righteous man's endurance, because he did not complain and say: "Why do I bring this woman along, when she has become the cause of such a storm for me? What good is our marriage to me, when because of her I am about to face mortal danger? What do I gain, when she not only brings me no comfort but even brings death upon me with her beauty?" He neither said nor thought any of these things. He rejected every such thought, did not doubt God's promise, and was concerned with one thing only: how he might escape the danger he foresaw. Consider here, beloved, God's inexpressible patience. He does not step in anywhere or comfort the righteous man. He waits for the dangers to reach their peak, to grow, and to come to the point of despair, and only then does he show his providence. "Say, then," he says, "'I am his sister,' so that it may go well with me because of you, and my soul shall live on account of you." The righteous man did not say this as though his soul were going to die ("Do not fear," it says, "those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul"). He was simply using an ordinary way of speaking with his wife. "So that it may go well with me," he says, "because of you, and my soul shall live on account of you." It is as if he were saying to her: "Say, 'I am his sister.' Do not let me, who fled Canaan because of the famine, fall prey to Egyptian hands. Be the cause of my safety, so that it may go well with me because of you." Pitiable words! His fear was great, both because of the madness of the Egyptians and because the tyranny of death had not yet been overthrown. That is why the righteous man chooses even to share in his wife's adultery, and very nearly to help the adulterer outrage his wife, in order to escape death. For death's face was still terrifying. The bronze gates had not yet been broken, and its sting had not yet been blunted. Do you see the bond of love between husband and wife? Do you see [?]

came into Egypt, "the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was very beautiful." Not simply beautiful: her beauty drew everyone who saw her beyond measure. "And Pharaoh's officials saw her and praised her before Pharaoh." Do not pass over these words carelessly, beloved. Marvel instead that none of the Egyptians laid hands on the woman as a foreigner who had come from a strange land, and that they did not treat her husband with contempt, but went in and made her known to the king. This happened so that the affair might become better known. Since the punishment fell not on some ordinary person but on the reigning king himself, the event would be spread everywhere. "And they brought her to Pharaoh." At once the righteous man was deprived of his wife, and she is brought to Pharaoh. Consider how great God's patience is. He does not show his providence from the beginning or at the very start. He lets everything happen, lets the woman fall almost into the very throat of the beast, and then makes his power plain to all. "And they brought her into Pharaoh's house." What state was the woman's mind in at that time? How troubled were her thoughts? How high did the waves rise? And how did she not suffer shipwreck, but stand firm like an immovable rock, looking to help from above? But why do I speak only of the woman? Imagine what the righteous man must have felt as she was being brought into Pharaoh's house. "And they treated Abram well because of her," as her brother, clearly. "And he had sheep, and calves, and donkeys, and male servants, and female servants, and camels, and mules." These very things were given to him for his luxury and comfort. What a fire they must have kindled in him! How could they not have burned up his mind and set his thoughts ablaze, as he considered why the gifts were given? Do you see the dangers come almost to their very end? Do you see that, as far as human affairs go, no hope of putting things right was left? That by human reckoning matters were beyond hope? That the woman had fallen into the very gullet of the beast? Now see God's unspeakable love for humankind, and be astonished at the surpassing greatness of his power. "And God afflicted," it says, "Pharaoh and his house with great and grievous afflictions because of Sarai, Abram's wife." What does "afflicted" mean? He made him pay the penalty, it means, for his audacity and his wicked attempt. "With great afflictions": he did not simply afflict the king, but afflicted him "with great afflictions." Since the audacity was no ordinary one but very great, the punishment too was great. "And his house," it says: not him alone, but his house as well. And why, when only the king sinned, did everyone in his house share in the punishment? This too did not happen without reason. It was so that God might reach the king's madness through this as well. A heavier blow was needed, so that he would be struck with terror and turn away from the abomination. "But where is the justice," people say, "in punishing these others because of him?" They were not punished because of him alone. It is likely that they too helped and took part in the crime that was about to be committed. For you heard Scripture say above: "Pharaoh's officials saw her and praised her, and brought her into Pharaoh's house." Do you see that they acted as procurers to win the king's favour, for the [?] [?]

…after being put to bed with an Egyptian, a king, a tyrant, a man so frenzied and so lewdly inclined, she came away untouched, her chastity kept whole. For, as I said a moment ago, what God arranges is always like this: wonderful and beyond expectation. When people have given up hope of a situation, that is when he shows his invincible power in everything. It was a wonderful and astonishing thing to see the man of desires surrounded by those wild beasts and suffering nothing, but coming up out of the pit unharmed, as if he had been ringed by sheep. It was the same with the three young men in the furnace, who spent their time there as if in a meadow or a garden, took no harm from the fire, and came out of it like statues. In just the same way, what happened now deserves our wonder: the wife of the righteous man suffered no outrage at the hands of the king of Egypt, that tyrant, that lewd man, and came away safe. For it was God who did it all, God who makes a way where there is no way, and who can always bring affairs out of despair into good hope. "And now, here is your wife before you. Take her and go." Do not think, he means, that we have wronged you. Even if we made the attempt in ignorance, now we know what a protector you have. The anger turned against us has taught us how much favor you enjoy from the God of all. "So take your wife and go." From then on the righteous man was feared by them, and so they hurried to send him on his way with great honor, trying to appease his Master through the way they treated him. 8. Do you see, beloved, how great a thing patience and endurance are? Here I would have you recall the words the patriarch spoke when they were about to draw near to Egypt: "I know that you are a beautiful woman. When the Egyptians see you, they will kill me, but they will keep you alive." Keep those words in mind as you consider what is happening now, and marvel both at the patience of the righteous man and at the power of the loving God: with what glory he has the righteous man return, who came in such fear and dread! "And Pharaoh," it says, "gave his men orders about Abram, to escort him on his way, with his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him." So the righteous man went back in complete splendor and with great wealth, and through what had happened he became a teacher not only to the people of Egypt but also to everyone along the road and to those living in Palestine. For those who had seen him going down in fear and trembling, driven by the famine, and now saw him again in such splendor, abundance and wealth, came to learn the power of God's providence over him. Who ever saw such a thing? Who ever heard of it? He went away to find relief from famine, and he comes back clothed in wealth and in glory beyond words. Do not be surprised, beloved, and do not [529] marvel at what happened; or rather, do marvel, be astounded, and glorify the power of the Master we all share. And look at his descendants too: in the same way they went down into Egypt again because of the famine, and from there, after long slavery and hardship, they came back up again with abundance. That is how resourceful our Master is. When he allows troubles to reach their peak, he then scatters the storm and brings about calm, and [?] a great reversal of affairs, teaching

…of the righteous endured, having made his way through the present life by the road of affliction, listen to Christ saying, "In the world you will have affliction, but take courage." So that they would not lose heart on hearing this, he at once filled them with courage and promised them his own support: "But take courage," he says, "I have conquered the world." You have, he means, one who lightens your troubles, who does not let you be swamped by the onset of temptations, who [?] along with the temptation also provides the way out, and who does not allow hardships beyond our strength to be laid on us. Why are you vexed? Why are you distraught? Why are you resentful? Why are you so faint-hearted? If we contribute what lies in our power, I mean patience, endurance and a thankful spirit, will he ever allow us to be overlooked? Even if things come to the point of despair, do they ever get the better of our Master's wisdom? Let us show what is ours to show and keep our faith sincere, knowing how resourceful is the protector of our souls. He knows our good better than we do, and he will surely arrange it as he ought, in a way that both befits him and benefits us, so that we may receive the reward of our patience and be counted worthy of his love for humankind, by the grace and compassion of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory, might and honor to the Father together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen. "Now Abram was very rich in livestock, and in silver and in gold. And he went back to where he had come from, into the desert as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at first, between Bethel and Ai, to the place of the altar [?] which he had made there at the beginning." 1. Seeing your eager gathering here today and your longing to listen, I want to pay you a debt that we owe your love. I know that you may well have forgotten it, since many days have passed in between and our preaching has been drawn off to other subjects. The arrival of the holy feast interrupted our sequence. It would not have been reasonable, while we were celebrating the Master's cross, for our teaching to deal with other matters; at each season we had to set before you the table that suited it. That is why, when the day of the betrayal came, we broke off the sequence of our teaching and turned to what was pressing: we let our tongue loose against the betrayer, and then set before you the events of the cross. Then, when the day of the resurrection arrived, it was necessary to teach your love about the Master's resurrection, and again in the days following to offer you proof of the resurrection from the miracles that happened afterwards. That was when we took up the Acts of the Apostles and served you a continuous banquet from it, giving much exhortation each day to those newly counted worthy of grace. So now it is necessary to remind you of the debt and then to pay it. Even if you, pulled about by many cares, do not even know what the debt is, since you have a wife to look after, and children to care for, and

…"there Abram called on the name of the Lord God." Let us not run past what has been read without thought, but let us learn clearly the precision of the divine Scripture, how it tells us nothing idly. "Now Abram," it says, "was very rich." Notice first this very point: it did not remark on this casually, and it is not for nothing or at random that it now calls him rich. Nowhere else has it mentioned that he was rich, but only now for the first time. For what reason, and why? So that you may learn how resourceful God's wisdom is, and the surpassing and [555] boundless power of the providence he exercised over the righteous man. The man who had gone abroad into Egypt because of the famine, because he could not bear the hardship in Canaan, suddenly became rich, and not merely rich but very rich, and not only in livestock but also in silver

2. Do you see how great God's providence is? He went away to find relief from famine, and he came back not only with the famine relieved, but clothed in great wealth and in glory beyond words, and having become plain to everyone for who he was. From then on, the people living in Canaan also came to know the righteous man's virtue more exactly, seeing such a sudden reversal, and the stranger who had gone down into Egypt like a fugitive and a vagrant now overflowing with so much wealth. And notice that the great prosperity and abundance of wealth did not make him more slack or more careless; instead he hurried back to the place where he had been before he reached Egypt. "For he came," it says, "into the desert as far as the place where his tent had been at first, to the place of the altar which he had made there at the beginning, and he called on the name of the Lord God." Consider, I ask you, what a lover he was of quiet and of a life free from business, and how constantly devoted to the service of God. For he went back, it says, to the place where he had earlier built the altar and called on the name of God. Already, long before and from the very beginning, he was fulfilling what David said: "I have chosen to be cast aside in the house of my God rather than to live in the tents of sinners." Because there he called on the name of God, the desert was dearer to him than cities. He knew, he knew well, that what makes a city great is not the beauty of its buildings or the number of its inhabitants, but the virtue of those who live in it. That is why the desert was more honorable than the cities, adorned as it was by the righteous man's virtue, and appeared more splendid than the inhabited world. "And Lot," it says, "who traveled with Abram, also had sheep and cattle and livestock, and the land could not hold them living together, because their possessions were many, and they could not live together." It was not only the patriarch's wealth that grew; Lot too had, it says, sheep and cattle and livestock. Perhaps Abram, being generous, gave some of them to his nephew himself, while others were given to Lot by other people out of respect for the patriarch. "And the land could not hold them," it says, "because their possessions were many." See how the abundance of wealth at once becomes a cause of division, brings about separation, breaks up harmony, and cuts the bond of kinship. "And there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot. And the Canaanites and the Perizzites were then living in the land." Consider how those who belong to them [?] reckons to them [?]. Savile, in the margin, conjectures οὐδείς ("no one").

…that men who were going to live here as sojourners should fall into such contention, when they ought to be setting themselves up as teachers of fairness, gentleness and every kind of wisdom for all these people. Let those listen to this who think they are free of blame when, out of familiarity with their own people, they look the other way while those people rob, grab more than their share, and do countless wrongs to their neighbors in cities and in the countryside, seizing one man's field and another man's house, and who even show their own people more favor for it. Even if the deed of injustice was someone else's, you have shared in it, not only by taking pleasure in what was done and thinking that your property is growing and your wealth increasing because of it, but also by not preventing the injustice before it was carried out. For the one who could stop the wrongdoer and does not do so will be held no less accountable than the wrongdoer. So let us not deceive ourselves, I beg you. Let us ourselves shun robbery and greed and the increase of our wealth by such means, and let us teach our own people to do nothing of the kind. For this does not leave us free of blame; it brings us heavier condemnation. Those people, betraying their own salvation in order to please us, venture on injustice, and drag us down with them into their own ruin. But if we are willing to be sober, we will both escape the harm that comes from this ourselves and turn them away from their wicked undertaking. And do not tell me those feeble words: "It is nothing to me. Did I seize anything? I know nothing about what someone else did; I had no share in the injustice." That is an excuse and a pretext. If you want to show that you had no share in the injustice, did not help bring it about, and were not an agent of the greed, put right what was done, comfort the one who was wronged, give back what was taken. In this way you will free yourself from blame, you will correct the wrongdoer by showing that what he did was not done with your approval, and by comforting the poor man you will not let him be swallowed up by the despair he would otherwise suffer because of what was taken from him. "Let there be no strife," he says, "between me and you, or between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are brothers." Do you see his gentleness? Do you see his fairness? Listen to what follows as well, so that you may learn how surpassing his wisdom was. How, then, can the strife be resolved and the contention quenched? "Look," he says, "the whole land is before you. Separate from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; and if you go to the right, I will go to the left." Consider the righteous man's wisdom and how intense his humility was. But before this, consider, beloved, how ruinous wealth is, and what discord great abundance brings. The flocks increased, great wealth [556] came to them, and at once harmony is broken. Where there had been peace and the bond of love, there is now strife and contention. For where there is "mine" and "yours," there is every kind of strife and occasion for contention; but where this does not exist, harmony and peace hold sway in every detail. And so that you may learn this, listen to what blessed Luke says about those who first came to the faith: "The heart and soul," he says, "of all of them were one." Not that they all had one soul, for how could they, being in different bodies? But he is showing us how intense their harmony was. And had the righteous man not been very long-suffering and known how to practice wisdom, he would have become angry, and [?]. So although Lot ought to have done this toward

…the patriarch, like a youngster carried away by desire for more, he leaps at what he took to be the better share and makes his choice. "And Lot," it says, "lifted up his eyes and saw all the region around the Jordan, that it was all well watered, before God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of God and like the land of Egypt, as far as Zoar. And Lot chose for himself all the region around the Jordan, and Lot set out from the east, and they separated, each from his brother." Do you see the surpassing virtue of the righteous man, how he did not let the root of evil even sprout, but at once cut out from below and destroyed what was about to grow? He showed great fairness, and for the sake of virtue an indescribable disregard for everything else, and he showed everyone that peace and freedom from contention were more precious to him than any wealth. So that no one should condemn the righteous man as ungrateful toward Lot, as if, having taken him from his home and brought him to a foreign land, he were now throwing him out of his household, and so that no one should think he did this out of hostility, but that we might all learn that he did it out of devotion to peace, he gave Lot the choice, and when Lot took the better share he was not displeased. In this way we can all know the goodness of the righteous man's disposition and the aim of his peaceful soul. Besides, another mystery was also being prepared in advance: that many things would happen to Lot, that Lot would be taught by events that he had not chosen as he should, that the people of Sodom would learn Lot's virtue, and that, once the separation had taken place, the promise made to the patriarch would come to fulfillment, the one that said, "To you and to your [558] descendants I will give this land." We will see these things as we go on little by little, since the divine Scripture makes everything plain to us.
