"And Abram," it says, "lived as a sojourner in Canaan, but Lot settled in a city of the surrounding region and pitched his tent in Sodom. Now the men of Sodom were wicked, and very great sinners before God." Do you see that Lot looked only at the nature of the land and did not consider the wickedness of its inhabitants? Tell me, what use is good land and a rich harvest when the inhabitants are depraved in their ways? And what harm could come from a desert and the poorest land when the inhabitants are decent people? The chief of all goods is the right-mindedness of the inhabitants. But Lot looked at one thing only, the fertility of the land. That is why Scripture, wanting to point out to us the wickedness of those who lived there, says, "Now the men of Sodom were wicked, and very great sinners before God." Not only "wicked," it says, but also "sinners"; and not simply "sinners," but "before God," that is, their sins were extremely intense and their wickedness surpassing. That is why it added, "very great, before God." Do you see how great the evil was? Do you see what an evil it is to leap at the first place and not consider what is truly beneficial? Do you see how great a thing fairness is, and yielding the first place, and accepting the lesser share? As our teaching goes on, we will see that the one who chose the best gained no benefit from it, while the one who took the lesser became more illustrious every day, and

[?]… excess. For it was no ordinary thing that the old man, who had done so many kindnesses and enjoyed such favor from the Master of all, should show such equal regard toward the young man, his nephew, as to yield him the first place, take the lesser share himself, and accept anything in order to stop the conflict and remove the occasion for contention. Let us all strive to imitate him. Let us never exalt ourselves over our neighbors or think highly of ourselves, but, showing great humility, let us give way and be eager rather to take the lower place in deeds and in words. Let us not be hostile toward those who wrong us, even if they happen to have received kindnesses from us (for this is the highest wisdom), and let us not grow savage at [540] insults, even if those who quarrel with us are our inferiors, but let us calm our anger with fairness and gentleness. For nothing is stronger than this, nothing more powerful. It sets our soul in unbroken calm, makes it ready to anchor as if in a harbor, and becomes for us the source of all rest. That is why Christ too, when giving that divine teaching, said, "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." For nothing so sets the soul at rest and in deep quiet as gentleness and humility. To the one who possesses it, this would be more precious than any crown, more profitable than any splendor and glory. What could be more blessed than to be free of the war that arises within? Even if we enjoy peace and attention from outside ten thousand times over, but turmoil and storm arise within us from the agitation of our thoughts, the peace outside is of no use. In the same way, nothing is more pitiable than a city that suffers betrayal from those living inside it, even if someone surrounds it with ten thousand walls and ramparts. So, I beg you, let us strive for this before all else: to keep our soul untroubled, to settle it in quiet, to be free of all bitterness, so that we ourselves may enjoy great rest and be pleasant to those who spend time with us. For this above all is the mark of a human being honored with reason: to be mild, fair, gentle, humble and quiet; not to be dragged and hauled about like a slave by anger or by the other passions, but to master the stirrings within by reason, to preserve one's own nobility, and not to fall through carelessness into the savagery of irrational beasts. And so that you may learn how great the strength of gentleness and fairness is, and how this virtue alone was enough to win ineffable praise for the one who achieved it with precision, listen to the proclamation of blessed Moses that comes from it, and the crown woven for him out of it: "And Moses," it says, "was the gentlest of all people on earth." Do you see the greatness of this praise, which declared him equal to the whole of human nature, or rather ranked him above the entire human race? And again Scripture says of David, "Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness." From this the patriarch also drew down much greater favor from above, and because he contributed his own part, he was counted worthy of greater things by the loving God. You will know this when we set before you what follows. Other manuscripts read "could be more pitiable." Seven manuscripts read "through carelessness."

…saying these very words to him openly: "Out of your great gentleness you gave up the finest land to your nephew, and you showed the utmost humility. You took such care for peace that you accepted anything so that there would be no quarrel between you. For this reason, receive a lavish reward from me." "Lift up your eyes," he says, "and look from the place where you now are, to the north and the south, to the east and the west; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever." Do you see a reward that far exceeds what Abraham had done? The loving Master uses the very words the patriarch used when he gave way. Abraham had said, "Is not the whole land before you? Separate from me. If you go to the right, I will go to the left; if you go to the left, I will go to the right." In the same way the Master says, "Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever." Here, I ask you, notice how great his generosity is. "You," he says, "gave him the choice. You let him have the part he wanted, and you accepted what was left. But I am so generous that all the land your eyes can see on every side, north and south, east and west, all the land that you see, I will give to you. And not only to you, but also to your offspring forever." Do you see generosity worthy of the goodness of God? Do you see how much he gave up, and how much he was given? Let us learn from this to be very lavish in giving alms, so that by giving little we may receive great things. Tell me, how can these be equal: giving a little silver and receiving forgiveness of sins? Feeding someone who is hungry, and being granted confidence on that fearful day, and hearing words worth the kingdom: "I was hungry, and you gave me food"? The one who gave you such abundance could surely have relieved that man's need as well, could he not? But he lets him be worn down by poverty so that he may receive a great reward for his endurance, and so that you may store up for yourself in advance the [?] that comes from almsgiving…

3. Do you see the Master's love for us, how he arranges everything for our salvation? So when you consider that this man is wrestling with poverty and wasting away from hunger for your sake and your benefit, do not pass him by without pity. Be a faithful steward of what the Master has given you, so that by relieving his need you may draw great favor from above. And glorify your Master, because for your sake and your salvation he allowed that man to live in poverty, so that you might find a way [?] to wash away your sins. Then, by managing well what the Master has given you, you will be found worthy of praises that surpass all speech and thought. For you will hear: "Well done, good and faithful servant. You were faithful over a few things; I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord." With this in mind, let us look on the poor as benefactors who can give us the means of salvation. Let us give lavishly and with cheerful eagerness. Let us never refuse to give, but speak to them very gently and show them great kindness. Incline [?] [?]

See how the loving Master trains the just man's virtue little by little. He said earlier, "To your offspring I will give this land"; now he says again, "And to your offspring I will give it forever, and I will make it like the sand of the earth." Yet so far the promise has gone no further than words, and a long time passes in between. This is so that we may learn both how much the patriarch loved God and how far God's power exceeds all things. God delays and puts things off on purpose. He waits until those who received the promise have reached deep old age and, so to speak, have given up hope by human reckoning. Then they experience their own weakness and see the overwhelming greatness of God's unspeakable power. 4. Consider with me, from the length of the time in between, how firm the patriarch's mind was. He looked past everything human and fixed his mind on the power of the one who had promised, and he was neither alarmed nor troubled. You know how often, when someone has promised once and twice and still has not done what he promised, we become slower to believe him when he promises again. With a human being that is reasonable. But with God, who manages our affairs with great wisdom, it is different. Once he has promised, even if countless obstacles get in the way, we must look to the greatness of his power and take courage. We must keep our thinking steady and know that whatever he has said will certainly come to pass. Nothing can ever cut short what he has promised, for he is God, and all things are possible for him. That is why he changes things to suit his will. He can find a way where there is none, and after we have despaired he leads us to good hopes, so that in this way we may learn more clearly how great his resourceful wisdom is. "Arise," he says, "and travel through the land, through its length and its breadth, for I will give it to you." See how in every way he wants to give the just man full assurance. "Arise," he says, "go around and learn its length and its breadth. Then you will know how large the land is that you are going to enjoy, and you will be nourished by hope and full of good cheer even before you enjoy it. For whatever land you walk around, I will give to you. So you will learn that what you gave up is not as much as what you are now going to receive. Do not think, then, that you have received the lesser share because he leapt at what looked like first place. Before long you will learn from events themselves that choosing first place did him no good, and he too will learn what an evil it is to love first place. Meanwhile, receive the reward for the humility and gentleness you showed your nephew. Accept the promise, and survey even now all the land of which you are lord, which before long you and your offspring will hold forever." "And to your offspring," he says, "forever." How great is God's promise! How abundant the generosity of the Master of us all! How far the reward of the loving and all-compassionate one exceeds anything given, the reward he gave to this blessed man and to the offspring who would be born from him! When the patriarch heard this, he was amazed at God's unspeakable goodness. "Moving his tent," it says, "he came and settled [?]…" […] [?] he opened up for us a road of repentance, if he has arranged countless other things for our salva-

-tion, he will clearly also give us the good things stored up for us in the future. He prepared these things out of his own goodness before we even came into being; how then will he not also grant us to enjoy them? To see that he prepared these good things for us in advance, listen to what he says to those standing on his right: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you before the foundation of the world." Do you see how great his goodness is, how much love he has shown our race, preparing the enjoyment of the kingdom for us even before the foundation of the world? So let us not be ungrateful, I beg you, or make ourselves unworthy of such great gifts. Let us love our Master as we ought, and do nothing that would cut off his goodwill toward us. After all, we were not the ones who started this. He showed us great and unspeakable love first. Is it not absurd, then, not to love him in return as much as we can, when he has loved us so much? Out of love for us he gladly endured everything. He leapt, so to speak, from the Father's very bosom and consented to take the form of a slave. He went through everything that belongs to human life and endured insults and dishonor from the Jews. In the end he accepted a cross and a shameful death, so that by faith in him he might set free us who were crawling on the ground, weighed down by countless burdens of sin. Blessed Paul thought about all this: Paul, the ardent lover of Christ, who ran around the whole world as if he had wings, and who strove while in the body to show the qualities of the bodiless powers. He cried out, "For the love of Christ constrains us." See his gratitude! See how great his virtue is! See his burning longing! "The love of Christ," he says, "constrains us"; that is, it drives us, compels us, urges us on. Then, wishing to explain what he had said, he says: "We have concluded this, that if one died for all, then all died. And he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them." Do you see how fitting it was for him to say, "The love of Christ constrains us"? "If he died for all of us," he says, "he died so that we who live might no longer live for ourselves, but for him who died and was raised for us." So let us accept the apostle's exhortation and not live for ourselves, but for him who died and was raised for us. "And how," someone asks, "shall we manage not to live for ourselves?" Listen to this blessed man again: "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." See how, though he walked on earth and was bound up with flesh, he lived as though he dwelt in heaven and spent his time with the bodiless powers. That is why he said again elsewhere, "Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." This, then, is what it means not to live for ourselves, but for him who died and was raised for us: to be as good as dead to the present life, and not to be carried away by anything we can see. For this is why our Master was crucified: so that instead of this life we might enjoy [?] that one, or rather, so that through this life we might gain that one for ourselves. For the present life, if we are willing to be sober and watchful, [leads] to the enjoyment of the [?]… Some manuscripts read "from the foundation."

…[?] he showed. But whatever we may be able to show, we do nothing great when we try to repay him who came first with such great benefits. […to be guided to the understanding of what is written, and to reap great benefit from it [?]…] For what comes from us, if it follows at all, is only repayment and debt; what comes from him is grace, kindness, and a great gift. Bearing all this in mind, then, let us love Christ as Paul loved him. Let us count the things of this world as nothing, and keep longing for him firmly settled in our souls at all times. In this way we will laugh at everything in the present life, and in this way we will live on earth as though it were heaven. We will not be puffed up by the good things here or crushed by the painful ones. Passing over everything, we will hurry from here toward the Master we long for, and we will not even chafe at the delay. Like this blessed man, we too will say, "The life we now live in the flesh we live by faith in the Son of God, who loved us and gave himself for us." Then we will pass through the present life without grief and be found worthy to enjoy the good things to come, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ. With him, to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, be glory, power and honor, now and always, and to the ages of ages.

HOMILY 35. "And it came to pass in the reign of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of the nations, that they made war with the king of Sodom." 1. Reading the divine Scriptures, beloved, is a great good. It makes the soul wise. It lifts the mind up to heaven. It makes a person grateful. It keeps us from being carried away by anything in this present life. It keeps our thoughts always dwelling there, so that we do everything with our eyes on the Master's reward and take on the labors of virtue with great eagerness. From the Scriptures we can learn exactly how God provides swift help, how brave the just are, how good the Master is, and how great his rewards are. From them we can be stirred to imitate the wisdom of noble men with zeal. We need not grow sluggish in the contests of virtue, but can trust God's promises even before they are fulfilled. So I beg you, let us read the divine Scriptures with great diligence. This is how we will gain knowledge: by going over their contents continually. Whoever reads the divine words with diligence and great longing will never be overlooked. Even if no human being becomes our teacher, the Master himself enters our hearts from above. He illumines the mind, enlightens our thinking, reveals what is hidden, and teaches us what we do not know, if only we are willing to contribute our own part. "For call no one on earth your teacher," he says. So when we take a spiritual book in hand, let us focus our minds and collect our thoughts, and drive away every worldly concern. Let us read in this way, with great reverence, with great [?]… Some manuscripts read "we do," others "let us do." The word "words" is added from a Coislin manuscript.

…the Jewish worship, so that he might offer worship to the Master. And when he had done what he longed to do, "Returning," it says, "and sitting in his chariot, he was reading." 2. Then Philip came up and said to him, "Do you understand what you are reading?" Do you see a soul full of concern? He did not understand what he was reading, yet he kept at it, longing to find a teacher to guide him. The apostle at once stirs up that longing with his question. And the man's own answer shows that he deserved to find someone to guide him to understand what he was reading. When the apostle said, "Do you understand?" and came up to him in humble clothing, the man was not annoyed or indignant. He did not think he had been insulted, as many foolish people do. They often choose to stay ignorant forever because they are ashamed to admit their ignorance and learn from those who can teach them. But this man felt none of that. He answered with all gentleness and reverence, revealing the state of his soul: "How could I, unless someone guides me?" And he did not merely answer gently and then move on. Instead, showing us the virtue of his character, this potentate, this barbarian riding in a carriage, said this and then invited the man who looked so lowly, whose clothing marked him as someone to despise, to come up and sit with him. Do you see the eagerness of his soul? Do you see how intense his reverence was? Do you see the God-loving mind of a barbarian, and how he fulfilled the saying of a wise man: "If you see a man of understanding, go to him early, and let your foot wear out the steps of his door"? Do you see how rightly he was not overlooked? Do you see how rightly he enjoyed providence from above? Do you see how he left out nothing that he ought to have contributed himself? That is why, once he had found a teacher, he learned the meaning of what he was reading exactly, and his mind was enlightened. Do you see how great a good it is to read the divine Scriptures with attention and diligence? This is why I have set before you the story of this barbarian: so that none of us will be ashamed to imitate the Ethiopian, the eunuch, who did not neglect his reading even on a journey. This barbarian is able to teach all of us. He can teach those who have chosen private life, those enrolled in the army, and those in high positions. In short, he can teach everyone, not only men but also women, who spend all their time at home, and also those who have chosen the monastic life. All of them can learn from him that no circumstance prevents us from reading the divine oracles. We can keep up this pursuit not only at home, but also while walking in the marketplace, while traveling, while in the company of many people, and while busy with our affairs. Then, if we contribute our own part, we will quickly find a guide. For when our Master sees our desire for spiritual things, he will not overlook it, but will give us light from above and enlighten our minds. So let us not neglect reading, I beg you; but whether we know the meaning of what we read…

…Kadesh, and they cut down all the rulers of Amalek, and the Amorites who lived in Hazazon-tamar. Let us not pass over these words lightly, beloved, or think the story is useless. The divine Scripture has told us all this in detail on purpose. It wants us to learn how strong these barbarians were, how much courage they showed, and how fiercely they rushed into war. They even defeated the giants, that is, men of great bodily strength, and routed all the nations living in that region. Like a torrent that crashes down and sweeps everything away and destroys it, these barbarians fell on all these nations and wiped them out completely. They routed even the rulers of the Amalekites and all the rest. But perhaps someone will say, "What good does it do me to know how strong the barbarians were?" Scripture did not put these things into the story idly or at random. Nor are we urging you to remember their courage now for no reason. We do it so that, as the teaching goes on, you may learn how far God's power exceeds all things, and how great the patriarch's virtue was. Against these men, then, who had so much power and had routed so many nations, it says, "the king of Sodom went out to battle, with the king of Gomorrah, and of Admah, and of Zeboiim, and of Bela (that is, Zoar). And they drew up for battle against them in the Salt Valley, against Chedorlaomer, Tidal, Amraphel and Arioch: four kings against five. Now the Salt Valley [was full of] pits of asphalt." Then Scripture shows how the five kings were terrified by the others' courage and the strength of their forces, and turned to flight: "And the king of Sodom fled, and the king of Gomorrah, and they fell there where the pits were; and those who were left fled to the hill country." Do you see how strong those men were? Their very appearance terrified the others and made them run. Now see how easily, once all the others had fled, they took everything that belonged to them and went back. "They took," it says, "also the hill country [?], and all the horses of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and went away. And they also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, and his belongings, and went off; for he was living in Sodom." Look: what I said yesterday has now come true. Lot gained nothing by choosing first place. Events themselves taught him not to love first place. Not only did he get no benefit from it, but he was even carried off as a captive. He learned from experience that it would have been much better for him to enjoy the just man's company than to be separated from him and, for all his freedom, suffer such disasters. He separated from the patriarch and thought he would be safer, that he had won first place and was very well off. Then suddenly he became a captive, with no house and no home. This is so that you may learn what an evil division is and what a good thing concord is. We should not leap at the greater share, but should rather be glad to have less. "They took," it says, "Lot and his belongings." How much better it would have been for him to stay with the patriarch and [?] everything…

…the magnanimity of the just man's courage: how, trusting in the power of God, he was not daunted by the strength of those men, even though he had learned of the rout they had inflicted. First they had attacked all the nations and overcome the Amalekites and all the rest, and then they had engaged the people of Sodom, put them to flight and stripped them of all their possessions. This is why divine Scripture told us all these things beforehand, and everything they had achieved by their courage: so that you may learn that it was not by bodily strength that the patriarch overcame them, but by his faith in God. Fortified by help from above, he accomplished all this without wielding weapons, drawing bows, hurling arrows and spears, or taking up shields. He went instead with the…

And why, someone asks, did he number three hundred and eighteen servants born in his house? So that you may learn that he did not just take everyone, but only those born in his house, who had been brought up together with Lot. That way they would carry out the vengeance with great goodwill, as men fighting for their own master. And observe, please, the surpassing power of God, and how swiftly the victory came about. "He fell upon them," it says, "by night, he and his servants, and struck them and pursued them." For the hand from above was taking part in what was done and sharing the command. That is why they needed neither weapons nor engines of war. Simply by appearing with his household servants he struck down some and put others to flight, and he did both in complete safety, with no one to trouble him. He brought back the cavalry of the king of Sodom, and Lot his nephew, and all the possessions, and the women. Do you see why, when the others had fled, Lot alone was allowed to be taken captive? It was so that the patriarch's virtue might become plain to see, and so that through him many others too might be saved. And so he returned bringing a great and splendid trophy, carrying with him Lot, the cavalry, the women and the possessions. He was proclaiming to everyone in a clear voice, crying out louder than a trumpet, that he had not brought about the rout or won the victory by human power or bodily strength, but that the hand from above had done it all. Do you see how the just man becomes more illustrious through everything, and at every turn shows everyone God's providence toward him? See him now also eager to become a teacher of godliness to the people of Sodom. "For the king of Sodom," it says, "went out to meet him after he returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him." Consider how great a thing virtue is, and what it is to enjoy God's alliance. The king goes out to meet the stranger, the old man, and pays him every honor. For he was learning that his kingdom was of no use to him without the alliance from above, and that nothing could be more powerful than a man aided by the hand of God. "And Melchizedek," it says, "king of Salem, brought out bread and wine; and he was a priest of God Most High." 5. What does this remark mean for us: "king of Salem, and priest of God Most High"? He was king, it says, of Salem. For blessed Paul too, writing to the Hebrews who had believed, brings him forward, and as he turns over his name and his city he also interprets the name…

…[?] of the things God has provided for us. Then the king of Sodom, astonished at the patriarch's magnanimity, says to him: "Give me the men, and take the cavalry for yourself." The king's gratitude is admirable, but look at the just man's wisdom. "And Abram said to the king of Sodom: I will stretch out my hand to God Most High, who made heaven and earth, that I will not take anything of yours, from a thread to a sandal strap, so that you may not say, I have made Abram rich." Great is the patriarch's disdain for money. And why does he make his refusal on oath, saying, "I will stretch out my hand to God Most High, who created heaven and earth"? 6. He wants to teach the king of Sodom two things at once. He shows that he is above the king's gifts and displays great wisdom, and he is also eager to become the king's teacher of godliness. He is all but saying to him: As my witness that I will take nothing of yours, I offer you the Creator of all, so that you may come to know the God who is over all and not think that things made by human hands are gods. For he, the maker of heaven and earth, is the one who won this war and caused the victory. So do not expect me to agree to take anything you give. I did not carry out this vengeance for pay. I did it first out of affection for my nephew, and then for the sake of justice itself, to snatch those who had been wrongly carried off out of barbarian hands. "If I take anything of yours," he says, "from a thread to a strap": that is, not even the merest trifle, nothing cheap, nothing thought worthless. For the word for "strap" was used for the tip of the shoe that ends in a point, since barbarians are in the habit of wearing shoes of that kind. Then he also gives the reason for his refusal: "So that you may not say, I have made Abram rich." I have the Giver of countless good things, he says. I enjoy abundant favor from above. I do not need your wealth, I have no use for human plenty. I am content with God's generosity toward me, and I know how lavish his gifts are. When I gave up small and cheap things to Lot, I was granted great and ineffable promises. Now I am gaining greater wealth for myself and drawing more goodwill from him, so I do not accept your wealth. This, I think, is why he also added the oath and said, "I will stretch out my hand to God Most High": so that the king would not think he was merely putting on a show, as is likely to happen, but would learn that he had firmly resolved not to take even the least thing from that source. He was fulfilling the command Christ gave to the disciples: "Freely you have received, freely give." Did I contribute anything more to this war, he says, than my resolve and my eagerness? The victory, the trophy and everything else, He accomplished by his invisible power. Then, so that the king would not think it was out of arrogance and contempt that he refused his gifts, he shows in this too his gentleness and the wisdom of his mind, and says: I will not take anything "except what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me, Eshcol, Aner and Mamre; they shall take a share." I will allow these men to take some share, he says, since [they gave] proofs of great friendship [?]…

…[?] lying upon it, so the desire for present things darkens the reason and does not let it see anything it ought. Again, it is impossible for someone who longs for those unchanging and secure goods to feel any desire for these perishable things, which fly away and wither before they even appear. For whoever has been wounded with longing for God and has come to desire the things to come sees the state of present things with different eyes. He knows that the present life is a mere outward show and a deception, no different from dreams. That is why blessed Paul said in his letter, "For the form of this world is passing away." He was showing that every human thing exists only in outward form and runs past like a shadow and a dream, with nothing true and nothing secure about it. Surely, then, it is the mark of a childish mind to get excited about shadows, to pride oneself on dreams, and to cling to things that will pass away a little later. "For the form of this world," it says, "is passing away." When you hear that it "is passing away," what more do you want? When you hear that all human things are mere form, empty of truth, why do you put up with the deception willingly? Why not consider how changeable and insecure they are, run past them, and turn your desire to the things that are everlasting, unchanging, secure and not subject to change? 8. To learn the understanding of the teacher of the world, see how elsewhere, wanting to show how worthless everything bright in the present life is, he used this expression: "For the things that are seen" — whether you mean abundant wealth, or glory, or renown, or office, or power, or kingship itself, the man who wears the diadem and the highest throne — all these "things that are seen are temporary." They last only a short time and do not let us enjoy them for long. What, then, do you want us to seek, if all these things that are seen are temporary? Those, he says, "that are not seen": not these things that are seen, but those that are not seen by these bodily eyes. And who, someone asks, would advise us to run past what is seen and seek what is not seen? Let the very nature of things teach you, he says. These things, though they are seen, quickly slip away. Those things, even if we cannot see them now, are eternal and last for ever. They know no limit, admit no end and know no change; they remain fixed and unchanging. Perhaps by now I seem tiresome, giving advice in vain every day. But what am I to do? Vice causes great ruin, the tyranny of money is great, and virtue is very scarce. That is why I want to overcome the disease, if only by persisting in my exhortation, and to bring those who gather here to perfect health. This is why we take pains to expound the Scriptures, bring the virtues of the just before you, and do not shrink from ringing the same things in your ears: so that by every means we may lead you to imitate the just. So let us, late as it is, take thought for our own salvation. Let us make proper use of the time we have been given as the span of our life, and while there is opportunity, let us hasten to repent and to correct our faults. Let us use our abundance of money for the good of our souls and spend what is left over on those in need. For tell me, why do you allow your silver and gold to be eaten away by rust… [?]

…to relate his story briefly, so that you may know both the just man's surpassing faith, which he showed in God's promises, and the generosity of the loving God, who gave him rewards so lavishly. For this just man is able to teach us all to strip eagerly for the contests of virtue, trusting in the rewards from above. Knowing our Master's generosity, we can accept with ease everything in the present life that is thought hard, nourished by the hope of recompense. Pay attention, I beg you, to how from the very beginning he enjoyed God's appearing, because he contributed his own part from within himself, from the knowledge implanted in our nature. He had no teacher from outside and was even brought up by unbelieving parents. Since even in his early youth he did not follow his father's error at all, but showed reverence toward God, he soon received a visitation from above while he was still in Chaldea. Blessed Stephen sets this out for us more clearly, saying: "The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran." Do you see how the vision raised him up from there? It is likely that, along with his worship of God, he also showed reverence to his parents and drew his father into great affection for him. In this way he himself became the reason his father left that place, and for love of his son the father agreed to leave his own homeland and live in a foreign one. But observe carefully, please, how the very visitation God granted him because of his earlier virtue makes his virtue more illustrious in turn. For he chose to leave the country of his fathers and live in a foreign one in order to put God's command into practice. He was ready, it seems to me, to set out on the journey alone, even without his relatives. But, as I said before, the man's virtue and his great devotion to his parents led his father to become his fellow traveler too. Then, when they reached Haran, they pitched their tent there. And when Terah died (that was his father's name), God again commanded him to leave that place. "Go out," it says, "from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I will show you." Since they had moved to Haran with the whole household, when God commanded him here to leave, he added "from your land and from your kindred." He was showing him that he wanted him to make the journey alone, by himself, and not to take along his brother, I mean Nahor, or anyone else. He said "from your land" because they had lived there no little time and now lived in it as if it were their own homeland. His mourning for his parent was still fresh, and journeys in those days were very difficult and there were no roads. Even so, he carried out the Master's command with complete eagerness, and that without knowing where his wanderings would come to an end. For "come," it says, not into this land or that, but "into the one I will show you." And although the command was so indefinite, he put it into practice without any prying questions; and his nephew too [?] … [Notes:] Savile: [?] providing. b "Raised up": so the editions and five manuscripts; [?] "pitched their dwelling"; Morel: "pitched their tent." … he made him return from Egypt to Palestine.

Consider how the loving Master brings in his own favor between the trials and makes his athlete vigorous again for the next contests. He does not leave him without his help, but arranges things so that it is shown to him plainly at every point: though he himself contributes little, he is granted great things, very great things, beyond human nature. Do you see, then, the just man's endurance? Look again at the greatness of his humility and his great gentleness after his return from there. For when he came back from Egypt having gained great wealth (and not he alone, since his nephew was with him too), "the land could not support them," it says, "living together, because their possessions were many." So a quarrel broke out between Lot's herdsmen and Abram's. But this just man showed the gentleness of his soul and the surpassing degree of his wisdom. He called Lot and said to him: "Let there be no quarrel between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are kinsmen." He was all but saying to him: Nothing equals peace, and nothing is more grievous than contention. So that we may remove every cause of quarrel, choose whatever region you want and leave me what is left, so that we may be free of all strife and contention. Do you see the man's virtue? He gave the young man first choice and was content with the poorest land. But see again how great a reward he receives once he has done his part. For as soon as they had separated, after Lot had parted from him, God said to him: "Lift up your eyes and look at all the land on every side, for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever." Consider how generously he is treated for the humility he showed his nephew. He gave up small things and was granted far greater ones, while Lot, who leapt at first place, soon fell into danger. Not only did he gain nothing from his choice, but he suddenly became a captive, without home or hearth. Through the events themselves he learned the surpassing virtue of the just man, and was taught never to do such a thing again. For as soon as Lot had settled in Sodom, a terrible war flared up. The kings of the neighboring nations came with a great force and utterly devastated the whole land. They killed the giants, drove back the Amalekites, put the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah to flight, and seized the whole hill country. They took the cavalry of the king of Sodom, captured Lot and the women with all the baggage, and then went home. 3. But see again God's great care. Wishing both to free Lot from captivity and to make the patriarch more illustrious, he roused the just man to rescue his nephew. When he learned what had happened, he set out with his household servants against those kings and struck them down with great ease. He brought back Lot, the women and all the king's cavalry, winning splendid trophies. He made God's goodwill toward him plain to all, and showed that he had brought about so great a rout not by his own power, but fortified by help from above. And now, through the events themselves, he was eager to teach…

…the things that were done [?] of Christ, and the very offerings foreshadowed a kind of mystery. That is why he accepted them; and Abraham, having received them, showed the greatness of his own virtue by the gift he gave in return. For he gave him a tenth, revealing in this too his God-loving purpose. Perhaps our sermon has run on to great length, but not in vain or to no purpose. For we have learned in brief, from the beginning up to today's reading, the just man's courage, his magnanimity, his surpassing faith, his wise mind, the greatness of his humility and his surpassing disdain for money. We have also learned of the constant providence that came from God's goodwill toward him, and how the help he received on each occasion showed the just man ever more illustrious and splendid. But if you are willing and not yet weary, let us also touch on what was read just now, add a little, and then bring the sermon to a close. Then you will learn how great a reward he is granted once again for disdaining what the king of Sodom offered him. What does it say? "After these words the word of the Lord came to Abram." Why did it begin this way, "After these words"? What words, tell me? Clearly, surely, the words he spoke to the king of Sodom. After that disdain, it means, after he shook off the king's gifts, after the teaching he gave by refusing them, as he led the king by the hand toward godliness and the knowledge of the Creator of all. "After these words": after he gave the tithe to Melchizedek. When, it means, he had fulfilled his whole part, then "after these words the word of the Lord came to Abram, saying in a vision of the night: Do not fear, Abram; I shield you; your reward shall be very great." 4. See the Master's love for humankind: how he follows good deeds at once with repayment, anointing his athlete and making him fresh again. "The word of the Lord came in a vision of the night." Why at night? So that he might receive what was said in quiet. And he says to him, "Do not fear, Abram." Consider the surpassing care. Why did he say "Do not fear"? Since Abram had despised such wealth and cared little for what the king offered, God says to him: Do not be afraid because you refused such gifts, and do not be anxious as though your property had been diminished. Do not fear. Then, to stir his soul still more, he adds his name to the words and says, "Do not fear, Abram." For this too is no small thing for rousing a person: to speak the name of the one being addressed. Then he says, "I will shield you." This expression also carries great emphasis. I who raised you up from the Chaldeans, I who brought you here, I who freed you from the dangers in Egypt, I who promised once and again to give this land to you and your offspring: I shield you. I who make you more illustrious before all every day: I shield you. That is: I fight on your behalf, I become your champion, I take care of you, I make every difficulty easy for you, I shield you. "Your reward shall be great…" [Note:] b In [?] it reads "O Master, Lord"; Hebrew [?]; Vulgate…

…yourself, since your heir will be the one who is to be born from you." Then, because the promise was beyond nature and surpassed human reasoning (for the obstacles of nature stirred up a great storm in him: his own old age, Sarah's barrenness, the deadness of her womb), God enlarges the scale of the promise, so that the righteous man, looking to the generosity of the one who made it, might take courage. "He brought him outside," it says, "and said to him, 'Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.' And he said, 'So shall your offspring be.' And Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Why did Scripture point out that "He brought him outside"? Because it said above that God appeared to him in a vision of the night and spoke these words to him; and since he wished to show him the countless number of the stars in heaven, it says, "He brought him outside and said, 'Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.' And he said, 'So shall your offspring be.'" Great is the pledge, vast the scale of the promise; but if we consider the power of the one who promised, nothing will seem great to us. For he who formed a body from earth, who brought it from non-being into being, and who created all things visible, will also be able to grant what is beyond nature. [5.1570] Do you see the Master's generosity? Abram had said, "I am departing childless," as though he were already at the very doors of death and no longer able to beget children; that was why he uttered those words, "The son of Masek, my household servant, will inherit me." Therefore, wishing to raise his spirits and restore vigour to his thoughts, God both frees him from the fear that pressed on him and sets his mind upright again with the promise; and by the greatness [?] of the gift, by showing him the multitude of the stars, and by promising that those born from him would equal them, he led him to bright hopes. For seeing the Master's promise, Abram shook off all human reasoning; looking neither to himself nor to Sarah, who faced still greater obstacles, but rising above everything human and knowing that God is able to bestow even what is beyond nature, he took courage from what was said, admitted no doubt, and did not waver at the words spoken. This is truly the mark of faith: when the promise does not follow the human course of things, and yet we take courage from the power of the one who promised. For faith, as blessed Paul says, "is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen"; and again, "For who hopes for what he sees?" This, then, is faith: when we believe in things not seen, fixing our minds on the trustworthiness of the one who promised. This is just what this righteous man did, showing great and genuine faith in what was promised; and for this he is proclaimed by divine Scripture, for it added at once, "And Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Do you see how, even before the promises were fulfilled, he received an ample reward for the mere act of believing? For it was reckoned to him as righteousness that he believed the promise from God, and did not pry with human reasonings into what God had said to him. Let us be taught, then, —

…let us cut short [?] our labours. For the hope of good things is enough to make us bold even in the face of dangers, let alone to bear nobly the labours of virtue. When you consider that, having struggled for a short time and kept the lamp of virginity bright, you will be counted worthy of that blessed life and will be able to go in with the bridegroom, if you have your lamps lit and holding enough oil—that is, the working of good deeds—how could you not run through every hardship with complete ease, bearing in mind the saying of blessed Paul: "Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord"? Do you see how he yoked peace together with holiness? So that we might learn that he requires not only purity of body but also peace, he aptly mentioned both, wishing to secure each person on every side and to have our thoughts settled, so that there may be no disturbance or tumult within us, but that we may live in calm and quiet, be at peace with all, and be gentle, meek and kind, so that all the colours of virtue may bloom upon our face. In this way we shall be able to look down on the glory of the present life, preferring true glory; to take great care for humility; and to laugh at all the prosperity of the present life, so that we may enjoy true and lasting prosperity and be counted worthy to see Christ. For "Blessed," he says, "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Let us therefore cleanse our conscience and order our lives with care, so that, having traveled through the present life with all virtue, we may be counted worthy to receive the rewards of our labours here in the age to come, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, be glory, power and honour, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

"And the Lord said to Abram, 'I am the God who brought you out of the land of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to inherit it.' 'Master, Lord, by what shall I know that I will inherit it?'" 1. Great is the power of divine Scripture, and vast the wealth of meaning hidden in its words. That is why we must attend carefully and search diligently, so that we may reap abundant benefit from it. It was for this reason that Christ too commanded, "Search the Scriptures," so that we might not simply attend to the bare reading, but, tracking down the depth, be able to grasp the true sense of Scripture. For this is Scripture's way: in a few words one can often find a great multitude of meanings. Its teachings are divine and not human, and so one can see that it is composed in every respect contrary to human wisdom. How so, I ask? There—I mean in human wisdom—all their effort is devoted to the arrangement of words; here it is entirely the reverse. Scripture has no concern for beauty of words or arrangement, for what it says has, of itself, divine grace and beauty blooming upon it. And there, after much unspeakable babbling, then of the meanings [575] [?] … did I lead you out from there in vain? This is why I wanted you to reach

Palestine, to leave your father's house and come into this land: so that you might inherit it. So, reckoning how much providence you have enjoyed from me from the time you left Chaldea until now, and how you have become illustrious, shown more glorious every day through my alliance and my care for you, take courage in what I tell you too. Do you see the surpassing loving-kindness? Do you see the greatness of his condescension? How he wishes to steady Abram's soul and make his faith firmer, so that he might no longer look to the obstacles of nature but, considering the power of the one who promised, might take courage as though the promises had already come to pass? 2. But look again at the patriarch: since he had gained boldness from what was said, see how he seeks fuller assurance. He says, "Master, Lord, by what shall I know this, that I will inherit it?" Although divine Scripture had already testified that he believed what God had said, for which it was reckoned to him as righteousness, still, since he heard, "For this reason I brought you out of Chaldea, to give you this land to inherit it," he says: "I cannot disbelieve what you say; yet I would like to learn the manner too—how I am to inherit it. For I see myself now advanced into old age, and until now wandering about here like a vagrant, and I cannot grasp by human reasoning what is to come—even though," he says, "I have already believed what was said, since it was spoken by you, who are able to bring things from non-being into being, and who make and transform all things. So I do not ask this out of unbelief; but since you have reminded me again of the inheritance, I would like to receive some more tangible and clear sign, able to strengthen the weakness of my thoughts." What then does the good Master do? Condescending to his own servant, and wishing to brace his soul, since he saw him confessing his weakness, believing the promise yet wanting to receive some assurance, he says to him: "Take me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a ram, a turtledove and a pigeon." See how he makes the covenant with him in human fashion. Just as among people, when we promise something to someone and wish to persuade the recipient of the promise not to doubt it, we offer some sign and pledge, so that, looking to it, he may know that what was promised will surely come to pass; so too the loving Master, since Abram said, "By what shall I know?" says, "See, I grant you this too: take me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, a ram, a turtledove and a pigeon." Consider with me to what concreteness the good Master consents to descend for the patriarch's assurance. Since in ancient times it was their custom to make covenants in this way and to confirm them by such means, he too goes this way. "And he took," it says, "and [Note: one manuscript reads 'passing by.']

…number of years, but up to four hundred years. "But I myself will take vengeance for them, and I will judge that nation which enslaves them, and so I will make them return here with many possessions." At the same time he foretells to him precisely what would happen afterward, revealing the slavery, the descent into Egypt, the wrath the Egyptians would suffer on their account, and their glorious return. And he shows him that it will not be in his case alone that things beyond nature will occur, and that after so many obstacles God's promises will be brought to fulfilment, but this will happen in the case of all his offspring as well. "I have told you these things now," he says, "so that before you end your life you may know what will befall your descendants too. But you," he says, "shall go to your fathers, nourished in a good old age." He did not say, "You shall die," but "You shall go," as though he were about to travel abroad and move from one homeland to another. "You shall go," he says, "to your fathers"—not meaning those according to the flesh. How could that be, since his father was an unbeliever, and the faithful patriarch could not go to the same place as he? For "there is a great chasm," it says, "between us and you." Why then did he say, "to your fathers"? He was hinting at the righteous: Abel, Noah, Enoch. "Nourished in a good old age." Perhaps someone might say: what kind of good old age could his be, to have passed his whole life amid so many afflictions? But do not look at that, O man; consider rather his renown on every occasion, and how the stranger, the man without city or hearth, became glorious, and how much of God's help he enjoyed throughout all his time. So do not judge things by present opinion, and do not think a good old age is living in luxury and gluttony, possessing wealth, [577] a crowd of household servants and herds of slaves. These things would not make a good old age; rather they would bring great condemnation on the one who is not brought to sober sense even in old age, who does not take thought for what is needed even at his last breath, but every day stuffs his belly, pursues banquets and drunkenness, and before long will be called to account for all of it. But the one who has traveled through life with such virtue truly ends his life nourished in a good old age, and finds at last the rewards and recompense of his labours here. That is why he says: these things will befall your descendants, but you shall go nourished in a good old age. Consider again here: had the righteous man's courage not been great and his wisdom surpassing, how even these very words could have thrown his thoughts into confusion. For he said, "in old age." [Note: Savile and six manuscripts read: "and the evil [?] of wealth, and of servants."] …that what concerns his descendants will certainly come to pass, and

from what had been foretold he might again acquire firm faith, so that what concerned himself must already come to fulfilment. Then, when he had completed the prophecy and Abram had received a sufficient sign of what had been done for him: "When the sun was setting," it says, "there was a flame, and behold, a smoking furnace and torches of fire, which passed between the divided pieces." The flame, the furnace and the torches came about to make known to the righteous man the firmness of the covenant and the presence of God's working. Then, when all was fulfilled and completed, the fire having consumed what lay before it: "On that day," it says, "the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying, 'To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites.'" See how again by repetition he confirms his promise to him. "He made a covenant," it says, "saying, 'To your offspring I will give this land.'" Then, so that from the breadth of the land and the extent of its borders the righteous man might know how far his offspring would spread, he says, "From the river of Egypt to the river Euphrates"—so great, he says, will your offspring be. Consider how by every means he wishes to show him the surpassing multitude. Having said above that he would make it countless like the multitude of the stars, here he also made plain the length of the borders, so that from this too he might learn the extent of the multitude [579] that was to be. And not only this, but he also names the nations one by one whose possession he was to give to his offspring, so as to give the righteous man full assurance by every means. And though so many promises had been made, Sarah still remained barren, and their old age advanced, so that, after they had given the greatest proof of their faith, they might then see both the weakness of human nature and the greatness of God's power. But so as not to stretch our teaching to great length again, let us halt the subject here and end our discourse, urging you to become imitators of the patriarch. Consider, beloved, for those words he spoke to the king of Sodom—or rather for all the rest of the virtue he displayed throughout his life—what reward he was counted worthy of, and how great a condescension the Master showed toward him, demonstrating to all of us, through what was done for the patriarch, his surpassing generosity: that if we can first show even a little, he does not delay in the least but repays us with great gifts, provided only that we show sincere faith, as this righteous man did, and are never shaken in our thoughts but keep our resolve firmly fixed. For it was from this that he too won approval. Hear blessed Paul proclaiming his faith, which he displayed from the beginning and from the very outset. He says: "By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place he was to receive, and he went out not knowing where he was going"—hinting to us at what God had said: "Go out [?]" … [Note: [?] seven manuscripts read: "the king of Sodom for those words which he made; or rather." [?] (In LIII.]

…of that day, neither the fear of hell, nor the greatness of the promises, nor the fact that our common Master of all takes to himself what is done to our fellow human beings; but, as though they had hearts of stone and were outside of nature, they now think that, because of the clothing they wear, they are even above human nature, not considering how much they make themselves liable for, by badly managing what the Master has entrusted to them, and by refusing to give any share to their fellow servants, but gladly leaving these things to be consumed by moths—are they not already preparing for themselves a more abundant fire of hell? For even if the rich distributed to the needy everything they had stored away, even so they would not escape punishment for the luxury they lived in, in their clothes and in their feasts. [581] What punishment do they not deserve, those who strive in every way to wrap themselves in silk garments again and again and strut in the marketplace, some wearing clothes woven with gold, others embroidered in other ways, while they overlook Christ naked and lacking even necessary food? This word would especially suit women. For among them one finds more love of finery and extravagance, and the wearing, along with gold-shot garments, of gold itself on the head, on the neck and on the rest of the body, and taking great pride in these things. How many poor people's bellies, tell me, could they have comforted, and how many bodies of the naked could they have covered, with what merely hangs from their ears, in vain and to no purpose, for no gain, but only for the harm and ruin of the soul? That is why the teacher of the world, having said, "Having food and covering," turned his discourse again to women and says, "not with braided hair or gold or pearls or costly clothing should they adorn themselves." See how he does not want them to be adorned with these, nor to wear gold, nor pearls and costly garments, but to transfer true adornment to the soul and make the soul's beauty shine through the practice of good works, and not, being infatuated with these things, to overlook the soul while it is filthy, squalid, clothed in rags, wasting with hunger, frozen with cold. For this zeal and this beautifying of the body reveal the soul's ugliness; the body's luxury makes the soul's hunger plain; and extravagance in clothing exposes its nakedness. For it is impossible for anyone who cares for the soul and values its comeliness and beauty to be infatuated with outward adornment; just as, again, it is impossible for someone devoted to outward show, to the beautifying of clothes and the adornment of gold, to take any thought whatever for the soul. When will such a soul bear to perceive any of the things it should, or come to think of spiritual matters, once it has given itself up to earthly things and, so to speak, drags along the ground, never able to draw breath, but bent over and weighing itself down with countless burdens of sins? How many troubles are born from this, it is not possible now to set out in words; it is enough to leave it to the conscience of those devoted to these things how much distress they receive from it every day. Either some piece of gold jewellery has fallen and is lost, and a great storm and uproar has seized the whole house; or a servant has stolen it, and all [are threatened with] the whip [?] … [?] to be at odds, but to compete with each other in bearing one another's burdens, and to consider domestic peace above all

…more highly valued. But we also need to hear the words themselves, so that the teaching may become clearer to you. "Now Sarai," it says, "Abram's wife, bore him no children; and she had an Egyptian maidservant whose name was Hagar." From this, beloved, consider for me the unspeakable long-suffering of God, and the surpassing faith of the righteous man, and the good sense he showed regarding the promises made to him. God had promised him so many times that he would give the land to his offspring, and that it would spread into so great a multitude as to equal the multitude of the stars. Yet although he saw none of the things promised coming to fulfilment, and the promises still remained mere words, he was not troubled in his reasoning or shaken in his resolve, but stayed unwavering, trusting in the power of the one who had promised. That is why divine Scripture has noted it here too, saying, "Now Sarai, Abram's wife, bore him no children." It all but shows us that after all these things, after the covenants made with him, after the promise that a countless multitude would come from him, he did not grow vexed and did not hesitate, though he saw none of what had been said coming to fulfilment, but everything to the contrary. That is why it says, after all those things, "Now Sarai, his wife, bore him no children": so that you may learn that nothing more had come to him after so many promises. And yet Sarai's barrenness and the deadness of her womb were enough to cause the righteous man great perplexity. But the patriarch no longer looked at the obstacles nature posed. He knew the resourcefulness of the Master, and that, as the creator of nature, he can find a way even where there is no way. So, like a right-minded servant, he did not pry into how things would come about, but yielded to God's incomprehensible providence and believed what had been said. That is why it says, "Now Sarai," after so many promises, "bore him no children. And she had an Egyptian maidservant whose name was Hagar." Here too divine Scripture did not mention the maidservant to us idly, but so that we might learn where Sarai had got her. That is why it added "Egyptian": so that we might go back to that earlier story and learn that she was one of the gifts given by Pharaoh, when Sarai enjoyed such vindication from the God of all and returned having received her. Divine Scripture deliberately made known to us both her name and her nation. But now see here Sarai's wise mind [?] and the surpassing degree of her self-restraint, and the patriarch's unspeakable compliance and obedience. "And Sarai said," it says, "to Abram in the land of Canaan: 'See, the Lord has shut me up so that I do not bear. Go in, then, to my maidservant, so that you may have children by her.'" Consider the woman's good sense. She said nothing like what Rachel later says to Jacob: "Give me children, or else I die." But what does she say? "See, the Lord has shut me up so that I do not bear." Since, she says, the creator of nature has made me childless and deprived me of bearing children, then so that you may not reach a deep old age and remain childless because of my barrenness, "go in to my maidservant, so that you may have children by her." Great and unspeakable is the woman's wisdom. For what woman would ever choose to do this, or advise her husband to do it, or yield her bed to her maidservant? [?] (Savile and six manuscripts: "promises. But still also.") (Thus Savile and [?].) [?] …and she gave her to Abram her husband as a wife. Consider

the precision of Scripture. It wants us to learn that not even after the words Sarai spoke to him did he leap at the thing, and that is why it says: "And Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her own maidservant." Divine Scripture all but shows us that he accepted the matter to comfort his wife and because he wished to please [?] her. And so that you may learn precisely the patriarch's chastity and surpassing self-control, it says: "After ten years of Abram's living with her as her husband in the land of Canaan." Nor did it note the time idly, but so that we might know for how many years the righteous man persevered and nobly bore his childlessness, and how, rising above every passion, he displayed great chastity. And not only this, but so that we might learn something else from it too. That is why it added: "After ten years of Abram's living with her as her husband in the land of Canaan." For it has not made known to us here the whole period of their marriage, but only the time they spent in Canaan. For what reason, and why? Because as soon as he arrived in Canaan the loving Master promised him, saying, "To your offspring I will give this land"; and again afterward, once and a second time, he made promises to him. So you may know, beloved, for how many years the Master kept putting it off [?] and bringing none of the promises to fulfilment, while the righteous man was not troubled in his mind, but put what God had said before his own reasonings. That is why it says, "After they had lived together ten years in Canaan." Have you seen the courage of his soul? Have you seen the training-ground of wisdom, how the Master delays and puts off because he wishes to make him more illustrious? For since he cares for his servants, he does not wish merely to bestow his benefits on them, but also to show them to be illustrious and to make their faith evident to all. If, as soon as he had promised to give the land to his offspring, he had opened Sarai's womb and granted him a line of children, the miracle would not have appeared so great, nor would the righteous man's faith have become evident to all. God's power would indeed have been plain even then, for by his own command he would surely have brought back to life the workshop of nature, which had been deadened and become useless for bearing children. But the patriarch would not have won his crown as he now did, with his virtue tested over so long a time and growing more radiant every day.

3. And so that you may learn that he not only wishes to do good and grant his gifts, but that it is also his custom to want to make those who receive them more illustrious, see him doing this in the case of the Canaanite woman as well. For this reason he delayed and postponed, so as not only to grant her the healing but also to make her known throughout the whole world. When she came begging and saying, "Have mercy on me, Lord, for my daughter is cruelly possessed by a demon," the compassionate and loving one, who always anticipates our requests, does not even deign to answer her. And the disciples, not knowing what was going to happen, and that he cared for the woman and did not wish to hide [?] her treasure… [?] (And six manuscripts: "deemed her worthy"; [?] and others: "her.")

…[he did not] simply grant her request, but proclaimed and [?]… (obeying you and your command he did this) [?]… crowned her. By saying "O woman," he showed how amazed he was at her faith; and by saying "Great is your faith," he made the woman's wealth plain to us. Then he says, "Let it be done for you as you wish": as much as you want, as much as you wish, so much I grant; for such persistence shows you worthy of your request. You have seen the woman's perseverance. You have seen the reason for God's long-suffering: he kept putting it off because he wished to make her more illustrious. But let us return, if you please, to the story before us, so that we may learn that for so many years he did not bring the promises made to the patriarch to fulfilment for no other reason than to grant them to him with great renown and make the righteous man's faith evident to all. That is why it says, "After they had lived together ten years in the land of Canaan," so that you may learn how much time had passed since he received the promise. For as soon as he arrived in Canaan he heard, "To your offspring I will give this land," and through all that long time he himself remained childless and Sarai's barrenness grew worse. "And she gave Hagar," it says, "to Abram her husband as a wife."

4. See how much wisdom was practised among them in olden times: the men were self-controlled and took great account of chastity, and the women were free of jealousy. Scripture deliberately keeps saying, "And Sarai took Hagar the maidservant," and again, "She gave her as a wife," so that you may learn how dispassionately she handled the matter and how great the wisdom among them was. "And he went in," it says, "to Hagar, and she conceived." See how Sarai learns that her childlessness was not the fault of the righteous man but of her own barrenness, for the union at once produced a conception. But see again the maidservant's ingratitude and the weakness of women's nature, so that from this too you may learn the patriarch's great gentleness. "And she saw," it says, "that she had conceived, and her mistress was dishonoured before her." For such is the character of servants: if they come upon a little good fortune, they cannot bear to stay within their own bounds, but at once forget their station and rush into ingratitude. That is just what happened to this maidservant. When she saw the swelling of her belly, she gave no thought to her mistress's unspeakable wisdom or to the lowliness of her own rank. Puffed up and proud, she looked down on the mistress who had shown her such care as even to bring her to her husband's bed. What then does Sarai do? "She said," it says, "to Abram: 'I am wronged by you. See, I gave my maidservant into your bosom; but when she saw that she had conceived, I was dishonoured before her. May God judge between me and you.'" Here, I ask you, consider the righteous man's unspeakable long-suffering and the respect he shows toward Sarai, asking her pardon over this unreasonable charge. For the woman who handed the maidservant to her husband with her own hands, who said, "Go in to my maidservant," who urged him to the union of her own accord and on her own initiative, now changes her mind and says, "I am wronged by you." Did he rush into union with the maidservant, woman? Did he leap at the thing driven by lust? It was in obedience to you… (Five manuscripts: "into the rank.")

…[it was not that,] moved by any passion of my own, I consented to intercourse with her, so that, moved by partiality on that account, I should give her unreasonable precedence. I know the honour due to you; I am not unaware of the ingratitude of servants. I have no regard for her, no concern. One thing alone is my care: that you should be free of grief and untroubled, established in all honour and rid of every distress.

5. This is true marriage; this is a husband: when he does not split hairs over his wife's words, but makes generous allowance for the weakness of her nature and makes it his one aim to remove her grief and bind fast peace and harmony. Let husbands hear and imitate the righteous man's gentleness. Let them render such respect and honour to their wives and spare them as the weaker vessel, so that the bond of harmony may grow stronger. For this is true wealth, this the greatest abundance: when a husband is not at odds with his wife, but they are joined together as one body. For "the two," it says, "shall become one flesh." Such people, even if they live in poverty and lowliness, would be the most blessed of all, reaping true pleasure and living in unbroken calm. But those who do not enjoy this, who are given to jealousy and destroy the blessing of peace, live the most pitiable life of all, even if they are awash in wealth, keep sumptuous tables and enjoy high renown. Every day they stir up waves and turmoil for themselves and suspect one another, and they can have no pleasure, since the war within throws everything into confusion and fills their life with misery. But here there is nothing of the kind. By his own gentleness the patriarch softened the anger of the lady of the house, and by giving her full authority over the maidservant he filled his house with deep peace. "And Sarai afflicted her," it says, "and she ran away from her presence." Since Sarai perhaps punished her insolence, the maidservant took to flight. For such is the habit of servants: when they are not allowed to act as they please and their undertakings are checked, they at once rebel against their masters and rush to flight. But see again here how much help from above the maidservant too enjoys, out of honour for the righteous man. Because she carried the righteous man's seed within her, she is also granted the vision of the angel. "For an angel of the Lord found her," it says, "by the spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur." Consider the Master's love for humankind: he overlooks no one, but whether it is a manservant or a maidservant, he shows his providence in all, looking not at differences of rank but at the disposition of the soul. Here, however, the angel appears not because of the maidservant's worth but out of honour for the righteous man. For, as I said earlier, she had to be granted great providential care because she had been found worthy to receive the righteous man's seed. "And having found her," it says, "the angel said to her, 'Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where are you coming from, and where are you going?'" See how even the angel's words brought her to remember her own rank. To make her more attentive, he at once brought her name forward and said, "Hagar"; for we are somehow accustomed to pay more attention to those who call us by name. Then he says, "maidservant of Sarai." He reminds her of her mistress, so that she may know that even if she had shared her master's bed ten thousand times, still… (Five manuscripts: "providence from above." In [?]: "by the multitude.")

…your offspring will be beyond counting, "because the Lord has heard your humiliation." So let us not be vexed either when some turn of circumstances humbles us. For nothing benefits our nature so much as having our pride checked and humbled and the swelling of our soul subdued. The Master listens to us most when we call on him with an anguished soul and a contrite heart, persisting long in our supplications. "Because the Lord has heard," it says, "your humiliation." Then he foretells the way of life of the child to be born. "He shall be," it says, "a rustic man; his hands shall be against all, and the hands of all against him; and he shall dwell in the face of all his brothers." He tells her beforehand that the child will be brave and warlike, and that he will labour hard at working the land. Have you seen how the things done for the maidservant honoured the patriarch? For the providence shown to her reveals the goodwill the Master displays toward the righteous man. Having given this counsel and brought Hagar the good news, the angel departed. But see again the maidservant's good sense. "And she called," it says, "the name of the Lord who spoke to her: 'You are the God who looks upon me'; for she said, 'Indeed I have seen face to face the one who appeared to me.' For this reason she called the well 'The Well of Him Whom I Saw Face to Face'; it lies between Kadesh and Bered." Consider how she too wishes to lay up an abiding memorial in the place through the name she gives it. For she called the place, it says, "The Well of Him Whom I Saw Face to Face." Have you seen how the maidservant gradually grew wiser through the affliction that surrounded her? How she showed great gratitude for the kindness done to her, and repaid, in the ways she thought fit, the one who had granted her such care? "And Hagar bore Abram a son," it says, "and he called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore him, Ishmael."

7. From this we learn how great a good gentleness is, and how great a gain it is to reap something even from afflictions. We learn about gentleness from what the patriarch displayed: he calmed Sarai's indignation, gave her authority over the maidservant, and in this way filled his house with peace. The gain from afflictions can be seen in the maidservant's case. When she was afflicted by her mistress and ran away, she endured great hardship and called on the Master with an anguished soul, and she was at once granted a visitation from above. So that she might learn that she was granted such care because she had been humbled and brought low, the angel says to her: "You are with child, and you shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your humiliation." We know, then, beloved, that if we stay sober, afflictions bring us closer to the Master, and that we will be able to draw his help to us when we approach him with an anguished soul and hot tears. So let us not grieve at afflictions, but count the gain that comes from them and bear meekly all that befalls us. Let us be trained to be gentle and mild toward all, but especially toward our own wives. Let us take great pains, whether they find fault justly or unjustly, not to split hairs but to devote ourselves to one thing only: removing the causes of grief and establishing deep peace in the home… [?] …ninety-nine; and the Lord appeared to Abram.

…[not only did he care for] Hagar as she wandered in the wilderness, having run away for fear of her mistress, but he also granted the birth of Ishmael. In this way he devised great comfort for the righteous man and repaid him for such endurance. And when Ishmael was born, divine Scripture, wishing to teach us the patriarch's age, also noted the number of his years for us, saying, "When Ishmael was born, Abram was eighty-six years old." Now let us see what follows, so that from what comes next we may learn once more both the righteous man's great endurance and the Master's unspeakable and surpassing love for humankind.
