We will know this precisely if we can again trace the stages of the righteous man's life, and how the good God ordered his affairs, testing his own servant at each stage and uncovering how dear to God his mind was. God himself clearly knew his servant's good disposition beforehand; he understood the beauty of his soul and knew the pearl precisely. But he wished to make him plain to everyone alive at the time as well, so that in later generations too the righteous man's virtue might draw those who are willing to emulate and imitate it. For this reason he reveals the wealth of the righteous man's mind little by little, so that we too may be taught never to distrust God's promises or chafe at delay. Whenever the Master of all makes a promise, we should trust things unseen more than things seen and in hand. We should know that what God has promised can never fail. Even if a long time runs by and things turn out contrary to God's promises, we should not be shaken in our reasoning even then, but should know the resourcefulness and invincible power of the one who promised, and that when he wills to carry out what he has decided, everything gives way and yields. For since he is Lord and creator of nature, he is able to bestow even what is above nature. So let us not look at our own weakness and pry into what God does, or look at the natural course of things and let our reasoning be divided. Instead, like right-minded servants who know our Master's surpassing power, let us believe his promises and rise above our natural weakness, so that we may obtain what was promised, enjoy his goodwill, and honour God as far as we are able. For the greatest honour we can pay him is to trust in his power even when what the eyes of the flesh see points the other way. And why are you surprised that with God the greatest honour is not to doubt? Even with our fellow human beings, when they promise us one of these perishable and corruptible things, if we do not doubt but trust the one who promised, every one of them considers that he has been paid the greatest honour: that we did not hesitate, but trusted his promises. If this holds even with human beings, who often change their minds or through weakness cannot carry out what they have decided, much more ought we to trust God's promise, even if a long time intervenes. I have not said this now idly, but so that, when we come to the beginning of what has been set before us today, we may know how the loving God, wishing to make the patriarch illustrious to all,

…his. Great is the gratitude of the righteous man, and surpassing is the love that the good God shows toward him. "For I am," he says, "your God." It is almost as if he were saying: "I who have managed your affairs in many ways up to now, I am he. I who raised you up from your home and brought you here, I am he. I who at every moment have been your champion and have set you above those who plot against you, I am he." And he did not say, "I am God," but "I am your God." See his great goodness, how even by this addition he shows his affection for the righteous man. The God of the whole world, the Creator of all things, the maker of heaven and earth, says: "I am your God." Great is the weight of the honour paid to the righteous man. The prophets too are accustomed to speak this way. He himself, though he is the common Master of all, now consents to be named after his servant, and we shall find him saying later, "I am the God of Abraham and of Isaac and of Jacob." In the same way the prophets are accustomed to say, "O God, my God." They do not confine his lordship to themselves; they are showing their own unrestrained longing for him. Yet there is nothing remarkable in human beings doing this. But when he himself does it in the case of human beings, that is what is new and astonishing. But let us not marvel, beloved. Let us rather listen to the prophet saying, "Better is one who does the will of the Lord than ten thousand lawless people," and again to blessed Paul saying, "They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, of whom the world was not worthy." So the prophet declared that one who does the will of the Lord is better than ten thousand lawless people. And blessed Paul, the teacher of the world, recalling all the righteous who lived in afflictions and distress, says, "Of whom the world was not worthy." He named the whole world and set against it these persecuted and afflicted people, so that you might learn how great virtue is. That is why the Creator of all says to the patriarch: "I am your God; be well-pleasing before me, and be blameless." For I will not overlook the sweat of your great virtue, but "I will set my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly." I will not simply make you grow into a multitude, but "exceedingly", which shows how great the increase will be. And what he said earlier, "as the sand and the stars," he expressed here with "exceedingly." But the grateful and God-loving servant saw God's great condescension and his care for his servant, and he was astounded. He came to consider both his own nature and God's goodness and infinite power, and "he fell," it says, "on his face," showing his gratitude by his posture. Not only was he not puffed up or proud at the goodwill shown to him; he was humbled all the more. "And he fell," it says, "on his face." For such is the grateful soul: whenever it enjoys greater freedom of speech with God, it shows all the more reverence toward him. [?]

…his parents gave him the name at the beginning, showing from the very start and from the outset that he would be a migrant, and would cross the river and come to a foreign land. "Since, then," he says, "the name given by your parents foretold that you would cross over from there to here, accept also the addition of the letter, so that you may learn what it signifies to you: that you will be the father of many nations." And see the precision of the words. He did not say "of all nations," but "of many nations." There were also other nations, which were to be driven out of that land so that the seed of the righteous man might receive the inheritance, and that is why he says, "I have made you the father of many nations." Knowing how great your virtue is, I will make you the teacher of many nations, "and I will increase you and multiply you exceedingly, exceedingly, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come forth from you." Let us not pass over these words lightly, beloved. If we consider the patriarch's age, and that he heard these things in extreme old age, we shall be amazed both at the faith of the righteous man and at the surpassing power of the loving God. This man was by now, so to speak, already dead, his limbs enfeebled, and he pictured his end every day. Yet God declared that his seed would increase so greatly as to become many nations, and not only this: "And kings," it says, "shall come forth from you." Do you see how the promise grows stronger? "I will increase you," it says, "exceedingly, exceedingly." He did not add the doubling for nothing [?], but to show the righteous man how vast the multitude would be. By adding the letter he had inscribed the pledge of his promise for him, as on a monument, so that it could never be erased. Now he says again: "And I will establish my covenant between me and you, and your seed after you throughout their generations, as an everlasting covenant, to be your God." Not only toward you, he says, will I show great care, but also toward your seed, even after your departure. See how he revives the righteous man's soul by promising him that he will provide richly for his seed as well. And what does the covenant amount to? "That I may be your God," it says, "and the God of your seed after you." For this will be the sum of all blessings for you and for your seed. "And I will give to you and to your seed after you the land in which you sojourn, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession; and I will be their God." Because of your virtue your descendants too will enjoy my providence, and I will give them the land of Canaan as an everlasting possession, "and I will be their God." What does "and I will be their God" mean? It means: I will show them great care and great providence, and in everything I will give them my help. Only "you must keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations." I ask nothing else of you but obedience and gratitude, and I will carry out everything I have promised. 4. Then he wished to claim as his own those who would be born of Abraham, and to make the people his own. He also wished to keep the multitude, as it spread, from mingling with the nations whose land they were to inherit. Above all, they were later to endure slavery in Egypt, as he had foretold, and he did not want them to be mixed up with the [?] even there… [?] …that he will migrate and cross. In the Bible the reading is: "and I will be God to them."

…to receive, when the purpose of the matter reaches its end, and the sign is then removed. So it is here too. This sign was introduced among you [?] so that the patriarch's people might be clearly marked out. Of the nations on whose account you received the sign, some have been utterly destroyed, and the rest, after them, have hastened to the light of the truth. So you ought no longer to carry around the proof of your own ingratitude. You should be rid of it and return to your former nobility. For consider that wonderful man, I mean the patriarch. Before he received the commandment of circumcision (he was ninety-nine years old when it was given), he had already become well-pleasing to God and had been praised by the Master countless times. Then, when the promises were about to be fulfilled, when Isaac was about to be born, the race to increase and the patriarch to depart this life, he received the commandment of circumcision and was circumcised at such an age, so that what the patriarch did might become a kind of law and rule for all who came after him. 5. And so that you may learn precisely, beloved, that this contributes nothing to the virtue of the soul, we can see it from the facts themselves. Why does it say, "A child of eight days shall be circumcised"? I think the loving God fixed this time for two reasons. First, so that at a tender age the child might bear the pain of the circumcision of the flesh more easily. Second, so that they might be taught by the facts themselves that what is done contributes nothing to the soul and is done only as a sign. An infant does not know what is happening and has no awareness at all, so what benefit could its soul receive from this? The achievements that properly belong to the soul are those that come from free choice. It is the soul's achievement to choose virtue and flee vice. It is the soul's achievement not only to stop wanting more, but even to give what one has to those in need. It is the soul's achievement not to cling to present things but to despise them, and to picture the things to come every day. But to receive the sign on the flesh: what achievement could that be? Yet the senseless and unfeeling Jews still sit by the shadow, though the truth has appeared. The Sun of righteousness has shone and sends its rays of light everywhere, yet they are still fixed on lamplight. The time for solid food has come, yet they still feed on milk. Nor will they bear to listen to blessed Paul, who cries aloud and says of the patriarch: "And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while he was uncircumcised." See how he taught us both points here: that he received circumcision as a sign, and that he showed the righteousness that comes from faith while he was still uncircumcised. The Jew might shamelessly say that circumcision won him his righteousness. To prevent this, this blessed man, who was taught at the feet of Gamaliel and trained in the strictness of the law, says: "Do not think, you shameless Jews, that circumcision contributed anything to his righteousness. For in the time of his uncircumcision [he showed] faith…" Morel.: "since, so that the people of the patriarch might become conspicuous, the sign, this by you, in[?]". Six manuscripts: "since because of the evident [?]". Savil.: "since, so that the seed of Abraham might be evident and not be mixed with the nations, this sign by you". Savil. and some manuscripts: "of milk".

…[spiri]tual. Ordinary dishes, once they grow stale, do not give the same pleasure to the guests, and if they are left over for a day or two they become completely useless. But these leftovers, not just for a day or two but even if they are kept for all eternity, give the same benefit and do not lose their delight. For they are divine and spiritual and suffer no harm from time. Every day they show their grace fresh, and they fill with great joy those who wish to enjoy them. Since these leftovers have such power, come, take your fill of the enjoyment they give, and let us, trusting in their power, set them before you, beloved. But so that the discourse may be clearer to you, I must recall the end of what was said yesterday, so that we can pick up the thread and take up the teaching. We brought forward the commandment about circumcision and told how God said to the patriarch: "Every male among you shall be circumcised, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. A child of eight days shall be circumcised. And whoever is not circumcised, that soul shall be utterly destroyed, because he has broken my covenant." There we ended the teaching, at the discussion of circumcision. We did not let ourselves go further, so as not to bury your minds under the mass of what was said. For our only concern is not to say a great deal and then leave. We want to measure the teaching to your capacity, so that you may all reap some benefit from what is said and then go home. Come, then, let us add what remains to what has been said, and see what else the loving God said to the patriarch after the commandment of circumcision. "And God said," it says, "to Abraham: As for Sarai your wife, her name shall not be called Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name." He is saying: just as I added the letter to your name to show that you will be the father of many nations, so I likewise add the letter to Sarah's, so that you may learn that the time has now come for what I promised long ago to be fulfilled. For "her name," it says, "shall be Sarah. And I will bless her and give you a child from her, and I will bless him, and he shall become a nation, and kings of nations shall come forth from him." That is why I added the letter beforehand, so that you may learn that what I say will certainly come to pass. Do not lose heart by looking at the weakness of nature. Look to the greatness of my power and take courage from what I say. "For I will bless her and give you a child from her, and I will bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of nations shall come forth from him." What was promised went beyond human nature. It was as if he had promised to make human beings out of stones. As far as bearing children was concerned, they were no different from stones. The patriarch was by now impotent from old age and incapable of begetting children. Sarah, besides being barren, was also weighed down by her age. But the righteous man heard these things and thought that the promise God had made long ago had been fulfilled in Ishmael. For God had said, "To you and to your seed I will give this land," but he had not made it clear: "I am foretelling everything to you, not only that she will bear, but also

what you will call him, and that I will establish my covenant with him, and not only this, but "also with his seed after him." God is always generous with his gifts and goes far beyond our requests. He had roused the righteous man's spirit, and through his promises he had, so to speak, made the old man young again and brought him to life by his words, though he was, so to speak, dead. Now, lavishing his kindness, he says: I will carry out these things I have promised. And along with this he accepted his plea for Ishmael [?]: "For I have heard your prayer, and I have blessed him. I will increase him and multiply him exceedingly, exceedingly. He shall father twelve nations, and I will make him a nation." Since he is your seed, he says, I will increase him and multiply him so greatly that twelve nations will spring from him. "But my covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sarah will bear to you at this season next year." See here, beloved, how in a single moment the righteous man received the reward for all his years. That saying of Christ to the disciples was fulfilled: "Whoever leaves father or mother, or house or brothers, for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold even here, and will inherit eternal life." Consider this righteous man. He readily obeyed the Master's command, left his own homeland and preferred a foreign land to the one that bore him. Then, little by little, he showed great endurance and climbed to the very summit of virtue, and so he became so renowned and illustrious that his descendants were made equal in number to the stars. If one were willing to consider it fairly, what this righteous man received here was perhaps not only a hundredfold but ten thousandfold. And if he was counted worthy of so much here, what words could describe the share he will enjoy there? Or rather, as far as possible, our discourse can show even this. For you hear that all the righteous, from his time until now and until the end of the world itself, make it their prayer to come to the bosom of the patriarch. What greater honour than this could you name? Do you see what endurance is, how great virtue is, how great a thing it is to love God and to show great gratitude for the Master's benefits? He contributed his own part at every stage, accepting everything with thanksgiving, both good things and bad. For this reason the loving God finally gave him the crowning blessing, the very thing the righteous man most desired. Consider how he tested the righteous man's virtue for twenty-four years. When he left Haran in obedience to the Master's command, he was seventy-five years old, it says. But now, when he heard these things, he had already reached his hundredth year. 3. Hearing these things, beloved, let us learn to show great endurance, and never to grow weary or slack in the labours of virtue. Let us know that our Master is generous and bountiful and repays small labours with great rewards. He not only stores up the immortal blessings for us in the age to come, but also lavishes many gifts on us in this present life, to encourage the weakness of our nature. For this patriarch too, not a few [?] in

…to give thanks to the Master, but also to show the same gratitude in adversity. This is how this patriarch too won approval. He obtained such freedom of speech before God that he received gifts surpassing human nature. 4. But we must return to the thread of the discourse and see the righteous man's obedience: how he carried out what God commanded without asking the reason or demanding an explanation. Many foolish people do that. They pry into what God does and say: "What is this for? What is that for? What good comes of this or that happening?" But the righteous man was not like that. Like a servant who loves his master, he hastened to carry out whatever he was commanded, without prying. To learn this, listen to what follows. As soon as the Master had made the promise to him and finished speaking with him, the righteous man at once did as he was told. He applied the sign God had commanded, I mean circumcision, to Ishmael, to all those born in his house and to those bought with money, as God had told him. And he circumcised himself too. "For he was ninety-nine years old," it says, "when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, and Ishmael was thirteen years old." Do not think that Scripture recorded the number of years for no purpose. It gives their count so that from this too you may learn the righteous man's great obedience: in extreme old age he meekly bore the pain because of God's command. And it was not he alone, but Ishmael too and all those born in his house. For it is no small thing, beloved, to cut off healthy flesh and suffer for it [?]. Even when physicians' assistants cut off a diseased limb, the pain is not the same, because they cut it away when it is, so to speak, already dead and deprived of its vital power. But here an old man, advanced in years (for he was about a hundred), meekly bore the pain. At the same time he hastened to carry out God's command and made his son and all those born in his house more eager, so that they would not hesitate but would carry out God's command with great speed. Do you see how great a virtuous man is, how he trained all who served him to walk in his footsteps? I will say again now what I said yesterday: this is why God commanded from then on that children should undergo this at a tender age, so that they would undergo the cutting of the flesh without awareness and would feel nothing of the pain. But consider, beloved, God's love for humankind and his unspeakable kindness toward us. There, what was done brought pain and suffering, and circumcision had no other benefit than this alone: that by this sign they were recognisable and set apart from the other nations. But our circumcision, I mean the grace of baptism, brings a painless cure. It becomes the source of countless blessings for us and fills us with the grace of the Spirit. Nor does it have a fixed time, as circumcision did. One may receive this circumcision not made with hands at a tender age, in middle age, or in old age itself. In it there is no pain to endure [?]; instead one can lay down burdens of sins, and of [the sins] committed at every time… Five manuscripts read: "they then cut off a diseased [limb]."

[?] … and awesome table, they spend the whole day at the horse races. They have gained nothing more from our earnest efforts. Instead, like slaves to a habit, the moment the devil merely beckons they hurry of their own accord to those lawless shows and willingly throw themselves into the nets of the evil demon. Neither our warnings, nor experience itself, nor the uselessness of the time they spend there has taught them anything. With what eagerness, then, could I carry on the work of teaching among men who want to gain nothing from what we say? Do not be surprised at this. A farmer, too, when he sees that after much toil and hardship the land proves barren and gives no return worthy of his labor, grows more reluctant to sow his seed and no longer takes up his farming with the same eagerness. And when a physician sees that a sick man does not obey his orders but makes it his business to aggravate the disease every day, he often lets him remain in his illness, so that experience itself may teach him what is good for him. And those who teach children their lessons, when they see them spurning what they learned before and forgetting what they have already been taught, often turn away from them, to correct their laziness and bring them back to greater diligence. The farmer, however, is understandably more reluctant, since he knows that his loss grows when he bears the toil and the expense but is deprived of the fruits. Nor is the physician unreasonable when he often leaves the sick man alone. It is a body that he is treating, and so he lets him be, so that the growing pain may bring the man to feel his disease and so to accept treatment. And because children are young and immature, their teacher often does well to raise the rod over them. But we today, going beyond all of these, are preparing to show fatherly affection toward those who have stumbled, and to teach them that if they persist in the same laziness, this very thing will bring them greater condemnation. For the farmer does not sow his seed with the same eagerness, because he thinks of the expense he has already laid out in vain and to no purpose. We, however, are free of this anxiety. Even if we sow this spiritual seed and get no fruit because our hearers are lazy, our reward will be complete. We have paid out the silver entrusted to us and carried out the Master's command. It remains for the hearers to answer to him who will demand back with interest what was paid out. Yet we do not dwell on the fact that we are safe from loss and have done our part. We want you too to do a great deal of business with what has been paid out to you, so that you will not be liable to the punishment suffered by the man who buried the talent, who not only did not multiply his Master's silver but even dug it into the ground. Such are those who receive the word of teaching (for this is what he calls the talent and the silver) and do not strive to bear fruit and to do a great deal of business with it. But perhaps someone will say that this parable of the talents was spoken about teachers. I say so too. But if we go through it carefully, you will see that the teach— [?] [Variant: three manuscripts read “often turn back the.”] … suffers great harm from this. For the one’s …

… is worn down by poverty, while the other, as his money increases, also heaps up a multitude of sins for himself. That is why, from the very beginning and outset, he laid down this commandment for the Jews, who were of a coarser disposition, saying: You shall not lend at interest to your brother and your neighbor. What defense, then, could they deserve who become even crueler than the Jews? After grace and such great lovingkindness from the Master, they are found to fall short of those who lived under the Law, or rather to be even worse. In spiritual matters, however, he himself promises to demand interest. Why? Because spiritual interest is the opposite of interest on material money. There, the one who is charged is suddenly brought down to the depths of poverty. Here, the one who is charged, if he shows great good will, receives a richer reward from above the more interest he brings in. So each of you, beloved, when we pay out what has been entrusted to us, ought to show twofold labor and vigilance. The first is in guarding what has been paid out, so that it stays secure. The second is in putting it to work, so that you share it with others and lead many by the hand onto the road of virtue. Then your gain will grow twofold again, for your own salvation and for the benefit of others. If you do this, you will make us blessed as well (for it says, Blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of those who listen), and you will enable us to set this spiritual table before you more abundantly. So do not neglect your brothers, and do not look only to your own affairs. Let each of you strive to snatch his neighbor from the devil’s gullet and from those lawless spectacles, and to bring him back to the church. Show him with great gentleness and mildness both how enormous the ruin is and how great are the good things here. And do this not just once or twice, but continually. Even if he is not persuaded by what you say today, he will be persuaded tomorrow. And if not tomorrow, perhaps when he sees you pressing him again he will be ashamed, and out of respect for your care he will keep away from what harms him. And never say, “I have spoken once, twice, three times, many times, and achieved nothing.” Do not stop speaking. The longer you persist, the more your reward grows. Do you not see how much patience we receive from the God of all? Every day we disregard his commands, and yet he does not give up his care for us, but supplies everything on his part: he makes the sun rise, gives rain, and all the rest. In the same way, let us take great pains over our brothers and stand against that evil demon, so as to make his schemes come to nothing. If each of those gathered here can win over one person, think how much joy the Church will have at the multitude of her own children, and how the devil will be put to shame when he sees that he has spread his nets in vain and to no purpose. If you do this, you too will hear on that day: Well done, good and faithful servant; you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. 3. But I am fully convinced that you will do this. I see your faces, and I can guess how with [?] [Variant: six manuscripts read “showing him” in the singular.]

… in my name receives me. Let us listen, beloved. When we are about to offer hospitality, let us never pry into who someone is or where he comes from. If the patriarch had pried into this, he might well have missed his chance. “But,” someone says, “he knew the dignity of those who came.” How is that clear? And how could he have been admired if he had done this? His hospitality would not have been as admirable if he had inquired. As it is, he did not know who the visitors were, and yet he approached them with great eagerness and honor, like a servant approaching his masters. He all but bound them in chains with his words, and pleaded with them not to refuse him and not to inflict the greatest loss on him. He knew what he was doing, and that is why he reaped with great fervor the abundance that came from it. But let us listen to the writer’s own words, so that you may see eagerness youthful in the deepest old age: the old man made young again, all but overjoyed, thinking the presence of his visitors a treasure he had found. And lifting up his eyes, it says, he looked, and behold, three men stood over him; and when he saw them he ran from the door of his tent to meet them. The old man runs and flies. He had sighted his quarry, and taking no account of his weakness he ran after the catch. He did not call his servants or give orders to a slave or show any laziness, but ran himself, all but saying: “A great treasure, a great business deal! I must trade in it myself, so that so great a gain does not slip past me.” And the righteous man did this thinking that he was receiving unknown men, travelers. 4. Let us learn and emulate the righteous man’s virtue. If we act in this way, we too will likely come upon such a catch some day. Or rather, we always come upon it, if we wish. This is why our loving Master, so that we do not shrink from such kindness or pry into those who pass by, says: Whoever receives one of the least of these in my name receives me. So do not look at how lowly the passerby is, and do not despise him because of what you see. Consider that through him you are receiving your Master. When you serve this man for the sake of his name, you will receive your reward as though you had received him. Even if the one who enjoys your kindness is lazy and neglected, do not take any account of it. You will be given a complete reward, because you do this out of honor for the Master and in emulation of this patriarch’s virtue. And when he saw them, it says, he ran from the door of the tent to meet them. The words “he ran” are rightly added, so that you may learn that they were passing by as strangers and would not have come to the tent of their own accord. That is why, so that this spiritual gain would not escape him, the aged man, gray-haired and a hundred years old, runs toward them and shows his eagerness by running. And when he saw them he bowed down to the ground and said: Lord, if I have indeed found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant. Let water be brought, and let them wash your feet, and rest under the tree, and I will bring bread, and you shall eat, and after that you shall go on your way, since you have turned aside to your servant. Great is the [?] of the righteous man’s words [?] [Variant: … and four manuscripts read “Let us listen, beloved, and never …”] [?] Gen.

… do not disregard my old age, do not refuse my request. I know how much hardship you have endured, and I can guess how fierce the heat has been. That is why I want you to rest a little.” What loving father would have shown his child such kindness as he showed to unknown men, strangers who until then were in no way known to him? But because he approached with earnestness and great intensity, his hunt succeeded and he was able to bring his quarry inside his nets. And they said, it says, We will do as you have said. The old man was set aglow again. “I hold the treasure in my hands,” he says. “I have laid hold of wealth; now I have forgotten my old age.” See how greatly he rejoices at this, all but leaping, as delighted as if he were carrying countless good things in his hands. And Abraham hurried, it says, into the tent. When he was hastening after them as his quarry, divine Scripture showed his intensity and eagerness by saying, He ran to meet them. So now too, after he has seen the men and achieved what he desired, he does not let his eagerness halt even then, but shows his love more fervently still. Nor did he grow lazier now that he was secure. This often happens to us: at the beginning we sometimes show great zeal, but once we are inside the undertaking we do not put in the same effort. Not so the righteous man. What then? Again the old man hurries and hastens and runs into the tent to Sarah, and said to her: Hurry, and knead three measures of fine flour. Consider how he takes Sarah as a partner in the hunt too, and how he had trained her to emulate his virtue. He urges her as well not to go about the task lazily, but says, Hurry. “We have come upon a great business deal; let us not lose the treasure. Hurry, and knead three measures of fine flour.” Since he knew how great this good deed was, he wanted the one who had become his partner in life to be a partner in its rewards and recompenses as well. Tell me, why did he not give this order to one of the maidservants, but to his aged wife? For she was ninety years old. And Sarah does not refuse the order, but brings equal eagerness of her own. Let men hear, let women hear! Let men hear, so that they may train their wives in this way: whenever some spiritual gain comes their way, they should not have it done through servants, but do everything themselves. Let women hear, so that they may hasten to share in such good deeds with their husbands, and not be ashamed of hospitality and of serving guests. Let them imitate the aged Sarah, who at such an age consented to toil and to do the work of maidservants. But I know that no one will put up with what we say. Today everyone is eager to walk the opposite way from her. Women are very soft, and their zeal is for fine clothes, for gold jewelry and necklaces and outward beautification, while they take no care for the soul. Not even Paul reaches them when he cries out and says: Not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing. See this soul that reached to heaven, how she did not think it shameful for herself to [?] to children [?]. [Variant: it is better to read “none” (feminine), since the maidservants are meant. Three manuscripts read “easily caught.”]

But this righteous man knew what he was doing, and he showed the eagerness of his soul in everything he did. Because he sowed hospitality abundantly and with great cheerfulness, he immediately received sheaves with an abundant hand. He fulfilled everything on his part and left nothing undone; the hospitality was brought to completion and the righteous man’s virtue was displayed. Then at last the visitor reveals himself, so that the righteous man might learn what guests he had come upon and how many good things the occasion of hospitality had brought him, and little by little he shows him the greatness of his power. Seeing him standing beside the oak and showing great honor and service by standing there, he says to him: Where is Sarah your wife? With this question he at once hinted to him that the visitor was no ordinary person, since he even knew his wife’s name. And he says: Here, in the tent. And since he was about to promise him, as God, things beyond nature, by speaking Sarah’s name he signified that the one who had lodged in his tent was more than human. For returning, it says, I will come to you at this season next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son. Behold the fruits of hospitality, behold the reward of intense eagerness, behold the recompense for Sarah’s labors! She, it says, was listening at the door of the tent, standing behind him. And when she heard this, she laughed to herself, saying: This has not yet happened to me until now, and my lord is old. To defend Sarah, divine Scripture noted beforehand that Abraham and Sarah were advanced in their days. And it did not stop even there, but says: The manner of women had ceased to be with Sarah. The spring, it means, had dried up, the eye had been blinded, the very workshop had been disabled. Looking at these things, Sarah reckoned within herself her own age and the patriarch’s old age. But while she was reckoning these things in the tent, he who knows the secrets of the mind wished to show the surpassing greatness of his power and that no secret escapes him. So he says to Abraham: Why did Sarah laugh within herself, saying, Shall I truly bear a child, now that I have grown old? For she was reckoning these things within herself. Is anything impossible with God? he says. See, he has openly revealed himself. “Do you not know,” he says, “that since I am the Master of nature I can do whatever I wish, even bring a deadened womb to life and make it fit to bear? Is anything impossible to God? Do I not make all things and refashion them? Do I not hold power over life and death? Is anything at all impossible with God? Did I not promise this already? Is it possible that what I have spoken will not come to pass? Hear, then: At this season I will return to you next year, and Sarah shall have a son.” “When I return at this season,” he says, “Sarah will know from the events themselves that neither her old age nor her barrenness will be a hindrance. My word will not be broken, and the birth will teach her the power of what I have said.” Then she, hearing that not even the thoughts in her mind [?] [Variant: … and five manuscripts read “advanced in days. And not even.” … below: “Is anything impossible with God.”]
